Yesterday is full of dry British wit and one-liners. It's not a headlong tribute, but fantasy fiction that celebrates the spirit of John, Paul, George and Ringo.
It's a chocolate egg of a film: sweet and satisfying enough to distract you from the fact it's completely hollow inside.
Himesh Patel has a wide-eyed charisma; Lily James, although underused, is a delight, and the earnestly-covered songs ensure this is a magical mystery tour worth boarding.
Yesterday is ultimately a romantic comedy, but a conceptually complex one, built on a peculiarly reactionary framework of private life and a culturally conservative pop classicism.
There's a good-natured, barreling charm to the film.
Ultimately, Yesterday is a victim of the amnesia it inflicts upon its characters.
This finally feels like a rather small, forlorn movie... Yesterday, for all its sly, often smart irony, is closer to cinematic Coldplay than it realizes.
Fuelled by the engaging chemistry of its leads and the unflagging wonderment of the music, it zips along. But it can never quite reach escape velocity from the weight of its silliness.
The movie is fun, largely because it proposes that fun is the principal legacy of the Beatles.
The structure is a mess. The characters are plastic. And the lines are Seventies sitcom bad.

Give "Yesterday" credit for taking a sideways approach to honoring the Beatles. But this Boomer fantasy only pretends to dive into a true appreciation of what made the group a once-in-a-lifetime phenomenon.
The possibility of a Beatles-less reality opens up a new world of storytelling, but not in Yesterday, which uses it to tell a disappointingly familiar story about falling in love.
As enjoyable as the movie can be it oddly flatlines right at the moment it should be building to a knockout crescendo.
You wish that Curtis could be prised away from the karaoke machine and let someone else pick a tune.
This seemingly sure-fire movie misses the mark. I felt like I was watching a balloon as the air inside it leaked out. I can only rate it as a disappointment.
Alas, after a promising first hour, Yesterday plunks one wrong note after another (including one particularly sour interlude), and eventually collapses under the weight of impossible expectations.
Feelgood has become a dirty word, but when it's pulled off with this much energy and actual feeling, it really is fab.

title: The Beast (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The Beast gives a sense of an artist burrowing deep inside his material (and his moment) and emerging with something vital. It’s fearless filmmaking.

About halfway through Bertrand Bonello’s insanely knotty new picture – a Spaghetti Junction of semi-discrete timelines – one version of Léa Seydoux gives in to frustration. “What the f**k are you talking about!” she yells into the ether. What indeed?
Against any rhyme or reason, it works.

The Beast won’t be for everyone, but submit to its looping structure and beguiling dream logic, and this extremely loose adaptation of a novella by Henry James weaves a bewitching, if a trifle head-swimming spell.
Like a painting, The Beast is best seen once, pondered and then left as a memory.
To paraphrase the smartest line from Tenet, don’t try to understand The Beast, you just have to feel it.
Instead, this sensual, cerebral work simply reminds us what is possible when ambitious filmmakers put their mind to it — and how long the result can stay in ours.
Bonello has created a wholly original work that pulses with prescience.

This is a bold and visionary film, an innovative modern sci-fi that feels both fresh and original. It delves into generational trauma and female oppression, whilst exploring an array of modern issues such as alienation and toxic masculinity. A must-see.
"The Beast," a riff on a 1903 Henry James novella that has flashes of remarkable atmosphere but has trouble congealing into a cohesive whole.
[Bonello] comes nowhere near achieving anything as insightful in two and a half hours that James manages in 30 pages.
A multi-genre/multi-century sci-fi philosophical whatchamacallit that wears out its welcome two-thirds of the way into a nearly two-and-a-half hour running time.
Even when it's not entirely clear where or when we are, Bonello's filmmaking is so hypnotic, and Seydoux's performance so subtly mesmerizing, that you can't help getting caught up in the flow.
Classical and ultramodern, The Beast is an experience both bold and rich.
It's very slow and convoluted.

Its devotion to the untamed territory of the human heart, its artfully discombobulating time and locale shifts, the shifting personae handled with marvelous fluidity by Seydoux; it takes you somewhere, and more than one somewhere.
Although the film can be talky and didactic at times, Seydoux and MacKay sell the high concept, generating a real erotic charge just by touching hands.
It’s a textually dense, formally ambitious, and supremely engaging, genre-melding treatise on fear and love.

The film can be mystifying at time, even confusing, with all that switching around and lack of explaining, but it’s never confused. Keeping an eye on Seydoux’s hairstyles is the best way to follow when’s when and where’s where.
It’s easier to admire the structural gambit of the film — to marvel at the scope of its genre-blending, century-jumping architecture — than to be drawn into its melodrama.

title: Always Be My Maybe (2019) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film's funny, contemporary, and uniquely tender take on the friends-to-lovers formula is further bolstered by its cultural specificity.
I thoroughly enjoyed this perfectly lovely little romantic comedy.

This literal LOL-filled film from sitcom showrunner Nahnatchka Khan doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it does provide a genuinely sweet, truly funny film that is sure to be watched and rewatched on many Saturday afternoons on the couch in pajamas.
Fresh, charming and laugh-out-loud funny
Netflix's romantic comedy Always Be My Maybe relies a bit too much on recognizable genre tropes, but Ali Wong and Randall Park are fantastic.
Past the performances, the remarkable part of Always Be My Maybe is how the film inhabits Asian-American culture.
Always Be My Maybe has that made-for-the-small-screen quality, almost a movie but not quite-it feels rushed, rough and a bit too casual, as if the script needed just another draft or two.
It's not new, but it's just as powerful (and, yes, still funny) as it ever was.
Always Be My Maybe's take on romance and relationships is both brutally honest and breathtakingly refreshing.
One of the better romcoms made in recent years, and smarter when it comes to its characters, too.
This is a high-quality crowd-pleasure that delivers on laughs, joy and cultural encouragement...
Netflix seems to have found its true purpose in original movie programming over the past year: clever, endlessly meme-able rom-coms meant to be watched on the floor in your weird pajamas.
Rather, the screenplay - which was co-written by Wong and Par.k, with help from Michael Golamco - settles into a relaxed groove that allows its main characters to play at what they do best
Always Be My Maybe hits all of the beats we have come to expect yet fails to do so well enough, as if the mere existence of a technically well-structured romantic comedy is better than nothing.
It's a film that delivers on all its promises, gives a lot of funny people a chance to shine and - yes indeed - provides some much-needed representation...
Ultimately, Wong and Park and their mutual affection carry the movie, assisted by a gut-busting cameo by Keanu Reeves, of all people, portraying a do-gooder rival for Sasha's affections.

An Asian-Asian romance is rare in Hollywood, making this romantic romp both irresistible and quietly revolutionary. No maybes about the dream team of Ali Wong and Randall Park, they're too good to miss.
Moving, thoughtful, tender, and hysterical.
Park and Wong are both innately likable, which makes the movie pleasant enough to watch, but also a bit of a slog given the ostensible inevitability of where it's heading.
The positive influence of When Harry Met Sally is noticeable in the undercurrents, but this romantic comedy has its own unique identity.

title: UglyDolls | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: With the school holidays on, this movie is a colourful and entertaining 90 minutes for kids under 10. The songs are easy on the ear and there are a couple of good jokes for the adult minders.
It's all pretty derivative but also pretty wacky, and there's meaning, if you look for it, on a whole lot of levels, from Freudian imagery and hints of religious allegory to the satire of reality TV.
Not so much a movie as a contemplative space wherein the viewer ... explores the shifting dynamic between the eponymous plush toys and the hegemony of play.

Positive messaging about celebrating our unique imperfections and seeking your own truth has never felt more urgent to children in the age of Instagram. Pity, then, that this toothless and derivative marketing exercise doesn't practise what it preaches.
The songs are horrifically soppy.
This paean to body positivity and living your own truth is more than welcome, but you just wish UglyDolls' message could be more charmingly argued, adroitly assembled and just plain funny.
The animation style of UglyDolls is so off-putting that it may be more worthwhile to watch any other children's film that offers the same messages about self-acceptance instead.
The script underwent a lot of sweetening after animation finished, with plenty of one-liners and exposition yelled in from just off-camera, almost all of it either unnecessary or just plain flat.

For a film about weird, colorful dolls, one hopes for something wackier, funnier, edgier. But "UglyDolls" is so soft - literally, the felted textures are startlingly realistic - and tame, that it feels like watching those PBS cartoons aimed at toddlers.
UglyDolls is less a movie than an infomercial for the plush Hasbro toys.
For a movie about supposed ugliness, "UglyDolls" works overtime to be pretty.
Movies don't skew much younger than this - anyone who isn't still attached to an umbilical cord might roll their eyes at some of the story beats...
The message of the screechy new kids' movie "UglyDolls" may appear to be "Be yourself," but the real takeaway here is "Buy our merch!"
"UglyDolls" is a mind-numbing, low-rent version of "Toy Story," with saccharine songs and a plot with echoes of, no kidding, the Holocaust.
UglyDolls are already adorable. You don't have to work that hard to convince anyone.

One must give in to the fantastical elements in films of this kind, but some of the plot details in this mashup production (Toy Story + Monsters Inc. + a generic stage show) are as visibly defective as its heroes but much less huggable.
Buyer beware.
Every aspect of this computer-animated movie directed by Kelly Asbury seems equally overdetermined and tossed-off, as if it were a caffeinated weekend project for everyone involved.
Like their Troll ancestors, the UglyDolls combine an evergreen cuteness with a why-now lack of currency.
An imbecilic eyesore that could lay claim to being one of the worst movies ever made if it was worth such hyperbole.

title: Poms | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: These women deserve so much better... It feels forced and problematic.
I found it, in order, depressing, moving and uplifting.
Director Zara Hayes, to her credit, mixes some dark humor and blistering social commentary into this otherwise frothy cocktail of pratfalls and platitudes.
Why worry about dying when you can spend your time dancing? Although "Poms" is an imperfect package, one can't help but take the message to heart.

There's a reductive and bland "women be worrying about their appearance" arithmetic happening. And it does a real disservice to the almost heartbreakingly game actors struggling to bring this thing to life.
The main cast does far better than the script in conveying both a sense of sisterhood, and the exquisite poignancy of the friendships that bloom as the end of life approaches.
Look, films need conflict, otherwise there's nothing for the characters to do. "Poms" never comes up with anything worthwhile to fight against, let alone cheer.

Even by the elastic standards of mass-market escapist trifles the creators of POMS might consider the challenges of growing old and confronting death without infantilizing both characters and audience.
Poms isn't going for any awards, but its rah-rah spirit is in the right place.
It's all as predictable as it is preposterous.
I can't necessarily recommend the movie, and yet I'm rooting for it this weekend.
"Poms" is an embarrassment.
The first narrative feature from documentarian Zara Hayes, who wrote the script with Shane Atkinson, making his feature debut. Neither have much background in comedy, and it shows.
It's uneven at times and hits a few too many clichés for my taste, but if my preview audience was any indication, the movie's still pretty effective.
It's fine to make a film that's just supposed to make an audience smile (hello, "Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again") but this film doesn't even get close to that level of joy.
The women in Poms deserve better and so do we.

An uncomfortable blend of sickness and silliness, this dancing-past-the-graveyard comedy suggests that the many travails of aging can be endured if you only gather enough friends and surrender enough dignity.

Weaver and Keaton sometimes manage to tease out the movie inside the movie, the one drawn to the connections between death and joy, youthfulness and mortality. Mostly, though, Poms just wants you to cheer.
The blueprint for a genuinely inspired, warm-hearted dramedy is indeed there, it's just that the filmmakers can't figure out how to properly utilize what they have.
Like a busy teenager who barely acknowledges her grandparents, this movie doesn't seem to realize what treasures it has.

title: The Vast of Night | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "The Vast of Night" is an entertaining sci-fi nostalgia piece that's made with an unusually high level of technical flair.
A low-fi genre gem that proves the age-old maxim that less is often more-especially when such minimalism is wielded by gifted artists.
The technical proficiency of Patterson's debut is off the charts, and it'll be interesting to see if and how this gifted filmmaker manages to maintain his independence...
Writer-director Andrew Patterson and cinematographer M.I. Littin-Menz are at times breathtakingly mobile as their camera navigates a tiny world frozen in nicotine amber.
The story of The Vast of Night is nothing particularly special. The storytelling, though, is spectacular.
This awful moment in America, beset by sicknesses both cultural and epidemiological, is precisely the moment for The Vast of Night, the rookie feature by director Andrew Patterson.
Working with a minuscule budget, Patterson pulls off a feat as amazing as any flying saucer.
The Vast of Night consistently entertains, and its mixture of vintage aesthetics and spooky subject matter feels like the beginning of the summer movie season.
Captures the live-wire immediacy of a few people in a small town stumbling across something monumental.
This witty and audacious sci-fi mystery arrives like a persistent and unexplained radar-bleep from the heavens: low-budget, high-concept.
That a film with such an apparently familiar narrative can keep us this intrigued is a credit to the film-makers - particularly Patterson, from whom we should expect to hear much more in the future.
Patterson and his talented team do wonders with this material, the performances from Horowitz and McCormick both outstanding.
It's remarkably sharp, funny, and ominous. A terrific debut.
It is very low-key and obviously extremely low-budget, but also stylish and clever.

What really makes "The Vast of Night" work isn't the film's climax - which is fine and creepy, if more obviously hampered by budget limitations - but the two main characters and the dynamic that grows up between them.
The Vast of Night sells its mystery as a package deal, firing on all sight-and-sound cylinders to immerse its viewers in its story.
The Vast of Night [is imbued] with terrifying vibes replete with a restless hunger to experience the fantastical.
[A] sense of immediacy is essential to the salty-sweet contrast of the film, which combines a throwback premise with an unstintingly modern sensibility.
Impressively, the quietest moments in The Vast of Night are as creepy and effective as the loudest.
Part Close Encounters of the Third Kind, part American Graffiti, and wholly its own stunning self, The Vast of Night is a debut of captivating weight and ingenuity.

title: Shaft | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Quintessential blaxploitation that launched a thousand imitators, Gordon Parks’s Shaft is much more than a rollicking crowd-pleaser, as it’s also a snapshot of a bygone era.
A good, gutsy crime yarn in the 'forties style.
If Shaft were indeed a hard-hitting, fast-paced, action-packed detective thriller, as it was meant to be, then it would be an acceptable entertainment. But it isn't.
A blaxploitation pic that's never quite as cool as its theme song.
Excellent cast, headed by newcomer Richard Roundtree, may shock some audiences with heavy dose of candid dialog and situation.
Forty years of gumshoe noir collided with black power in this 1971 action classic, the most popular of the blaxploitation pictures.
A hip, cool, entertaining thriller.

Parks isn't especially good at action direction, but the heart of a private-eye movie is in the mood scenes, anyway, and he supplies a scene in a bar and another one with the Harlem rackets boss that are very nice.
The attraction to them will be the stylish conversation and attitudes, as well as Richard Roundtree, who lends Shaft the right amount of charisma, swagger and untouchability.

title: The Public | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's heart is in the right place in many ways, but it just outlines everything so clearly in red marker that it doesn't let you discovers things for yourself. Still, it's an estimable effort in some ways.
That everything ends on a weird happy-clappy high is indicative of a scattershot project that could have done with less ambition, more focus.
The Public presents a heartening story of triumph of good over evil, but sadly lacks the gravitas one would usually expect from these types of stories.
It's all a bit old-fashioned and earnest but with US civil liberties under attack, it's a timely celebration of humanity.
It is a film with its heart in the right place, but the dialogue and characterisation are both plonkingly unconvincing.

Making a feature that pleads the cause of the homeless is a laudable achievement, so it's all the more unfortunate that Estevez is unable to eliminate some of the obvious flaws in an otherwise compelling, and timely, drama.
It's hard to play a good man doing the right thing. Saints are dramatically dull, but Estevez gets away with it here.
Estevez's drama gets a little preachy in the second half, but "The Public" is passionate about its cause and the cast... deliver like the pros they are.
Alec Baldwin, Jeffrey Wright, Christian Slater and Gabrielle Union all look like they'd rather be somewhere else.
Writer-director-star Emilio Estevez turns a library occupied by homeless citizens as ground zero for our under-fire democracy. Bravo!
It's not an easy task to direct yourself but Estevez turns in a top-notch performance, fired by his passion for the subject matter.

The story's moral has obviousness problems, the plot's predictable, and its sweetness will annoy as many as it pleases. But it's still warm, winsome and droll, and the spectacular cast fills underwritten roles with radiant star power.
The problem is, there's only just enough story to go round. You can hear the creak as both characters and subplots get jacked up out of proportion.
Its heart is in the right place, but because it's mired in too many of Estevez's questions about public duty versus public safety, The Public struggles to stay on track and keep the viewer involved.
It's a noble effort, but "The Public" never makes a convincing case for its cause.
Its presentation of real, painful issues is too simplistic and its approach too preachy.
Estevez does an elegant job with this setup, creating a low-key, uncondescending portrait of lives on the edge.
Well-intentioned parable about the plight of the homeless falls flat.
Estevez, directing himself, knows what emotions Estevez, the actor, is trying to put over. He's the only one.

It's hard to disagree with anything in "The Public." Estevez is fighting the good fight. But it's also hard to swallow an argument, however well-reasoned and emotionally compelling, when it feels like it's being shoved down your throat.

title: The Perfect Date | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I liked The Perfect Date better when it was called Loverboy.
"The Perfect Date" feels engineered by Netflix algorithms.
It's a perfectly middle-of-the-road teen flick, and it is notable mostly because it gives [Noah] Centineo plenty of opportunities to do what he does best: gaze longingly at girls.
This isn't quite going to scratch your romcom itch in a satisfying way... But by the end, I was essentially on board.

title: Annabelle Comes Home | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Thiis is an uncommonly handsome scary movie, one that respects the audience's intelligence while delivering all the requisite chills and just the right amount of gore.
It felt like like a made-for-TV, disposable [film]... It's not anything special.
Middle-school horror in its near-perfect form.
A back-to-basics take on the ghost-story gauntlet run; compared to the previous films, it's worth its weight in spare doll parts.
Annabelle Comes Home is mechanical and unambitious, thereby falling between the quality levels of the fairly dire first film and the taut, surprising second.
Proudly retro and coyly innocent, it's the perfect movie for a tweeny sleepover.
Annabelle Comes Home is an enjoyable Saturday night flick with great rewatch value.
Sluggishly paced and lacking in inspiration, Annabelle Comes Home proves that this doll works best when the filmmakers are willing to really play with it.
As for Annabelle herself, her case may be closed, but we now know that it can be reopened anytime by the guilt-ridden, the transgressive or the curious, which is, at times, all of us.
Here's a horror sequel that wants to be anything other than what it is: a picture about an evil doll.
Annabelle Comes Home is such a massive amount of sinister fun it might be my favorite entry in The Conjuring universe outside of the 2013 first film.
The reason the movie works, I think, is simple. The actresses are all strong.
"Annabelle Comes Home" is so low stakes it's barely a movie - more like a very special "Brady Bunch" episode in hell.
The scares are there but Annabelle Comes Home also has a playful haunted house vibe that makes it stand out from the rest of the Conjuring franchise.
If the film falls flat as horror, it succeeds little better as a symbolic coming-of-age story: the lesson imparted is about the importance of playing it safe.
What follows is excellent, uncomplicated and well-wrought house-of-horrors fun, complete with a message about self-blame and the real things that haunt us.

It's a mostly effective thrill ride of lo-fi scares, and the script early on dispenses with the most obvious question: Why not just throw Annabelle away, or destroy her? That would only make things worse, the Warrens explain.
A smart, controlled film, made with considerable integrity.
When the doll has more vitality than the movie around it, there's a problem.
Annabelle Comes Home delivers on its title with the best "Conjuring" spin-off so far, in large part because it has such modest aims.

title: Someone Great | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Netflix's romantic comedy Someone Great is extremely of this time, a sugar rush that adds a millennial gloss to genre tropes.
Someone Great certainly lives up to its title.
A fluffy romp with a sobering truth: relationships and your twenties may end, but neither signals the end of the world.
A movie that's best experienced while lazing on the couch, preferably on the morning after a wild night out.
Someone Great is both sentimental and melancholic, and feels a bit disjointed in the way these movies always do.
This character is, for the moment, a mess, and Rodriguez really digs in, especially when Jenny's drunk. Who knew Jane was a fun filthy-mouthed drunk?
It's raw, visceral, and highly relatable.
It's not quite as charming or winning as other Netflix rom-com originals, but it does have a more meaningful message: Find yourself, then find the guy.
It's designed to be the perfect movie to rewatch for the 40th time while putting on your makeup.
The "someone great" of the title isn't some mythical romantic object. It's each of them, bringing out the best in each other.
It's very funny and offers up plenty of heartwarming fodder for the sentimental among us.
The hooks on which "Someone Great" chooses to hang its emotional hats are a little clichéd, but Rodriguez, Snow and Wise have enough chemistry to pull it all off.
The film plays like a mixtape of various sensibilities, partly beholden to the self-contained form of the bildungsroman.
What makes Something Great, well, so great, is that it is both rom-com and female-buddy comedy.
Rodriguez squeezes humor out of the bland writing regularly, but there aren't too many actual jokes. It's all hyperactive situational stuff.
Someone Great is a solid debut for a promising young filmmaker, and a welcome addition to the ever-growing Netflix rom-com canon.
While the latest Netflix-produced rom-com struggles to decide what it wants to be, it seems clear from the outside - this should have been a TV series instead.

Robinson's big-screen debut feels like a newer breed of movie: the scrappy female-POV in which the love story at the center is as much about friendship or the face in the mirror as it is about any one man.
While this debut film from "Sweet/Vicious" creator Jennifer Kaytin Robinson is a raunchy good time, don't discount its moving message about the lasting power of female friendship.
What "Someone Great" is missing is anything that punctures its rom-com bubble. At no point is there any doubt that the power of friendship will triumph.

title: Room for Rent (2019) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's essential viewing for Lin Shaye fans, and that's more than enough.

title: Mothers' Instinct | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: These perfect housewives serve each other passive aggression like petits fours and protestations of affection like they're macarons iced with arsenic.
Half the time, you don't know if you should be rolling or shuddering in your seat, though you mostly do the latter.
Masset-Depasse deftly handles a plot which flirts openly with ripe melodrama, but keeps the audience guessing about which household the madness and paranoia lurks within.

title: Changing the Game | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Incisive about the complex issues involved and emotionally compelling, this documentary might help clarify the rules so the game can be changed.
There's all-out bigotry, and there's all-out triumph. Changing the Game does well to offer both in a way that hits all the right notes.
During this time...documentaries like Changing the Game are more important than ever.
"Changing the Game" goes beyond those dehumanizing headlines to show the real people affected by harmful anti-trans policies or lack of any meaningful legal protection.

It tries to get so many different perspectives in. It's so emotional, personal, and complicated, and there are no easy answers, but I appreciate that this film exists to at least inspire the conversation.
"Changing" challenges long-held perceptions and hopefully, in the process, can change minds.

"Changing the Game" could have gone further, analyzing how fairness in sports is a myth to begin with. But the movie isn't interested in rewriting the rules; it would rather introduce us to the brave young people who are.
Changing the Game gracefully examines the dilemma of young transgender athletes.
Landing amid politicization of the issue, this sensitively told Hulu documentary won't settle the debate, but it does put faces to those thrust into the center of it.

That rare documentary about a social issue that is not preaching to the choir. If someone is uncertain or on the fence about this issue, this movie should allow them to make a logical conclusion about it.

Subtle and nuanced... Changing the Game radically asserts the humanity of Mack, Sarah Rose, Andraya, and Terry, and the rest of us whose lives are under assault by the current political establishment.
Barnett gives the viewer a clear overview of just how tough transgender athletes have it in gender-segregated sports.
A smart, poignant tribute to young athletes changing the rules.

title: Murder Mystery | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Murder Mystery's predictability and cliches are comforting - which has entertainment value if you're not looking to be challenged for 90 minutes.
Watching Murder Mystery is a slog, and I still can't comprehend how the same dude who wrote Zodiac wrote this, and oh, did I mention this movie steals one of its final reveals from Legally Blonde?
It's no Punch-Drunk Love, but it's on the better end of the spectrum when it comes to Sandler's streaming selections.
Aniston and Sandler, paired before in 2011's Just Go With It, relax into their roles as if their only stake in Mystery is to enjoy the free trip to Italy and have fun running down cobblestones.
Every Adam Sandler comedy abides by a trope as hoary as "the butler did it." At some point in the shenanigans, Sandler's schlub has gotta get a chance to prove he's the bravest boy in the world.
The crime? A truly boring movie.
It would be uncomfortably cynical to assume that Sandler thinks these novocaine-like comedies are what common people want to watch, but the guy doesn't leave us much choice.
Still, the movie proves a cheery enough diversion, during a summer movie season leaden with underwhelming blockbuster offerings.

Even grading on a curve, though, Murder Mystery is a tired, bordering on tiresome endeavor -- feeling like the pilot for a not-very-good TV show -- as well as a reminder that Netflix's content buffet caters to all kinds of tastes.
Adam Sandler is a genius, sure. But I'd love it if he were to smarten up, too.
For something that's top of the landing page, thus doesn't even require thumb movement, Murder Mystery is surprisingly entertaining.
It's just the kind of movie to pop on one night when you're looking for something fun, silly, and a little mysterious.
Just entertaining enough to make you wish it was actually good.
Capably directed by Kyle Newacheck from a suitably twisty-turny script by James Vanderbilt, it serves its purpose as a lighthearted comedy.

Murder Mystery... isn't going to dispel the longstanding rumor that the Sandman mostly makes movies as an excuse to go on paid vacations, using his Happy Madison production shingle as a personal travel agency
Aniston and Sandler have a goofy, relaxed rapport that is often amusing despite the film's best efforts to smother any sign of verve.

Aniston, not for the first time, seems more engaged and wide-awake than her material, and you can sense her mental gears grinding away as she tests out bits of business and digs for stray moments of comic gold. None, alas, are forthcoming.
Murder on the Bore-ient Express.
Murder Mystery is a satisfying standout, albeit one that exists in a field with a very low bar.

title: 4x4 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Cohn's point is that we are all victims - of ourselves.

The success of [Mariano] Cohn's film rests almost entirely on the performance of [Peter] Lanzani, and he turns in a remarkable performance that runs the gamut of emotions from disbelief to dawning horror as the reality of his plight begins to sink in.

title: Blow the Man Down | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A tightening of the screws would have helped this thriller immensely. But Cole and Krudy are after something a little different here than just two sister and one downward spiral.

It's normally not a great sign when the lead characters are less compelling than anything around them, but the Connollys' predicament opens up the weird bits of village mythology and feminine conspiracy that secretly drives the film forward.
[A] murder movie with momentum...
I was in from the opening prelude, a quasi-Greek chorus of fishermen singing an old sea shanty, their great voices mixed with the musicality and rhythms of their tools and work.
It's an incredibly cunning mystery with a charming cast of characters who ultimately crack under the pressure of keeping up with their appearances.
It is really singular and unique and cool and strange and very ambitious.
I really did not know where this was going almost the entire time, and and that's an all-too-rare feeling watching a movie these days.
Blow the Man Down hasn't great ambitions but fulfills its modest goals nicely. It's well worth streaming, especially if you have a cup of chowder handy.
Blow The Man Down is salty, savage, and sensational, offering a dark tale with a suitably subversive wit as pointed as a harpoon.
Once it got going, I thought it was a hoot... Stick with it.
I thought it had a very vivid sense of place... It has some smart dialogue and some very offbeat characters.
"Blow the Man Down" creates a well-realized world with layers that keep revealing themselves. You don't want to live there, but it's well worth a visit.
In its own gentle but sure-eyed way, this movie cuts deliciously deep.
Which is fine, because the movie's pretty great - not quite "Fargo" with lobsters but close enough, and about as good as regional filmmaking gets.
Blow the Man Down isn't an earth-shaker, but it's a small pleasure that makes you wish for more from its filmmakers, and soon.
A compelling cinematic world that lingers in the memory.

A briny Northeastern noir powered by women with secrets, "Blow the Man Down" is a pleasantly spiky slinging of small-town sin that should prove to be eminently companionable viewing for these sequestered, streamable times.
It serves handily as a staycation inside whatever walls currently proscribe your field of vision.
As small town crime stories go, Blow the Man Down is intriguingly low-key, but it's in the filmmakers' quietly bold decisions that it swells above most of its ilk.
The result is intriguing enough to make you wonder what these writer-directors might accomplish if they applied their vision to a more expansive canvas.

title: The Hustle (2019) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A generally unfunny and regressive remake.
This is a slab of cold, unfunny comedy, just lying there, very very odd given the two talented performers at the center of it.
The Hustle just isn't very good, and the only con being pulled is on any audience member who has found themselves coerced into buying a ticket.
Hathaway is a pleasure to watch but this role is beneath her pay grade.
The Hustle wants to say something about the inherent sexism of the rich... but it never manages to overcome its weak jokes and tired plot points.
It's the irony of all ironies that one walks away from "The Hustle" feeling a little, well, hustled.
Wilson's energy level never falters. You would sympathise with such a natural, engaging talent for the narrow typecasting if she hadn't done it to herself. Rebel, Rebel, your film is a mess.
Sexism is structural but yet again, female empowerment and sisterhood are presented as individual, economic imperatives and personal acts of revenge.
Simply not funny.
An embarrassment to the heist genre, an insult to all existing comedies, a disgrace to feminism.
Even with a running time of 93 minutes, The Hustle felt about an hour too long.
Who's conning who here? In "The Hustle," everyone's a sucker, most of all the audience.
Every barely competent line or gag from the original has been deleted or replaced with gobsmacking doggerel.
The Hustle is just plain dumb. Wilson's shtick is so overdone, it's growing mold, and though Hathaway is the scene stealer she's doing all the work for zero reward.
The gender-swapped Dirty Rotten Scoundrels remake The Hustle may be born out of a lazy idea, but its misandrist energy carries it along nicely.

It's not terrible. It's not anything, really, except an excuse for Hathaway to swan about in a series of clingy dresses and fake accents and Wilson to pratfall and deadpan her way from one outlandish scheme to the next.
They (Wilson and Hathaway) deserve better than a movie that feels like it's just checking boxes, and an ending that's completely off.

"You could've been more!" is something I wanted to stand up and scream during the closing credits of The Hustle... starring Anne Hathaway and Rebel Wilson. Instead, I packed up my popcorn, left the theatre and wondered how it all went wrong.
The Hustle will fail to seduce the most important mark in any heist movie: the audience.

Even with Anne Hathaway and Rebel Wilson as con artists, the setups are flat, the jokes don't land and the actors strain for laughs that never come. Be warned about this femcentric spin on Dirty Rotten Scoundrels-it's the audience that gets hustled.

title: Brightburn | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is an interesting idea that I wish they had done more with.
Despite its simplicity, Brightburn's premise is filled with potential, but it struggles to find anything meaningful to say.
The conceit works brilliantly until, in the closing 20 minutes, it clatters disappointingly into a fatal uncertainty.
As an antihero with an oedipal complex, neither Brandon nor Dunn is sufficiently creepy or conflicted to launch a new franchise.
This is primarily a character study, about that thin line between heroism and horror.
Because the film that this broadside of brass describes is ultimately, seriously, "Duuuumb!"
The final effect... is a disheartening vacuum. Having torn down a myth, it leaves little but a dropped mic in its wake.
Director David Yarovesky does the fantasy stuff with flair. And the dafter the plot gets, the better the acting conjured from Elizabeth Banks as foster mom.
That this story's riddled with silly plot holes isn't make or break but, less forgivably, Brightburn is slow and often boring.

What it lacks in any greater meaning, it makes up for with good old B-movie gore. It's a demon child story wearing the mask of a superhero film, twisting an age-old myth into something quite unsettling, even if it isn't all that deep.

Crossbreeding superhero tropes with horror staples was an idea laden with promise. Brightburn is enlivened by trademark James Gunn black comedy, but hamstrung by sketchy writing and a botched sense of dread.
This film draws its strength in part from its willingness to be a more humbly scaled operation than the tentpoles weighted down by mandates for billion-dollar grosses.
It leans heavily on jump scares and creeps before engaging with its premise, but when it does it's as chilling as Superman's freezing breath.
It's a fine and distinct funhouse ride designed to elicit cackles, then be forgotten about by the next ride.
A cure for superhero movie fatigue, this lean, gory horror film...has a coherent narrative and pays off with a bang.
Its harsh, pitiless violence could earn it a cult, but it's ultimately a workmanlike movie playing at being something more renegade-an unconvincing disguise.
If the filmmakers had a modicum of curiosity about the implications of their own idea, the movie might have had something interesting to say.
Although Brightburn's final seconds hint at James' more finely attuned cinematic sensibilities the film is not nearly as strong as its villain. It is, however, just as immature.
If the goals were a little more clear, the film could've been better...they could've played with the audiences' expectations much more, but this is an enjoyable horror movie, almost a slasher film.
The premise is intriguing, but this gruesome origin story plays like just another slasher film with idiots for victims.

title: The Souvenir | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [Joanna Hogg] makes brilliant use of shallow focus to keep you keyed in to specific details.
Superbly crafted and acted on every level, The Souvenir is one of the best British films of recent years.
Hogg's lighter touch discourages easy judgment. Despite this she has a knack for the kind of vignette that speaks volumes about a relationship.
Hogg's approach to this material is classical and literate.
Hogg's work with actors has always been exceptional, but here she is at the top of her game, making each role count by maintaining that balance of closeness and separation that is her trademark.
The absolute specificity of this story makes it universal too. It's the best British film for a long time.
Julie unfolds slowly, as does the film, and sometimes conversations start, stutter, stall, go nowhere. But the leads are both sensational and it's not paint drying, whatever anyone may say.
It is ... Hogg's way to leave us in a state of tantalising incompletion. We collapse out of The Souvenir wanting more of everything.
As rousing and exhilarating as anything you'll see in a Hollywood blockbuster or high-level horror.
The sense of real life rerun is vivid. Hogg keeps you in the palm of her hand as few film-makers could.
The skill of the film lies in how coolly its evidence is assembled.
Poetic, fascinating and enigmatic, it's a remarkable showcase for two peerless leads. Possibly the finest film of this year and there's part two to come next summer.
Joanna Hogg paints a precise picture of a woman trying to develop her own artistic vision while caught in the slipstream of a toxic relationship. An understated, exquisite gem of a film.
Tender and charming, but the bitter sting elevates it to greatness.
A visceral, open-hearted exploration of grief and the implacability of loss. Led by extraordinary performances this may well be Hogg's best film so far.

Swinton Byrne and Burke make for one of the year's most intriguing screen couples, although this is a romance based on anxiety, narcissism and opportunism rather than anything resembling genuine affection.
This is not a movie that lets life simply play out as it is or was - it is instead a collection of memories, some sharp as shards but others smoothed down.
"The Souvenir" is an oddly alluring piece of filmmaking, rich and quiet and sneakily affecting.
The Souvenir doesn't get under your skin. It clasps your hand tightly, and when it finally lets go, you will feel its absence.
"The Souvenir" reveals itself slowly, calmly, with great deliberation.

title: Porno | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Porno is a funny and frightening time-machine trip worth taking.
For a film unafraid of occasional full frontal nudity, this is surprisingly puritanical, especially when you consider the plot.
Even if the sophomoric Porno doesn't make the grade, it represents a promising start for the talented filmmaker.

This gory teen comedy blends laughably outrageous carnage with a legitimately scary plot to delightful ends. Throw in a winking fetish for cinephile culture and audiences are sure to go wild for the gutsy film.
There's an amiability of intent and execution that keeps "Porno" watchable.

Porno's playfully amusing critique is woven into the fabric of its plot, although just as integral to the saga's charms is Racela's fondness for rubbing his audience's noses in the shocking, the lurid and the grotesque.

title: Dark Phoenix | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The spectacle is entertaining, up to a point, but even the digital wizardry wears thin, and Dark Phoenix turns into a standard-brand miasma of explosions, collisions and swirling force fields.
Turner delivers a solid performance as a young woman coming to grips with an unknown force, and James McAvoy and Michael Fassbender maintain the frenemy bond we've grown to love.
A middlin' X-men effort that cheats the saga of its past, present and future, messing with the story-line in unacceptable ways. Plus, it looks big and cheap - but mostly cheap.
Outgunned on the action front by box-office rivals and too nervous to tell a more intimate story, Dark Phoenix leaves the franchise running on empty.
It's as if the writer-director [Simon Kinberg] is using a superhero movie to rediscover the roots of soap opera. His emphasis on everything Young about the franchise swamps everything that's Adult.
It felt terribly, terribly scrappy.
Of course it's best not to make too much of this. It's just a movie about mutant superheroes and mutant or alien super-villains, after all...
Dark Phoenix is the greyest (pun intended) superhero spin-off yet.
There are strong action set pieces here, but for the most part, Dark Phoenix chews through story so quickly that the narrative ultimately lacks impact.

The franchise never established the foundation needed to tell this story. That amongst other problems keeps it from being an emotional character journey and makes it yet another blockbuster spectacle that coasts on surface level entertainment value.
The movie's weaknesses make more glaring the movie's hollowness where the storyline's feminism once was.
A stupendously dull series-ender without a shred of wit, narrative thrust or genuine emotional force.
Even by the uneven standards of the X-Men movies, this is a glum exercise in film-making by rote.
Worst of all, because Jean isn't at the center of her own story, the film's climax ends up being something of a bizarrely unemotional irritation.
It didn't have to end this way...It didn't have to end with so little emotion, so little meaning - with a sad little speech about evolving, for Phoenix's sake.
If future filmmakers can learn these lessons from the travesty of "Dark Phoenix," it won't have been a total waste.
This is the end of an era, 19 years, and...they really played it safe. The characters say and do things that don't lead to anything. It should've been so much better than it was.
The final battle takes place aboard a moving train that feels like it's headed nowhere. At this point, it's a perfect metaphor for the "X-Men" series.
It's either an origin story or a series finale, but it's definitely a low point in the "X-Men" franchise.
It's hard to be engaged when the characters themselves seem so detached.

title: Child's Play | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Unfortunately, [Child's] Play isn't campy or fun, either. It's not much of anything at all.
Has the marks of a cult horror hit.
Child's Play is junk fun.
The acting is good. The plot is interesting. The characters have common sense. And the villain has a nasty sense of humor.

Child's Play pads the premise effectively to feature length and supplies enough dreamlike disorientation to make you forget that the film is a retread of a gimmick at least as old as talking pictures.
Everyone tries to kill [Chucky] for good, even nice Chris Sarandon and nicer Catherine Hicks, but they can't, and I fear a sequel.
When the little devil finally tackles its enemies head on, matters become unbearably silly.
Technically speaking, quite a neat exercise in Petit guignol.
The result is a watchable, occasionally fun, but thoroughly contrived outing.
Once Holland turns on the scare and shock machine, Child's Play is just another game.
Holland takes the safe course of pandering to the kids with a resort to conventional splatter.
Child's Play is fairly preposterous for the genre.
The real star is Chucky, who's far more interesting than his human counterparts.
Once Chucky goes public and becomes nothing more than a pint-sized slasher, Child's Play turns into cheesy kid stuff.
a Hitchcockian blend of high tension and dark comedy, with a rich seam of psychological subtext, as little Andy must decide between maternal influence and peer pressure.
A rip-roaring low-budget screamer.
The filmmakers seem more than aware of the logical and dramatic deficiencies of their material, and so they flee to that last refuge of movie scoundrels: self-conscious campiness.
Scary, yet darkly funny, this thriller of the supernatural from the director of the terrific "Fright Night" moves with the speed of a bullet train and with style to burn.

The sequences without Chucky are as stock as they come, and so are all the flesh-and-blood characters around him, but he's still a hugely entertaining mischief-maker, and what he lacks in physical gifts, he compensates for in sneakiness.
Making a good horror-thriller, or even a good horror-comedy, is not child's play, as this schizoid film all too unfortunately proves.

title: Come to Daddy | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Brutal violence abounds in these coastal mysteries, but they're not all show.
Incredibly violent and very fun and very strange.
Any film that opens quoting William Shakespeare and Beyoncé is meant to be regarded with skepticism and giggles, but this dog gets sillier by the minute.
Providing both a tight script and interesting directing, and blending the best of indie horror with B-movie violence and gore, it's exactly what it needs to be for both the audience and Norval.
For anyone who can suppress the urge to gag, Come To Daddy's enthusiasm can be catching.
A film that's as clever as it is strange.
Unfortunately, the movie is far more effective in its first half than its second, which degenerates into cheap shocks, absurd plot contrivances and vulgarism for its own sake.
If you're a fan of action or crime movies and you're prepared to wait halfway through a 94-minute film for the violence to start, you might be glad you stuck around.
Is it "The Tell-Tale Heart"? "Cape Fear"? "Manchester by the Sea"? "Home Alone"? "Come To Daddy" borrows something from all of those, but feels wholly original at the same time.

Come to Daddy is a stylistically impressive and disconcertingly lovely shot across the absurdist bow that plays havoc with genre conventions and as such impresses with its utterly unique take on father/son reunification and the perils thereof.
Enjoyable performances... hold the film to its redemptive goals, even as it descends into what can only be described as bloody bedlam.
"Come to Daddy..." does deliver a good, sick twist; and sometimes that's enough.
Wood's excellent and empathetic performance proves to be the anchor point, the port in this bloody, vulgar storm.
And though the eventual reveal is certainly strange, it's almost distractingly so; it's less an "aha!" moment and more a "wait, what?"
[Wood] has to do a lot of selling here, but I bought most of it.
Wild, weird and yet nothing less than wholly sincere in its focus on the father-son relationship at the core of the film, Timpson's brilliant debut feature reveals an unambiguously great filmmaker
As the plot thickens and the genre keeps shifting, this will turn out to be a funny, violent, increasingly unhinged caper of simple men
While "Come To Daddy" dials up its gruesomeness to maximum noise, even the collectively therapeutic "ewws" and stress-release claps wear thin, as the onscreen gore starts feeling like a bore.
Director Ant Timpson's feature debut is a messed-up, funny exploration of the fraught familial relationship, defying genre and expectation at every hairpin turn.
If you're looking for something that's a bit ghoulish, gross, and goofy, check out Come To Daddy. It's a deranged bit of fun for the whole deeply f*cked up family.

title: Men in Black: International | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There are some jokes that don't land, and the tone can be unbalanced, but overall, this is an enjoyable buddy cop film that takes its characters around the world.
This is just a good, quality, second base summer blockbuster.. Very big, bold, and funny.
Having Molly guide us back into the supernatural buddy-comedy universe really should've worked. To her credit, Tessa Thompson works very hard to make it work.
It's garbage, of course, the aesthetically undistinguished result of pure avarice and laziness, with nothing in it to command the attention of an adult with a functioning visual cortex.
This is Men in Black. It should be extravagant and nuts, not, well, civilised and sanitised. It's like they forgot to have fun.
For all its oddball aliens and fantastical technology, the most unbelievable thing about Men in Black: International is just how thoroughly it wastes Tessa Thompson and Chris Hemsworth.
Tessa Thompson carries it to the best of her mighty abilities but it's a pulverising load to bear.
Unfortunately the smarts, the sass and the wit of the original MIB is MIA.
Three sequels in and we've yet to get something as good as the original film. I think they should just stop.
It felt like they threw a bunch of stuff at the screen..some of it stuck, some of it felt terribly perfunctory...

A self-referential Thor joke comes across as forced. The plot about a mole buried deep within the MIB organization offers up a very short list of candidates, and it's beyond easy to decipher which one will turn out to be the turncoat.

In this uninspired MiB reboot, the effervescent biplay between Hemsworth and Thompson almost compensates for the vacuum where a live-wire alien invasion comedy should be. Almost being the operative word.
The film, which is helmed by Straight Outta Compton's F. Gary Gray, is still slick, well acted and pretty freakin' witty.
Very little about Men in Black: International feels new or fresh, despite the buddy-comedy energy well-exhibited by Chris Hesmworth and Tessa Thompson.
One of those memory-erasing flashes would be nice right about now, please.
The uninspired approach of director F Gary Gray does nothing to mask the staleness of the formula.
Sufficiently entertaining, but a little rough around the edges.
Every so often a movie gets so thoroughly shellacked by critics that, when you see it and realize it's actually quite good, you can't help but feel sorry for the filmmakers.
It's unfair to expect the franchise-launching chemistry between Smith and Jones, but the mere adequacy of Hemsworth and Thompson disappoints nonetheless.
This fourth chapter in the long-running franchise is oddly unremarkable and is seemingly against taking anything akin to a risk.

title: Above Suspicion | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's all interesting stuff, but not fodder for a movie. There's not enough there for a movie like this to fill in.

There's more than enough meat on the bones of this true story for a film like Above Suspicion, but director Phillip Noyce can't figure out how to tell it in a way that's more interesting than a Wikipedia entry.

Shot way back in 2016, but only now reaching American theaters and digital services, Above Suspicion plays exactly like a movie you'd expect to sit on the shelf for years, no one pushing hard for its release.
Sex, drugs and J. Edgar-sized violations of FBI ethics rules.
What Above Suspicion lacks in flashy direction, it makes up for in strong performances and gripping true-life material to draw from.
Shy of committing either to its rural noir trappings or its hovering air of mordant black comedy.
The stranger-than-fiction weirdness and emotional dysfunction are what's interesting here, and the film doesn't quite take the lid off it. But Clarke is effective as Smith and carries the picture.

title: Kalank | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Kalank offers unexpected and welcome nuance for a mainstream Bollywood film.

Kalank doesn't really lift off the screen. The whole feels like a giant set, stately and ponderous and minus impact; the cast all costumed and perfumed and largely life-less, sparking only in bits and pieces.
The film is an operatic fantasy filled with staggering sets, swirling fabric and heartache, but to enjoy it, you must wholly suspend disbelief.
The excesses - be it the protracted length, the over-the-top lines, the wordplay, use of metaphors or the constant repartee between lovers - bore rather fast.
Dialogue scenes can be static, stand-and-deliver affairs. And Mr. Varman leaves the actors at sea; when the script calls for character complexity, the result usually reads as incoherence.
A superlative piece of technical craft, one that rolls off several of the year's most beauteous shots.
A lavish but ponderous Bollywood extravaganza that springs to life during a few exuberantly over-the-top production numbers.

title: Her Smell | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There have been plenty of movies about self-destructive rock musicians, but none quite like this.
There's a claustrophobic, almost airless feeling to this -- it's almost suffocating, but it's always compelling.
You won't forget it. You can't forget it.

We basically don't get any escape [from Becky Something]. We are either right up in her face, with those close-ups and handheld camera, or they're employing a steadicam that follows her around as she stalks the rooms and corridors backstage.
Stretched over 135 minutes and overloaded with shout-to-the-rafters confrontations, Her Smell has too much talking and squawking, and not enough rocking and rolling.

Movies about self-destructing rock stars, whether based on real idols or centering on wholly invented characters, are often hackneyed. But Perry's pulsating, quicksilver film, boosted by Moss's jagged magnetism, vivifies the genre.
Moss is endlessly fascinating, basking in the liberating comfort of surrendered glamour. She inhabits every cranny and crevice of the character's despairing, terrified, burnt-out, blasted self.
The genius of Her Smell is that it's not about Becky. It's about the chaos she causes.
You can quibble with this movie's title, but it gives redemption stories a good name.
But by opening at rock bottom, instead of the heights, Perry makes it difficult to care about Becky's fall from, and slow crawl back to, grace.
If the writer-director has a gift, it's for orchestrating caustic confrontation, and for a while, that's mainly what Her Smell offers, impressively and at length.
New material from the challenging auteur, one that reflects a deeper sense of maturity, displayed mainly in the idea of the possibility of redemption.
Despite all the claustrophobic airlessness of Her Smell, you won't be able to quit it if you stay with its jumbled dialogues and dizzying pace long enough.
We're getting a portrait - albeit flawed - of a woman, disintegrating before our very eyes.
Her Smell is a journey through hell and back that feels more gratifying for being difficult.
A fame-to-flameout movie that leaves scorch marks on the brain.
For all its yelling and theatrics, Her Smell can't even be bothered to figure out where the outlet is.

Moss, so perfectly calibrated in everything from her career-making role on Mad Men to her small but brilliant turn in Jordan Peele's Us, does the best she can with the material here, though it never quite rises up to meet her.
Her Smell is an uneven movie, occasionally dipping into clichés. But Moss's performance works...
Elisabeth Moss is a primal, predatory force in "Her Smell," a female-centric spin on the classic debauched rock star story.

title: Pet Sematary | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Reduced to its plot outlines, King`s work no longer functions; its meaning lies in the obscure tensions and anxieties that shape the fantasy, not in what happens, but why.
Overall, the acting in Pet Sematary is hit or miss. But when it hits, it's a bullseye.
Aside from its blatant foreshadowing, the main problem with Pet Sematary is its hit-you-over-the-head approach to characters' inability to "let sleeping dogs lie."

title: Playmobil: The Movie | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There is a gentleness and simplicity to the adventure-seeking vibe of Playmobil: The Movie that will work particularly well for very young audiences.
This is a vastly inferior toy-to-film IP expansion, with duller songs, dumber jokes, and forgettable voice work.
There's a plot in there somewhere, but most of the time it's subsumed by a frenetic attempt to showcase the whole Playmobil range in an extended kinetic eruption of primal sound and primary colour.
Playmobil: The Movie isn't as funny as some of the direct-to-video Lego-related movies, either, and that's very much the field it competes in, theatrical release or not.
Best watched running in the background of a playdate for pre-schoolers, buried under the noise of kids' own imaginations but offering the occasional distraction from a total toddler meltdown.
It does not even work as a commercial, never showing us why these toys could be especially fun to play with.
Something with a passing resemblance to The Lego Movie, but one that doesn't fit together and isn't any fun.
But much like the Playmobil toys, with their poky feet and weird, lobster-like hands, Playmobil: The Movie is similar but inferior to the Lego equivalent.
[F]or a movie so clearly doubling as product placement, it's also fun, a cartoon (bookended by live-action sequences) which allows talented actors to riff on unexpected themes.
Disappointingly, it is a borderline dopey, sentimental children's adventure mostly without the wit and spark that converted grownups and kids to the Lego films.
It feels like exactly what it is: an ugly, interminable, devoid-of-substance advert.
This is a film that exists because it has to exist -- it has no interest in justifying itself any further.
[Playmobil: The Movie] is a fun but bumpy ride.
Maybe it's fitting Playmobil: The Movie is old-fashioned, stiff and only suitable for those between the ages of four and ten, but it sure isn't much fun.
Lino DiSalvo's hyperactive film never transcends its blatant product-flogging purpose.
It's safe to say that anyone who has already reached double digits will find little to enjoy in this generic and lifeless promotional tool...

title: Changeland | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Not everything in the script shows that same care, but this is still an interesting, if not wholly successful first feature from the star.
Everyone from boat-tour guides to shot-bar patrons find time to ask our hero solicitous personal questions. If only he, or the film, had more interesting answers.

title: The Tomorrow Man (2019) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Always worth seeing these two actors, but not necessarily in this movie.
An apocalyptic septuagenarian romance that leads with its heart rather than its head, "The Tomorrow Man" is warm in spots but never quite comes together.
Ronnie? She's just looking for someone to sing Muskrat Love with. If you are as well, this quaint, doting film might be your thing.
The Tomorrow Man gives off a feeling of having seen it all before.
For all its eccentricities, The Tomorrow Man plays it too safe.
There's a lack of chemistry that makes for a listlessness of narrative.
John Lithgow and Blythe Danner make an offbeat and winning combination, with total belief that they're in a really good movie. Unfortunately, they're not.
The movie's ending could be called a twist. But it's really more of a belly flop.
Debut writer-director Noble Lincoln Jones' dramedy is a delightful oddity in our superhero era.
If you cherish the rare opportunity to watch magnificent actors as perfect as Blythe Danner and John Lithgow giving it all they've got, in a film about grown-ups, then the line starts here.
The actors bring a great deal of humanity to keep a wobbly script from going too far off balance.
A cloying, at times disturbing tale of two dotty seniors whose eccentricities unexpectedly mesh.

Makes some astute observations about the coping mechanisms we use to protect ourselves from the world, with Jones eliciting solid performances from John Lithgow and Blythe Danner as two troubled senior citizens embarking on a tenuous courtship.
While the film's last 30 seconds are refreshing, they hardly redeem the previous 90 minutes of utter predictability.
The film is content to peddle the naïve notion that love is the panacea for all that ails you.
[T]he film's packaging has an attractive simplicity - amplifying an overall effect of everyday strangeness that's finally more reassuring than truly bizarre.
Keeps chasing a quirky scenario that never settles in.

Noble Jones' first feature... would have worked superbly as a half-hour Twilight Zone episode, but this December-December love story between two mild eccentrics in a small town is remarkably unremarkable.

title: Sibyl | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A mess Sibyl is, although at times it is a glorious one.
It's amusing, but it's not terribly novel... It's very well-acted, funny, and Sandra Hüller, who plays the director of the film within the film, is hilarious.
Virginie Efira gives a tour-de-force performance.
A film filled with quick-witted observations about vanity and delusion (self- and otherwise), Sibyl bracingly concludes with no moral to impart, no character truly redeemed.
Rich in impulsive sensuality and knowing humor, the film captivates even as it stumbles through too many subplots.
Triet's direction is witty, regularly finding clever and disorienting ways to break in and out of scenes while the more predictable developments of the plot take unexpectedly elongated paths.
That earlier film and its off-camera drama remain more compelling than anything in the busy and ultimately banal "Sibyl."
It's a comedy of self-discovery, a drama of lingering addiction and a study of how even seemingly conquered traumas can devastatingly reassert themselves.
Whether psychological drama or sexual farce - and, really, there's no way to tell - "Sibyl" is a soapy mess.
Audiences may likely experience an emotional distance from and not an emotional attachment to the main character.
I came away liking the movie's world, even as I marveled at the carelessness and heavy-handedness of the screenplay.
Perhaps the version of Sibyl we have has been cut down from a significantly longer version, which no doubt would be even messier, but also potentially more compelling as psychodrama.
[Virginie Efira] holds this film together through its various swings, and comes off stronger for it.
Throughout, Justine Triet is committed above all else to the tricks that memory and language can play on us.

There's much to appreciate about the meta-commentary at the center of this lively work, but "Sibyl" ultimately becomes a victim of the same pressure to deliver a big, showy narrative that its troubled protagonist so desperately wishes she could tell.
It is a formulaic story about a woman who has zero redeeming features, and lacks the charm to carry that repugnance off.
Triet handles the material gracefully and altogether skillfully, directing star Virginie Efira to one of her most impressive all-encompassing performances to date.
It is not convincing, and some of the acting is not of the highest order.
Sibyl is far less than the sum of its parts, and never manages to shake off a heavy tone which consistently threatens to capsize even the rare funny interludes.
A film that effectively plays as cinematic dessert - albeit less a choux puff than a lemon tart, with sharper notes than expected to its creamy pleasures.

title: The Curse of La Llorona (2019) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The performances are good, but I wanted more complexity for the original folk tale of La Llorona.
I was so bored, and so depressed by the mechanics of it.
A formulaic slab of supernatural dirge destined to be forgotten by year's, or perhaps even month's, end.
The creaking-doors-and-wind-gusting-through-windows routine becomes tiresome, though, as does Raymond Cruz's hilariously taciturn Hispanic exorcist.
In spite of the absurdity of the plot and the flimsiness of the concept, there are enough bloodcurdling moments here to make you cower, jump or hide beneath your seat at least once or twice.
The Curse of La Llorona could have been better than average.
Without an original or fresh bone in its body, The Curse Of La Llorona smacks of unelevated horror for the very easily scared, not to mention pleased.
You'll have better luck running into the actual Llorona in a desolate alley than finding cultural significance in the darkness of a movie theater invoking this cash grab of a spirit.
Spooky bathtubs, flickering flashlights, old wooden crosses perfect for dispensing with nasty spirits: "The Curse of La Llorona" is haunted by a reliance on musty horror tropes.
It's rather boring, and even if some individual moments do strike a suitably unnerving tone this is still a rather forgettable affair difficult to get excited about.

It may further the brand a bit, but it's the opposite of frightening: a sludgy collection of tired jump scares, inexpertly mounted period décor -- this time we're in a too-shiny 1973 Los Angeles -- and a continued slump into generic blahness.
A cool set-up, they just didn't do anything with it...this could have been a lot better.
Wail as she might, the silly, not scary "The Curse of La Llorona" never reaches the operatic heights that the best of the franchise can offer.
What's missing from La Llorona is the element of world-building, the mapping of the myth onto the wider world in some more explicit and ample form than a mere sudden apparition.
The legend of La Llorona could inspire a whole universe of films on its own, but not with a kick-off like this.
It is a terrifically scary movie that I wish were more haunting.
With The Curse of La Llorona, the Conjuring universe has damned itself to an eternal cycle of rinse and repeat.
...we were cursed with the annoying and shrieking but not even close to terrifying La Llorona.
This is what happens when franchise greed is put ahead of storytelling basics.
"La Llorona" is another lame trip down a long, darkened hallway where the anticipation of the scare is always more frightening than the scare itself.

title: Hellboy | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film may not be thrill-a-minute entertainment like Superman, Spiderman or Batman. But this is precisely what makes it tick.

When the movie's story line concentrates on the character of Hellboy and his relationships with those important to him, the film becomes a unique romp, with an exciting yet vulnerable superhero at the center who just happens to be the spawn of Satan.

Director Guillermo Del Toro captures some of the visual color, tone, and beauty of the comic book. But he sometimes makes you feel like you are reading it over someone else's shoulder, and that person takes too long to finish a page.
Played by Ron Perlman, he's the most magnetic action hero I've come across in a long while, though I couldn't make heads or tails of this story.
Unfortunately, after setting up this fresh blue-collar scenario in the movie's first hour, Del Toro wallows in pyrotechnics.
Del Toro, in love with his source but never overawed by it, keeps things moving; Perlman ties it together with some of the driest witticisms this side of Indiana Jones. Like we said: fun.
Del Toro's energized adventure has humor, excitement, and soul to burn.
Most effective as a brief window into an era. It captures the bitter aftertaste of a counter-cultural movement gone stale
It hasn't got the breakout potential of less eccentric comic book heroes, but fans will thank the dark squid gods for del Toro's admirable loyalty to the source material.
A richly imaginative comicbook world is unveiled in Hellboy. If only the story was as strong.

Perlman plays the adult Hellboy to perfection: part blustery, stogie-chomping tough guy in a mean leather duster, and part angsty teenager, sick and tired of being confined to the BPRD lest his appearance incite a riot among the general populace.
To his credit, del Toro does not flinch from the ridiculous. But he is equally sensitive to Hellboy's pulp poetry.
This is the kind of movie you watch for its aura, for its appealing characters, for its marvelously sustained seriocomic romantic mood.
Del Toro moves his story along with unrelenting energy and wit while introducing the opposing parties with admirable efficiency.
Comic book fans are sure to be delighted by Hellboy, Guillermo del Toro's surprisingly smart, graphically faithful live-action adaptation of the Mike Mignola series.
Easily the most adept comic book adaptation since Ghost World.
[del Toro] doesn't quite knock it out of the park like X2 or Spider-Man, but that's not because of a weak swing.

If you don't normally go to films where the lead characters look like giant Pez dispensers, the slogging fights of Hellboy may seem like purgatory. But there's enough going on in between the big action sequences to save the movie from mediocrity.
While the character of Hellboy is entertaining, the film in which he appears is largely an exploitative jumble.
I don't know if Hellboy has had a Beauty and the Beast relationship in his comic-book life, but if he did, the filmmakers did right by him in casting Ron Perlman.

title: Daughter of the Wolf | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The filmmakers adeptly blur the lines between the heroes and anti-heroes, constructing a dynamic, character-driven portrait of rage and redemption.
An entertainingly scenery-chewing Richard Dreyfuss performance intermittently livens up a movie that's otherwise fairly unremarkable.
Alas, David Hackl's film doesn't give its gifted star much to do, despite a wealth of natural challenges and even one nifty car stunt early on.
A subpar vehicle for an action star who deserves better.

title: See You Yesterday | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Though the movie encounters some of the usual pitfalls of time-travel plots (predictability, muddled rules) and sports some hokey, eighties-style special effects, what it offers in terms of diversity and messaging is a treasure.
No matter the inspired cinematography or considered, authentic performances, these stories carry a weight of inevitability as they suck every particle of hope out of the air.

The teenagers speak with authentic voices, and Bristol builds a believable world for them (they conduct their science experiments inside Sebastian's grandmother's garage) without bogging them down in science.
Undeniable,... is the powerful impact of watching a cycle of violence that cannot be broken, no matter how many ways it plays out.
An ambitious, striking debut that takes unexpected creative risks and heralds the arrival of an exciting new filmmaker.
At its core, "See You Yesterday" is a story about grief and the inevitable question so many mourners have asked themselves: Could I have done anything to forestall my loved one's death?
Is this really an appropriate movie for serious topics like excessive policing, shooting bias, and institutional racism? The answer is... sure, why not?
See You Yesterday finds a striking-yet-natural balance between genre concept and a harsh reality that is achingly familiar to the people who have to navigate it every day.
Eden-Smith makes the film her own, right up to the surprising, challenging and altogether sharp final note.
See You Yesterday is an instant sci-fi classic that's as timely as it is terrific.

Would end up being a very dark movie indeed if it didn't have Duncan-Smith at its center, determined to think her way out of a set-up that is stacked so heavily against her that time travel changes only the victims, but not the violence.
A smart, often ingenious, new film that takes a depressingly familiar scenario and then adds some time travel to the mix.

title: We Have Always Lived in the Castle | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film adaptation of We Have Always Lived in the Castle understands Shirley Jackson's novel as a tale of male abuse and female rage.
Emotionally high-stakes drama.
Passon makes the creepy stuff too low-key, less a case of building dread than growing impatience.
Allows Passon to work with a larger, more complex canvas while still displaying her intuitive understanding of women seeking to overthrow repression and societal expectation.

The movie, though, which was adapted by Mark Kruger, is all surface polish and play-acted oddness, from the cloying symmetry of the stalely composed shots to the cartoonish depiction of some awfully complicated - nigh perverse - family relationships.
Under Stacie Passon's precise direction, this gothic fable of isolation and violence expertly treads a fine line between tragedy and camp.
Passon's attempt at slow-burn never really ignites. And so We Have Always Lived in the Castle is not exciting, eerie, or intriguing, just boring.
We Have Always Lived in the Castle shows off Stacie Passon's directorial flair, and both Farmiga and Daddario are exemplary in roles that would be difficult to translate off the page.
Passon... sharply channels the author's atmosphere of dread, paranoia, and isolation, making the past feel prescient.

title: Wine Country | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: In Wine Country, Amy Poehler, Maya Rudolph, Rachel Dratch, Ana Gasteyer, Paula Pell, and Emily Spivey all seem to be having a blast, but the resultant movie is unfunny and forgettable.
All in all, it's a drinkable, if at times indulgent, affair.
A curious letdown.
A pleasant and perfectly watchable comedy that would have died on the vine in theaters, "Wine Country" is casual viewing done right.
...if you saw this group of friends in a restaurant or at a wine tasting or walking down the street, you'd either feel grateful you have a similar crew, or you'd sure as heck wish you did.
But while this isn't the most original project that any of these women have ever done, it is as warm and comfortable as a cashmere blanket draped around one's shoulders by a considerate friend.
A waste of talent that makes Wine Country even more forgettable than its jokes.
Unlike basically every other drunken comedy ever made, this one has experiences of womanhood baked into every layer.
Despite having only one character trait apiece, the cast each slip into their semi-fictionalised roles as comfortably as a trusty longline cardigan. If only there were a bit of edge on show.
For a group of actresses with improv comedy chops, it feels labored at times. And it doesn't have the zany, unpredictable energy of a movie like Bridesmaids.

There's plenty of drinking, bonding, and bickering. But none of the jokes feel as barbed-wire sharp as the material you know these brilliant comic actresses could have come up with if they tossed out the script and just ad-libbed.
Wine Country is basically Poehler's version of Adam Sandler's Netflix-funded vacations, but with some introspect in place of Sandler's crass gags.

Star Amy Poehler's directing debut about six female friends on a weekend break in Napa trips up on its journey from silly to soul-searching. No matter. Poehler seems to think that the pleasure of their company is enough. She's right.
Amy Poehler's directorial debut never really leaves its Eileen Fisher-clad comfort zone, but it'll probably be a hit regardless with women of a certain age.
By slyly acknowledging the clichés of "this type of movie," it distances itself from them before diving in. More importantly, it clears space for its mega-talented performers to pour on the laughs.

It may proffer fart jokes and pratfalls, but it also has profound and insightful things to say about what it is that keeps old friends returning to each other, even after the inside jokes are exhausted-and the limits of those bonds.
Wine Country goes down like a decent pinot grigio -- something that might not be a medal winner, but which isn't half bad.
Because the talent amassed here is so impressive, I wish the film had been more focused.
Wine Country springs to life here and there, but there's something dispiriting about the way these women seem to be working hard for laughs rather than just being funny.
What's most painful is that Wine Country isn't as funny as just having brunch with this talented bunch would be.

title: The Furies (2019) | Rotten Tomatoes
