Not a fan of football, but a fan of overcoing adversity , which is exactly what this "dirty dozen" orphans accomplish under the guidance of Rusty Russell. It's a feel good story delivered at exactly the right time

Football fans, or those longing for bygone days of old timey sayings and men with conventional character, may find enjoyment in the film's spelled out structure. Others will be at the mercy of its barrage of inspiration, devoid of insight.

The script is littered with misogynistic locker room talk, from the use of "ladies" as an insult, to immediately objectifying Vinessa Shaw, who plays Russell's wife Juanita, as soon as she appears on screen.

title: In the Heights (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: You can practically see the heat rising off the pavement in Lin-Manuel Miranda and John M. Chu's perfect return-to-the-cinema summertime musical.

The choreography (by Christopher Scott) is always terrific and there's that unstoppable energy which, given the film's running time, might eventually have you shouting: "Stop. Stop with the unstoppable energy! I'm over it!" But, you know, what the hell.
Ramos instantly secures his future as a leading man, but every single member of the cast is giving it their all, infusing their vocals and movements with life.
While the individual musical sequences range from the exciting to the charming, the film drags in spots. Despite that it's a must for musical lovers...
With its big-hearted, vibrant celebration of community, hope and heritage, In the Heights is a movie that's infused with life and verve.

The musical numbers here tend to be over-edited and visually cluttered -- and there's clutter too in Miranda's lyrics, which are clever if you think it's clever to rhyme "falling hard" with "calling card" in a love duet.
If found it celebratory, despite the dark stuff in it. It was what I wanted, a great big everything-and-the-kitchen-sink romp.
Unpeel the song-and-dance romance and escapism and there's a socially engaged, issue-led drama under the sparkle and pizzazz.
Whither the urban grit? There's plenty of razzle dazzle here but little that passes for oomph.
Miranda mixes hip hop flavours with latin beats to give us a gorgeously layered and robustly performed love letter to Latin America and its people.
They don't make 'em like this any more, truly. For just a second, even those among you who won't be seeing this anyway might wish they did.
From top to bottom, I had such a good time with this.
It's all very much in the shape of that era of [the musical] Rent that has been upon us for about 20 years now.
Its highest accomplishment is that it succeeds as the star vehicle Hollywood seemed to demand: Ramos, Grace, Barrera, Merediz, Diaz -- the world will be hungry for more of them. And soon.

Why are the visuals so relentlessly static, and boring? Why doesn't the movie soar away from the stage, doing what film versions of stage shows are supposed to do - broaden, rather than strangle, the virtues of the material?

All characters are beautifully cast, but a standout is Hawkins, who has the soulful voice of a young Christopher Jackson (the original Benny, who has a cameo here) and charisma that burns through the screen.

Musicals are magical because sometimes a character can just open his or her mouth and proclaim something-and do it with such force-that it can take your breath away ... In The Heights had half a dozen such moments for me.
While the adaptation doesn't reach Hamilton heights, a movie celebrating communal creativity and joy in adversity is a fine fit for our return to theaters.
To dramatize such binding ideals, for almost two and a half hours, and to conjure precipitous revels from next to nothing, as Miranda and Chu have done, is no small feat.
The vibrant film adaptation of Lin-Manuel Miranda's musical couldn't be more welcome

title: Mortal Kombat | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Let's just say that Mortal Kombat is "way cool" (something I am rarely inclined to do) and leave it at that.
The result has a pleasing, unpretentious B-movie verve, putting a new sheen on the old-time Saturday-matinee serial.
Mortal Kombat isn't the worst movie of the year, but it's easily the most forgettable.
Mortal Kombat does a good job of giving its customers what they want.

The best thing Anderson does is steer the combat to a backdrop of driving techno drumbeats... But in an old complaint with the action genre, all the in-between storytelling takes its toll on the viewer's patience.
Like the risible Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat originated as a video game. Unlike Streetfighter, however, Mortal Kombat is a lot more fun.

It's that simple and stupid but for fans of the game, Mortal Kombat transcends its obvious limitations by pushing a series of visceral buttons that have been hard-wired into our brains by too many hours in front of a game console.

The results range from passable to hokey, with the latter worsened by screenwriter Kevin Droney's lame sense of humor. In fact, the only real laughs come from Christopher Lambert's tongue-in-cheek turn as [Raiden].

High adventure by video-game standards is low-brow entertainment in the movie theater. What seems like an engaging two-minute plotline to a 13-year-old joystick-meister becomes a tedious affair indeed after an hour and a half.
The movie gets to its mysterious combat island with cool buildup and a sense of wonder. But once the battles start, it's all special effects wrapped inside one giant yawn.
"Finish him!," exhorts Shang near the end of many of the contests, a catchphrase of the original game. "Finish it!," you feel like shouting back at the screen.
Incoherent, poorly edited and laughably acted. The neo-gothic sets are not bad, and the special effects are the best part of the movie... But even on its own terms, Mortal Kombat is kablooey.
Less than perfect but eye-catching.
Such games thrive on interactivity, so watching the movie is like peering over someone's shoulder in an arcade, while heavy metal is blasted in your ears and a strobe light thrust into both eyes.
It is too violent for children and too silly for anyone else.
Novices may find the ground rules difficult to follow, though if you cut away the baroque detail you are left with a blunt, noisy, violent fight between good and evil.
The only decent video game turned into a movie. Why? Obviously because the filmmakers have really tried to offer some eye-popping visuals that can provide the same stimuli as the video game itself.

A martial arts action-adventure with wondrous special effects and witty production design, it effectively combines supernatural terror, a mythical slay-the-dragon, save-the-princess odyssey and even a spiritual quest for self-knowledge.
The guys in the recording studio who made the ooofff! augghhhh! sounds are the ones who really had all the fun.
Anderson does a good job of edging humour into dumbness - Lambert gets a few witty looks - and the art direction and effects are okay.

title: Dream Horse | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a small, sentimental and straightforward film that offers little in the way of surprises. Instead, it wins on heart and a simple message about the value in fighting to keep one's dreams alive.
"Hywl" is a Welsh word that is described on-screen as a "feeling of emotional motivation and energy" - and Dream Horse has certainly imbued its likeable story with plenty of "hwyl".
This is a character-driven movie and the horse is not the main character...

It's a story with all the hallmarks of a typically British feel-good movie in the tradition pioneered by the Ealing comedies of the post-WWII years when the country needed all the laughs it could raise.
The feelgood Brit-com is back!
Shamelessly predictable and thoroughly feelgood.
What it lacks in originality, it makes up for in the sheer force of its sincerity.
Its saving grace is a wonderful - and convincingly accented - lead performance by Toni Collette...

Dream Horse is predictable and manipulative to a fault but, sparked by Toni Collette, there is a strong sense of sincerity and commitment to the subject matter that helps it across the finishing line.
The resulting movie may be a bit schmaltzy - actually, a lot schmaltzy - but I couldn't help enjoying it: like Chariots of Fire, only with horses.
I didn't find any great pleasure in seeing a story play out [the way] I knew exactly how it was going to play out.
It's super cheesy and formulaic, but it is also a total crowdpleaser. If you like that kind of film... I think it really fits the bill.
Poetic licence nudges forward backstories of marital strife, but the film's touch is deft. Likewise, the comedy of small-town eccentrics, rowdily played without tipping into snobbery.
Toni Collette is a sure thing in Dream Horse, a thoroughly predictable but ultimately winning underdog sports movie.
While there's nothing remarkable or surprising about this movie from director Euros Lyn and screenwriter Neil McKay, it's nearly impossible to dislike.
The racetrack tale's uplifting story, heartwarming moments and beautiful scenery pay off in a big way.

Sure it's hokey, but this fact-based crowdpleaser starring a terrific Toni Collette as a struggling Welsh villager who risks everything on a racehorse she breeds and raises is an underdog story that works like a charm.
Sit back, let your resting pulse rate slow to an easy Acorn crawl, and watch Collette and Co.'s sweetly scrappy dream come true.
Watching the film navigate... clichés has a special satisfaction. It's like watching Dream clear the fences in the Grand National at Aintree.
It feels familiar because of its clichés, but it's a rousing enough story that those clichés don't hold it back from making an impact. Plain and simple, Dream Horse just works.

title: Tom Clancy's Without Remorse | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The good news is that "Without Remorse" is pretty great when it comes to the action, and there is a lot of it.
It made me think, I should just be playing the video game...boring, boring, boring.
While it's no Hunt for Red October, this stripped-down, unapologetically retro thriller still gets the job done.

The film doesn't reinvent the wheel when it comes to action thrillers. But where it does succeed is presenting a character that is entirely different from either Harrison Ford's or John Krasinski's Jack Ryan, which exist in the same Tom Clancy Universe.
Without Remorse is sleek, formulaic spectacle anchored by a charismatic, durable hero.
Amid a multitude of sins committed by the aggressively unimpactful Without Remorse, underusing Colman Domingo might be the most unforgivable.
The charismatic leading man Jordan isn't at his best in by-the-book spy thriller...
I didn't know Michael B. Jordan could be charmless or so boring.
It's an experience much like watching someone play Call of Duty for 110 minutes straight - action-packed, maybe, but oh so dreary.
Without Remorse is a convoluted thriller that's far too scenically modest for its supposedly wide canvas, and way too shortsighted to maximize its Black lead character.
With his outrageously articulated physique and an unsmiling visage featuring faraway eyes conveying both determination and recently experienced loss, Jordan is more than up to the task.

No knock on serving up an action-jacked Michael B.Jordan in an R-rated, red-meat, military thriller. But this clumsy update of Clancy's 1993 bestseller should have been way better than a generic, one-note, cash grab
Something to kill 100 minutes or so while you're avoiding something else, delivered in an impersonal but not unskillful manner.
I wish the movie broke as many rules as its characters.
Sollima knows how to film violence, so individual moments stand out. What Sollima can't do is make a good movie from a bad script.
The action is sharp and imaginative, and Jordan strongly establishes his action-flick credentials. But story-wise it's all very familiar and more than a little dour.
It takes itself more seriously than it should, but you can take it with as much seriousness as you like. Personally, I advise little to none.
Jordan makes a sturdy enough action hero, but the character as portrayed doesn't give him any contours to play.
[I]t still feels like a made-for-television movie, a Friday night time passer whose characters, dialogue and plot all feel purely stock.
[E]ven with a star as charismatic and physically formidable as Jordan, audiences won't be hungry for a single sequel.

title: Here Today (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is more indulgent, and the more it goes on the more mawkish it unfortunately becomes. It's clearly a very personal project, but it just loses its way very badly.
A film with a big heart and more zingers than actual laughs.
A glossily disingenuous piece of work.
A very heavy and indigestible meal of emotional correctness.
Sure, there is a fair bit of whimsy and jarring dialogue, but Crystal is able to bring his usual self-deprecating style to an otherwise unoriginal story. Haddish is hugely likeable.
The handling is soggy and often tone-deaf, the kernel of mournful humanity the closest thing to a saving grace.
If anything, "Here Today" proves that the dynamic Haddish can ably downshift and still be winningly charismatic.
This is maybe one of the worst movies I've ever seen. It's just terrible, awkward, stiff, and never funny.
It can be saccharine, syrupy and silly... But I got to tell you, I just didn't care. I love Billy Crystal and Tiffany Haddish, and when they mix it up, man they really mix it up.
It's amusing at best, deeply uncomfortable at worst, and always capable of stopping the movie's emotional undertow on a dime.

Here Today serves up slow pitches for Crystal and Tiffany Haddish to knock out of the park, delivering another comedic odd couple with carefully massaged heart. As thin star showcases go, it's an occasionally effective bit of comfort food.
The movie certainly has heart; its purpose is unmistakable. But the spark -- for which it has all the necessary ingredients -- is somehow missing.
Crystal largely avoids the pitfalls of a movie about friends of different races.
A dementia subplot torpedoes the laughs, leaving Tiffany Haddish and writer-director-star Billy Crystal adrift in a comedy fizzle that forgets to be funny.
While Here Today never works, there is a confessional quality to it that makes it intermittently interesting.

Mr. Crystal directed, from a script he wrote with Alan Zweibel. But he did no favors to himself or anyone else by pushing his cast to TV-sketch excess while playing Charlie on the sticky margin between unctuous and smarmy.
Crystal writes himself a honey of a role that he performs with his signature charm and wit. But he seems to have forgotten to write any of the other roles with the same depth, which is a darn shame.
Movies are allowed to be more than one thing - "Terminator" has robo killings and romance - but all those qualities must harmonize. "Here Today" is a mess.
Crystal's first directing effort in 20 years produces dubious results.
Too peculiar and heartfelt to be truly bad.

title: Finding You | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Even as an amorous daydream, "Finding You" is dated and generic, Disney Channel-movie-esque, but without the charismatic teen stars.
Scores around six on the logarithmic PH scale - Paddywhackery Hazard - that leads from acceptable neo-realist films at one to the herb we won't mention again at 10.
Tiny specks of grit get entirely smoothed over in pearlescent sentimentality by the end, eased through by lashings of flute-and-fiddle noodlings on the soundtrack.
[T]here's not much here outside of glossy stargazing and fluffy daydreams, except for the exquisite greenery of Ireland. That's so real you couldn't fake it if you tried.
It's as if Finding You was written by a computer program that studied 2000s rom-coms, taking the worst tropes and clunkily blending them together.

A rom-com (with splashes of drama, care of death, cancer, and the price of celebrity, surely all stellar romantic hallmarks) that never met a contrivance it didn't love, right down to its winking take on "Notting Hill."
If you like rom-coms, this will win your heart.
But the film forgot to graft a personality onto its protagonist and seems so determined to be PG-clean that sparks between the leads are ... hard to "find."
A not-insignificant miscalculation aside, effervescent performances from an ebullient ensemble make Finding You a palatable and compelling female coming-of-age tale.
It would never work, Finley warns us, and it seems she might as well be talking about this cornball movie. But thanks to something ineffable... "Finding You" kinda, sorta does.

title: The Forever Purge | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Wry and satirical...a blunt tool that works rather well.
It's a timely argument against self-regulation instead of safeguards, and an admonishment of a government that views human collateral damage as an inevitability.
A visceral rip-roarer, it plays out like Max Mad crossed with The Walking Dead - but amid the spurting jugulars and the gunsmoke, director Everardo Valerio Gout chucks in barrel-loads of idealism.
The fifth Purge outing goes for broke and comes out wanting, working neither as political commentary nor horror-action-thriller. In this case, bigger is definitely not better.

"The Purge" movies still want you to believe they stand for something, but they're just cheap window dressing on conventional genre tales, this one a race to the border. Anyone else feeling Purged out?
Even in light of such shortcomings, The Forever Purge is just incendiary enough to suggest that, though it must inevitably come to a close, the franchise hasn't yet run out of gas...
The Forever Purge does have its finger on the pulse of America at a particularly violent moment in time, but for a series defined by glorious chaos, this one paints pretty much by the numbers.
The Forever Purge's once-over-lightly politics don't merit much of a fuss, playing like a cynical exploitation of real-world issues.
That idea was fun once, maybe even twice, but by the fifth outing the formula has given way to preachiness and predictability.
Bad people take over; American civilization fall down, go boom.
There's nothing subtle about this fifth entry, and I can't help but feel that's exactly as it should be.
One is left to wonder who The Forever Purge is for.
The most confrontational and nihilistic of the films as well as the most somber and contemplative.

It's hard to know how seriously we're supposed to take any of this when it's so unclear what the makers' intention is and so the film's deeper cuts fail to truly wound because so much of it is mired in silliness.
Words like "colonialism" and "the American dream" are thrown around, to little avail. This movie ultimately cares more about monotonous shootouts than making points about border relations.

Watching these violent events unfold feels just a bit too plausible, but DeMonaco and Gout cook up such delicious comeuppance that you can't help but indulge in the pleasure of revenge, even if the terrors and pleasures are incredibly fraught.
As it strives for a grander metaphor of life in America, The Forever Purge resorts to sweeping generalizations that make the prior films in the series feel like pinnacles of subtlety.
The Forever Purge reads less like a horror movie and more like news headlines that offers no reprieve or semblance of fantasy. It's delivered with blunt force that makes for a grueling experience.
[The Forever Purge] which struggles to justify its lurid fascination with mayhem by burnishing the plot with a patina of class and racial awareness...
DeMonaco is not at all subtle with his script and maybe that's for the best.

title: Audible | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Matt Ogens' exceptional 39-minute documentary sneaks up on you, revealing complexities to the story that address bullying, sexuality and suicide.

title: Four Good Days | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Perhaps the most fascinating aspect of this shallow movie is left unexplored: why doesn't Deb look in the mirror at her role in Molly's addiction?
Mila Kunis does her finest acting work alongside Glenn Close...
It is a couple of good performances in a movie that feels like we have seen it a thousand times before.

The subject matter will certainly resonate for many, but even with its fact-based underpinnings Four Good Days feels like a bit of a Frankenstein monster, stitched together from past addiction movies.
Character actor Stephen Root, 69, plays the largely understanding stepfather in this contemporary tearjerker released in the shadow of the Oscar-nominated Hillbilly Elegy.
These are important stories that should be seen, but audiences need more than scripts that are primarily acting exercises.
What sets "Four Good Days" apart from the many other films of its ilk are Close and Kunis, who sharpen and elevate its well-worn contours with vivid performances that are honest and grounded.
Scene by scene, Close and Kunis drag us into their family problems, and we end up caring.
"Four Good Days" is more complex than its outward trappings and preachier scenes - like an anguished Molly addressing a high school class - suggest.
[C]o-writer and director Rodrigo García (who worked with Close on "Albert Nobbs") knows where to keep his focus and how to frame his story.
Both Glenn Close and Mila Kunis are very talented actors, but Four Good Days gives them absolutely nothing interesting to say or do.
Still, "Four Good Days" nails what addiction is like for the afflicted and those who love them. Close and Kunis work well together.
"Four Good Days" could be a better movie, but I'm not sure that matters.
Though this agonizing weeklong ordeal reaches a shrill climax, the denouement feels rushed, opaque, leaving us only with more questions.
Four Good Days doesn't have much to offer to the audience, except for an occasionally effective Glenn Close.
Even with two strong lead performances, "Four Good Days" feels awfully well-worn.
As a performer's showcase, "Four Good Days" does the job. But there's not much to see here otherwise.

Persuasively acted, compassionately observed and thoroughly unsurprising, this is well-intentioned material that never quite gets beyond its inspired-by-a-true-story, issue-driven TV movie-of-the-week template.
"Four Good Days" is based on a true story, and the way it plays out is both watchable and plausible. Yet the movie doesn't shake us to our souls.

title: Aloners | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A reflective interrogation into modern loneliness, as well as the silent brutalities of today’s urban life defined by competition, technology and nonstop productivity.
While the message is pat, the way it’s presented is poignant, thanks to an arresting lead performance from Gong, who manages a tricky balance of chilliness and charm.
The bittersweet Korean drama “Aloners” works best when it’s a character study about an isolated thirtysomething’s behavior instead of whatever her creators think should be done about it.
Hong’s greatest strength is restraint. At every moment in which she could turn the film into an easier, feel-good story about a woman being taught how to wake up to life, she pulls back.
Aloners transcends its limitations through acute character observation, impressive directorial control and a strong performance from lead actress Gong Seung-yeon.

A low-key, thoughtful meditation on the difference between being alone and loneliness, isolation and independence, Aloners is a quiet, thoughtful and sensitive debut feature from a filmmaker to watch.
Aloners manages to delicately infuse what otherwise seems like a slice-of-life drama with shots of mystery that keep us invested in Yu Jin's otherwise humdrum life.

title: The Ice Road | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The ratio of exposition-heavy dialogue to things-a-real-person-would-say lines is roughly 20 to 1. Any bit of visual wit that manages to slip through feels accidental.
The setup has potential, with trapped miners needing saving but icy roads making rescue efforts difficult. But it hits the skids and ends up formulaic and cliched.
Piles cliches atop cliches with an end result of mush - not content to be the story of a dramatic rescue, it's also a conspiracy movie and a revenge thriller.
The film arguably works best prior to this gearshift, when it appears to be primarily about keeping huge vehicles moving steadily and horizontally rather than abruptly and vertically.
The Ice Road doesn't share a trucker's discipline, and it speeds up and up and up until it bleeds into a different, more conventional action sub-genre altogether.
This is a big, dumb, often gripping action movie.

Neeson's durability as an action hero seems more remarkable as the years go on. Yes, he's older and brittler and paler here... But, just like Mike, he gets the job done, and he's the reason to watch this.
[It] has its blunt charms, and offers more than one instance of Neeson punching a guy in the face. And admit it: that's part of what you came here for, isn't it?

[Neeson's] action hero schtick... has become so repetitive that one imagines him just shuffling from one set to the other dragging his rifle, wearing the same costume, each role boringly interchangeable.
As The Ice Road goes on, [its] matter-of-fact approach increasingly feels at odds with what's happening onscreen. Such a smart movie probably shouldn't have been so stupid.

Simply put, Neeson has been in a bit of a rut, one that Ice Road exemplifies almost literally, since at several points in the movie the challenge involves extricating big trucks from slushy situations.
But while the Irish actor reliably hits both his marks and the bad guys, he's doing so in a film that's leadenly predictable when it's not unintentionally laugh-out-loud funny.
The by-the-numbers screenplay feels predictable from first moment to last.
The film lacks slam-bang, signature action sequences that would make it more memorable.
"The Ice Road" is what we used to call a B-movie, but there's no shame in a B-movie that carries out its mission with such competence and star power.
An increasingly implausible action movie that will entertain most viewers, but also perhaps make them feel a bit played for fools.
Even "The Ice Road's" dumbest turns are stabilized by the presence of Neeson, a real Kenworth of a man if there ever was one. Even when big rigs are dieseling next to him, he commands the screen.
Despite its many perils, both natural and human, The Ice Road is surprisingly dull. It's definitely not as crazy as it should have been, given the setting and the stakes.
Sadly, Neeson's dander is no match for a hackneyed plot, poorly visualized stunts and characters whose behavior can defy common sense.
The film is a muddle of clichés and unremarkable action sequences that bleed together into a cacophony.

title: Ride or Die | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Right at the moment when it seems like "Ride or Die" might run out of gas, someone drops by to remind us how powerful it can be when people let their most primal emotions take the wheel.
In the end... Ride or Die boasts strong performances, and its beautiful cinematography takes viewers from metropolitan restlessness to the liberating seaside.
A frustrating experience as much as a sentimental one.
[Has a] liberating, inexhaustible energy.

title: Those Who Wish Me Dead | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Those Who Wish Me Dead wants to be a neo-western with a heart, but its damaged heroes are straight from the cliche playbook.

Those Who Wish Me Dead has a tendency to veer into the over-sentimental and it has an ending that is heart-on-its-sleeve earnest. But this taut, contained story with well-directed action is as an effective thriller.

It's very very by the numbers, ticking all the genre boxes, and the cliches sometimes become too much, but it is what it is as popcorn entertainment doing a lot of subversive things around the edges...
Those Who Wish Me Dead ends up offering something quite radical within its understated package.
It was far-fetched and there were lots of plot holes.
This is a really well-meaning, predictable, attempting-to-have-an-emotional-hook action movie that just didn't work well.
That grounding in reality helps "Those Who Wish Me Dead" stand out, and it's backed by a solid, straightforward game of cat and mouse.
Sheridan's flair has always been in ensembles, but here that trait is caught in a stalemate with the desire to provide an underwhelming Jolie with a star vehicle.
Those Who Wish Me Dead could have risen to meet Jolie's ability. But the film reflects the industry's lack of imagination for an older female action star.
Unfortunately, the second half is over-reliant on flashy disaster set pieces, blazing towards a predictable, melodramatic conclusion.

Angelina Jolie continues her seemingly unstoppable run as a gifted film director (see First They Killed My Father) who makes terrible choices in front of the camera by following the execrable Come Away with this preposterous mishmash thriller.

The fiery explosions and chase sequences are handsomely shot, but the plot is undeniably absurd and the ominous/rousing soundtrack downright hokey. It's the performances and banter that make the project worth watching.
"Those Who Wish Me Dead" has an awfully twee title. It comes from Michael Koryta's 2014 novel. But the twee-ness is OK, since this adaptation is pretty good, if also violent and a bit overblown.
But sometimes you simply want to see a movie star stab a guy in the chest while a raging inferno burns in the background. Even if it's not August.
"Those Who Wish Me Dead" - an enjoyable, absorbing, characterful testament to shuffling the whole deck of genre conventions, and then politely setting it on fire.

Angelina Jolie, back in action mode as a haunted smokejumper seeking redemption, gets the job done if you're looking for action escapism, but those who wish for something deeper and more resonant are out of luck.
The contours of this story, and the tinges of genuine melancholy thrown into our path along the way, are very much to the point. They make it all work, and make it worth it.
Angelina Jolie's bare-knuckled performance in Those Who Wish Me Dead easily outclasses the film that contains it.
If Sheridan's film is meant to convey the long stretches of boredom before brief moments of excitement, it succeeds.

A lean, engrossing, action-packed shot of adrenaline that is striking in its aesthetic decisions and boasts some exceedingly fun turns from its actors. Most important, it proves once more why Jolie is a star.

title: Run Hide Fight | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film has no psychological depth beyond offering up the occasional cliché - one of the shooters was bullied at school, for instance.

So somebody somewhere one day had a thought: "What if 'Die Hard' except a school shooting?" and not only didn't they immediately check themselves for other symptoms of lead poisoning but thought, "Yep, that's a winner."
It often feels like an insanely poor-taste experiment.
It's hard to say what's more offensive: That Rankin is pissing into an overflowing reservoir of national pain, or that he's doing it so poorly. Just kidding, it's not hard at all.
"What would you do?" the film tastelessly needles its viewers throughout, presenting the brawniest, most impossible answer all the while.
What's most notable about Kyle Rankin's slick and compulsively watchable genre entry Run Hide Fight is the utter shallowness of its psychological perspective.
It feels fundamentally tasteless, indeed just plain wrong.

title: Oxygen (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: All I will say is that after watching this movie you will want your passwords etched in stone.
Absolutely pulpy, but gripping and well-done...
"Oxygen" takes us on a thrilling voyage and lands at an unexpected destination.
What Oxygen's really about doesn't pack enough of a punch, but it is an especially well shot contained thriller with a phenomenal lead performance from Mélanie Laurent.

There's a twist midway that only the most naive viewer will not see coming (we know exactly where she is, from the opening frame), but it's good wholesome fun, and Laurent certainly brings conviction to an otherwise paper-thin role.
Decent tech specs, including some nifty shots from veteran horror cinematographer Maxime Alexandre, offset the slightly cobbled-together feel.
A neat little sci-fi nightmare; a cool-toned exercise in claustrophobia that nearly pulls off the innate improbabilities of its high-concept nonsense.
The excellent Mélanie Laurent sells it hard, and it's a rather elegant contrivance, more restrained than usual from this director, the shlock-horror specialist Alexandre Aja.
Aja knows what sort of product he is turning out and does it ably, if without much excitement, as though understanding he is filling a hole in a lineup.
A modest, taut nailbiter. It lets itself down in the final third, but for the most part Oxygen leaves you gasping for air. And Mélanie Laurent, in practically every frame, is terrific.
Aja maintains tension throughout, using horror conventions - and a few cheap jump scares - to routinely shock the audience back to attention.
Alas, "Oxygen" is too busy gasping for itself to embrace the Socratic method, and so there's precious little payoff to the answers that it gradually teases out from MILO.
Oxygen doesn't do anything new with its familiar setup, but Aja brings taut, propulsive energy matched by his talented lead.
With robust direction in an incredibly confined space and Laurent's phenomenal work, Oxygen should feel like a breath of fresh air for people looking for something to watch on Netflix.

As one might expect, much of the responsibility for keeping Oxygen compelling rests on Laurent, who runs through all the stages of grief, from denial to acceptance, as she thrashes against her high-tech prison.
Oxygen won't quite leave you breathless, but it should leave you thinking -- and surprised. For this sort of movie, that's perhaps the most precious fuel of all.

A locked-in-a-box conceptual thriller that more or less succeeds almost entirely due to Mélanie Laurent's resourceful performance as a woman who has no idea why she's become trapped in a tiny cryogenic pod.
Executed the way Aja approaches it, the plot holes become apparent. Some are big enough to push an asteroid through. But it's an intriguing journey all the same...
Laurent is terrific, deserving of top billing even were she not the only actor in sight.
A tight exercise in breathless unease.

title: I Am All Girls | Rotten Tomatoes
Oslo (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: At 118 minutes it is an hour shorter than the play. As with any theatrical adaptation, it relies on the dialogue and the acting, and both are strong. You come to know the men in this room, and the husband and wife who want them to succeed.

The film is at its strongest when it uses their individual journeys during the negotiations to serve as metaphors for the complicated emotions and human suffering intertwined in the larger Israeli-Palestinian mess.
Ruth Wilson in particular embodies a plaintiveness that's heart-wrenching.
Directed by Bartlett Sher and adapted by the play's author J.T. Rogers, "Oslo" serves as a haunting portrayal of what was, and a sobering reflection on conditions as they currently exist.

Rogers' stage play is a smart, mature piece of writing, but one that transfers rather clumsily to the small screen, in part because its makers don't show quite the same confidence in their audience's intelligence.
The film never shuffles off its theatrical roots ... there's an almost visceral feeling of how much better this probably worked onstage before a live audience.
Oslo provides a sense of grim irony. The side with which it aligns our perspective tip its hand toward a certain version of history that feels jarringly out of step with our current reality.
Scott is enormously sympathetic walking on eggshells among the spiky guests and jokingly wondering if they'll be murdered in their sleep by Asfour.
The actors sell most of this stuff... along with lots of information, some of it elementary but much of it steeped in gnarly transactional mechanics.

title: No Sudden Move | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Praise Soderbergh, and pass the ammunition.
This is a crime thriller with great acting that once again illustrates Steven Soderbergh's mastery of the genre.
"No Sudden Move" is a remarkably effervescent affair: not so much frothy as high-spirited, even when the story seems to be moving with the studied grace of a mime.

The intersection of criminal gangs and the American auto industry during the vast freeway expansion boom of the post-war years makes for fascinating bedfellows. And Soderbergh knows how to make the most of it.
A story about race and class and hidden pollution.
It's well-crafted and thrilling in a way that feels oddly reassuring.
Slouch back and enjoy the prolific Soderbergh's 35th movie. It might not move you straight away. By the end, though, you'll be buzzing.
The performances are unanimously on point. Even in his weaker movies Soderbergh seems incapable of drawing out a single substandard line-reading from his ensembles.

No Sudden Move has something different from the crackerjack noir swagger a younger director might have brought. Decades since his Out of Sight prime, Soderbergh invests it with a deluxe sense of fatigue.
A grown-up film that credits you with the brains to enjoy not knowing everything at once.
We all are in the river. Some of us are strong swimmers, some of us are not, and we have to decide whether to let the raft pass or climb aboard.
Bonus points for a regally menacing extended cameo by the great actor-director Bill Duke, who barely has to move (or speak) to impose his will on scenes.
Part of the fun of No Sudden Move is that we figure out what's going on almost as the characters do.
[It's] about characters who insist on trying to exert their freewill despite living in a world in which they have none - that itself is never insistent.
It's gorgeous to look at and, even though the plot might seem flimsy, it speaks with authority and says much about big business and the times lived, not just back then but now.

Every moment of exposition, every flare-up of personality: none of it comes off as mere talk, no bit of swindling feels as straightforward as a mere "Gotcha!" plot twist. It always feels active, alert, contained, stylish.
This movie intentionally doesn't offer the pure dopamine hit of Ocean's Eleven, but Soderbergh's ability to play so broadly within a single genre is just as thrilling.
The film's got plenty of ideas that you've heard before. (All it needs is Mark Ruffalo popping in to scream, "The system is rigged!")
With One Sudden Move, Steven Soderbergh mixes an old-school 1950s noir with a modern sense of social self-consciousness.

"No Sudden Move" offers a look at a city in a period of transition and what that transition does to everyone around it. The big beats crackle, the smaller ones hang around like an aftershock. Don't be surprised if it ends up knocking you out.

title: Together Together | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Together Together suffers a little from being too polite, as a comedy it lacks snarl, and as a drama it lacks, well, event.
Just Helms' and Harrison's expressions at these situations are enough to bring about chuckles.
Harrison is tremendous.

Beckwith's script does have a few moments of grace and humor. Helms gets a particularly beautiful monologue about why he wants a child... But there are far more clichés, contrivances and threads left unnecessarily dangling.

Watching Matt and Anna discover the parameters of their friendship, and the impact they have on each other's lives, is quite rewarding. Both Helms and Harrison nail the fluid nature of the tonal shifts as their bond tightens, loosens, and tightens.
Opposite Ed Helms, the likable Patti Harrison is funny and endearing as a surrogate mom in a comedy that's a joy to experience.
"Together Together" is a sweet film about connection that leaves some large questions unanswered and open-ended.
Together Together is not just smart, it's sneaky-smart.

Beckwith's film never condemns going it alone. Rather, it finds the hopefulness in what society might deem hopeless, reminding us to go after what we want, while savoring togetherness, in any form it takes, along the way.
Sweet, funny, a little melancholy and a little obvious, Together Together is an odd-couple parable with a fertile comedic premise.
The easeful, unvarnished rapport Helms and Harrison generate through their touching performances is the steady cradle to this brisk two-hander.
That the softness of the whole endeavor never quite turns to squish is a lot to do with how naturally the principals underplay it and how genuine their G-rated chemistry seems.
"Together Together" is a big warm hug of a movie, a pregnancy dramedy that upends expectations and pulls on your heart strings with a tale of two very different best friends.

Harrison gives the character more life than the screenplay does, yet both she and Beckwith seem to collaborate on the film's final image, which - like much of this odd, daring, and surprisingly resonant film - lands with a light touch upon hard matters.

Sweet, sensitive and surprisingly insightful, Nikole Beckwith's "Together Together" fashions the signposts of the romantic comedy - the meet-cute, the misunderstanding, the mutual acceptance - into a wry examination of a very different relationship.
A delightfully undemanding film that will put a huge smile on your face.
It's an ode to the way that even impermanent relationships can be profoundly meaningful.
This is a small, simple story, free from emotional pyrotechnics and, mostly, false notes.
The high points - and there are several - make the film worthwhile viewing, especially a breathtaking finale that will linger in the minds of those who watch.
It doesn't have the predictable, tidy feeling like a lot of films of this nature. It's quite appealing and charming.

title: A Perfect Enemy | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Maíllo, making his English-language debut, effortlessly sustains the tension and sprinkles in some dinky visual touches...

title: Mainstream | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Once "Mainstream" locks into its purpose - showing the vapidity, cruelty and calculation of certain YouTube stars - it soars.
A more incisive film would have something to say about using empty spectacle to comment on empty spectacle.
[Mainstream] drills down hard into its subject, jettisoning Coppola's previous restraint in favor of a more confrontational and graceless hyperactivity.
The film has the knowing swagger of something on the cutting edge but none of the self-awareness to realize it's late to the party.
A horrifically empty "social media satire"...
Mainstream takes a while (and a lot of hipster costume changes) to get there, but it eventually throws up some pertinent questions to ponder...
A big, blunt, sanctimonious satire of YouTuber idolatry that, for all its bug-eyed, pin-balling energy, never feels remotely ahead of the curve.
It's a messy, childish scrawl of a film, but it is high on energy.
Mainstream never transcends the impasse of being another update of the old story about hipster radicals challenging the system only to be devoured by it...

The plot is just as predictable as the themes. Everyone watching will know where it's going, although the viewer's imagined version of the screenplay will likely be shrewder than the one written by Coppola and Tom Stuart.
Soon becomes the very thing it sets out to expose: a glittery, jangly image machine that manufactures little of actual substance, except the conclusion that social media = bad.
Mainstream is a cautionary tale to approach with caution, deserving of a like but perhaps not quite a subscribe.

title: Paper Spiders | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The screenplay from Natalie Shampanier is astute and purposeful. "Paper Spiders" doesn't put a happy face on any of this, but it does instill hope and understanding.
If the film's flirtations with full-tilt melodrama occasionally strain credibility, a pair of intuitive, thoughtfully inhabited performances pull proceedings back from the edge every time.
Personal experience brings a rare honesty and authenticity to this film about mental illness.
It is a pleasure to see Lili Taylor sink her teeth into a starring role, and she plays her character's manic descent with a palpable and heartbreaking practicality.
A sensitive blend of YA, PSA and nuanced characterizations.

title: Army Of The Dead (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Zack Snyder's ridiculously entertaining latest is a zombie heist movie with gore at its core.
If nothing else, Zack Snyder knows how to craft a stimulating visual tableau and he knows how to put on an extravagant show.
Not great. Not terrible, but it really could have just been 90 minutes and done the same thing.
Zack Snyder lives for excessive storytelling by stuffing as many insignificant details into his stories as possible.

Death comes for us all, and if we're fortunate, it's a very slow walker. Enjoying "Army of the Dead" doesn't require much more than appreciating that. Our collective starvation for thrills and wonder probably sauces its appeal even more.
Working with the Netflix charge card, Snyder has a ball proving that trash can triumph on the largest stage if played with elan and enthusiasm.
In its own bizarre way it works like gangbusters, partly because Snyder doesn't care whether you take any of it seriously or just hoot throughout.
Snyder understands the tonality of a modern zombie film. Like Dawn of the Dead, it's where his trademark snark shines best.
The Army of the Dead is too scattershot, perhaps too derivative and definitely too long. But it's definitely a movie, as well as a perfectly acceptable turn-your-brain-off entertainment.
[Zack Snyder] has made a light-footed zombie epic. I guess you'd have to call it an epic when it's that long -- two-and-a-half hours.
The best aspects of "Army of the Dead" are hindered by undue excess.
Army of the Dead grills its cheese to a crisp, but Bautista adds some healthy flavor. His headshots never miss your heart.
It's mindless fun - no more, and no less.
On the whole, the film is sharply cast with a group of actors we haven't seen in a zillion things and who distinguish themselves well.
Expertly paced and with top-notch special effects, "Army of the Dead" is a popcorn zombie movie for our time. Long live the undead.

Its grim images of quarantined refugees and rotting hordes summon a bleakness at odds with its most fun creation: An elite zombie power couple with functioning brains. Snyder should probably have given them final cut.
"Army of the Dead" is more than the sum of its basted-together parts - barely.
Snyder shoots with a blockbuster strut and plots like a 14-year-old raiding their parents' drinks cabinet.
Army of the Dead is exactly the kind of uber-stylish, ridiculously muscular, exceptionally juvenile storytelling that he's made his bones on.
This movie was an absolute blast. I had such a good time with this movie.

title: In for a Murder | Rotten Tomatoes
Zola | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The filmmakers, writers and cast are so criminally funny they should all be hailed for shining a light on a serious subject and then arrested by the vice squad for their naughty humor.
All in all, the tale of what happened in the aftermath of her extended saga sounds a lot more fun than the adventure itself.
It's very arch and very funny in its tone... It's sort of vibrating at this slightly scary frequency, and it really walks the line between comedy and drama.
A film that brashly merges traditional and disorientingly new ways of telling stories, and finds both chaos and wisdom in the chasm between them.
The story Bravo tells in Zola about innocence and experience – and who is allowed to have each – makes this slim, runaway road movie something else entirely.
That rarest of things: a film inspired by new media that deftly acknowledges the platform on which the story originally played out without becoming enslaved by it.
Domingo brings both charm and terror; Braun is the ideal wet noodle.
Keough is exquisite.
Raw, boundary-pushing cinema.
Time will tell if the social media thread is set to become the epic poem of the new millennium. For now, Zola feels like a triumphant lunge into fresh territory.
What's funny about exploitation? You'd be amazed.

A whip-smart critique of the very modern, not especially psychologically steadying notion that our life experiences can now be repackaged for strangers' amusement as "content", rather than honestly reckoned with.

Bravo stylishly delivers a dreamlike odyssey with slick, character-driven performances full of conviction, but that courage dissipates by the final act with nary enough steam to power a satisfying ending for its eponymous hero.
If the subject matter is bleak, and the story itself grim, the film is lifted by the comedic bounce of the performances and the sheer audaciousness of the filmmaking.
An icily slick and funny Florida urban thriller in the style of Carl Hiaasen, carried with great deadpan style by Paige.
It's the perfect visual language for a movie about the comedy, terror, and life-changing perspective of being along for the ride.
The smart, hyper-stylish, coded and colorful direction of Janicza Bravo, who wrote the script with playwright Jeremy O. Harris, is what really makes it all swagger and singe.
Ultimately, Zola is the perfect summer film; it's a freewheeling joyride through the seamy side of stripping that balances the thrill of voyeurism with the dangerous reality.
Yet as an extravagant, not-meant-to-be-taken-as-gospel yarn, it's like a rollicking group chat brought to life, and it makes one hell of a story.
In Janicza Bravo's Zola, the tale is preserved -- repackaged as not just a comedic thriller, but as a way to explore social media as testimony, a source of perspectives we never had access to before.

title: Trigger Point (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [A] cinematic bag of pain.

title: The Amusement Park | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "The Amusement Park" is the only one of Romero's films that feels deliberately episodic without losing its through-line.
"The Amusement Park" is a concise film (only 52 minutes), but Romero packs it so full of detail and ambition that it contains more to appreciate than most films that run three times as long.
The Amusement Park is sharp social commentary rooted in brutal reality, a clear cousin to Romero's Living Dead movies despite the fact that it was a work-for-hire project.
It's not horror in the conventional sense, nor is it even a feature film. That doesn't make The Amusement Park any less unnerving, which makes this restoration all the more impressive.
It's really more of a wild curiosity, though-a footnote on a towering career. All the same, to receive even a minor work from this major artist feels like a blessing...
The film's view of a mind thrown back on itself, and the profound vulnerability, mental derangement, and physical degradation that result, is, true to form, a political horror.
Romero died four years ago, but the strength of this posthumous work - to say nothing of his existing corpus - ensures that his legacy will live on.
The important thing is to be disturbed.

tracks its ageing protagonist's journey from assurance and optimism to disorientation and despair. Carnivalesque both literally and metaphorically, it is a surreal affair, but for all its unnerving strangeness, the depressing subtext is spelt out...

Finally recovered from the archive by the George A. Romero Foundation, and restored by New York's IndieCollect from two faded 16mm prints, its mere existence as a lost Romero is enough to make it worth watching.
With The Amusement Park, George Romero holds a cracked (funhouse) mirror up to a callous and ultimately terrified society.

The Amusement Park is one of Romero's trademark hammer-over-the-head metaphors. It is blunt in its message, and repetitive in its stylistic execution. But it is also a genuinely horrifying thing to watch...

title: Buckley's Chance | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Fortunately, Ben Nott's very handsome location photography impresses as do most of the performances, Nighy's included once you get used to the fact that, like his screen grandson, he seems alien to the Australian wilderness.

None of it brings any freshness for the formula. Swap the dingo for a mustang and the Outback for the American West and you have a storyline very like the one anchoring Dreamworks' latest animated feature, Spirit Untamed.
The film is like one of those old, bad Disney dramas nobody remembers, in which everything feels fake - even real outdoors sets, as if nature itself has been hoisted upon a soundstage.

title: Werewolves Within | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's a film that wants to please and to some extent succeeds in doing so, without ever being very funny or very alarming.
Starring a delightful Sam Richardson, at its best Werewolves Within feels like a cross between the 1987 vampire film The Lost Boys and the 2002 and 2004 live-action Scooby-Doo films.
This goofy horror comedy, based on an online game of the same name, just goes to prove that if you have a great cast, smart direction and witty script you can just about get away with murder.
Werewolves Within is fun without ever rising to frightening or frightfully funny.
A new comedy classic whodunnit in the honored tradition of Clue, Werewolves Within finds the laughs in the jump scare, and brings back the uproarious joy of the "it's behind you!" creeping fright.
She's equal parts angel and devil, and as the counterpoint to Richardson's plucky go-get-'em do-gooder, Vayntrub is a bedeviling ingénue who's the ideal yin to his yang.
A goofy and skillful [horror story], with a lot of charisma across the board to paper over its shortcomings.
Both funny and snappy, the horror-comedy "Werewolves Within" isn't just easy to like, it's easy to "get."
"Werewolves Within" joins the rarified club of video game film adaptations that don't make me want to gouge my eyes out.
The film possesses a strong touch of Edgar Wright in how it manages both the humor and horror of its conceit...
The film becomes unexpectedly, effectively violent just when you've written it off as a glorified SNL sketch.
This overstuffed script drips with blink-and-you'll-miss-them jokes that lampoon everything and challenge nothing, least of all monstrosity itself.
With a dream cast and a shrewd commentary on our fractious times, "Werewolves Within" is delightful, one the best surprises of 2021.
The sole purpose of this hysterical horror comedy is to perfectly deliver the right amount of gore and guffaws.

Sam Richardson shows off his delightfully understated demeanor as the lone voice of reason in this town of oddballs and malcontents, proving to be the most entertaining element of a strained whodunit.
That starts with Richardson, who steps into a leading role with more than enough charisma and clear-eyed goodness to anchor the rest of Ruben's ensemble cast.
Unafraid to sink its teeth into current affairs, "Werewolves Within"... has the kind of sharp bite that feels fresh, even fearless.
Ruben's latest plays like a joyous hug of a comedy-horror movie full of charisma, violent antics, and entertaining character-driven mystery.

title: Deliverance | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It is also a finely structured allegory about America and Americans. But at least it works properly on a more basic level. It’s good to watch, and then to think about.

The movie casts a spell through images both ugly and beautiful, and other sounds, none of them really reflecting the idea of "nature in harmony." All here is dissonance, and the best one can do is find a thread of consolation within.
Each of the four lead performances is exceptional, none more so than Burt Reynolds' beefy, supercilious Lewis.
John Boorman's 1972 film of the James Dickey novel has a beautiful visual style that balances the film's machismo message.
It's the stuff of which slapdash oaters and crime programmers are made but the obvious ambitions of Deliverance are supposed to be on a higher plane.
This man-versus-nature story is also about man indulging his most uncivilized instincts, and in their various ways the four men on the canoe trip are transformed.
It's a haunting, nightmarish vision.
A fantasy about violence, not a realistic consideration of it.
So many of Dickey's lumpy narrative ideas remain in his screenplay that John Boorman's screen version becomes a lot less interesting than it has any right to be.
To this day, 'Dueling Banjoes' still gives me the willies.
There's real substance in themes, performances and John Boorman's superb direction.

title: One of These Days (2020) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Watching them [Khani Le and Matt Robertson] nurture a budding relationship while enduring one of the worst eras of modern human history is suspenseful.
Günther executes stray powerful moments, but his lack of a handle on the material leads to two hours so meandering that the story drifts away in a haze of boredom.
We know from the film’s antecedents that bleakness is not the only way of telling this tale, nor is it necessarily the most truthful one. Yet Günther gives us his own version with conviction.

title: The Power (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The Power elegantly knits together atmospheric terrors and institutional ones, providing a reminder that it's not always the things that go bump in the night that are the true threat.
An eerie chiller...great soundtrack, but the thing it really gets right is that it has its own atmosphere.
The movie's period spookiness and its #MeToo outrage have virtually nothing to do each with other, diminishing the efficacy of both and making it feel like a tract.

The Power is a masterclass of the contemporary feminist horror film, a movie that simultaneously looks back at the past to tell us urgent, important and, yes, some extremely uncomfortable truths about our present.
"The Power" is built on subtle elements, but the director's more ambitious jumps are just as electrifying.
A ruthlessly efficient screenplay is realized with vision and viciousness.
"Power" is smart, scary and angry as hell - a potent mix.

[W]hile Williams and Faith do a fine job of capturing the frustrating powerlessness of a low-wage-earning woman in a sexist and classist society, "The Power" never generates much in the way of shocks or excitement.
The peculiarity of the setting and the overall mood make it worth an evening watch.
Most of the items on [its] formulaic checklist are used well enough, but none of them are surprising or so well-realized that they're still compelling.
The film stumbles in delivering a cohesive vision.
Smart special effects, atmospheric visuals and an impressive physical performance from Williams enhance this timely ghost story but the horror doesn't hit as hard as the rages against misogyny.
A raw and painful watch.
Faith uses a familiar period ghost story as a foundation to create an emotionally powerful tale full of claustrophobic dread and nyctophobic-induced scares.
There's a dark, enticing world at play in the Stygian gloom of a rambling Victorian-era East End hospital at night which will be a calling card for Faith and her players.

title: The Deep House | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A haunted house tale whose clammy underwater setting provides the chills.
The Deep House more than unsettles through an eerie, otherworldly atmosphere and an exhilarating new twist to the haunted house.

title: The Woman in the Window | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A clockwork noir of diabolical determinism.
A strong and decidedly suspenseful murder melodrama.
The Woman in the Window is mostly notable as a dry run for the following year's Scarlet Street.
It's not merely a dazzling piece of suspense, but also a characteristically stark demonstration of Lang's belief in the inevitability of fate.
The Woman in the Window is a humdinger of a mystery melodrama.
A masterful film noir from Fritz Lang's rich American period.

title: Lansky (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Harvey Keitel takes a swing at portraying the "Mob's Accountant" and Keitel is as reliable as he's always been - but while this is a well-filmed and well-acted story, much of the material has been covered in superior movies.
Harvey Keitel, 82, is perfectly cast in the title role as Meyer Lansky... With his lizard's watchful gaze and age-stiffened body, it's an epic performance at the center of a modest true-crime drama.
For Keitel completists only.
Keitel infuses his performance here with more than enough lion-in-winter gravitas to dominate every moment he is on screen, and quite a few when he isn't.
Hits all the major bullet points in the gangster's life but ignores almost all the connective tissue that would make this outline of intriguing anecdotes really come alive.
The gangland clichés can be cringe-worthy at times, particularly when the film emphasizes Lansky's Jewish background.

title: Stowaway (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Such a tightly written and engaging character piece that it overcomes an unconvincing premise.
Stowaway, it turns out, is just as intricate and immersive.
Just about every confusing plot point is overcome by a powerful human moment.

Collette, who makes rare use of her native Australian accent, is especially good. There's a hardness to her performance that speaks not to cruelty, but to a knowledge that the price of leadership is often some small chunk of humanity.
It's a clever take on a familiar genre with a terrific cast, but the slow burn may be too slow.

The obligatory suspenseful spacewalks are perhaps less impressive than in recent similarly themed movies, but there is still a commendable philosophical thread running through the narrative that makes up for any shortcomings
Stowaway, Joe Penna & Ryan Morrison's latest, is a suspenseful survivalist drama well-plotted to sweaty-palmed effect.
The ending will frustrate as much as it satisfies. But, really, like any two-year mission to Mars, it's the journey that counts. And this one does.
Moral crisis in space!
Once the moral dilemma emerges, not a whole lot happens for a too-long stretch, despite solid performances from the cast, as their characters reel under the psychic toll of their situation.
By paring their story down so much, the filmmakers only end up highlighting just how little it contains.
In space, no one can hear you scream. But watching Stowaway, there's a good chance that you'll hear muffled cries of frustration. They'll be coming from inside the house.
[Penna] maximizes a simple premise by spinning it into an intriguing story about the difficult decisions that need to be made when best laid plans go sideways.
Penna and his co-writer Ryan Morrison handle this existentially challenging material with grace, and Kendrick, Collette, Kim and Anderson deliver equally impactful, intense performances.
For all the empathy it expects of its viewers... the film is troublingly removed from human reality.
Even at nearly two hours, "Stowaway" feels rushed, particularly toward the end. It's a matter of pacing and choices, what Penna chooses to focus on and what he ignores.
An engrossing and surprisingly touching addition to a genre already bursting with splashier, more extravagant and more overtly sentimental titles.
Empathy and compassion aren't vulnerabilities in this narrative. They're resources, with which you can defy the cold cosmos - though not without cost.
Nothing is being sacrificed for the sake of storytelling, no patronising over-explanation, just the realities of an agonising scenario, unfolding at a steady pace.
Stowaway pulls plenty of pages from the generic space-movie handbook, but it still builds a mood of dread and contemplative ennui...

title: Voyagers (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "Lord of the Flies meets Sex Education in space" sounds like an unmissable yarn, yet nothing at any point in this criminally undernourished sci-fi lives up to the potential of its premise.
A low-grade thriller that plays out like a zero-gravity Hollyoaks.
Voyagers is not a film blessed with subtlety, especially not when it comes to laughable wild animal montages when the kids go, err, wild
Burger doesn't bring anything new to the material, which was lifted practically beat for beat from William Golding's classic novel Lord of the Flies.
Most of the youthful actors give performances of a startling lassitude, although, to be charitable, that may be the fault of the plot...
"Voyagers" shows that Burger can still move a story along with craft, pace, and skill, even if that story is, in the end, awfully predictable. Maybe it's time he got back to the grown-ups' table.
The characters have so little development, they don't even reach archetypes level.
This curious but engaging parable has its own speculative side, grounded mostly in the soft sciences: sociology, for instance, with a hint of the nature-or-nurture debate.
It's the kind of premise that you can imagine would have been better served by a limited series with time to get to know and like at least some of the characters so that there are some stakes.
It's a lazy film, one whose future will most likely live on in mediocre undergraduate term papers. Oh, the humanity.
You want it to be a little more cosmic-sloppy, more hormonal, more unbridled. It needs more WWLCD: What Would Larry Clark Do?
But despite the familiar nature of the themes writer/director Neil Burger is exploring, his film still offers plenty of tension and his trademark visual panache.

Despite an intriguing premise that suggests a "Lord of the Flies" in space, this thriller about young hotties playing astronauts quickly devolves into a dud that never makes sense of its borrowed convictions or any sense at all.
A smart and effective little sci-fi thriller about the best-laid plans of scientists crumbling in the face of teenage hormones and human frailty.
Voyagers, in keeping its focus where it does, feels like a waste not just because of how predictable its beats are, but because it ends just when it feels like it's getting interesting.
The story is all over the map, and "Voyagers" never capitalizes on its intriguing premise.
While almost none of what transpires is a surprise, the film is solidly crafted and features a handful of strong performances.
"Voyagers" is drunk on its own Kool-Aid, too intoxicated to realize it's nothing new under the sun.

The film's ponderous pace, its deficit of emotional energy, its ugly colors, its repetitive chases down more corridors... and its actors' shared penchant for mumbling and scowling make those 108 minutes seem interminable.
Burger's half-assed attempt at an updated "Lord of the Flies" makes you long for a good old-fashioned school bus and a pig's head on a stick.

title: Holler | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Holler is a gorgeously-textured exploration of the way ruthless corporatism trickles down through each layer of a country, and a system, until it falls on the shoulders of a young girl and obscures her future. Jessica Barden pens sonnets with her silence.
Miss Barden is just wonderful in this movie, but so is everyone else.
Honest, gritty, and thoughtful.
Jessica Barden, Pamela Adlon and Gus Halper knock it out of the park with the girtty tale of escaping the trash heap of poverty for a better life. Kudos Nicole Reigel for sharing your heart!
While the broad strokes of Nicole Riegel's story might sound familiar, "Holler" finds its power in the particularities, especially Jessica Barden's unfussy and wholly believable performance.

Barden's central performance is as tough and honest as the film calls for, and even if a closing riff feels slightly borrowed from "Good Will Hunting," "Holler" is a solid entry in the Midwest Desolation canon.
A modest classic -- hopefully the first of many from a major new voice in American cinema.
An unflinching autobiographical work about what it takes to lift oneself out of this marginalized life.
Holler is a compassionate film, and a worthwhile one, even if Riegel gets her points across bluntly.

For all the scenes of desperate people doing desperate things in order to stave off literal starvation while working dead-end or downright criminal jobs, Riegel somehow manages to imply short, sharp shock of actual hope by film's end.
Even the medium - Super 16-millimeter film, in the era of digital - adds to the ambience of rusting, abandoned machinery.
The film's bleak outlook is leavened with a ray of hope, when she decides to take a road less travelled.
A film that is heart-rattlingly poignant, haunting, and among the best of the year.
[A]side from the scraggly forests and ominous smokestacks that writer-director Nicole Riegel films in gorgeous, grainy 16mm there's not much that's memorable about this story.

Holler is a compelling, confident film about family, loyalty, hope and self-care, executed with a firm directorial vision and speaking with an authenticity and genuineness that is unambiguously refreshing.
Riegel seems to still be hung up on Winter's Bone, making a slavishly imitative film with few flourishes that allow it to stand on its own.
The director has a secret weapon in Barden, who makes Ruth's story relatable, even to those who've been fortunate enough to avoid such hardship.

title: Gaia (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The innovative visual effects, which combine CGI and practical makeup, are truly mesmerising.
A thought-provoking and disturbing experience.
Even when the story takes on biblical overtones, the melodrama never blossoms. And in terms of suspense, Gaia doesn't so much tighten the screws as endlessly turn them in the wrong direction.
Bouwer takes material that could have been laughable and makes it terrifying and intense.

As a feat of carefully imagined, economically realized world-building... "Gaia" compels to the end, making the most of the natural resources at its disposal while constructing its own dreamy, tactile visions.
After a while, the film's elaborate, often breathtaking special effects come to feel like it's only source of complexity.
Fans of Jeff VanderMeer's "Southern Reach Trilogy" and its Annihilation adaptation, and lovers of the defiantly feminine and vengeful natural world will find plenty to chew on in Gaia.
[Gaia] is most significant for its excellent make-up and select special effects.
This slow-burn horror-fantasy narrative prefers a different approach to eco-horror by creating a stunning assault on the senses.

title: Spiral: From the Book of Saw | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I like being scared; what I don't particularly like is being grossed or winced out.
Director Darren Lynn Bousman, on his fourth Saw film, keeps things fresh while also nodding, via the pig mask and a scene involving handcuffs and a hacksaw, to where it all began in 2004.
In trying to save itself, the Saw series got caught in a convoluted trap of its own making.
Here you have really good actors in a really mediocre movie.
I was just happy watching Chris Rock having fun in this movie, even if I wasn't really having fun watching people get their limbs torn off.

The film conveys no coherent message, except as a warning to makers of mash-ups: throwing an unusual set of ingredients into the blender may be a way of creating something fresh, or it may simply result in an indigestible stew.
An earnest, overproduced piece of Saw fanfiction without the cheap thrills.
Even the "torture porn" murders have lost their gross-out value, and are now just brutal and kitsch.
Spiral's too-restrained storylines here are clearly an unfortunate side effect of its ambitions toward a more venerated generic bent...
No matter who the killer is targeting with his latest schemes, it's Rock who's the victim here, and he does not escape unharmed.
If the title implies a certain motion, the main direction the movie heads is essentially down the drain.
It's hammy and predictable, where it should be lean and nasty.

It can't decide whether it wants to be a horror movie attached to a police procedural, a police procedural attached to a horror movie, or a Bulgarian knock-off of Law and Order: Special Hostel Division.
Spiral: From the Book of Saw is more frustrating than the average mediocre horror sequel because you can easily decipher the wasted opportunity up there on the screen.
"The last three traps weren't gory enough" feels among the more depressing critical judgements I'll ever bestow.
Spiral: From the Book of Saw is a mixed bag of gruesomely bloody tricks.
The Spiral team gets the traps right, but that's about it. A hugely disappointing installment loaded with so much untapped potential.
Spiral returns to the roots of the franchise, with its Se7en-like grungy aesthetic and grisly murders that nourish the cravings of extremity horror hounds.
Though plenty gory, there's no suspense, or even scares, to speak of in "Spiral," as the story just sort of happens at the audience rather than drawing us in.
If only this ninth installment in the "Saw" series carried more weight than Monopoly money, its 93-minute runtime wouldn't feel like we hit a "Go to Jail" space.

title: We Broke Up | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: We Broke Up is a breeze to watch thanks to its fully-committed leads, who go wherever the story takes them.
There are a million reasons why couples break up. If only We Broke Up had landed on one, they might have really had something here.

A relationship isn't necessarily a waste of time just because it doesn't lead to the altar, Rosenberg affectingly reminds us, just as a movie isn't necessarily a waste of time just because it doesn't seem to be leading anywhere else.
Harper and Cash are ideal, and the writing and direction make this one broken affair to remember.
The best thing about it is William Jackson Harper... If you're looking for something that doesn't just follow the tropes of a romantic comedy, this might just be the film for you.
This was okay -- maybe even more than that... It's just never as funny as its first joke.

While "We Broke Up" is focused, lean and heartfelt, it does feel at times a bit insubstantial. It's missing the "why" at the center of this conflict, particularly with Lori, who remains an opaque character.
Cash and Harper have an oddly appealing chemistry. Their intimate portrayals make Lori and Doug feel sincere.
Although the relationship at the heart of We Broke Up may be messy and complicated, Rosenberg ties all of the story's elements together into a neat, bittersweet package.
The film's ambitions are impressive, but the characters are too thinly written to support them, despite the best efforts of the actors.
Rosenberg can't stick the landing after so much mediocre clowning.
"We Broke Up" catches a rom-com ripple and rides it toward sweet laughs and some authentic insights.
The film is tense through scenes that might have been funny and maudlin when addressing the emotional stakes for the former couple. The overwhelming impression is that of shrillness.

title: The Virtuoso | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Lethargic direction and bland acting drags down what could have been a decent neo-noir.
Michael Caine famously bought a new house with his fee for making Jaws 4. What Anthony Hopkins splashed out on after completing The Virtuoso remains unknown.
Too dumb to actually be any good and too dull to at least be entertainingly bad.
This is a committedly mediocre movie. The script reads like a rough draft that should be gathering dust.
"The Virtuoso" covers well-worn territory - the assassin story is almost a genre unto itself - and director Nick Stagliano, hampered by a predictable script, can't bring much new to the game.
When it's all over and the big twist you saw coming in the first 15 minutes has been revealed, you feel empty, a bit depressed, and like you need another cup of coffee.
"The Virtuoso," directed by Nick Stagliano from a script by James C. Wolf, misses its shot in a spectacular, and sometimes spectacularly pretentious, fashion.
Making the best of a shabby job? Funnily enough, even if it all too rarely heeds its own brief, that's what The Virtuoso is all about.
Hopkins isn't awful in "The Virtuoso," but the movie that surrounds him is.
The payoff makes sense, but it delivers far less than intended.

title: Are You Lonesome Tonight? (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: One of the most invigorating debuts you’ll likely to see this year.
If the premise of “Lonesome” feels a little familiar, the director Wen Shipei still manages to keep us guessing.
The unlikely presence of Guangzhou, steamy by day, gritty by night, and the shifting viewpoints on the accident add an engaging originality.

title: Censor (2021) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Indie movies like this one aren't out to make a killing, but consider me slain.
This thrilling, dizzying debut from Welsh writer-director Prano Bailey-Bond is a nostalgic treat for anyone old enough to remember the infamous "video nasties" scare of the early 80s.
Censor feels lovingly worked-at, slathered in period detail and aesthetic beauty.
Algar's intense performance ... keeps the momentum surging throughout. A clever concept carried out with great invention and some emotional honesty.
This half-baked horror is all context and no content.

If Censor isn't in the same class as last year's outstanding British horror debuts, it remains a promising start, and it will be fascinating to see what this film-maker can do once she engages more emphatically with the world.
All of this is good fodder for a frightener, and first-time director Bailey-Bond is clearly sufficiently steeped in vintage slashers to give it the hum of authenticity.
A psychedelic rabbit-hole-drop of a movie from one of the most exciting new directors working in horror today.
Sharp social commentary mixed with copious amounts of claret.
It's as much a movie about genre fandom as it is a genre movie, especially that find the phrase "Video Nasties" doubling as a Proustian Madeleine.
It sometimes feels like the film is so enamored of its mood and style that it forgets to prod the story along, but the mood and style are indeed worthy of savoring.
Achieves a very difficult balancing act of showing a character who makes choices that aren't really good choices, but because you can understand the state of her mind... You go with it.
Censor expertly uses color and style to blend atmospheric tension and suspense.
There are a number of compelling books about the Video Nasty scare -- two immediately come to mind: Kate Egan's Trash or Treasure and James Simpson's Video Nasty Mayhem -- but Censor works, too.

As an experience of mood, tone, performance and dazzlingly macabre style, it's a striking and wholly original piece, a cinematic experience that has no obligation to offer the audience pat conclusions wrapped up in a tidy bow.
"Censor" gazes on movie history with style and commitment, but little apparent purpose beyond simulation.
Censor is a brilliant, original and head-in-the-door-slammingly creepy horror film.
Censor wears its genre influences on its sleeve, but it's very much its own thing.
The film unfortunately pulls back from its social interrogation just when it's working up a head of steam.
It's more than emulating a cinematic look, like those faux-gialli. It's creating an engrossing, disturbing, yet authentic world that cracks wide open like Enid's fragile psyche.

title: Every Breath You Take | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A deeply pedestrian psychological thriller that uses the hoary old cliché of a dead child as its emotional ballast.
