Dwayne Johnson is at his most uninteresting as an ancient Egyptian bodybuilder who must learn (like Drax in Guardians of the Galaxy) that sarcasm is cool and that (like Arnie in Terminator 2) torture and murder is not.
The film ultimately overloads us with so much amazing nonsense that we sort of give up and give in.
The issue with Black Adam might not be that the movie is too interested in being a darker take on superheroes -- it’s that it’s not willing to go further.
A fascinating mess.
The messiest superhero movie this side of Morbius, Black Adam nevertheless has a certain charm and even a few intriguing — if not downright radical — ideas on its margins.
Black Adam gives the audience everything they wanted, along with things they never expected.

Question for Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson: What happened, dude? How did your passion project playing a Black DCEU posterboy for anger management become a humorless, chaotic bummer that leaves you holding the bag for an epic failure to launch?
Black Adam is two hours of cinematic soup, the ultimate statement from the god-king of movies that everyone sees but no one remembers.

Black Adam is what happens when you build a movie from the outside in — when you start with the visuals and figure everything else will just fall into place. More to the point: Black Adam doesn't work.

Nothing exemplifies the randomness better than a ... pointless explosion of computer graphics to the rhythms of Kanye West’s Power. It’s as if the producers suddenly realised they needed to confirm they were hip to popular beats of the first Obama term.

title: The Pale Blue Eye | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The Pale Blue Eye falls flat in the conventionality of its final, fiery conclusion.
I found the mystery itself a bit dull, but I liked the setting of this and the character Christian Bale is playing.

It’s made by a good director, has a fine cast, a compelling plot and an intriguing historical link to Poe’s fascination with death. Such elements make it worth watching, even if it does become predictable and silly by the end.
It’s a fine Hollywood film. But Poe’s mysteries aren’t so easy to pin down.
It’s a film that, on an aesthetic level, casts an eerie spell. Shame about its story, though.
A serious disappointment.

Those who are intrigued by the history of Old New York, and Poe, might respond to the film’s portrait of both. Those who insist on stories making total sense might need to chase The Pale Blue Eye with a cask of amontillado.

It’s a troupe in service of a story that’s only barely satisfying when it finally decides to tie up loose ends. The real pleasure, it turns out, was always meant to be the weirdos we met along the way.
A mystery that’s more about mood than ingenuity. But the chill you feel in your bones may actually enhance the suspense; Cooper clearly understands that mysteries live or die on their atmosphere.

“The Pale Blue Eye” isn’t biography but invention, and Melling is the merry wind-up toy at its center. Watch it for him and for the way Bale anchors the younger man’s performance to the movie’s here and now.

Christian Bale tries to solve a murder at West Point, circa 1830, with the help of young cadet Edgar Allen Poe (Harry Melling). But what should be a gothic mesmerizer ends up a dreary exercise to doom and gloom that’s an endurance test for audiences.
Subtly says something meaty about the military mindset, family lineage and the hazards of prolonged grief.
A stylish and smart telling of what is at heart macabre malarkey.

The Pale Blue Eye marks the film-maker’s third collaboration with Bale. Many other actors mill about to no real avail. It’s not a career high for any party, but it’ll serve well enough as silly Christmas entertainment.
While pacing and believability issues in “The Pale Blue Eye” cannot be overlooked, this finely made period mystery’s virtues should still be savored.
While the picture looks wonderfully atmospheric throughout, with its frostbitten monochromes and consumptive colour palette, the story disintegrates into a lurid and rather silly final act.
It’s a handsome adaptation, albeit with an unnecessary bit of literary celebrity dragged alongside it.

Its plot is riddled with holes and its ending is overcooked, but it’s packed with terrific actors and achieves the light chill of a Christmas ghost story. Not one Poe would have been proud to write, but perhaps the sort of thing he’d read on holiday.
Maybe, in truth, it never really does get going. But the story’s stately pace is part of the attraction, and perhaps key to its pleasurably somber tone.
The Pale Blue Eye is all at once a melancholic romance, a revenger’s tragedy, and an intriguing mystery. Its one problem, though, is that it comes with a glacial pace to match its wintry setting.

title: Is That Black Enough for You?!? | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Film critic, curator, ace interviewer, and all-around bon vivant Elvis Mitchell has put together a provocative scrapbook documentary that both celebrates and examines the history of Black cinema in the 1970s.

The style is anything but dry, yet Mitchell subtly crafts an overview that is both studded with detail and allows for terrific commentary from the likes of Samuel L Jackson, Zendaya, and Laurence Fishburne.
Mitchell is smart. It’s pleasurable to be along for this tour of his mind and its nimbly kinetic knack for association and sharp inference.
It tells a collective tale of long-frustrated and marginalized talent finally getting some breaks.
Among the many virtues of “Black Enough” is that even if you don’t feel quite so strongly about that time as Mitchell does, it makes you share his excitement.
From a film archivist’s standpoint, the work serves as a remarkable corrective on cinematic memory...
As Mitchell puts it, “Being Black in America is often about remembering that what you think you are isn’t what people see, and figuring out the distance between those two perceptions.”
An absorbing and nourishing documentary.
“Is That Black Enough for You?!?” ultimately does what the best films like this do: make you wish there was more.
It should be shown in film schools. Wonderful.

With his outstanding analysis, dazzling clips, and compelling reflections, Is That Black Enough For You?! will undoubtedly be a staple in cinema studies and for the causal cinephile for decades to come.
A reclamation of the traditionally white canon of film history that pulses with the passion of its creator and the voices that inspired him.
A glossy and breezy summation of Black cinema history this is not, and thank goodness for that.
Ambitious in scope, rich in substance.
There is a sense of celebration and discovery that lets us see a whole world of lesser-known films just waiting to be viewed, re-viewed and appreciated in new ways.

Mitchell answers the call by not just checking a box, but by fluidly weaving these players and these movies into their larger cinematic fabric. And in the process, elevating Blaxploitation to its rightful cultural perch.
“Is That Black Enough for You?!?” is built in a formally simple yet elegant kaleidoscopic way, examining one movie after another but looking at each through a different lens.

title: Roald Dahl's Matilda the Musical | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A serviceable screen adaptation of a vastly popular stage play.
A spirited adaptation of the book and stage musical.
"Matilda the Musical" serves as a textbook example of how to adapt a stage production adapted from a book to the screen without sacrificing the spirit of its author.

A rewarding example of the perilous practice of building such efforts around children. Of course, it helps that the young star, Alisha Weir, is terrific, aided by wonderful turns from Emma Thompson and Lashana Lynch.
‘We are revolting children, living in revolting times!’ Tim Minchin’s genius lyrics make this a smash hit, with Alisha Weir, for all ages. See you at the singalong version.

For a film that takes this much glee in cruelty — Matilda is called “a brat,” “a bore,” “a lousy little worm” and “a nasty, little troublemaking goblin” in her first three minutes onscreen — it also includes scenes of genuine loveliness
This is a story about the family you choose, versus the one you were born into. And for some people, the chosen family is the one that makes all the difference.
Stage directors, by and large, are inept at making movies and yet we keep allowing them to make movies. Still, “Matilda” has her moments.

Just the blast of wicked fun we need, using song and dance to enhance Dahl’s timeless tale of naughty children vs uncaring adults distilled as bookish Matilda (Alisha Weir is a one-girl talent explosion) battles with Emma Thompson’s hellish headmistress.

The film is directed by Matthew Warchus, who is the artistic director of the Old Vic in London and worked on the original stage production. He has done a wonderful job transferring the musical’s energy to the screen.
Matilda dances exuberantly onto the screen and into your heart.
There’s no arguing with the songs. And the young actors are uniformly excellent, most notably Alisha Weir as Matilda, who has a wonderfully intelligent face and a pinging singing voice.
Matilda the Musical may not be as fierce and feisty as Dahl’s book – almost every adaptation has toned it down – but it’s still plenty entertaining.
Matilda the Musical is both thrilling and engaging, even if at just under two hours with no interval, some parents might struggle to keep their young ones in their seats.
An enjoyably bright and chipper adaptation of a moving, melancholy story I’ve loved since childhood.

Warchus brings together the cast with craftspeople behind the camera to create an intoxicatingly colorful and hyperreal world that is visually witty, highly stylized and mischievous, offering the audience a great big wink.
The filmmakers don’t try to tone down Dahl’s darkness or sentimentalize the children’s plight. They recognize how condescending that would come across...
It seems fitting... that the best thing about Warchus’s film should be the energy of the children.
Faithful to both the surreal nature of the Roald Dahl story and the playfulness of the musical. Emma Thompson stands out, as always.
Flamboyantly mounted and CGI-sprinkled as it is, it feels less a fully reimagined screen adaptation, more like a deluxe souvenir programme with pictures that move.

title: The Big 4 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's like The Three Stooges with bazookas. The Big 4 is way too long and talky, but you feel its impact when it explodes.

title: Monster High: The Movie | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It retreads familiar themes from high school musicals that came before, but the spooky twist adds a fun layer that could make an excellent gateway for a budding monster kid.
Between all the magic and mayhem and singing and dancing and general spooky revelry in Monster High, there’s all kinds of good lessons about accepting ourselves and each other, exactly as we are.

title: The Amazing Maurice | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It could be because of deviations from the source, the film's bland visual style that’s just unambitious enough to be annoying, or the unengaging story, but “The Amazing Maurice” is, well, less-than-amazing.
What should be a cute story about a mischievous orange tabby cat instead becomes an ironic, even vaguely smug movie in the vein of something like “Deadpool.”
An entertaining way to convince kids to pick up the book.
It’s genuinely eccentric enough — with its sly talking cat, intrepid band of gold-hearted rats and chronic aversion to keeping the fourth wall intact — to come off as charming rather than smarmy.
It’s a film that’s extraordinarily clever and proud of itself, even though it rarely manages to make that cleverness fun for the rest of us.

The overwritten script is laden with insider jokes for older viewers, but the film seems to fall between two stools – the animation isn’t ­especially distinguished and the screenplay is both derivative and overstated.

Funny, wacky, fast-paced and somewhat hollow. It’s a tad shrill and exhausting, especially when non-stop talker Malicia arrives inside the frame, bouncing around like a caffeine-fuelled teen know-it-all.
A fun, if slightly macabre option for family audiences.

Just what every kids’ movie needs: creaky gags about poststructural textual analysis! This might not have mattered... if the characters around Malicia were lively, witty or even, yes, animated. Instead these educated rodents are oddly interchangeable.
... A breezy little film, about how it’s cool to be a rat.
This is a film with a lot of charm, and gives cinema its most lovable rats since Ratatouille. But I did wonder at points who the audience is.

title: Disenchanted (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Disenchanted starts with promise but largely drops those interesting threads when the over-the-top action really kicks off.
The abundant charm that elevated "Enchanted" to the status of a minor Disney classic has been excised from this sequel
How much you enjoy yourself depends on whether you’re a fan of the original, or of Amy Adams.
It’s worth catching up with Giselle and crew one last time, even if the madness of the Big Apple is swapped for the bake sales of suburbia.
The production value is less awe-inspiring and more, "Ah, right. This is a straight-to-TV sequel."
The original dared to push back, to think a little differently, to admit that it was time for Disney to evolve. Its follow-up goes in the other direction, searching for safety in easy familiarity.
Disenchanted feels muddled, half-cocked and dragged down by its need to constantly talk us through its indifferent high concept.

This isn’t an organic continuation of Giselle’s story so much as an uninspired knockoff of the original, yet another attempt to use existing IP to attract viewers and subscribers besotted by the prospect of watching something familiar on a Friday night.

Amy Adams nimbly steps back into the role of an animated princess trying to adapt to the live-action world, in an epilogue to Enchanted that has moments of magic without completely delivering on the premise.
By the time Idina Menzel, famous for the showstopping “Frozen” anthem “Let It Go,” belts a new ballad that includes the lyric, “Let it grow, let it glow,” you may find yourself craving fresh ideas.
Director Adam Shankman hurries the film to its climax before anyone has really gotten the chance to have fun with the new world created by Giselle’s foolish wish.
Its lack of legitimate wit, cleverness, and focus makes a promising concept feel like a wasted wish, conjuring little of the magic that made its predecessor feel so memorable.
As in the first film, [Adams] strikes a graceful balance between the silly and the sincere, embodying and even humanizing everything people love about fairy tales.
Disenchanted fails to truly rekindle the magic, or the biting wit of its predecessor.

Like “Enchanted,” “Disenchanted” plays with the idea of stepping from the world of an animated fairy tale to the real world (albeit a rather prettified version of it) and back again; it’s a journey worth taking again, even after so many years.
Disenchanted is a welcome addition to Gisele’s story, serving up catchy tunes and all the sweetness of the original with a new level of knowing.
Did we need a sequel to “Enchanted”? Not really, but it’s cute enough to cast a bit of an escapist spell this holiday season.
Aims for the deft mix of slapstick comedy and poignant messaging of the original, but struggles to find its footing, resulting in a film as vanilla as its setting.

Adams almost makes it work through sheer force of musical-comedy will: her mimicry of “classic wicked stepmother poses” is a scream, and despite the thin material, she never looks less than fully, beamingly engaged.
“Disenchanted,” at times, is like a kiddified “Don’t Worry Darling” crossed with “Cinderella Strikes Back.” At others, it’s a light show in search of a movie.

title: Something from Tiffany's | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It is pretty predictable, even if guessing what comes next in a movie isn’t your strong suit, but that doesn’t take away from the fact that Something From Tiffany’s is a cozy, comforting holiday watch.
Deutch and Mitchell are so likable that it’s easy to root for their characters — and to root for the actors too, to someday get cast in more enduring films.
Overlong at a mere 87 minutes, there's nothing timeless or elegant about this flop entirely composed of elements derived from much better films.
Do these two feel like they belong together against all odds? Despite the pushy urging from Ethan’s daughter and Rachel’s business partner, the unfortunate answer is “not really.”
True love has a funny way of revealing any current or previous imitations, but the lethargic Something from Tiffany’s doesn’t offer any of the laughs that ought to go along with that.
“Something From Tiffany’s” rides the line between Hallmark cheese and the Hollywood gloss of big-screen rom-coms once headlined by its producer, Reese Witherspoon.
Deutch and Sampson have an abundance of screen chemistry, and Wein lets it simmer, holding on glances as it builds slowly to a last-act boil.
In a season of oversaturation for both Christmas and romantic comedies, there’s something here that feels worth picking up.
It seems unlikely that this will enter anyone’s consistent holiday rotation, likely doomed instead to the bowels of Amazon Prime Video and forgotten by January.

title: The Independent (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Cox is fabulously acerbic fun and, as he proved on Succession, a master swearer, while Turner-Smith is effective enough in an underwritten role. But so much of the film is derivative, and a melodramatic cancer subplot doesn’t help.

If nothing else, this solid, by-numbers political thriller serves as a star-making vehicle for British actor Jodie Turner-Smith, who is nothing short of mesmerising as dogged cub reporter Elisha James.
Insipid and unsatisfying, and completely lacks any kind of authentic insider knowledge of Machiavellian political skullduggery.
An undercooked serving of political skulduggery that nevertheless provides a showcase for the magnetic Jodie Turner-Smith. Like most of the cast, she’s better than the material.
Passably entertaining, even if the fourth-act bait-and-switch registers less as a shocking twist than a mechanical revelation.

Parter's basic structure is fairly solid and his characters are well chosen, but all of his dialogue consists of the sort of hyperbolized declarations of plot exposition that only gets by on guilty-pleasure TV shows.
Flat direction makes the writing feel weaker than it is, while full-bodied performances make the drama feel stronger than it was on the page.

title: Stay the Night (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Jeyapalan's two actors, with sparkling chemistry between them, allow their characters to emerge, tentatively, towards a connection. It's such a pleasure to watch this relationship develop.

title: Accident Man: Hitman's Holiday | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A movie for adrenaline junkies who want to watch as many slapstick fights as can fit into about 90 minutes of screen-time.
If you want a movie filled with kills, blood, fights galore, and more than a little Scott Adkins, Accident Man: Hitman’s Holiday is for you.

title: My Name Is Vendetta | Rotten Tomatoes
Empire of Light | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Its final, confused assertion that the power of cinema is capable of salving the wounds of major social ailments is too ambitious a sentiment for a film that never really does anything to prove its own thesis.
Empire of Light is a dull historical romance that isn’t even amusing enough to be offensive. It has its moments, but you’d be hard pressed to remember them later.

These are tricky scenes to bring off, but Mendes has written them with such care and Colman performs them with such a delicate awareness of just how far they should be taken that the swift changes in pace and tone don’t hit a false note.
The main location for the film was a real cinema that had fallen into disrepair and was restored to its former magnificence. It provides a vital centre for this poignant, intelligent, handsome film.

The central romance between Hilary and the devastatingly handsome new usher, Stephen, played by Top Boy’s promising star Michael Ward, never rings true. Nor does Hilary’s sudden shock at discovering racism in Margaret Thatcher’s Britain.
Watching the misguided artistry at work in Empire of Light, it’s hard to fathom just what attracted so many top-tier talents to a project of such torpor.

Hilary and Stephen have been buffeted all their lives by the message that they are less-than, undeserving, unimportant. Empire of Light highlights the ineffable joy when both discover that none of that is true.

Empire of Light is neither a convincing age-gap love story, nor does it authentically evoke the 1980s. It is baffling anyone could have managed to set a film in an old cinema while failing to capitalise on the potential for film-loving romance.
Mendes has called it a tribute to his own mother. Others have declared it a love letter to cinema. So why is it so oddly impersonal? So cold? So closed off from its audience?

Empire of Light is... very much another film about the glory of cinema itself. That message comes within a conundrum of a movie: well-acted and well-meant, strikingly melancholy, but prettified and artificial too.
Little convinces as anything other than a first-draft screenwriting exercise.
Throws more into the pot that it knows how to deal with, but some good stretches.
For all its visual flair, courtesy of veteran cinematographer Roger Deakins, there’s little to suggest that Mendes has the writing chops to match his directing skill.
At its best, it is genuinely evocative, and while the script is patchy, it also wisely leaves the camera — plus Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’ delicate, pensive score — to do a lot of the talking.

The magic of film-going is the theme but there is almost no film-going in it and what there is isn’t magic. Peculiarly soulless, pedestrian and plodding, it is, however, wonderfully shot by Roger Deakins.
The way to celebrate cinema is to make a good film, not to lecture about it in a bad one.

Late in the film, Hilary asks projectionist Norman (Toby Young, appealing) why he made a particular momentous decision; his mystified reply may match the viewer’s own as to what Mendes had in mind here.
There is nothing subtle about writer-director Sam Mendes’ Empire of Light.

Empire of Light is so dewy and sentimental, it’s practically moist. What’s more, it’s almost desperate to be the kind of film that wins awards. A shame, because it wastes an excellent Colman performance.
Colman, talented trooper that she is, gives it her all — but I wasn’t buying.

title: Wendell & Wild | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Sometimes there’s too many cooks in the kitchen. Sometimes there are too many storylines in a movie. Same difference.
This needs a lot more chaos energy to power it past the rough spots. None of this should detract from the movie’s good elements and better-angels best intentions.
The story is a touch convoluted, but it’s a gleefully grim good time.
As offbeat and personal as the director’s best.
Wendell & Wild’s biggest narrative problem is its lack of a strong central focus.
A pleasant, plotty resurrection with a superb soundtrack.
A brave young heroine (Lyric Ross as Kat), wildly imaginative visuals that reward a second and third viewing, and some nicely satisfying twists.
“Wendell & Wild” may not succeed, but I took heart from this: At least it doesn’t succeed in unconventional ways.
Fans of “Key & Peele” will love their latest duet. Much of their dialogue sounds improvised, and the pair work off each other like the pros they are.

Wendell & Wild marks the anarchic return of one of the most exciting directors in animation, retooling his idiosyncrasies in service of a boundary-pushing children’s horror with strong political messaging.
Stop-motion movies — and films this bizarre — aren’t easy to get made. Wendell & Wild is something special: a little messy, but so weird and wonderful.
The story lines feel far-flung and disconnected, and the limits and rules of this world’s magical logic are at turns underdeveloped and inconsistent.
It’s the perfect Halloween movie and one of the best animated films of 2022.
In many ways, this film has the creepiness of The Nightmare Before Christmas fused with the girl-power of Coraline but for less pay-off than either.
This is a very strange movie in its moments, even if the execution is dull as anything.
[Selick has] made another creepy holiday classic with “Wendell & Wild,” and if some of it makes your tummy ache, that’s OK. It was most likely intended to.

It’s so packed with gloriously demented visuals and bold thematic swings that try, with varying degrees of success, to lift the film out of the realm of pure fantasy, that we’re not entirely bothered by the convoluted story.

“Wendell & Wild” actually has a few things to say (about teenage grief, the privatization of prisons, and raising your parents from the dead), but mostly it’s content to fly off in all elegantly cracked directions.
Given its authorial heft, the greatest sin of “Wendell & Wild” isn’t that it’s flawed; it’s that it’s forgettable.
It's a busy plot — too busy by about half — but Selick's vision is as fresh and unfettered as ever, and his black and purple color tapestry is a window into a dark and colorful world.

title: The Wonder (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The blessing of The Wonder is how it acknowledges the things we most want to believe and still proposes, in the end, that human acts and faith in others can be the most miraculous things of all.
The Wonder is entirely fresh -- and equally brilliant.
A compelling drama shorn down to its essentials, both visually and emotionally.
Pugh is very much at home in this kind of role, but it’s no less arresting in its familiarity.
Beneath its satisfying surface mystery, “The Wonder” levels a steady gaze at a faith-ruled culture where the miracles of women are sometimes the only way to cope with the sins of men.
[A] perverse, provocative story about women, their appetites and a world that barbarically tries to control them both.
The Wonder crosses a line between eerie ambiguity and aimless floundering.

Not every story can or should be a movie, despite Hollywood’s insistence otherwise. Some should remain books. Some should remain silent. And some, such as this, provide a fresh reminder of the power of visual storytelling.

Largely thanks to Pugh, Leilo’s semi-experimental attempt at blending an old-fashioned melodrama with Media Studies 101 commentary never makes you feel like you’re watching something created in a dorm-session smokeout.
If this film is nominated, I will not be surprised, particularly when it comes to cinematography...

Basically, the film is a waiting game, with Lelio, a sophisticated technician, using every available trick to keep us engaged... Mainly what we’re asked to do is keep watch on Pugh, who is equipped to make Lib into a mystery in her own right.
The Wonder coheres as a powerful study of the way in which people are cloistered by their own stories.
Equally haunting, heartbreaking and heartening, it’s a narrative about narratives’ ability to transform, destroy, resurrect, imprison, and liberate.
There’s a deep emotional seam that runs through The Wonder which viscerally challenges your preconceptions of faith, morality and care.
It's an interesting and compelling premise, but it feels pretty dull and empty.
Finds a very human way into a conversation about how we measure and value truth.
A clever prestige project whose neat assembly of themes and talent can sometimes seem to have started in a flat-pack.
Science and belief clashes aside, The Wonder is a transfixing, transportive film, anchored by the incomparable Pugh.
Wonder's spare, muted intrigue hangs mostly on Pugh and atmosphere, an elusive minor-key mystery.
Thanks to a typically mesmerizing leading turn from Florence Pugh, it’s a film that can hold up a mirror to believers and nonbelievers alike as the best stories of faith do.

title: Troll (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “Troll” succeeds by getting back to basics. Like way, way back — all the way to the Old Norse.
While light on narrative, it’s when director Roar Uthaug embraces the film's monster that Troll reveals its magic.

title: Mister Organ | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: An unhinged character study.
It's less an examination of the psyche of one man than a PSA about manipulators.
At the risk of his sanity, Farrier has bottled one of the darkest ways a law-abiding human can be made.
If its title, “Mister Organ,” initially strikes you as humorous, you won’t be laughing long.

Mister Organ offers a somewhat lucid glimpse of the danger that people like him pose to the public. If only it didn’t feel like Farrier himself were standing on the outside looking in, perhaps Mister Organ could have offered more than just a glimpse.

title: The Curse of Bridge Hollow | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The story isn’t wholly original or even new, but it delivers on what it promises. It’s difficult not to be charmed by a cute family-friendly Halloween movie that instills the importance of Halloween while embracing it on a massive scale.
Jeff Wadlow’s film is competent enough to serve as relatively harmless background noise while kids sort candy after a night of trick-or-treating.
Despite a clever premise, decent special effects and an amiable tone, the horror-comedy “The Curse of Bridge Hollow” never makes the jump from “mildly pleasant time-killer” to “entertaining.”
It’s all very familiar, and dispiritingly so.
Adults are advised to enjoy the living Spirit Halloween aesthetic of it all, and remember that you love your children while enduring the rest of this hollow experience.
This setup promises a gleeful escalation of comic pandemonium, but the film fails to deliver.
Parents looking for Halloween fare to share with the kids -- it’s hard to imagine them going in alone -- might find that all the wacky chaos is just overkill.

title: Blueback | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A lovely, sweet family film.
You can feel barnacles on the dialogue, like when a corporate bully (Erik Thomson) growls, “You and your mom really think you can stop this, don’t you?”

Manages to be pensive and breezy at once, a reflection on the way those who raise us sometimes impart their most noble values to us even as they’re driving us crazy—and their little ways of annoying us are often the things we miss most when they’re gone.
“Blueback” is beautiful to look at and touchingly sincere about the urgency of protecting the oceans, but it is also thinly scripted.
A transporting mother-daughter (and fish) drama as well as a beautifully shot memory piece that will reward patient viewers able to settle in and enjoy the film’s accessibly low-key vibe.
It all goes down easily, with editor Nick Meyers’ pace never growing slack despite a general laid-back vibe.
An exceptional cast brings this very beautiful and ultimately moving film vividly to life.
[A] wholesome and modestly affecting coming-of-age story...
A love letter to Western Australia’s Ningaloo Reef and the sea creatures that make their home there.
Against [its] gorgeous backdrop, Connolly sets a coming-of-age tale that’s downright silly, never finding a tone that does anything beyond manipulation.

title: The Lost King | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Reveals a distinctly British obsession with royalty and propriety that doesn’t always translate with the same reverence abroad. But the more important story is the one about discrimination and misinformation; that fact can be twisted into fiction
A true story, potentially inspirational but mostly just peculiar.
The viewer will recognize a classic David vs. Goliath tale at the heart of The Lost King, which is what makes it such a good story.
It's sweet and nice, but it didn't need the extra stuff.
Stephen Frears gives us something really comforting, sweet, solid and sincere.
As it ticks along from one small but crucial development to another, this climax is far more exciting than any part of any superhero movie I’ve seen in recent months.

The Lost King often seems distinctly underpowered. But it has one big thing in its favor: Sally Hawkins’ performance as Langley. She’s perfectly cast, which, as a general rule, does not always translate into a perfect performance. Not so here.
'The Lost King' is a thoroughly entertaining and enlightening film for grownups, and well worth seeing
[Hawkins] radiates a brazen confidence that shines through any surface impression of timidity.
With Sally Hawkins playing Langley as a woman undeterred by pompous academics and condescending naysayers, The Lost King makes for a charmingly droll tale of long-ago and not-so-long-ago reappraisal.
It’s comfort-food cinema but also appreciably more, since Hawkins invests Langley with deep reserves of doubt, dreaming, and resolve.
The fact that The Lost King never quite reconciles this tension between striving for noble recognition and the fallacy of divine majesty feels like an implicit damnation of both.
"The Lost King" gets sidetracked. Still, it's a great story.
Hawkins evokes a certain British contrariness, a polite determination to do the right thing, and a quiet indignation when the same is not done for her.
It’s a tale made for the movies, and a character perfectly suited to the great Hawkins, who specializes in wispy-voiced women with cores of steel.
The film, a shabby account of the story behind the story, muddles its themes and only superficially conveys the importance of the historical insights it contains.
Sally Hawkins is a gift, to directors and audiences alike.

Its pleasures and compensations lie not in plotty complications or some third-act twist, but in the humanity that suffuses an enterprise that is borne of obsession but achieves a form of transcendence.
Despite its flaws in emphasis, “The Lost King” has a story that was just impossible to kill.
Sally Hawkins’ compassionate rendering of Philippa rounds out some traits that could have come off as far more self-righteous and off-putting.

title: Fantasy Football | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Although the film... can be lightly charming, it is mostly perfunctory.

title: Call Jane | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Elizabeth Banks plays a radicalised housewife in need of a life-saving termination in this well-intentioned and timely drama.

If Call Jane’s narrative is largely paint-by-numbers, its closing scene eschews narrative conventions. We are left with names, circumstances, the then-as-now cries for help, and the knowledge that there is so much more still to burn.
[An] entertaining, if not exactly heavyweight, movie.
Well told and well acted, but go seen the documentary [The Janes].
A crowd-pleasing feel-good movie of personal empowerment.

There is much to admire about it... However, it is painful to report that the script is a hot mess, often egregiously on the nose, and feels like the product of both pre and post-production editorial triage.
Hardly as revolutionary as the activists it draws inspiration from, Call Jane is nonetheless a charming, big-hearted story of a fight for justice, and might just change a few minds along the way.
Call Jane is a drama that carries the ring of historical truth.
Call Jane would be more effective if it stuck to human drama rather than having its characters make sweeping assertions that sound like stump speeches given at political rallies
[Nagy] is sensitive to the details, and sensitive to what the story needs.
The film, despite its heavy subject, has a bright, vibrant energy. It’s not so much optimistic as galvanizing.
We may all have the power to be Jane, but the image of Jane remains frustratingly hazy in Nagy’s depiction.

Banks, a gifted and spirited comedic actress whose dramatic work is underrated... brings the right amount of defiance, warmth, strength and sparkle to her role. Not all the pieces here fit into place, but her Jane is worth a call. [Full review in Spanish]
A career-best performance by Elizabeth Banks and a spicy, Earth Mother turn by Sigourney Weaver are more than enough reasons to see Call Jane...

Should you see “Call Jane”? You bet. And not just because it’s satisfying to watch Banks, Weaver, Mosaku et al as feminists fighting the patriarchy with wit, intelligence and medical know-how. This is a story that needs to be told, again and again.
Call Jane delivers a striking and affecting message that self-autonomy is crucial to survival, and that the fight for reproductive health is one that we can under no circumstances back down from.

The writers clearly intended to personalize the abortion conversation through their Everywoman protagonist, and Banks ably fills that role. Still, turning this into one woman’s story shrinks the narrative at least as much as it universalizes it.
Few know how to tease out threads of repression in a society like Nagy. The conventional approach of Call Jane is a statement, itself. This could be anyone’s story.
For a heavy-duty subject, Call Jane is anything but, moving along almost like a lighthearted Lifetime movie.
[Nagy] strains to shepherd a narrative that zips along in a haze of underserved storylines.

title: Causeway | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Year-end releases reveal a plethora of fine actors vainly trying to apply their extraordinary skills to raise the quality level of mediocre films. Jennifer Lawrence in Causeway is a perfect example.
Director Lila Neugebauer manages to keep the tone understated, focusing on the nuances of Lawrence and Henry’s performances that carry the weight of the heavy script.
A dour, paint-by-numbers contemplation on trauma and dislocation unfolds, and we see two actors capable of tremendous expression stuck in a place that won’t allow it.
Causeway is a small film with a big heart.
Soft-spoken yet gut-punching...
Causeway will offer plenty for fans of thoughtful, quality dramas that touch on humanity, trauma, connection and the kindness of strangers.

This is the kind of plain-and-simple story Lawrence hasn’t really made since her 2010 breakout in "Winter’s Bone." And that simplicity — though not always perfectly deployed — is still deeply captivating.
If we allow these wars to be reframed through a queer lens, through a hip A24 lens, we will see their errors repeated.
Neugebauer, making her feature debut following work in series such as the Netflix production Maid, opts for an unshowy realism that emphasises the chewiness of the actors’ work.
[The filmmakers'] approach to the two people at the center of the tale is honest and honorable, and the actors respond in gracious kind.
It may be [Jennifer Lawrence]'s best performance, surpassing Winter's Bone.

Lawrence seems to have found her footing again. Her performance marks a return to the kind of textured naturalism that won her so much acclaim in the first place; it gestures not only to her past but where she is likely headed next.
Causeway ultimately may be a little too languid, too restrained, but there’s catharsis to be found in its quiet moments and fine-tuned performances.
...if anything, its audaciousness lies in its restraint…all of the revelations are small-scale but meaningful.
Sit with it for a while, let it wash over you. It is here, in the quiet moments, where its brilliance lies.
A quiet, low-key drama that doesn't announce itself in any particular way, but has a way of sneaking up on you...
As a film, “Causeway” is perhaps too cautious and oblique about the story it wants to tell.

Neugebauer will not be hurried and the pared-down script is not going to tell us any more than we need to know and when we need to know it. It’s effective, although the dogged, humourless mood of it does bring on an urge for action.
It’s blessed and also a little cursed with having a duo at the center of it all that feel more compelling than the raw narrative material.
Any metaphoric meaning is left up to the viewer, who will be too busy basking in the fine performances to give it much thought.

title: Blade of the 47 Ronin | Rotten Tomatoes
Armageddon Time | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Armageddon Time is the rare case where the bitterness overwhelms sweetness, and true enlightenment comes from rejecting nostalgia at every turn.

Preteen drama is amplified by robust and fairly obvious musical choices, but more interesting is the sound design: the city is everywhere, grumbling and fractious, the sound of a short fuse burning out.

Gray’s latest, Armageddon Time, is a flawed work. But it sees the filmmaker at his most vulnerable, as he twists the camera back on himself and asks: of all the paths that brought me here, how many were carved out by my own privilege?
Both young actors give strong performances, which is more than you can say for Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway, both laying it on too thick as Paul’s highly strung parents.

Both a coming of age and an exploration of an era, this self-biographical reminiscence feels both regretful and hopeful – a filmmaker trying to make peace. It’s not sugar-coated, but it’s full of love.
The real nourishment comes from unflinching honesty, served with compassion, insight, and a bit of sadness. In that sense, Armageddon Time is a full meal.
His coming of age feels more like something out of the Marvel Universe than the childhood of a real living boy.
Armageddon Time is emotionally honest storytelling.

Am I bringing something to the table that keeps me from bonding with writer-director James Gray’s achingly personal – yet, to me, painfully pat – memory film? Or, to quote the Simpsons meme, is it the children who are wrong?
Sometimes it simplifies huge societal problems, but what makes it really great are the performances by Jeremy Strong, Anne Hathaway, and Anthony Hopkins.
The movie still uses its young Black character as a prop to process white guilt.
Gray isn’t just well-intentioned... while the world around Paul may want to move on from Johnny, we can’t.
[Gray has] given his life story the tidy, well-meaning structure of a college admissions essay.

Armageddon Time has a loose construction and a plot that follows natural beats rather than chasing grand, overly telegraphed moments. It comes back to themes of family, the promise of prosperity, and that precarious time in youth...
What it lacks in explicit moral structure the film more than makes up for in historic sensibility.

Looked at yet another way, this is a film about the temptation to sell out, clearly an ongoing practical issue for Gray, whose instincts are far from commercial but who has never given up hoping for a mainstream hit.
The self-congratulatory, back-patting nature of this film is what makes it so insulting.
It's a subtle movie, and Gray has cast it beautifully, including another great, valedictory performance by Hopkins.
Writer-director James Gray tells a personal story about class, race and survival.
An alternately tender and candid glimpse of what it feels like to be told one thing while knowing the opposite is true deep in your bones.

title: Soft & Quiet | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The formal conceit forces you, in fact, to pay attention to how easily combustible incidents like the ones you see in Soft & Quiet are, and acknowledge how embedded into our modern firmament this prettified poison is now.
Soft & Quiet is extremely effective as a piece of educational agitprop.
Within 90 minutes, their monstrous worldview turns them into murderous home invaders, and though the timeframe is arguably an exaggeration, it gets the point across succinctly.
The film is a palpable joyride steered by the kinds of women who, de Araújo seems to think, could easily get away with it.
Gave me the worst panic attack I’ve ever had during a film screening.
This is powerful filmmaking that goes beyond just vilifying racist scum, and asks hard questions about what hate hath wrought.
Araújo crafts a tense film that slowly reveals how simple racist rhetoric can escalate into physical violence on the turn of a dime.
This film’s treatment of the issues is erratic, highly extremist and less than fully coherent, but the turbulent and troubled impulses behind it are easy to discern.
A gripping and stomach-churning observation of contemporary white supremacy.
The film unfolds like a runaway train, a rapid-fire thriller and drama and horror film all in one, both breathless and breathtaking.
“Soft & Quiet” is deeply unpleasant to watch, but that’s the point.

title: I'm Totally Fine | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Everyone involved has clearly thought through how such a wild fantasy situation might play out — and more importantly, how it would feel.

The best sci-fi illuminates darker corners of the human condition and screenwriter Alisha Ketry has crafted a sci-fi context illustrating the destabilizing experience of grief in thought-provoking ways.

Despite its sci-fi bend, the greatest strength of “I’m Totally Fine” is its smallness. A stellar script and two standout performances from Jillian Bell and the sensational Natalie Morales round out this sweet little flick.
It’s a movie that purports to root itself in grief, but instead wraps itself in such a cloak of wispy, noncommittal vagueness that virtually everything about it dissipates on contact.

title: Bruiser (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “Bruiser” is an anxious film filled with unmistakable beauty and obsessed with conceptions of family, love, growth, the past, and the future.
What makes “Bruiser” so affecting is that Warren doesn’t keep any of these characters locked into types.
I have a feeling we will look back on “Bruiser” as the affirmation of two major talents in Hall and Warren. Like Darious himself, they’re just getting started.
[An] affecting study of masculinity, fatherhood and coming of age.
Insightful and universal in so many ways, Warren’s first feature is a confident if sometimes oblique coming-of-age story from an important new voice...
A mellow and compelling spin on a familiar story.
Warren’s feature debut succeeds in offering characters compassion, as well as navigating themes of toxic masculinity and fatherhood with the tenderness and heart that every child should be given.

title: Mr. Harrigan's Phone | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I would much rather have read this than watched it.
Hancock and his cast effectively convey the essence of King’s story, which is about a well-meaning kid learning how anything that comes too easy likely has dark strings attached.

Some may not go with this veering plot, but those who love Stephen King will enjoy the leap into speculative fiction. It’s what made him famous -- that ability to see how a little dark fantasy can illuminate the world.

Resists the urge to delve deeply into the mechanics of using modern technology to speak to ghosts; instead, it’s a rather depressing allegory for our innate refusal to give up things that are convenient but bad for us.
The story presents a title character so prescient about the woes of social media you’d think he was supernatural. Which he may well be.

Add Mr. Harrigan’s Phone to the relatively short list of really good Stephen King adaptations, garnishing a coming-of-age story with understated hints of the supernatural and thoughtful rumination about cellphones that finds true horror in their ubiquity.
Less a chiller than a diverting drama about technology with things that go bump in the night, along with some nicely apt ethical quandaries for Craig — and for us.

An early engaging performance from the great Donald Sutherland and a consistently grounded one from Jaeden Martell keep Mr. Harrigan’s Phone from completely going dead, but you’re going to want to send this one to voicemail.
It won’t keep you up at night, but it is a solid and surprisingly poignant effort.
Such bottom-drawer source material proves to be an insurmountable disadvantage for John Lee Hancock’s Netflix adaptation of the same name, a downcast and thoroughly dreadful supernatural drama.
It’s all rather unforgivably dull, a call to be swiftly ignored.

More akin to a stern lecture by a grownup than an eerie, unsettling cautionary tale, this adaptation of Stephen King’s short story might have succeeded better if it didn’t completely collapse into boomer-style commentary.
As with the greatest King stories, the best parts here are not the horror elements (of which there are few). It’s the time spent with the characters.
A strong start tapers off into a quiet and uneven morality fable that’s ultimately too vague to make an impact.
Unfortunately, despite its intriguing premise, Mr. Harrigan’s Phone lacks the necessary ingredient to make it truly memorable; it simply isn’t very scary.

title: The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A tale with way too much story and not nearly enough life.

title: Lamborghini: The Man Behind the Legend | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The period details are above par and Grillo is up for the challenge, but “Lamborghini” comes out as perfunctory and unenlightening as a school report from a bored teen.

Fortunately, the film is only 97 minutes long. But even this grace note comes at a cost to the viewer. The end of the story comes out of nowhere, as if the filmmakers ran out of money and stopped shooting before they were really done.
A pamphletized biopic that does the easy thing — beautifying Italy and vintage automobiles — but stalls with everything involving humans.

title: The Man From Toronto (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Although Hart, as the broadly comic version of the classic Hitchcockian Wrong Man, has a certain goofball charm, his frantic coward routine gets old quickly, with no appreciable change as the action-flick danger continues to escalate.

Hart is something of a stocky comic iron man, a scrappy pro with the ability to twist and bend even the lousiest dialogue into a pretzel shape that can make you laugh despite yourself. Afterward, you may be laughing more at yourself than anything.
Harrelson is as effective a foil here as he is a credible Canadian, which is to say, not at all.
Dreadfully unfunny.
The Man from Toronto wastes the talents of Woody Harrelson and Kevin Hart.
Despite a fun premise and a well-structured first act, “The Man from Toronto” tries to do too many things at once and devolves into a strange bouillabaisse of studio comedy tropes.
You know a film’s in trouble when it can’t be saved by a rocket launcher-toting Ellen Barkin.
When someone drops the ball, makes a mistake or otherwise blunders something, they've Teddied it. In that regard, "The Man From Toronto" Teddys it. Big time.

As directed/hacked out by Patrick Hughes, the film represents the nadir of the once-reliable buddy/action-comedy genre, whose descent into the eighth layer of Hollywood Hell was kick-started by Hughes’s own viciously awful filmography...
A throwback buddy action-comedy that offsets its run-of-the-mill sense of humor with a pair of appealing leads...
Brawn and bustling action with no bruise, no staying power.
As a 110-minute diversion, as a source of some laughs, as an opportunity for two funny guys to be funny — and to be funny with each other — what’s not to like? Just go in not expecting much.
By now you should be familiar with Hart’s banter in movies like this. When working with such witless material, his improvisational gags can land like comfort food.
“The Man From Toronto” plays like the walking corpse of better, far more entertaining movies.

title: Descendant (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Has the self-awareness not merely to put Black voices at the center, where they belong, but to underline those moments when white people step up and intervene in the situation—sometimes as allies and advocates, sometimes to stake their own claim.
Boasting a wealth of vivid subjects, this new picture illustrates in clear terms how the country’s past sins still stain communities, the damage perhaps permanent.
We meet so many people in Descendant who could be the primary subjects of their own documentaries, and Brown deftly peels back the layers of all of their stories and makes them heard.
What Descendant initially renders into something of a suspenseful hunt for the truth barely lasts for half of the movie -- alerting us to the fact that it is not the only thing on the movie’s mind.
While it tells a powerful true story, it could have benefitted from a tighter running time.
[A] fascinating film...
Brown... lets audiences make what they will of a rich tapestry.
One of the best films of the year... Brown roves across the land, crowding her film with a wide spectrum of voices for a living oral history that reckons with the long shadow of slavery.

Descendant is worth seeing no matter who you are. For viewers like me, however, it engenders the reality that, no matter how hard anyone tries to whitewash history, our stories will forever continue to be told in full, by us and for us.
We’re in for something different here, is the film’s opening gambit. It’s an unspoken promise that Descendent lives up to.
A feat of cinematic non-fiction storytelling, about the importance of storytelling itself.
If you’ve ever wondered what “holding space” looks like in practice, the director Margaret Brown’s deeply attentive documentary “Descendant” provides moving examples.
Brown knows this is not her history to tell but rather an unfolding story about storytelling she can diligently observe in meetings, get-togethers and intimate interviews.
“Descendant” isn’t just necessary. It’s urgent.

A bit slow-moving at first, the history gives way to a thoughtful conversation about how best to remember this history and honor its victims, while simultaneously highlighting the modern science surrounding identifying the ship.
With Descendant, filmmaker Margaret Brown finds poetry where most would see the opportunity for a polemic.
Descendant is an infuriating and enlightening look at how often white supremacy alters the truth in its favor.
The movie might have felt more comprehensive and compelling if driven by a single person. Rich community and uncovered history still make this documentary a must-see.
Despite finding Clotilda and the attention brought to Africatown, there is still so much to unpack, and many truths remain buried.
It is, frankly, terrifying to watch. What Descendant demonstrates is how ignoring the real story doesn’t just steal people’s history from them. It impoverishes the future.

title: R.I.P.D. 2: Rise of the Damned | Rotten Tomatoes
Sam & Kate | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Better with the in-between moments...When the chaacters are just interacting quietly they convey a great deal and the events interrupt the delicacy of those scenes.
These lessons are all fine and good, but it takes well over an hour into the 110-minute run time for “Sam & Kate” to reveal any conflict worth paying attention to.
Sam and Kate are such broad archetypes that it’s hard to feel the depth of their scars or the spark of their chemistry.
Sam & Kate doesn't try to elicit big emotional responses, but that's exactly why it gets them.

title: The People We Hate at the Wedding | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The movie has a brevity to it that makes the silliness and embarrassing antics pass by quickly, and it delivers a decent amount of chuckles and even some outright laughs.
It’s an ensemble cast but Bell is the star.
If your happiness or well-being absolutely depends on seeing every last romantic comedy, give it a shot.
“The People We Hate at the Wedding” will be all over your Prime Video home screen for the next few weeks – consider it not an invitation but hazardous waste signage.
From the predictable plot structure and series of overt zingers to the eye-rolling litany of on-the-nose needle drops, The People We Hate at the Wedding is awkwardly executed.
As with the chicken/steak/vegetarian entree you selected, this film will leave you unsatisfied and wishing you’d spent your evening at Red Lobster.

Sporting a game cast and efficient sitcommy pacing, it looks and sounds the part just enough to keep you diverted — until you notice, as the credits roll to upbeat electropop, that you haven’t laughed once.

The People We Hate at the Wedding doesn’t stray too far from the formula of our streaming-dominated visual landscape, but a witty screenplay from the Molyneux sisters and strong performances from Janney, Platt and Bell make it reliably diverting.

Underneath the plentiful high jinks in its physical-comedy-heavy scenes, “The People We Hate at the Wedding” ends up being a poignant enough good time that celebrates imperfect yet endearing familial love.
This a really tepid glass of chardonnay.
Who exactly are “The People We Hate at the Wedding”? Truly, all of them.

While “The People We Hate” may not be as refreshing as “Bridesmaids” or “The Hangover” or even “Father of the Bride,” it holds your attention. The problem is that it never sparks any deep emotional attachment.
Bell and co. are able to squeeze the dialogue for some extra flavor whenever the lines are a little more forgiving... but real warmth or charm is few and far between.

title: The Noel Diary | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Ditch the mistletoe and holly and it would still be a well-crafted, well-balanced character sketch, following two lost souls as they discover what they’ve been missing.
Director Charles Shyer brings a journeyman’s ease to the screenplay (based on Richard Paul Evans’s novel by the same name): embracing holiday movie expectations here, gently deflecting them there.

title: Dangerous Game: The Legacy Murders | Rotten Tomatoes
Shotgun Wedding | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Shotgun Wedding isn’t the worst rom-com ever made, but it’s the type of generically terrible offering that serves as a reminder of why my beloved genre fell out of fashion — a fate that Jennifer Lopez herself may be partially responsible for.

While the director Jason Moore spends much of the film demonstrating how good Lopez looks at 53, Coolidge steals every scene she is in as the mother of the groom (“when I’m in formal wear I like to pee standing up”).
This Wedding clearly wasn't meant to be a masterpiece, but even as mid-winter fluff it feels like a rush job.
At its best, "Shotgun Wedding" has the snap of Howard Hawks screwball romances like "Bringing Up Baby."

The direction by Jason Moore (Pitch Perfect) is cake-knife sharp, while Mark Hammer’s script never wastes a gag, especially one that involves pineapples. But what really helps is the casting of sleeper agents in the supporting roles...

An action movie/romantic comedy hybrid that’s too violent for comedy fans and not thrilling enough for thrill seekers. It’s not romantic at all, despite the best efforts of Jennifer Lopez and Josh Duhamel.

Once the plot kicks in and the characters separate (and settle down), “Shotgun Wedding” becomes much more entertaining, highlighted by the comic push-and-pull between its two leads, Jennifer Lopez and Josh Duhamel.
This is a slapdash effort on most every level, seemingly sold almost entirely on the notion of watching Lopez run through the jungle in a tattered wedding dress.

The film is mutinously bored with weddings, which is a start, and has a punchy aerial climax that’s much better value than the average first dance. In a sickly-sweet genre, it’s almost bracingly sour.
Fights and explosions fail to perk up the rom-com veteran’s latest mediocre walk to the altar.
There is a serious theme under all the silliness: no couple is perfect. We all do things that other people, even those who love us, find annoying.
The balance of humor and action is uneven, and it does not even try to make sense. But the overall tone is lighthearted, andnLopez is, as always, hard to resist.

... There’s lots of automatic gunfire and grenade-throwing and other mayhem that feels out of place any way you slice it — oh yes, knives too! — and this rom-com doesn’t end up feeling very romantic OR comedic.

The script, by Mark Hammer, falls under the category of modern screwball, or perhaps it's a pirate romance, with actual violence on top. Either way, it's neither fully one way or the other. There's enough to cut a good trailer, but precious little more.

All the charm and style in the world, and J.Lo has more than anyone, can’t make up for the bizarre tonal imbalance of Shotgun Wedding, a movie too violent to be funny and too funny (in the odd, weird sense) to be fun.
It navigates its story with an apathetic level of spirit in its moment-to-moment sequencing.
Lopez stars opposite Josh Duhamel: not exactly Clark Gable, but Lopez makes it work. She always does.
A romcom revelation, this ain’t – but it’s an entertaining vehicle for the ever-charismatic Jennifer Lopez, and frankly, that’s enough.
If you can put your cynicism aside, RSVP “yes” to Shotgun Wedding.
The only thing wrong with “Shotgun Wedding” is that it isn’t any good. Aside from that, it’s a pleasant experience.

title: Deadstream | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's hard not to begrudgingly admire a film as committed to its deliriously silly bit as Deadstream.
This comic horror romp has no pretensions and seeks only to goof around and dole out a few jump scares, but in its own sly way it offers a Gen Z version of The Blair Witch Project.
The film doesn’t quite live up to its promising premise and handful of clever camera gimmicks.
With a sharp script brought to life by a fantastic actor, and deliciously gross creature effects, this is one horror-comedy you want in your annual Halloween rotation.
Briskly paced, wildly fun, and surprisingly smart, Deadstream is a bloody terrific good time.
Deadstream is smart, sophisticated comedy horror that finds new ways  and new media  for resurrecting old ghost stories.
WritersDirectors Vanessa Winter and Joseph Winter eschew expectations and instead deliver a delightfully raucous splatstick horror-comedy thatll leave the midnight crowd cheering for more.
There is an impressive consistency to the way the filmmakers bounce this man whos used to living online around an unimaginably real nightmare.
A fun comedy-horror ride both driven and limited by the noxious onscreen character of its co-director/writer/producer/editor.
An absolute delight.
Deadstream is outrageous, delightful and deeply satisfying, a breath of fresh air in a genre that can far too often feel old and musty.

title: Strange World | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Everyone is delightfully lost in a softly Lovecraftian Osmosis Jones labyrinth with climate change overtones and lovely faceless critters everywhere, trying to pantomime meaning to these stumbling humans.

Strong familial conflict, magical adventures and timely social messaging make this animated feature a bit deeper than most. If Strange World can find its audience, those viewers will be pleased. Why? Because even the trees are cool!
Despite the film's rich CGI, it’s only when the humans and their conflicts, big and small, come to the forefront, that the film comes to life.

The director Don Hall and his co-director and screenwriter Qui Nguyen seem to have put all of their effort into gaudy backgrounds, wacky gadgets and strange ancillary monsters instead of into dramatic urgency or conflict.
So much of Strange World’s audaciousness is front-loaded into its concept, and so little of it comes through in the execution.
Why isn’t this an out-and-out recommendation? It nearly merits that, but the tangled environmental allegory winds up being a royal headache.
Hall and Nguyen deliver these messages with the subtlety of a wrecking ball, but the excellent voice-over work plus the score by Henry Jackman make the preachiness palatable and the film fun.

It’s Disney riffing in ways that are reminiscent of The Emperor’s New Groove and Lilo & Stich, making this Journey to the Center of the Earth-style adventure a visually imaginative treat the whole family is certain to enjoy.
Strange World breezes through a checklist of formulaic plot points and canned emotional revelations with enough style and sensitivity to make it work.
A rewarding continuation of the studio's recent narrative fascination with overcoming divides rather than evil.
Strange World has the makings of a fun, pulpy adventure story, and it is, but much of the plot is bogged down in strange, unfunny dialogue and a needlessly complicated storyline.

Energies have been focused on the visuals, and they make the experience worthwhile. That, and an appealing collection of human characters that look a lot more like the real world than usually seen in these films.
The visual beauty of the film isn’t enough. After all, pretty is as pretty does — and in “Strange World,” pretty doesn’t do much.
There's a lot of plot in "Strange World," which takes too long to get moving as a result. But the good news is that the characters are lively enough to keep us interested.
Strange World feels like a new iteration of Disney, one that is more thoughtful and inclusive without sacrificing any of the humor or fun.
It’s no Encanto, but the family-friendly fun fest offers plenty of ingenious visuals and upbeat messaging.

The takeaway is the difficulty of collaboration in the face of entrenched beliefs and ways of navigating the world that, ultimately, must be questioned — if not entirely dismantled — if any one of us expects to stick around.
A sweet, science-fiction family film with a loud environmentalist message that’s good fun.
The uneasy marriage of clunky psychodrama and overwrought special effects along with the fact that none of these characters are particularly likable make “Strange World” a chore to sit through.

Kids will love its primary-coloured wonderland that teems with weird and wonderful beasts, and only the stoniest-hearted grown-up won’t be moved by its inclusive celebration of family across generations.

title: Bad Axe | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a family story – of a time, a place, an event, a community – in all its rich and quiet nuance, with all the members, related by blood or by affection, given their space.
A stirring tribute to strong family ties and triumphing over adversity.
“Bad Axe” comes out the most organic, showing not telling about this family of immigrants and their bonds to get through the toughest times.

...a curious, compassionate portrait of a country, community, and family in flux. And as socio-politically topical as it is, what lingers are the emotionally introspective ways the family members change during this volatile time.
A penetrating assessment of American society at the time of the pandemic.
Even if Siev wants “Bad Axe” to emerge as an ode to his family’s strength, the film feels more like a home video exercise.
It is not just among the finest and most important films of the year, but it will stand as a valuable historical and social document of these times.

Captures the wildly disparate facets of small-town Michigan life, from Nazis and rampant gun ownership, the lack of recycling and cheap restaurant food, to the miraculous skies and beautiful greens, the local camaraderie and budding pockets of diversity.
The most essential film yet made about this era is David Siev’s moving and triumphant Bad Axe.

If you’ve made any missteps when it comes to how you changed your life... you’ll be able to see a lot of the messy artistic truth in Bad Axe — and it’s even easier to find emotional resonance in this family saga.

title: Raymond & Ray | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Raymond & Ray does have its moments, but it seems obsessed with trying to be different when it’s basically just warming up leftovers.

The third act is clunky and disappointing, as both men coincidentally encounter women who have been crudely shoehorned into the narrative solely to smooth our boys’ furrowed brows and, well, to cure them.
... It never rings true, a portrait of grief afraid to confront itself in any real way.

Garcia, the son of novelist Gabriel García Márquez, has made some good movies – “Nine Lives” (2005), “Albert Nobbs” (2011), the HBO series “In Treatment” – and some misfires, but this is the first time it feels like he’s running on autopilot.
A vamping, oddly inert dramedy that never for a moment transcends its paper-doll characters and forced quirkiness.
Garcia holds back too much, perhaps trying to avoid any phony epiphanies. As a result, his two main characters are too preoccupied with re-litigating old grudges to do or say anything notable.
Ewan McGregor and Ethan Hawke are outstanding in "Raymond & Ray," a movie that gives them the chance to focus on developing their characters rather than serving the whims of a plot.
Ewan McGregor and Ethan Hawke show great rapport.
“Raymond & Ray” is a restless seeker of a movie. There are far too few of those, which should make us all the more grateful to have this one.
For the most part, Raymond And Ray reaffirms the filmmaker’s command of gentle, emotionally complex human portraiture.
A funeral-as-exorcism movie, as inert as the image of the detested parent, sprawled naked in his coffin — a man so carelessly cruel he gave both brothers the same name.
A silly, pointless movie which never delivers on its promises of drama and comedy and contains not a single funny or believable moment.
Rodrigo García’s film is fastidious, tidy, and lifeless, with every obligatory gesture in its place.
An exercise in melancholic quirkiness that increasingly trades honest feeling for trite situations.
It gets really silly and mawkish.
Ewan McGregor and Ethan Hawke, both 51, make for an odd pair of estranged half-brothers sleepwalking through life.
In the end, Raymond & Ray doesn’t really get to know anyone, merely pushing them toward the inevitable finish line.
Despite some mild humor and A-list talent, Rodrigo García's ham-fisted story of grief and family feels too listless and inauthentic to matter.
The screenplay starts out strong, but then it becomes a slog. It’s impossible to discern which scene, if any, García has designated to be the climax, because the plot remains flat throughout.
A winning delve into contemporary masculinity and all its quirks that is as tenderly observed as it is laugh-out-loud funny.

title: Dear Zoe | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Too much of “Dear Zoe,” though, feels factory-designed to engineer emotion rather than aiming to earn it organically.

title: Savage Salvation | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Let there be no confusion: this is an unarguably bad film.

title: Sissy | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Barlow and Kane Senes, the film’s co-writers and co-directors, slip easily between satiric humour and gory ramifications. They get the genre’s conventions, but with Dee’s committed performance leading the way, they refuse to simply accept them.
It’s far from perfect, but it has a fresh tone and the desire to take risks.
Impressively unpredictable all the way to the bitter end – a very difficult and commendable achievement, in a genre as coded and conventionalised as horror.
Cecilia [Aisha Dee] achieves, within three minutes, one of the strongest and most depressing openings to a movie I’ve seen in a minute.
Sure to be a runaway hit for the social media crazy TikTok generation

A clever twist on the morality tales about the dangers of bullying, Sissy has a twisted sense of grisly humor, unleashing some impressively brutal practical effects as its protagonist becomes truly triggered.
There’s a lot going for Sissy. The cast is pretty great, led by Dee. She’s in nearly every scene and boy, the camera loves her.

Sissy is a fun and gutsy romp in the playground of horror, employing the genres codes and conventions to construct a hard-to-forget snapshot of the frequently volatile terrain of contemporary feminine identity.

title: The Inspection | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The Inspection succeeds in the end because this powerful real-life character study is firmly rooted in reality.
It’s Ellis’s story and [Jeremy Pope] keeps you on his side all the way with a performance so direct, intuitive -- and restrained -- that you feel as if he’s letting you in on his every thought.
Fiercely candid, in its condemnation of the brutality that is enmeshed in the training programme, and in its celebration of the bonds and brotherhood that grow between fellow cadets.
The ending is a tad contrived (it gets a bit O Captain! My Captain!), and Gabrielle Union seems slightly one-dimensional as French’s cruel and bigoted mother. But there is much to appreciate here.
The Inspection may be by the book, but the layers of personal detail and emotionally resonant core lend it an authenticity that hits home and hits hard.
Some brilliant performances, but mixed messages cloud the overall impression.
"The Inspection" does feel unfocused at times, or like it's playing the Greatest Hits of other movies that came before it. It's not until Union's character returns that the film comes full circle...
Observant, insistent and unsparing, wrapped around characters that feel real and rounded.
It is the type of film — brave, raw and poetic — that will rightly put Bratton on the map as someone to watch, not to mention the standout performances of Jeremy Pope and Gabrielle Union.
With The Inspection, Bratton has continued working with the humanist lens through which he shaped his captivating 2019 documentary Pier Kids.
A stunning look at a gay man’s terrifying, triumphant time at Marines boot camp.
Bratton’s unique perspective is so much more interesting when you hear him talk about “The Inspection” that you often wonder where it is when you’re watching it.
A powerful, poignant, and complicated look at what people will do for acceptance.
Elegance Bratton’s autobiographical story The Inspection is one of learning to accept love on one’s own terms.
Jeremy Pope gives a searing performance as the young man lacking direction, with Gabrielle Union a powerful force as the mother who initially disowns him.
Bratton brings a surreal, rubbed-raw realness to “The Inspection” — reflected in the performances, the film’s gritty look and unconventional style.
Where most films that recount military training ultimately lead to the battlefield, this one is preparation for a different sort of combat.
A well-meaning, sometimes moving, but at times exasperating movie.

Bratton, who has an eye for compelling framing and unexpected beauty, has made something more complicated than a treatise against the power structures enshrined in the military, though he’s very aware of them.

To be successful in confronting, understanding and dismantling the institutional homophobia that continues to be a cancer in American life requires depth, perspective, and a sense of inquiry—three qualities in short supply in The Inspection.

title: The Mean One | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: For a film with such a promising premise, it turns out to be a plodding example of how to squander potential.
A parody only by legal definition, The Mean One has no teeth as a naughty comedy or gory horror.

The Mean One has a handful of inspired lines, e.g., “Time to roast this beast!” but the production values, editing, score and photography are average at best, and we’re left with a film that will be remembered mostly for a cleverly twisted marketing hook.

Parodies are theoretically supposed to be funny... it’s almost as if there was an explicit directive not to crack any jokes, let alone exhibit any pleasure, in a film that deliberately skirts copyright infringement to bring a sadistic Grinch to theaters.

title: Nocebo | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a worthwhile, twisty little thriller with some genuinely smart ideas within.

An act of supernatural vengeance and a whoppingly crude metaphor for the western fashion industry’s shameful history of exploiting southeast Asian labour markets. If you insist on a message, it should be buried deeper than this.
I was once again impressed by Finnegan, and I suspect not for the last time.
Actress Eva Green is always a good indicator you’re in for something stylishly weird.

Finnegan and Shanley have artificially hefted more guilt onto poor Christine’s shoulders... Still, the use of deep-focus Persona-style shots of two faces aligned in uncomfortable proximity is striking, as are the eerie creaks and cracks

Director Lorcan Finnegan, working with a script by Garret Shanley, creates some unsettling moments and there are sharp prickles of commentary about our attitude to fast fashion and the workers who make our clothes.
A dreadful psychological/supernatural horror pic about a fashion designer who can’t get her mind around a recent trauma.
Even in a movie haunted by death, you need more signs of life.
Finnegan juggles the script’s disparate elements with some aplomb, making for a sleek whole that’s entertaining if not particularly depthed or plausible.

What would have made a great Tales From the Crypt episode becomes overlong even at 96 minutes—Lost-style flashbacks add depth but not revelation, as they merely make graphic what was already implicit.

title: Aqua Teen Forever: Plantasm | Rotten Tomatoes
Aisha (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Wright and O'Connor's arguably best work yet...

Writer-director Frank Berry’s film never devolves into melodrama – if anything, it may be understated to a fault – but he grounds her plight in an authentic mixture of daily frustrations and sporadic joys.
“Aisha” resists tidy answers through the gentle force of its performances and by staying on the rebuffs and uncertainty Aisha suffers.
Tom Comerford’s framing makes a coastal bus stop look like the loneliest place in the world. And Berry’s script – as with his star – is quietly seething.
Wright’s portrait of everyday heroism is stunning. It won’t earn her a Best Actress Oscar (films this low-budget don’t get noticed by the Academy). But that doesn’t make her work any less impressive.
Black Panther star Letitia Wright shows she’s not all about blockbusters with this small, moving story of a Nigerian woman seeking asylum.
It’s an absorbing drama given sympathy and life by two very high-calibre performers.
The scenes between the two leads are gripping and crackle with chemistry. The wider drama, and the incessant castigation of social inequality, sometimes feels slightly stilted.
This sobering ode to the immigrant experience will leave audiences unsettled and hopefully reflective.
A thoughtful and intelligent film, and it finds a gifted actor doing some very tricky things quite well.
It’s not an unfamiliar story, but Frank Berry’s delicate drama is immensely moving.
Eschews histrionics in favor of a docudrama-like approach that’s all the more affecting for how authentic it feels. The result isn’t quite Kafka, but it’s closer than it should be.
Beautifully observed and acted.

title: Halloween Ends | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: While Halloween Ends does provide something close to the catharsis that long-time fans of the franchise may be seeking, it does it in a manner that still feels a tiny bit lacking.
Some of it is gory; the opening is good. None of it is scary. Worse, none of it has any tension whatsoever.
“Halloween Ends” is a bummer. And everything about it makes it seem like it’s willing to go. We should let it.
Halloween Ends is notable mainly for its cockamamie plot and its reverence for the original.

“Disappointing, given the most recent films have had a grounding in a very modern context…. There’s nothing more disappointing than a sequel that’s just there for the sake of it, and that’s what this is for me.”
They say this is “Halloween Ends.” I say: Can we get that in writing?
