How the story resolves itself is one of the more inspired and thoughtful narrative gambits in recent memory, landing on a hard-won emotional maturity.
There's a low-key charm to the movie's knowing spin on familiar beats.
Brie is, as always, enormously appealing.
It’s a wasted opportunity. Brie is clearly a gifted comic actress who deserves better material than this.
A well-meaning dramedy with a great cast and admirable ambitions — but which never quite finds a good groove.
Not terrible, but nothing to wrote home about. Kiersey Clemons is the real revelation here.
A distinctly empowered subversion on My Best Friend’s Wedding and fellow rom-coms that came before it.
It’s a kitchen-sink approach. Not everything works. Especially perplexing is a half-baked subplot involving one set of parents, and this is where the story lost me.
Franco and Brie give Ally time to wrestle with these questions and herself, and to be imperfect. That's more than most romantic comedies allow their characters.
“Somebody I Used to Know” comes dangerously close to being interesting.

The romantic comedy genre’s broad, patented hijinks and hilarity are indeed on display, but cleverly cloaked by a beautifully-realized portrait of delicately faceted characters and their relatable conundrums.
A gratifyingly fresh spin on an old formula.
“Somebody I Used to Know” never fully finds its footing as a romantic comedy. It plays more like an unfinished script, one in which the kinks haven’t been worked out yet.
The film lacks the indelible details and authentic feeling necessary to encode it in long-term memory. Indeed, soon after finishing the movie, it already feels far away.
This is an odd combination of broad semi-satirical humour and deeply serious hugging and learning.
What could have been rote and predictable love triangle turns into a character-driven romance about loving yourself and not compromising who you are with anyone around you.

title: In My Mother's Skin | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This film’s unwavering depiction of children suffering will no doubt come across as excessive to some, but it’s what makes “In My Mother’s Skin” so beguiling and terrifying.
It’s miserable stuff, and not in an entertaining way.
Gory, glittery and irresistibly bleak, In My Mother’s Skin represents a stylish, ripe contribution to the folk-horror canon.
Well-executed, unusual and historically-tinged...
“In My Mother’s Skin” finds a rare sweet spot between story-book nightmare and historical allegory.

title: Money Shot: The Pornhub Story | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s titillation with a side of radicalization.
A thoughtful look at a controversy unlikely to fade away, so long as modern technology and prurient interests continue to exist.
A powerful and well-made documentary...
A pornucopia of issues handled with care by director Suzanne Hillinger.

Here is a documentary that casts a clear eye on the offenses of an industry driven by capitalism while never losing sight of the workers whose safety and success should be that profession’s number one priority.
It was the least exciting but the most important truth to come out of Money Shot: until there’s legislation and the threat of sentencing for executives, no one gives a toss.
If you like searing documentaries, you’ll love “Money Shot.”
From a divisive, combustible subject, [Suzanne] Hillinger manages to rise to the challenge of retaining journalistic distance and steering clear of both moralising prudishness and prurience.
As “Money Shot” persuasively argues, pornography may be a hot-button topic, but the closer you look at it the more you realize that nothing about it is simple.
A superficial exposé afraid of getting dirty.
The film interviews – and is on the side of – the models and the performers as creative entrepreneurs and heroes of consenting sensuality. Fine. But so what?

title: Marlowe (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s a deluxe nostalgia trip guided by a director who really knows his way around the genre.
Jordan does a competent job, but this is not a patch on his best films...
It lurches along, scene by perfunctory scene, with the narrative fluency of treacle.
There’s a little bit of fun and interest along the way and Lange has some fun with her eccentric persona, but this feels under-energised.
The story is laden with red herrings and punched-up dialogue, but little manages no land.
In his 100th movie, Liam Neeson is spot on as the flatfoot, just when it seemed like the Irish star’s career had devolved into one violent revenge fantasy after the next.
Ironies build, narrow escapes accelerate, and familiar fisticuffs multiply, to little avail, in William Monaghan’s yawning screenplay.
Thanks to the high-end production values, the juicy script and the vigorous performances from that first-rate cast, it’s great to see another iteration of Marlowe on the case.
Marlowe is no classic from the case files. It lacks the intricacy of Chandler's best mysteries, that sense of being helplessly pulled into a labyrinth of compounding revelations.
“Marlowe,” enveloped with a strong smell of mothballs, feels like an old pinstripe suit that’s been taken out of the closet for no apparent reason.
Marlowe is the cinematic equivalent of a word salad: It parrots all the right lines while striking all the right poses, without saying much of anything at all.
Liam Neeson's particular set of skills can't rescue this noir misfire.
Revisionist this may be, but it’s done with smarts and ... perceptiveness and sensitivity.
While the star adequately acquits himself, Neil Jordan’s throwback noir is a cover song that knows all the notes but can’t capture its predecessor’s spirit.
The cast is large and the costume and set designers have been kept busy with period details, but “Marlowe” neither dutifully copies nor cleverly updates detective-movie tropes.
Merely cosplays a 1930s detective movie, taking us from two-fisted private dick to icy rich client to corruption among the powerful as though we hadn’t seen all of this countless times before.
A detective movie so pulpy that it will make you choke.
Sticking to film noir traditions to a fault (minus the black & white), Marlowe feels mostly like cinematic karaoke.
With the exception of Jessica Lange, who tears into her fairly brief role as a wealthy and wicked former movie star, everyone in “Marlowe” is directed as if to seem groggy with depression.
Neil Jordan’s Marlowe is an homage so riddled with noir clichés that one may initially take it for a genre parody, except that the jokes never arrive.

title: Supercell | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The thriller-y bits are duly exciting, and there’s something almost endearing about a film that makes no attempt to find comedy or supernatural elements or airborne sharks within these dangerous-enough natural conditions.
Between the genuinely awe-inspiring storm effects and Corey Wallace’s rousing, old-fashioned score, “Supercell” feels like a cheaper but in some ways more heartfelt version of a ‘90s blockbuster.

title: The Old Way | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's just so bland and cheap-looking.
Two elements make the picture worth watching: one is Nicolas Cage, wearily brutal as Colton Briggs, a man who has already completed a lifetime’s worth of killing. The other is Ryan Kiera Armstrong...
Though Cage and Armstrong’s father-daughter dynamic merits praise, The Old Way tries so hard to emulate Westerns past that it squanders a gilt-edged opportunity to do something new.

At times you may find yourself wondering if The Old Way’s script, by Carl W Lucas, was adjusted to accommodate Cage’s availability: there’s too much of the four bandits and not quite enough of him, and the narrative balance feels off.
Ultimately, this is a movie with real personality, about a man coming to realize with no small amazement that he has an actual legacy to pass on — even if it’s a grim one.
Cage sleepwalks dead-eyed through this paycheque western, playing reformed gunslinger and now family man Colton Briggs...
Consider it a bump in the road of Cage’s long-overdue return-to-the-mainstream resurgence.
Hackily written but reasonably watchable thanks to Cage and Armstrong’s screen chemistry.
When it comes to re-writing the rules of Hollywood Westerns, they don’t exactly break new ground, but they do prove the old ways still work best.
The Old Way sputters to a conclusion we saw coming a mile down the road.
Donowho’s competent but uncompelling oater doesn’t have enough fresh meat on its bones to fill out its Western cosplay.
Perhaps if more Westerns were being made these days, The Old Way—which is more of a half-baked mistake than a total disaster—might have been a little palatable or at least easier to forgive.
The Old Way is a cold, uncompromising Western that tracks down suspense and tension by moseying down a conventional narrative trail.
The Old Way is at first glimpse merely a classic revenger, but it's also vintage low-key Cage, with that acid little twist that makes it all the more fascinating.
It’s a distinctly low-effort affair across the board, from the simplistic plotting (our heroes chase the bad guys, then find them) to Cage’s performance...

title: There's Something Wrong with the Children | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There’s something wrong with the children, all right. The filmmakers can’t figure out what to do with them.
Director Roxanne Benjamin never allows Children to overstay its welcome, resulting in a scare package worth seeking out.

There’s Something Wrong with the Children punches above its weight by doing all the little things right. T.J. Cimfel and David White’s script is built like a Swiss watch, setting up countless twists without ever wasting a line.

Benjamin infuses her latest with throwback stylings and a sense of humor that keeps the story zipping along. While it isn’t a complete reinvention of the subgenre, it offers enough fresh ideas to set this one apart from the pack.
There's not much wrong with this film on paper—there's just something wrong with the execution.

title: A Little White Lie (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I kept thinking to myself "This is a stupid movie -- but it got me."
The film's biggest con doesn't come from [its] imposter protagonist so much as the messy script and direction.

When we talk about small, finely crafted, dialogue-driven gems with interesting characters and little or no CGI, it’s easy to say, “They don’t make ’em like that anymore,” but the good news is that’s not really accurate.
Director Maren doesn’t trust Shannon to convey this inner monologue via his performance — just one example of the film’s plodding lack of wit or sophistication.
Hobbled by a lack of visual oomph or verbal sparkle, “A Little White Lie” pokes feebly at impostor syndrome and writerly insecurity.
Maren’s direction is tonally right, full of warmth and touches of humor; he makes it an inviting film to watch.
Not even the considerable comic chops of Shannon and Kate Hudson are enough to save this literary world comedy.

title: A Lot of Nothing | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There’s an earnest, yearning passion here that makes the film feel vital even at its clumsiest.
A Lot of Nothing presents a script simmering with buzzwords but ultimately no thesis.

McRae certainly shows promise as a director, if not a writer, with Noel, Coleman, Anderson, and Scott demonstrating they can handle complex portrayals well. It’s just unfortunate the story doesn’t live up to all their talents.
More of a trauma drama than a satirical thriller, it never lets up on the buttons it’s pushing or the characters it’s manipulating.
The opening scene is a phenomenal short film of its own, but McRae sadly can't quite get back there again.
McRae leaves the audience with a clear sense that nothing is as simple as it seems or we'd like it to be.
While it doesn’t end on a satisfying note, this is nonetheless an excitingly combustible piece that announces a vibrant talent unafraid to confront thorny issues head-on.
Even if the onyx-dark humor and sardonic formal control go MIA eventually, “A Lot of Nothing” is really quite something.

The points the film sets out to raise — about activism, police brutality and the function of race in society —  ultimately, and unfortunately, get lost in the twists and turns of James and Vanessa’s hair-raising story.

title: You People (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's so funny. I don't know if it'll change race relations, but it'll make you laugh.
Now, there are enough thoughtful screen examinations of racial politics along with normalized visions of inclusive casting to make "You People" stand out as a gormless throwback.
The film is much more interested in social embarrassment cringe and gags than it is in any sort of close examination of how racism affects interracial couples.
Here's a recipe for success: great actors, including Eddie Murphy and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, plus an affecting story and lots of droll, awkward comedy.

The one person to emerge with credit from the melee is Murphy, whose character grows ever more rigid with anger. Supporting actors as forceful as Rhea Perlman and Elliott Gould barely get a chance to speak.
The movie is much better when it relaxes its death grip on screenwriter-y punchlines and slapstick cringe and just allows its cavalcade of stars to act like actual, you know, people.
You People carries the unresolved, disjointed tension of a sitcom that’s been stretched to the two-hour mark.
The first third of the picture is promising, if frequently excruciating. But the points are painfully laboured and the jokes run out of steam.
A movie that so rarely rings true it starts to make your skin crawl.
In a movie where Jonah Hill and Kenya Barris process white privilege and affection for Black culture, the Black characters are treated with less generosity.
Without Murphy’s deadpan, steely reactions to the latest affront, You People would be all strain and little gain.
“You People” is so tame in its take on race that it makes “Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner” look like Spike Lee’s “BlacKkKlansman.”
For all its insistence that it’s a daring piece of social commentary, You People is, above all, a romance without a beating heart.
The film can’t figure out if it wants to be a love story or social commentary, and ends up doing neither very well.
A topnotch cast can’t fully redeem material that gets lost somewhere between satire and sitcom as assembled by star Jonah Hill and director Kenya Barris.

Most scenes stick to the same formula – awkward situation arises, characters verbally fumble their way through it – but Hill and Barris’s script seems unsure of just how wacky or eccentric it’s allowed to be...

Kenya Barris disastrously trades cutting social satire for romcom pablum when a Jewish podcaster (Jonah Hill) and his Black fiancé  (Lauren London) break up after her dad (Eddie Mirphy) and his mom (Julia Louis-Dreyfus) turn a wedding into a race war.
Funny, if a little formulaic. Murphy and Hill make for a very watchable duo.
Murphy playing it straight is one of his funniest performances, and the movie is not afraid to include some sharp commentary along with the sillier moments.
... A Guess Who's Coming to Dinner-style rehash which pits the two parties against each other but puts straitjackets on them both.

title: Appendage | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Appendage is first and foremost a lot of fun, and Zlokovic clearly delights in employing older horror movies as a palette through which she can tell her own story of the nightmare many women face as they struggle to live up to impossible expectations
A comically freaky look at the inner voices we must learn to live with.

while this feature debut is certainly body horror, it is also a psychological allegory, dramatising Hannah’s therapeutic path to both emotional balance and accommodation of her worst qualities alongside the best.
Despite the grotesque premise, its attack is a little too blunt to make much impact, whether taken as thinly-veiled satire or straight fantasy thriller.

title: House Party | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Clearly this is no masterpiece, but as its US reception indicated, it is a product overdue in the market, and it compares well with its anaemic counterparts.
All of the performances are good and the soundtrack pulses with humor as well as decibels.
This is the only House Party that counts.
An aged piece of ghetto-lore that has become less black-counterpart to Heathers and Dazed and Confused than pristine example of serendipity in film.

[It's] fast-moving, never dull, extremely funny, and manages to touch, with lighthearted (and R-rated) profundity on almost every youthful issue you can imagine, including police harassment, teenage sex, the all-too-easy road to jail and alcohol drinking.

There's a lot more energy and social reality in this picture than one is accustomed to finding in teen exploitation movies; the cutting is often dynamic, and Hudlin generally does a good job of keeping things moving.
House Party isn't a great movie, but it's heartfelt and enormously winning.
House Party is silly and high-spirited and not particularly significant, and that is just as it should be.

title: Brother (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Not entirely original, but does what it does very well indeed.
Virgo does a great job of confounding our expectations of macho masculinity, finding tenderness, protectiveness and even neediness beneath the street-tough exterior.

There are fine performances on display and Johnson especially is perfectly nervy as Michael. But the storytelling here could have easily squeezed into a short film or, even better, a slickly shot music video.
Not a lot is spelt out here, a strategy both brave and frustrating. But the cast has the chops to fill in some of the blanks with strong performances...
An example of strengths outnumbering flaws.
The thing I love about this film is the empty spaces where no one's talking.
I loved it... This is definitely a movie to check out.
Beautifully shot and anchored by two phenomenal performances by Johnson and Pierre, Brother does in the end tell a familiar story, but does so with poignancy and passion.
No feeling in “Brother” goes unfelt; every element of its filmmaking taps into the heart.

Even if writer-director Clement Virgo... can’t achieve the sustained aura of ineffable melancholy he’s striving for, the film still hits some lovely notes of grace and poignance that rise above the script’s manipulative nature.

The ultimately sparse dramatic elements here feel more suited to a short film; in a feature-length production, they become too thin to support the big feelings and weighty themes the movie wants to leave us with.
The spirit of what Scarborough represents – for Chariandy, and for Clement – is undoubtedly present in every lovingly composed frame of Brother.
The story is filtered through a familiar gaze that speaks to folks of specific communities while also broadcasting a universal message of what it means to be an outsider.
Ensembles don't get better than this. Brother is a delicately crafted, all-consuming piece that offers the opportunity to not just watch but wholly feel its characters' experiences.
A world is revealed, brilliantly.

The lives of two brothers, taking in timelines which span several decades and a devastating death, are threaded together in this supremely confident and affecting drama from Canadian director Clement Virgo.
There’s such gracefulness to the filmmaking here, cutting back and forth across time, building like a thriller.
Virgo’s “Brother” leaves you spellbound and grateful. Grateful for a filmmaker who cares deeply about the interior lives of Black people. And the light that shines within them.

title: Consecration | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Sure, it’s purest hokum, but real pride has gone into crafting it.

When the threat the characters are facing remains so vague for so long, it robs the story of tension. It doesn’t help that Smith keeps the horror elements to a minimum, or that the picture is so drably colored and dimly lit.
Through it all... “Consecration” grows increasingly murky and blood-drenched and contrived.
Jena Malone brings a biting charm to her portrayal of Grace, but the story’s straightforward revelations end up feeling far too muted for the holy surroundings.
Another retread of “spooky” Catholic-themed horror tropes without adding any insight or originality to the subgenre.
Consecration won’t be for everyone and finds itself at the more reflective end of the Catholic horror film spectrum, but for those who like a slow burn this is a captivating watch.
The plot... can’t quite find its momentum; it doesn’t help that most of the film’s scares fall flat on a visual and technical level.
The meager surprises it does contain aren’t particularly effective, considering that early clues suggest only one possible twist and the proceedings do little to mask it.

Consecration can’t muster up effective scares and is prone to repetitive tactics. Still, its enigmatic story, bloody finish, and scathing critiques of the Church make for a fascinating journey all the same.
Consecration ends up not just gimmicky but derivative of Christopher Smith’s own prior work.

title: Superpower | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is not a film about Zelensky; it’s a film about Penn’s feelings about Zelensky.
The movie's co-director, narrator, and onscreen guide, Sean Penn, can't decide what kind of movie he wants to make.
An undeniably intense and intriguing documentary that sheds as much light on Penn’s passion as on tenacity Zelenskyy.

Superpower may not alter that course or the downward trajectory of Ukraine's polling numbers with the public, but it might not have to. Penn has proven he has a way of getting in front of the people he needs to hear from or to be heard.
A powerful chronicle of Ukrainian courage and resistance, in a way that reflects Penn’s passion as opposed to journalistic detachment.

This film offers little in the way of Ukraine insight. Instead it serves as a queasy-making examination of the celebrity-blighted news cycle where somebody like Penn is the de-facto messenger of tragedy.
Penn appears to have one eye in the mirror, but at least he’s taking some sort of action.
“Superpower,” one of several documentaries about the war in Ukraine, doesn’t break any news, but Penn, a two-time Oscar-winning actor and director of several feature films, is a skilled storyteller.
Given how much informative, sober coverage the war has so far generated, it’s hard to imagine that viewers will really benefit from this frenetically-paced, awkwardly narcissistic piece.
Too often, the film’s well-meaning reportage is muddled with needless vanity sequences of the actor-director as an on-the-ground trailblazer...

It would be easy to write the whole thing off as one big and slightly dangerous vanity project, but let’s be honest: This war concerns all of us, and the actor is doing all he can to help the good guys.

title: Clock (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Agron throws herself fully into the role and the first 45 minutes of Jacknow’s disturbing commentary works wonders, but it strays and winds up losing its punch near its end.
Clock leans too heavily on too-obvious visual metaphors, but it’s still a vivid and visceral explication of one woman’s fears.
“Clock” is a psychological thriller, or perhaps even a satire, in horror clothing, tantalizing us with thought-provoking ideas, only to abandon them...
Writer-director Alexis Jacknow amps up the anxiety by blending science and religion into paranoia-soaked mayhem, conjuring resonant emotion and haunting menace in this psychological horror film.

Ms. Agron gives a highly intelligent performance -- at no time do we doubt Ella’s awareness of how badly things might go, and while we do have questions about her judgment, the pressures she’s under are made palpable.
Despite its fascinating intersection of societal pressures and personal guilt, Clock struggles in its horror approach.

title: Malum | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [DiBlasi] doesn’t have much sense of how to parse this hackneyed occult screed into sequences with any true tension...
"Malum" is [most] impressive when it turns its talented ensemble cast loose on material that was obviously a lot of fun to play with.

Malum has enough budget to be too glossy to be gutter fun, and adds little visually much beyond some very mediocre practical effects, often feeling that – yet again – its ambitions outstripped its grasp.

title: The Young Wife | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A movie about what we ask of young people when these take these large steps towards their future, and to respect how hard it's going to be -- and it does that will a lot of style.
Warm hearts and cooling feet is nothing new for movies, of course, but Kiersey Clemons’ portrayal of Celestina -- her head spinning -- raises the stakes of love and liberty.

These are familiar, even hackneyed themes, which make the film’s relentless theatrics feel gratuitous and somewhat exhausting. Style overpowers substance, though Poe’s fantastic eye for composition and Clemons’s vivacious screen presence are undeniable.

Watching “The Young Wife” is an immersive, often overwhelming experience, a whirlwind of well-meaning but stressful characters mobbing the camera and speaking at such an anxiety-inducing speed that you forget to breathe for a second.
The Young Wife can be a chaotic experience, but Poe has the skills to carry us through the noise and toward the future.

title: The Strays | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The execution of ideas here can be bumpy: sometimes you’d like more back-story, other scenes meander. But moments of social satire also land with real oomph. And Madekwe is terrific...
Despite messy plotting and occasional ill focus, fantastic lead performances help The Strays find its way before a knockout ending really carries Martello-White’s eye-catching debut home.
For all her co-stars’ gifts, the movie really belongs to Ms. Madekwe, upon whose eloquently expressive face Mr. Martello-White relies to carry much of his film.
The Strays sets up an intriguing examination of race, privilege and the difficulty of social mobility for Black Britons but... ultimately bails.

a provocative allegory of black experience in white Britain, as characters get caught in an evolving conflict between estrangement and assimilation, individualism and inauthenticity, pride and self-loathing.

title: Maybe I Do | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Gere is the movie’s saving grace and somehow makes it all seem worth it.
Diane Keaton, Richard Gere, Susan Sarandon and William H. Macy each get a star-turn at pretentious blather in this talky mediocrity.

While it's swell that these actors are getting roles and heartening that "Maybe I Do" acknowledges that older people remain sexual beings, all four leads have been in better projects that made that same point.
Despite one ongoing affair, one possible affair, and one relationship on the brink of marriage, each coupling is as chaste and sexless as an after-school special.
Despite the formidable star wattage and estimable talents on display... Maybe I Do fails to overcome its obvious stage origins, feeling all too schematic and talky.
Diane Keaton, Richard Gere, Susan Sarandon and William H. Macy  make the movie a lot funnier, and a great deal more compelling, than it might have otherwise been.
The ostensible comedic bits in which the oldsters duck each other soon give way to musty monologues on marriage — material that even the seasoned cast is unable to freshen up.
A film with barely any rom, and not enough com.

The older couples’ sparks have faded, perhaps because none of these people were characters to begin with. Macy, Sarandon, Keaton and Gere are operating with one adjective apiece and hitting that adjective until we’re exhausted by them.

title: The Siege | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The Siege attempts to update the bluffs and counterfeints of the Cold War spy thriller, not to advance any ideological point but to obscure the fact that it doesn't have one.
It's difficult to sustain a responsible subtext when you're delivering the jolts required to keep butts in the seats.

Even at its most unbelievable, The Siege has the performances of Washington and Bening to fall back on, and a theme that understands that what's difficult is not choosing right from wrong but 'choosing the wrong that's more right.'
The Siege is clumsily put together. Zwick is careless about plot details, so the movie is often needlessly confusing.
Just about distinguishable from several dozen predecessors in the same apocalyptic vein.
The Siege may well be based on a huge 'what if?' premise, but it's smart, taut and knows exactly what the hell it's doing. And it does it well.
The script is too muddled to be remedied by vigorous filmmaking.
[Benning] is the only fresh, compelling character in the film.
Could someone please turn down Denzel Washington's Righteousness Meter? It's set too high.
Typical summer popcorn fare.
Washington and Ms. Bening play smart, interesting characters who never quite connect, while Willis turns himself into the loosest military cannon this side of Dr. Strangelove.
The prejudicial attitudes embodied in the film are insidious, like the anti-Semitism that infected fiction and journalism in the 1930s--not just in Germany, but in Britain and America.

title: Chantilly Bridge | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [The cast is] better at evoking the kinds of in-jokes and easy laughter of old friends than conveying the intimacy of genuine connection.

title: Like Water for Chocolate | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Laura Esquivel's wonderful novel about the powers of passion has been adapted for the screen by her husband, director Alfonso Arau. The result is as rich and savory as Mexican hot chocolate.
It tells a dark, sad, horrific but heartening story in sweet, gleaming images that tickle ribs, quicken senses and awaken hungers. There's just one word for it: Scrumptious.
Deliciously offbeat and bittersweet, it is, entirely appropriately, a treat.
Like Water For Chocolate is an extravagant, playful romantic fable that celebrates passion, liberation and the spirit of women but never forgets that unbridled ecstasy comes at a cost.
Strong material has been wasted by inept filmmaking in Like Water for Chocolate.
Whether you approach this swift, eventful tale on the culinary or the cinematic level, prepare for a treat.
It's a privilege to partake of such a feast.
In the end, "Like Water for Chocolate" is an overwrought potboiler that punishes Tita for her sexual freedom.
It's the best movie to establish the spiritual link between food and the human condition since "Babette's Feast" or "Tampopo."
Like Water for Chocolate creates its own intense world of passion and romance, and adds a little comedy and a lot of quail, garlic, honey, chiles, mole, cilantro, rose petals and corn meal.

title: Assassin (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s sad to see Bruce Willis in his final film, lacking his trademark twinkle...
The multinational cast seems assembled for reasons other than serving defined character needs. None of them are able to rise above the vague material.

title: Atonement | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It is an elegant and sophisticated film, one that never condescends or shirks from the complexity of the novel and its grand themes - war, love, sex, memory, betrayal, redemption - but it's also strangely unfeeling.
Atonement is a film out of balance, nimble enough in its first half but oddly scattered and ungainly once it leaves the grounds of the Tallis estate.
[U]ltimately, the movie amounts to rolling lawns, lovely costumes, and characters that simply fail to resonate.
Sweeping, showy, and stiff, Joe Wright's adaptation of Ian McEwan's pedigreed bestseller traffics in florid staging and callow emotions.
Atonement's extraordinary qualities outweigh any quibbles.
Somehow the intensity of McEwan's voice hasn't survived and once we move beyond the magic of that lost summer's day, the film becomes a strangely cool and cerebral experience.
This is a film that might have contained itself better, but it still stings with bitter truth.
Imagination typically should be encouraged in children, but an excess of it leads to tragedy in this more than worthy adaptation of Ian McEwan's 2002 novel.

In its first 45 minutes, Atonement achieves a kind of perfection rare even for big Oscar-bait movies. Every facet of the filmmaking is the equal of any picture released this year. The rest of the movie isn't so bad.
Atonement is perfect.
Atonement has hints of greatness but I think it falls just short of Oscar contention.
A lushly shot, proficiently performed, and largely stultifying period piece that invites only mild, detached admiration.
It ranks with the best novel adaptations of recent times.
As good a film as one could imagine having been made from a great work of contemporary fiction.
Atonement is not only too polite but maddeningly orderly, resulting in a prettily cast, professionally performed, impeccably mounted bore.
On paper and on screen, Atonement is a story of rare beauty, both wrenching and wise.
Atonement takes a familiar movie environment, a setting that we think we know, and uses it for an examination of a host of dark impulses, such as jealousy, lust, cruelty and deceit.

Director Joe Wright and screenwriter Christopher Hampton not only blow the Merchant-Ivory dust off the British period movie, they transform Ian McEwan's interior novel into a sweeping epic that speaks to the 21st-century soul.
It is an amazing story, filled with quiet moments of profundity and more surprises than you could imagine.
Christopher Hampton's screenplay respects the literary focus of Ian McEwan's novel without falling into the trap of becoming uncinematic.

title: Acidman | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This film is what would remain if you deleted all the spaceships from “Close Encounters of the Third Kind”: the tale of a once ordinary man beset by an unworldly thirst that he can neither explain nor quench.
Though not without its flaws, this resonant, resourceful indie drama leaves a gentle imprint on audiences’ souls.
In this all too straight-forward drama, Church, an actor perfectly ripened for this role, gives one of the best performances of his career.

title: Baby Ruby | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: You can look at it as a dark comedy, a thriller, a horror movie, or as a psychological study. It gets to a lot of truth about how confused you feel when you're a new mom.
[Baby Ruby] operates at a high-pitched melodrama-horror level, and the constant frenzy becomes exhausting.
Disorienting, tense, funny and scary.
Noémie Merlant and Kit Harington's Instagram-perfect life unravels once their bundle of joy arrives in this tense, thoughtful, slightly unfulfilled debut feature from playwright Bess Wohl.
Retro visual flair, such as repeat cuts and mirror effects, add some aesthetic interest to Jo’s spiraling. But “Baby Ruby” hardly whimpers, let alone screams.
Baby Ruby makes a valuable contribution to the emerging cinematic literature on the unspoken realities of women’s lived experience — with style, disarming honesty, and a steady and intelligent hand.

Baby Ruby is a fervently uncomfortable and aesthetically compelling depiction of new motherhood, an unsettling horror exploration buoyed by strange imagery and a no-holds-barred lead performance from Noémie Merlant.
Baby Ruby employs a shaky narrative to deliver a rattling good commentary about every parent’s nightmare
Whether you’re angered or tickled, it makes for a mesmerizing film.
The film’s depiction of the fear and uncertainty of motherhood gives in to monotony.
This movie is exhausting in the best way possible.

Writer/Director Bess Wohl’s debut feature uses psychological horror to put viewers in the shoes of a new mother unraveling after giving birth. It’s a fascinating means to open up conversations on postpartum psychosis.
“Baby Ruby” is an audacious and riveting portrait of maternal life that’ll leave you wailing into the night.
New motherhood can be a very dark place indeed, both figuratively and, and in this case literally – the film’s lighting scheme goes beyond moodily murky and ends up being frustratingly indistinct.

title: Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: In spite of a first half that suggests greatness, Across the Spider-Verse lets itself down with a televisual cliffhanger of an ending.
It’s smart stuff, leaps and bounds beyond Marvel’s snarky hegemony...
Tempts you to think Spider-Man was always meant to be animated.
Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse boldly throws out any restraint and leans full-tilt into the zaniness of its visually and thematically kaleidoscopic world.
Animated Spider-Man sequel is worth the price of admission in this four-star movie.
Extraordinary animation and muscular transformations make the continuing Spidey saga(s) of Brooklyn teen Miles Morales and his family, friends and foes even more of a marvel.

It might be hyperbole to say that this state-of-the art animation is about as genius as it gets for the genre. But for kids, teens and twentysomethings, raised on MTV, comic books and TikTok, that isn’t an overstatement. It’s their truth.
It's really impressive how this movie has its cake while eating it, too.
As thrillingly rendered and technically innovative as it may be, the current Spider-iteration is little more than a gorgeously ornate two-hour-and-twenty-minute comma in a run-on Spider-sentence.
It takes the basic themes of the first film – adolescent isolation, communication breakdown, the messy, stressful business of growing, of finding your people – and builds whole worlds with them.
It’s hard to follow up such a success, but Across the Spider-Verse (the second of a planned trilogy) takes the action and the story to the next level and may just be a superior film.
...what once seemed brain-bendingly original now seems over-familiar...
Across the Spider-Verse avoids seeming like a physics lesson because its visuals are consistently thrilling; the most static bits of dialogue still pop because of how daring the animation is.

Plays with literally every possible form of animation to create a stunning spectacle that also still manages to tell a smart, character-driven story about fate, friendship, and the cost of being a hero.
This latest addition to the Spider-Verse canon reminds us why we love superhero narratives — not just for the action but for their humanity.
Full of the joy of discovery and the emotional generosity that is the soul of Into the Spider-Verse. It’s inventive, thrilling, funny, ridiculous, heartwarming, frenetic, and sad.
Into the Spider-Verse showed us that the myths and heroes we’ve created are important but mutable - they have to be. The sequel inventively and thrillingly continues that evolution.
I knew we’d get a sequel eventually, but I didn’t expect them to suck most of the joy out of it.

Across the Spider-Verse looks incredible, even better than the groundbreaking first installment, but what’s truly impressive about it is how willing it is to entrust its storytelling to its animation.
This new animation classic, the first in a two-part sequel, is out to make history. Consider it done. In a word—wow! You’ve never seen anything like it in your life.

title: Black Clover: Sword of the Wizard King | Rotten Tomatoes
The Kingdom | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [I]t fails in its attempt to be a serious drama with important things to say about the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.
The Kingdom works as an exotic action thriller, but its politics are so choked on checks and balances it cancels itself out.
When it's got the pedal to the metal, which is a substantial fraction of the running time, The Kingdom delivers the goods.
Sensationally directed by Peter Berg.
http://www.thisislondon.co.uk/film/film-23339226-details/The+Kingdom/filmReview.do?reviewId=23414945

If this mix doesn't entirely work, it's perhaps because there are so few surprises - the forensic elements of the investigation would be wrapped up in minutes by CSI's boffins. Still, it's possible to respect the effort while doubting the achievement.
Intelligent films about US involvement in the Middle East can be counted on the broken fingers of one hand, and this one makes Syriana look like Citizen Kane.
Rambo meets Syriana in this bloated action-thriller, which tries to be gung-ho and PC at the same time.
Macho lunacy.
A cut above the bullish jingoism that would have characterised a film of this ilk at the beginning of this decade.
In twenty years this will look as subtle as an episode of "Love Thy Neighbour".
A terrifically stupid film. Dumb, dumb, dumb.
Not quite as smart as it wants to be, and a better action movie than it is a political thriller, this is still a heart-pounding drama.
Everything moves so much and so fast that the movie seems both gutsy and brainy. But the main strategy is to keep viewers' pulses racing so they concentrate on the action, not the message.
Simplistic in the extreme and riddled with clichés, the quality of its execution can't excuse the dubiousness of its premise.
One could say [director Peter Berg] shoots first and asks questions later, if at all.
See this movie, but take a motion sickness pill first.
Every moment in The Kingdom is shrouded with the threat of violence, until it finally explodes in a last reel that's one of the most heart-pounding action scenes in years.
The Kingdom comes down to a police procedural, and one whose procedures prove none too interesting.

It attempts to say something profound about the war on terrorism and the human tendency toward an us-vs.-them mentality. But the finale feeds on a sense of bloodlust and then tries to pull back to show us the error of maniacal revenge.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Vol. 3 keeps much of the goofy humor of previous Guardians installments and melds it with a wonderfully bizarro and often deeply tragic narrative...
If the first two Guardians of the Galaxy films were pure lighthearted fun, the final story gives some punchiness and gravitas to balance that story out.

Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 manages to be more than honest-to-god entertainment, one that has the liberated weirdness of material (like a stealth We3 adaptation) that was never expected to find a mass audiences.

Remarkably, given the studio brand: this is absolutely Gunn's movie. It's cheerfully gross, frequently hideous to behold, nakedly emotional, indulgent to the point of bloat in its desire to tie off every narrative thread...and, happily, its own thing.
While better than most recent Marvel or DC films, it definitely lacks the fun, buddy-film aspects and sincere relationships of the original in lieu of an exhausting mission-based story.
Completes Rocket’ transformation from a footnote to one of Marvel’ greatest characters.
Too often it feels like James Gunn made a playlist of songs he likes and then came up with scenes to go with them.
Guardians 3 is a real warm and fuzzy movie that sometimes makes you forget that you’re a bit bored with the onslaught of superhero movies.
Be forewarned, it’s a slog for the first 90 minutes of its 2h 30m length. Then real energy kicks in.
The fact that Gunn himself, as writer and director, has an unusual degree of authority, and thereby seems to be largely constraining himself, renders the narrow results all the more oppressive.
A picture that balances a slightly overstuffed storyline with mischief, humour and the biggest of hearts.
A funny, big-hearted adventure.

When the Guardians get into a big group hug at the end of the film, it’s supposed to evoke love and solidarity. But it might better be characterized as the unity of capital, determined to offend no one and turn no one’s dollars away.
For "Guardian" junkies and kids of all stripes, this two-hour reunion with old character friends will have them singing Peaches & Herb’s 1978 soul classic “Reunited” -- and it feels so good.
Flirts with being interesting but I checked out after the 90 minute mark with nearly an hour to go.
As a final chapter for this trilogy, Vol. 3 works. But of the three films, it’s the weakest.
It trashes the camaraderie of its core ensemble in favor of one deafening, vicious flourish after another.
Mercifully, Gunn gives us a Phase whatever Marvel movie that is self-contained - more GCU than MCU.

For all its backsliding into bleak—stop torturing Bradley Cooper's talking raccoon—this spirited summer kickoff delivers the requisite thrill ride and ends the GOTG trilogy with the sweet sorrow of saying goodbye to these space dorks. It’s been a trip.
Overall, “Vol. 3” does everything a final film should — if it really is a final film, that is.

title: Nimona | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I think it's the third act's a little weak, but I enjoyed it very much and has got a lot to say.
Its message is powerful but subtle, and I like the animation style a lot.
Just as Stevenson somehow magicked Netflix into green-lighting She-Ra and the Princesses of Power's unmatched all-ages queer storytelling, he bamboozled them with Nimona too. This baby is gay.
It's awesome.
Nimona seems to proceed from the assumption that focusing on diverse protagonists relieves the movie of the need to train its creative energies on any other area.

Nimona significantly revamps Stevenson’s original story and swaps his sparer aesthetic for something more frenetic in style and conventional in its look. But at the film’s heart remains a relationship that’s radical and sad.
What could have been a generic piece of standard Netflix fare in less skillful hands ends up being a nuanced story of belonging that’s slightly less cliche-ridden than you might expect.
Nimona is imaginative and boisterous, just like its main character.
Bites off more than it can chew and doesn’t really hold together, but it has a whole lot of fun as it makes a mess of things.
A sometimes cute but mostly hyper and overextended animated sci-fi fantasy.
The tone is uneasy teetering on anarchic, veering from giddily moronic one-liners to — more shockingly — a climax with deep empathy and visual awe.
Nimona tells its story tenderly, poignantly and offers up a parable on learning not to fear those who are different from you and demolish the pious barriers that separate us.
... Seems so enamoured with its allegorical power that it neglects dramatic coherence.
A sequel, please.
I can’t think of a better time than Pride month for this beautiful LGBT story to be released and enjoyed by a wider audience of all ages.

This may not push the envelope much further than recent animated forays into more blatant depictions of same sex relationships, but it’s another tiny step in the right direction which is always helped when the movie is good, too.
Nimona is likable and engaging entertainment that finds its way through self-created chaos to some humane life-lessons.
That it’s so entertaining and unapologetic at this moment in history adds another component to the film’s kaleidoscope of qualities.
Both enthusiastically irreverent and deeply sincere, Nimona is a revisionist fairytale that forges its own path visually and narratively to beautiful effect. Insert celebratory shark-dance here.
A film that manages to put a distinctive spin on themes that are, it has to be said, very familiar.

title: Culpa Mia | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There's something wrong with this YA drama flick, and the myriad storylines aren't one of them.
This soapy story has plenty of attention-getting elements -- a forbidden relationship, high society young people, illegal fights, car racing, gambling, and gangs.
If this is your kind of teen rom-com, it's not my fault.
The lack of deep psychological character development and bland dialogue contribute to a completely unsatisfying movie experience. [Full review in Spanish]
The characters are insipid and rudimentary, crudely carved from the granite of countless hoary cliches.

While González ramps up a significant amount of heat here, the frequent tone shifts, lack of focus, and cheesy, Velveeta-like dialogue are too much for the likable young leads to overcome in such an overblown, soapy picture.
Unfortunately, the toxic romance between bad boy Nick (played by Gabriel Guevara) and his new step-sister Noah (Nicole Wallace) doesn’t quite work in translation.

title: Shooting Stars (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: With James’ Springhill Company behind the movie, we only see the sweet friendships, the glory of victory, and of course, James’ iconic celebrity. Too bad a lay-up of a biography isn’t interesting at all.

Every moment and image is so perfectly shaped and presented, and rings so true, that you can imagine the same story being told, beat-for-beat, with a cast of invented characters and being every bit as satisfying.
Unfortunately, LeBron James is the least interesting part of this LeBron James origin story... But this is a nice, inspiring film.
Basically “It takes a village to raise an all-star,” it’s a familiar B-level sports story about the strains of success buoyed only slightly by its talented young cast.
This adaptation of Lebron James’s and Buzz Bissinger’s 2009 book would have done better as a six-to-eight-hour limited series. There’s a compelling story here, but this version isn’t it.
Shooting Stars is an entertaining docudrama that rarely digs beneath the surface but serves as a bright and inspirational reminder of a time when basketball was the glue forging a bond.
It’s stubbornly undramatic.
It is an inspiring story, no surprise, told with a great deal of warmth.
Mostly hits its shots.
For what it sets out to do, detailing the bond of young boys under surreal circumstances, “Shooting Stars” is a relatively sturdy retelling.

title: Guy Ritchie's The Covenant | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Gyllenhaal is good as the intense American sergeant...

[Gyllenhaal 's] energy is perfect for the relatively sober-minded The Covenant — and allows space for Dar Salim to shine, in a more substantial lead than the majority of his Hollywood roles have afforded him so far.
Though the movie is fictional, the uncertain fate of thousands of real Afghan interpreters after the hurried 2021 US withdrawal gives it genuine heft.
This feels like a breath of fresh air [for Guy Ritchie]. He is really reinvigorated by paring it down.
This gripping look at war gets under your skin.
Swinging back to a more serious register, Ritchie presents his first film grounded in harsh real-world politics, and it’s the best film he’s made in years.
Jake Gyllenhaal stars in skillfully made and gripping film...

For much of its running time, director Ritchie’s war movie manages to be topical, suspenseful, and moving. But partly because the story is fiction, Ritchie takes a few genre liberties that threaten to undermine the sincerity of his tale.
The Covenant does merit bonus points for showcasing Salim, a terrific journeyman actor who finally has a meaty role in an American movie.
A muscular, overwrought war film.

A sober military thriller that excoriates Joe Biden’s decision to pull out of Afghanistan in 2021 and, in the process, to strand the thousands of local interpreters who had risked their lives to aid the American cause.
How does it honor these brave and essential people to make a movie that isn’t about any of them but rather a near-superhuman fictional character?

It’s good to see Ritchie branch out — just like after “Snatch” and “The Man From U.N.C.L.E.,” he made us all do a double-take with “Aladdin.” Not everything works in “The Covenant,” but he’s not lost in the desert, either.
For all its clichés, this furious and discomfiting film tugs on your conscience for days, making a powerful case to turn the American public’s attention back to a conflict it would rather forget.
The Covenant works best when the two leads are forced to be silent lest they tip off prowling combatants.
An oftentimes riveting war film which marks a new path for the 54-year-old filmmaker.

Gyllenhaal, who’s looking more and more like a trimmer Javier Bardem, uses that handsome-hangdog face of his to good effect. Salim, an Iraqi-born Danish actor, is very good. If he weren’t, the movie simply wouldn’t work.
Instead of layering on jump cuts, crazy camera angles and jokey subtitles like he usually does, he keeps things calm. Ritchie lets the action unfold swiftly and clearly.
The result is one of Ritchie’s finest films that’s made all the better by two extraordinary performances.

Director Guy Ritchie exercises considerable restraint in his depiction of action: again and again, he is content to pull back, hold the shot, and let what happens be enough to engage the viewer. And again and again, it's more than enough.

title: Eye of the Storm (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
The Super Mario Bros. Movie | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Without overplaying its hand, it hits all the major notes within the wild, inventive universe of block-breaking and Goomba-stomping.

This lively computer-animated take on the video game just opened and it’s already the biggest box-office smash of 2023. Despite lapses into dull and disposable, it’s also a godsend for parents seeking family entertainment for the 5-year-old in all of us.

Among the many errors of The Super Mario Bros. Movie, screenwriter Matthew Fogel plops him and his brother Luigi into a milquetoast Brooklyn family that doubts them and disrespects their small-business dreams.
It is the laziest possible version of a Mario movie, and for most viewers, young and old, that’ll be totally acceptable.
The whole package is a deranged mishmash of overstimulating elements.
A frantic Easter egg hunt of a film that does the bare minimum to please its loyal existing fanbase.
The film belts along with an assault of candy colours and a commendable command of canonical detail.
What it seems to have forgotten is creating an engaging story. It's bland, uninteresting and cobbled together.
While The Super Mario Bros. Movie’s ambitions don’t stretch far beyond telling a competent story featuring these beloved characters… it at least succeeds at that.
It’s emotionally bland and yet garish enough to psychologically sedate the pre-teen Easter audience.
Kids may have the time of their lives watching The Super Mario Bros. Movie, but for most adults, this is game over.

The 8-bit world is faithfully reimagined for the modern under-10. Much of this will be slightly dull for anyone else. But it can also feel refreshing when a studio children’s movie is this squarely made for actual children...
It’s all dispiritingly rote, aside from bursts of weird vitality whenever the film veers into action out of the games.
In terms of servicing fans who want more of their "Super Mario Bros." than they can get at home or in an arcade, the movie gets the job done.
This isn’t a movie; it’s a checklist of fan expectations.

For all its detailed worlds, like the Mushroom Kingdom and Jungle Kingdom, the Nintendo film is just another soulless ploy to sell us merchandise that doesn’t bother to disguise its creativity-starved greed.
The new film is so colourful, sweet and playful, while ultimately insubstantial, going to it is like being handed a bowl of Froot Loops cereal to munch on instead of a bag of popcorn.
Justice for Bob Hoskins.

While the details are meticulous, the attitude is all wrong, trading the simple, unaffected charm that has served the character so well since his introduction... for a snarky and fatuous air that leans hard on winking humor and bland, hackneyed irony.
The artistry is enough to keep children and adults watching... At its 8-bit heart, The Super Mario Bros. Movie is ultimately about family.

title: Elemental (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s almost as though the contours of what made Pixar great have been copied out here in vague watercolour.
Gentle and humane but never raw or vulnerable.

There are tonal parallels with Pixar’s Inside Out and Zootropolis, but while it has a peppy visual energy, Elemental lacks the wildly inventive storytelling of the former and the laughs of the latter.
A bit like Inside Out meets Zootropolis – but not as fully worked out as either – it’s a movie of lovely, radiant moments.
Busy, zany and sincere, the movie does a perfectly good job with the stuff of urban culture clash. But it is also fatally unfunny, and gets more so with every weird contrivance it whips up.
The problem is that there’s not enough storytelling muscle here for the allusion to really land.
Surely a reality where the elements are in charge should be more inventive, not limited by the trappings of capitalism and gender norms?
Elemental is overstuffed and inconsistent — but packed with enough moving sentiment, gorgeous design and punchy voice performances to mean it still burns bright.
A movie that encourages kids to be open-minded needed to be laid on our culturally divided doorsteps. Peter Sohn should take a bow.
The details of it are really beautiful.
Especially coming from a studio that used to be so terrifyingly fastidious about its world-building, the internal logic of Element City is wobbly at best.
As slight as it is, I found Elemental to be adorable.
Disney’s latest venture Elemental will make your heart melt, even if it’s not Pixar’s best.
A certain sweet, unworldly idealism in Elemental survives, the keynote of optimism – and this is the flame that Pixar has to keep alive.

It’s a muddle, frankly, and the beauty of the animation can’t wholly compensate, especially given the mostly witless dialogue and the fact the traditional Pixar ease with plot construction seems to have evaporated.
Elemental's story of earth, wind, fire and water isn’t top-tier Pixar, but its screen-popping visuals carry the day.

The animation is good without being spectacular. It’s fun to see fire, water, earth and air in human form. The flashback where Wade relives his childhood trauma with a sponge will make young and old laugh out loud.

Elemental, despite being a tableau rich with marvelous imagery of a world populated by the four elements (fire, water, earth and air), relies on the simplest of storytelling hooks: getting the audience engrossed in a sweet romance.
I was taken by the imaginative ways the animation explores societal inequities.
The crafty cartoon wondrously animates disparate elements and shapes them into relatable characters.

title: Unidentified Objects | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [Matthew] Jeffers and [Sarah] Hay have a strong chemistry, and they make Peter and Winona's vivacity and pain feel equally real, even when the movie around them is shading toward the phony.
Leland Frankel’s screenplay, the two lead performances and the compassionate direction from first-timer Zuleta make it a celestial wonder worth discovering.
Director Juan Felpe Zuleta and scriptwriter Leland Frankel haven't bothered to provide a plot, the film depends on what the pair of misfits see and do on the road to fill out the running time.

title: Extraction 2 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Occasionally, the dizzying filmmaking style, a mix of practical stunt work and invisible VFX, feels like a video-game cutscene. More often, it just sucks the air from your lungs.
With its bigger, broader swath of carnage, Extraction 2 improves upon the original and isn’t unpleasant (you know, unless you’re bothered by watching hundreds of deaths on screen).
A nutty movie that's just like the first. If you love the way that first movie was constructed, then it's a knockdown bang fest.
What counts in an action film is the action, and former stuntman-turned-director Sam Hargrave more than delivers on that promise.
It’s better than having a tooth pulled. But not by much.
The rare action sequel that works just as well as the original.
The second Extraction is more grandiose, full of pace and action, and dull as a box of rocks. It follows all the bad rules of sequels -- bigger, louder, dumber.
It's a lot for an anti-hero to handle, but our bruised and battered and bloodied hunk is more than up to the task.
The script, by the famous Joe Russo, is full of lines such as “copy that” and “reload”. It looks like the filmmakers thought a high body count is all an action movie needs. It isn’t.
The sequel, Extraction 2, hammers away at the same basic outline, while feeling particularly simple minded even by the standards of the genre.
All Hemsworth is asked to do is stare off into space. As a result, there’s an emotional void where the movie’s heart should be.

You might appreciate the series' attempts to anchor military-adjacent shoot-'em-up adventures in something like reality, and give all of its major characters situations to play that are a step above the standard action film tropes.
As per sequel rules, everything has to be bigger. But bigger doesn’t always equal better, as “Extraction 2″ proves.
Hemsworth has landed on his Bourne, and this is his Supremacy.
Now comes the sequel, which is even heavier on action mechanics and even thinner on character, as if that was even possible.
By the end it’s hard to care. But that oner? Wow!
Less an original movie than an assemblage of ideas pulled from other movies.
These sequences are nonetheless truly impressive; you watch in amazement as the complicated fight choreography, involving dozens of stunt men and hundreds of gunshots and explosions, goes on and on.
Feeling inessential and disposable, a cog in a machine rather than something unique, Extraction 2 is a snapshot of a sequel in this moment, bigger, expanded and even less necessary.

Even seasoned pros and cinephiles will gape and wonder how they pulled off any number of the shots and sequences here... This may not be a particularly good film, but you’ll definitely see things here in a way that you’ve never seen them before.

title: Air (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Affleck’s diamond-studded comedic timing and commitment to telling a compelling story well give it oomph.
Air is a quick-paced entertainer with glib dialogue, humour and a wonderful sense of nostalgia for the 1980s.
Once you’ve made peace with those really narrow parameters, what you see on screen – ie virtually nothing of Jordan himself – kind of works.
There’s not an ounce of fat on this film’s physique, and Affleck keeps the pace moving even though everything that’s happening is entirely driven by the dialogue.

Affleck is a fine actor and a better-than-fine director. As an actor since childhood, his skill at selecting the right actors and allowing them to do their best is to be expected. He also has an exceptional sense of narrative structure.
Affleck, the cast, crew and script put you in a time capsule and take you back to the ’80s.

Nostalgia is the only reason I can think of to explain why old friends Ben Affleck and Matt Damon reteamed for a movie that so artlessly sets out to make us love shoe company Nike for buttering up a college hoops star better than Adidas or Converse.
While much of Affleck's casting choices in Air err on the side of superb, one pivotal choice is repeatedly jarring: He doesn't cast Michael Jordan.
The script is pacy, the tone is consistent, and Affleck’s deft direction commands a raft of skilful performances from an ensemble who rarely puts a foot wrong.
For all its affable charm, there’s something slippery and disingenuous about this film.
"Air" is effortlessly entertaining, but it wants to be about more than just the marketing triumph of an underdog shoe company.
The film certainly invites fists to be pumped in celebration. It is less certain Air offers any meaningful critique of the society that gave us the sacred gutty.
Affleck’s return to the director’s chair is an exceptional success, stimulated by its script and cast.

The decision to deny Jordan a character presence... conspicuously muzzles a pivotal character and it’s clumsily out of step with a movie that is otherwise the definition of carefully considered, precisely told, error-free film-making.

As much as we can talk about the thematic resonance of Air, its impact is dependent on your personal connection to Michael Jordan. It’s like going to church as an atheist — you might be able to follow the story, but its meaning is lost.

Air mainly takes place in drab offices, yet the cast’s expert performances transform those spaces much in the same way that Michael Jordan transformed courts and sneaker racks -- by turning them into sites of magic.
It’s a feel-good fable for a culture that doesn’t know how not to win, and it’s going to be huge.
The film wants to be a wing-ding entertainment, but it also strives to say Something Important. The first half of that equation is what makes the movie eminently worth watching.
Air is great. Pitch-perfect, deeply entertaining.

The boldest thing I can say about Air is that it follows the tried-and-true underdog sports movie formula, only none of its main characters even attempt a shot much less sink the game-winner at the buzzer.

title: Hunger (2008) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: McQueen seems too enamored of his shorthand art-house symbolism for [the film] to truly resonate.
There is very little context, because on the inside, prison has no context. There is just horror. And maybe, sometimes, in the least expected places, beauty.

The stylistic palette of McQueen's picture, and its grasp of cinematic vocabulary, elevate the film to a purely visceral realm, so that it seems to bypass your eyes and ears and go straight for your nerve endings.
Steve McQueen's Hunger is a daring, brutal, vital piece of filmmaking.

Midway through the movie there's an epic 24-minute scene...in the claustrophobic cell block the protesters have already internalized their cause so deeply that the world of words seems distant and inconsequential.
It's a strength of this carefully composed, almost obsessively controlled picture that it has no interest in the conventional biographical focus on a subject.
Hunger is daunting and powerful work.

Hunger is not about the rights and wrongs of the British in Northern Ireland, but about inhumane prison conditions, the steeled determination of IRA members like Bobby Sands, and a rock and a hard place.

The film is stunning. Bare, minimalist, stark and based in a hardened reality that's as hypnotic as it is horrific, this is as gut-wrenching an exercise into documentary-like historical fiction as any I'm ever likely to see.
Hunger -- the disturbing, provocative, brilliant feature debut from British director Steve McQueen -- does for modern film what Caravaggio did to Renaissance painting.
Relying on images more than words, it's a plea for humanity in times of insanity.
Hunger is an upsetting, vivid film about going to the ultimate extreme in defense of one's beliefs.
It's horrific. But Hunger displays uncommon intelligence and visual panache, transcending the goal of making the situation seem real. It feels more than real. It's art.
McQueen has taken the raw materials of filmmaking and committed an act of great art.
In the end, it is not Bobby Sands but Michael Fassbender we are looking at, and this realization takes us out of the movie just as surely as (for me) De Niro's fattening up did in Raging Bull.
A visually ravishing tour of hell and a meditation on freedom that at best is wordlessly profound and at worst interestingly obscure.
In the end, even though I recognized the need to be reminded of Guantánamo and of crimes carried out there, I was awed but not moved by Hunger.
It's rigorous, evocative, and, in spite of its grisly imagery, elegant. It's a triumph -- of masochistic literal-mindedness.
A mesmerizing 96 minutes of cinema, one of the truly extraordinary filmmaking debuts of recent years.
Regardless of politics, one must grant McQueen's substantial gifts, which bring to mind Paul Greengrass in another Northern Ireland film, Bloody Sunday.

title: Transformers: Rise of the Beasts | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Transformers: Rise of the Beasts is bland.

If you can get on its wavelength as a film at odds with itself, Rise of the Beasts is an enjoyable summer blockbuster that plays the narrative hits, good guys and bad guys in a race for a MacGuffin, and supplies the requisite action sequence.
Certainly delivers on needless destruction and world-class stupidity.
It’s not spectacular enough to impress us, nor intimate enough to move us. It’s just kind of there — ready to be consumed and forgotten.
There’s not a morsel of joy to be found in the franchise’s latest ludicrous outing.
Even with its abundance of action, the franchise’s newest addition boasts little life or heart compared with its predecessors.

Beasts encourages you to let your eyes glaze over through the plot exposition and embrace the visceral nonsense. Beasts is dumber than a box of hammers, but it doesn’t drip with the rote cynicism of, say, Fast X.
Dominique Fishback totally outclasses her infantile dialogue...
The movie doesn’t have much going for it.
Transformers: Rise of the Beasts is arguably the best film with the word “Transformers” in the title and frees the series from its robotic shell, but that’s not saying a heck of a lot.
In terms of personality, the Transformers still only come in two varieties: annoying and [404 error: character traits not found].
This hunk-of-junk piece of IP commodification truly can’t be regarded with any further value other than that: a transactional piece of content.
Programmed to follow the loud, clunky formula...

Wait a hot minute here. Can a new Transformers movie actually be bearable? Let’s not get carried away, but a diverse cast and the absence of ham-handed former director Michael Bay qualify as a step in the right direction.
It pains me to say that Ramos and Fishback are let down continuously by a truly preposterous premise that seems to prioritise mindless destruction over any kind of plausible plotline.
A predictable return to rock-em-sock-em stupidity with nothing to add except Michelle Yeoh as a talking aluminum falcon.
It’s the safe and simplistic course correction that—neutered of the very absurdist immensity that was this franchise’s calling card, if not its sole reason for existing—lands with a crashing thud.
Rise of the Beasts lacks the disarming wit that somewhat elevated Bumblebee, and the attempt to turn Davidson’s character, Mirage, into plucky comic relief mostly comes up flat.
Quake, ye mortals, before the Toys R Us Cinematic Universe: accessories sold separately; batteries, entertainment and point not included.
At least there’s solace in the premise, however slapdash its execution. The very existence of a technorganic ape is evidence that computer-generated blockbusters know they still need a beating heart.

title: Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Lana Condor voices a shy teenager whose love of the ocean takes her on an endearing journey in this family-friendly parable about finding the bravery to be different.
The color experience, on the most primal, visual aesthetic level, will be fun for little kids and fine for their parents.
Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken turns into something bigger and better than your average kids’ pic.
A likable film that can’t decide if it’s a Turning Red-style menstrual metaphor, a generational conflict story, a Nickelodeon teen diary sitcom, or Harry Potter except with creatures of the deep.
Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken,” blends teenage angst with a fun and vibrant take on sea-creature lore that subverts fairy-tale expectations.
Beautifully designed and voiced, this has a solid message at its heart. But it’s a well-told tale that suffers from being too well-trodden already.

Despite game efforts by directors Kirk DeMicco and Faryn Pearl to imbue Ruby Gillman with some visual flair during the various underwater sequences, it’s an upstream swim to try to distinguish a fairly by-the-numbers story.

The look of Ruby Gillman has a TV-cartoon cheapness, but its frames are cluttered with all manner of objects and elements of odd design, almost as if the filmmakers hope we won’t notice how basic and uninspired everything looks.

Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken charms and woos in a predictable manner. This isn’t to say the film is bad, but its slower moments might have your mind wandering to other, more evocative versions of its familiar tale.
Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken was not made for me. At least, not the “me” of today. If I were seven or eight years old, I’m sure this colorfully obnoxious adventure would have thrilled me senseless.
It's derivative of Turning Red but a lot more fun and witty than expected.
One of the best family films of the year, "Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken" has humor and heart, buoyant energy, witty and imaginative visuals, and never-less-than brilliant voice talent.
Turning Red has been repurposed here as a charmless tale about yet another teenage girl who is secretly a monster...

Plays like the result of feeding the screenplays of recent Pixar titles Luca and Turning Red into Chat GPT and then animating the results. Unfortunately, this new coming-of-age tale doesn’t come anywhere near the depth or delight of its predecessors.

Enjoyable as it may be, Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken never quite rises above its straightforward title and one-note sounding premise—which the film still spends an inordinate amount of time setting up and explaining.
Not even the matriarchal link at the story’s center feels satisfying, its good intention strangled by the plotty chaos.
Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken fails to see its own potential -- it’s never quite sharp enough to work as a parody, nor sincere enough to make its adolescent insecurities relatable.

Kids are always in need of gracious tales about the power of being yourself in a world not necessarily built to embrace differences and stories like “Ruby Gillman, Teenage Kraken” can do that, with fun to spare. But why not get more splashy?
DreamWorks' house animation style is nice, with fun character designs and lots of elastic movement, but nothing ever pops.
Sweet but narratively thin and didactic, the latest from DreamWorks Animation always seems as if it’s trying to find its footing.

title: Praise This | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film reads like a faux-hip youth pastor in movie form, only instead of an acoustic guitar, it’s an 808 drum machine luring the kids toward God.

Adds a mostly delightful entry to the musical genre, even if it doesn’t offer a unique take. More successfully it acts as a winning introductory calling card to the acting and musical talents of its rising star, Chloe Bailey.

title: It Ain't Over | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: With the help of a slew of adoring talking heads, It Ain’t Over director Sean Mullin effortlessly validates his subject’s legendary career through the film's zeal to restore him to his proper place.
Berra’s ground-level appeal keeps the documentary from getting too full of itself.
He might have become more famous off the baseball field than on it, but there’s no denying that he was a great player, and “It Ain’t Over” provides an excellent reminder.
The film is a spin through baseball history, but also an examination of how media-molded personas can overtake genuine accomplishments.
The result is a home run in a field often flush with loud fouls.
A comprehensive encapsulation of an American icon known more for his ubiquitous turns of phrase... than for his exploits on the diamond.
I’m convinced. I’ll happily agree with what Billy Crystal says in the film, that Berra is “the most overlooked superstar in the history of baseball.”
"It Ain't Over" works the way it's supposed to work.

[It Ain't Over] has two purposes and succeeds delightfully at both. One is to make some sense of the famously self-nullifying sayings... The film’s other purpose is to re-establish Berra’s standing in baseball history.
Filled with game footage, home movies and knowledgeable talking heads, It Ain't Over ensures Berra’s exalted status in the annals of America’s pastime
It Ain’t Over offers a winning coda to the career assessment of the late, great Yogi Berra.
A lively, engaging and moving documentary...
[An] affectionate documentary.
More emotional than you'd expect from a doc about a hard-hitting catcher.
Yogi Berra lived the kind of life we wish our heroes to have: filled with love, respect, and integrity. This is a film fans can embrace and younger generations can learn from. I loved it.

title: The Fox (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Yes, it says all the right things about love and humanity and the folly of war. My problem is that it doesn’t say any of those things in ways that are particularly interesting or ultimately moving.
“The Fox” is not only a touching story about this poignant relationship between a human and an animal, but also a primer in how to forgive those who we feel have trespassed against us.

title: Fast X | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: While Fast X still delivers on propulsive stunts and fan service, as the 10th instalment and with the promise (or is that a threat?) of at least two more, it’s starting to run out of road.
The best thing about this movie is Jason Momoa. He just said "You know what, guys? I'm going to pull the top off this one and let it rip."

Fast X continues the franchise’s mission to scale bigger and campier heights, and there are moments that will have you full-volume hooting and hollering in your seat, but it’s undone by the gravest sin of this cinematic universe: it breaks up the family.
It's been a long time on the road but Jason Momoa's maniac villain gives the franchise a jolt.
It’s overlong and over-the-top, but the real trouble is that when a series like this starts acknowledging its its own absurdities, they become harder to enjoy.
If action/adventure fans are willing to throw logic out the window, they’ll like what they see.

Leterrier's achievement in assembling such a gargantuan, multi-stranded, globe-trotting, head-spinning blockbuster is impressive, but however many gruff sermons Dom makes about his family, it's impossible to care about any of it.

This is what summer movies should be! It's spectacular! It's thrilling! And it's the kind of movie you can't wait to yammer about to your friends. Truly, I walked out of Fast X with a big Momoa smile on my face, so wide it hurt.
The franchise hasn’t quite yet run out of ways to combine cars, guns, planes, and explosions… but perhaps it’s good that there are maybe only two films left until the franchise officially “ends.”
It would be OK if Fast X were merely loud and dumb; that much is to be expected. The problem is that it’s also achingly mechanical. It’s all car, no driver.
A decent diversion, though watching it feels like sustaining a head injury.
Fast X is the most absurd entry yet in the long-running franchise, and that’s saying something, considering the crew journeyed into outer space in the previous installment.

Only glints of the old whiplash magic remain in chapter 10 as thrills give way to thudding formula and paycheck acting—not you Jason Momoa—that slow down the action to forge the runt of the F&F litter.
“Fast X” is watchable, and its car chases are often exciting, but it’s not as satisfying as the best F&F movies.
[Momoa] seems to have modeled his bright, sing-songy delivery on Bill Murray's brilliant work in "Little Shop of Horrors," and darned if he isn't almost as funny.
Creatively speaking, the fuel gauge is pointing to E and the engines are sputtering.

Diesel no longer seems quite human enough to be vulnerable, with his bald dome polished to an ageless sheen and his life-coach mottos delivered in a gruff near-whisper. Still, there are moments that show that despite everything he remains an actor.
Momoa was drawn to the role because it let him tone down his masculinity. But the latest instalment in the Fast & Furious franchise is a let-down.
