This jolt-happy July programmer might be as dull and rusty as a nail in the coffin could possibly get without breaking apart, but Insidious newcomers should rest assured that they’ll be able to follow along with their friends’ exasperation.
Whether or not you’ll want to push this door open may depend on how much of a completist you are. For many, leaving it shut may be just fine.
'Insidious: The Red Door' isn't the absolute worst way to spend 107 minutes. I'm sure it is more fun than working in a uranium mine.
The leaden screenplay would be easier to overlook if there were more spooky sequences.
Callbacks to other “Insidious” films are half-hearted, and “The Red Door” seems to give up on trying to make all of the pieces fit after a while.

'The Red Door' makes a vague gesture in the direction of emotional resonance, but it can’t figure out what to do with its allegory beyond what’s been done more successfully elsewhere, flimsily mimicking Ari Aster with all the conviction of Neil LaBute.
Franchise fans will enjoy seeing the Lamberts again, but newcomers will be baffled by the under-developed story and nonplussed by the over-familiar scares.
Wilson comes at this like the star of a TV show who’s watched them make it for long enough that he figures he could do it himself.

title: Theater Camp | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Lampooning big dreams and high melodrama, this comedy about the kids and counsellors at a stagey summer camp is charming, and brilliantly brutal.

Mostly improvised, it’s an amusing celebration of community seen through a song and dance lens as the chaotic but devoted staff at a summer camp instruct their dedicated young charges, ignore their own failings, and make sure that several shows go on.
Achieves the rare trick of creating a fictional work-within-the-work that is supposed to be really good, and actually is.

The cast makes up such an effective ensemble that it’s hardly fair to single out individuals, but Noah Galvin is wonderful as the harried and ever-resourceful stage manager who has yet to experience the luxury of sitting down.

Depending on your level of initiation, Molly Gordon and Nick Lieberman’s pitch-perfect satire Theater Camp will either trigger mortifying flashbacks... or play like a psychoanalyst’s field study in hysteria.
It’s enjoyable stuff, particularly the bracingly catty sniping of the first two-thirds.
Having laughed all the way through, you’ll leave the cinema feeling moved too.
The mockumentary is in safe hands with this talented team. And at a breezy 90-minute running time their film is exactly what you need to ward off the end-of-summer blues.
Theater Camp is itself shamelessly infatuated with the great American musical, but it also enjoys poking affectionate fun at the kids’ creative tunnel vision.
A thesp fest with some great kids and cameos, but a little cliquey despite its intentions.
Like the Guest films, Theater Camp’s comedy springs entirely from personality: the jokes aren’t really quotable because they depend on you knowing who’s making them to work.
It’s a zippy 90 minutes or so, and packed with jokes.
Theater Camp is a feel-good delight, and a sign of impressive directorial talent from Molly Gordon and Nick Lieberman.
The film deftly captures the high emotional stakes of being a theater kid, whether you’re still a child or a full-grown adult.
For theater nerds, and the ambitious young thespians they foster, this Sundance gem is likely to be the summer’s funniest feel-good film.

If it doesn't reach the heights of Guest's works — "Waiting for Guffman" is its clear antecedent — it's recognizably funny, where you might acknowledge a particular joke is funny even if it doesn't leave you laughing out loud.
Even those who never did theater camp can enjoy Theater Camp.
It’s excruciatingly unfunny for the first 74 of its 94 minutes before suddenly revealing an impressive flourish of creativity.
Earnest and ridiculous in equal measure, Theater Camp makes clear that places like AdirondACTS are microcosms of magical weirdness.
The message of Theater Camp is clear: Its eccentric world of show tunes and show people is big enough (and funny enough) for everyone.

title: The League | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Both the history and the filmmaking here are extraordinary.

By presenting this crucial cultural phenomenon in a staid documentary form and in the reverent tone of a hushed docent, The League has the unintentional impact of making Black baseball seem like ancient rather than living history.
Ultimately, Pollard’s film is equal parts tribute and lament, as complicated as this country.
It’s a solid and stirring documentary – you should see it.
If one measure of a documentary’s quality is whether it inspires you to learn more about its subject after the credits roll, “The League” is an unqualified success.
The League revels in its subjects’ athleticism and the dynamic style the players pioneered, which now defines contemporary baseball. That emphasis on their talent makes the film a delight to watch.
The League is well worth watching if you’re an avid fan of sports and history.
I haven’t even scratched the surface of how much you’ll learn from “The League.” It’s a must-see for baseball fans and for anyone who loves a great American story.
Pollard’s “The League” is a rich, engrossing, and necessary tribute to a critical early wave in the Civil Rights movement.
The League is a reminder of the rocky road to inclusion in our great American pastime.
Interviews, photos and newsreel clips inform The League, which stands with the best chronicles of baseball integration.
This history has surely been well-covered elsewhere, but “The League” recounts it movingly.
At its most engrossing, the film vibrantly sketches out the historical roots of the Negro baseball leagues.
An exceptional documentation of the men who played the game of baseball their way and became role models in the process.

It not only proves fascinating itself but makes one want to see nearly every one of its episodes dramatized — after all, it’s been a long time since 1976’s The Bingo Long Traveling All-Stars & Motor Kings.

title: Muzzle | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The dogs give the film a touch of class, but as a whole this is forgettable.

"Muzzle" is filled with intriguing aspects not explored meaningfully. There are so many different threads, themes, and plots, even Scotch-taped together in the hopes it will come together. It doesn't.

title: Cobweb (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s as if Kim is testing himself to see if he could make a self-indulgent, unsubstantial lark of a comedy. He can. Sorta.
“Cobweb” falls victim, ironically, to its own punchline — becoming a movie that is too obsessed with itself.
A film containing another film; a filmmaker referring to the trials of a filmmaker: It's a movie of many layers, all of them garish and goofy, none of them great.

title: The Beanie Bubble | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The Beanie Bubble eventually runs out of steam. The snappy pace and colorful style — so attractive at first — later become alienating, keeping nearly all the characters locked into one dimension.
The film feels like a vapid cheerleader for late-stage capitalism. It is blithely unquestioning of what the frenzy over glorified Hacky Sacks actually tells us about society.
Zach Galifianakis captures the narcissism of Chicago’s Ty Warner.
It is dispiriting to watch such talented people try to animate this turgid blueprint.
Robbie is right that the beanie bubble represents a mad moment, as did tulip mania in 17th-century Holland, and other must-have investments before and since.
The Beanie Bubble is convinced there’s a victory buried in this story somewhere. It’s just not clear who or what we should be celebrating.
This is the weakest of the year's crop of pictures that purport to tell the inside story behind iconic products.
Outside of some easy irony given the cuddliness of the product at hand, there may not be enough that makes this iteration of such a familiar cycle especially interesting.
Despite its satirical tone, The Beanie Bubble largely plays things pretty straight -- indeed, a little too straight, when a bit more humor and whimsy would have helped.
By offering a lazy take on power and greed, Gore and Kulash short change their talented female leads and patronise the audience.

Barbie is hot, but this botch job about the Beanie Bables—another doll craze from last century—is no collector’s item as it runs off the rails and wastes such fine actors as Zach Galifianakis, Elizabeth Banks, Geraldine Viswanathan and Sarah Snook.
A breezy feminist demolition of self-made-man mythology, The Beanie Bubble is marred by clunky ironic retrospection, based on showing its characters unschooled in the internet...

It’s not as though Banks, Snook and the reliably charming Viswanathan don’t have their moments, but the film commits to a relentless hard sell on the Amazing Women™ each one is playing, and we don’t really believe a word.
The Beanie Bubble needlessly complicates itself. But it also makes a compelling reflection of history repeating itself.
Screenwriter Gore codirects with husband Damian Kulash and the film struggles to figure out what story it wants to tell.
It deploys every storytelling cliché in the book, from “you’re probably wondering how I ended up in this situation”-style voice-overs to pat last-act monologues that reiterate the themes.
The elements of a good story are here, and the talent to tell it is more than willing. The movie just never quite gets there.
The Beanie Bubble is less a tale of a corporate genius than a story, three times over, of a woman scorned.
There’s material here for a juicy backstage exposé yet unfortunately the story never pushes beyond the parameters of a Horrible Bosses set piece.
Sometimes the storytelling can feel like a stretch, but this is mostly a lively, well-told account of a bizarre toy craze gone wrong, and the big personalities behind it.

title: Haunted Mansion (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A story that mainly serves as an excuse to publicize the attraction ride, from which countless details and characters are extracted. [Full review in Spanish]
Disney’s Haunted Mansion is a fair enough choice for a family night in, experienced from the comfort of your couch, where the flaws are less glaring and the price of admission for Disney+ is cheaper.
No central theme emerges beyond a blandly generalised one about moving on from the past, which is to say that overtly at least, this Haunted Mansion plays it even safer than its 2003 predecessor.
Owen Wilson is a priest who may be a man of the con rather that the cloth. He does manage to exorcise a few jokes out of a demonically unfortunate predicament.
This is a grimly efficient IP cash-in that defuses any potential scares with a hot-pink colour palette and a bunch of oddly specific and distracting product placements.

The movie only gels once, in a sequence featuring Winona Ryder as Pat, a hilariously sour member of the heritage industry. Serenely quirky and coherent, this segment offers a haunting glimpse of what might have been.
Not scary. Not funny. Just depressing.
One imagines the skirls of funereal bagpipes sounding throughout this deeply puzzling slab of unthreatening horror. This must be the end of something. Must it not?
Haunted Mansion is played for family-friendly laughs, with much cobwebbed Scooby-Doobery and character comedy...
For a family seeking exciting entertainment, this Disney romp is a terrific choice.
Haunted Mansion comes so close to being good that it’s honestly infuriating that it comes up short. It’s frankly annoying.
Like the Disney theme-park attraction upon which it’s based, at its best it’s entertaining in a quaint, late-’60s way, which makes it a pleasant summer surprise.
Some actors are silly while some keep it real, but all work overtime to give viewers a good time.
Despite a lively cast and a promising director, this Disney comedy barely has a pulse.
Haunted Mansion is a big, plastic theme park ride of packaged fun. It’s funny-scary, not scary-scary.
“Haunted Mansion” is star-studded but shoddy at best.
It’s amazing that anything in Haunted Mansion works, even if most of it doesn’t.
I went into “Haunted Mansion” expecting a hot mess on par with Murphy’s movie. Instead, I found an engaging and sweet action comedy, one that’s not only very funny but also quite touching.

It could have been worse, but that’s no excuse for turning an exciting nine-minute theme-park ride into an overlong, star-stuffed 122 minute feature that is only fitfully funny and scary and soon wears out its welcome.

Even with a solid cast yielding good moments, there’s a general flatness to it, and a sense the movie is seeking to scare up what it can in theaters before settling into its natural haunting grounds on Disney+.

title: You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: What sounds like an excruciating work of nepotism emerges as something far better: a frothy and lightweight comedy that ends up having something of a genuine heart.
This has a lot of Judy Bloom in its DNA, in terms of dealing honestly with what young women go through.
The rare teen movie that recognises crushes are never as important or powerful as BFFs — and one that marks an intriguing new direction for Adam Sandler’s Happy Madison productions.
Open your heart and turn off your logic meter and you‘re going to enjoy “You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah.”
A comedy blessed with cultural weight.

Cry nepotism all you want, but the entire brood acquits itself quite well, and they seem to be having an infectiously good time together. It helps a great deal that the film is energetically directed and written.
Adam Sandler’s daughter Sunny -- the clear belle of the ball -- quickly dampens the “nepo baby” asides with her winning, natural performance in a familiar but very nicely done coming-of-age story.
You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah appreciates that being in middle school means still being a child in most ways, but with a new array of social weaponry with which to be cruel.
A love letter to the agonies and messiness of the kids on the brink of maturity.

It's basically a pricey home movie that lets Adam Sandler spotlight his wife and two daughters. It's also an unexpectedly sweet and sassy surprise. Dynamo Sunny Sandler, his youngest, gives nepotism a good name as a Jewish girl on the cusp of womanhood.
Proof that Sandler still has the capacity to spearhead (as opposed to just for-hire headline) a competent movie—including one featuring those closest to him.

The young cast proves deft with the film’s clever script, by Alison Peck (based on the 2005 novel by Fiona Rosenbloom), and the director Sammi Cohen indulges the virgin-mojito passions of preteens while avoiding nostalgia, thankfully.

Director Sammi Cohen takes an attention-deficit disorder approach to storytelling, in which every feeling and plot twist is punctuated by a current pop song, and any hint of emotion or thoughtfulness is interrupted by a needle drop.
The Sandlers’ affectionate rapport and palpable family chemistry lends the film, based on the book by Fiona Rosenbloom, a rare, sweet charm.
It's a breezy but heartfelt affair, light and colorful, perfectly suitable for family viewing.
An easily watchable treat for the entire family.
A fun family affair.

Playing like a cross between Judy Blume’s “Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret” and John Hughes’ “Sixteen Candles” in scale, scope and sound without being derivative, its characters, conflicts and conundrums are filled with potent, earned emotions.

title: Meg 2: The Trench | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Things might have felt more perilous with more finessed CGI.
What’s perhaps most damning about this big dumb shark movie, however, is how little it actually pays attention to its fine finned friends.
Definitively edible. [Full review in Spanish]
Eventually stops taking itself seriously and becomes the movie it's meant to be.
While there are undeniable instances of magic, there are just as many unintentionally laughable ones right along with them.

Attempts to bite off its 2018 predecessor by going bigger in every way, but rarely for the better. It’s a clumsy action movie with the occasional spurt of fun monster conflict amidst a sea of flat characters and a tiresome plot of corporate espionage.
What's all most astounding about this is that it's directed with zero panache by Ben Wheatley.
If Wheatley were inclined to release Meg 2: The Fun Island Cut, there’d be a lot more here to recommend. As it is, the film’s dead in the water.

This franchise needs to be buried at the bottom of the Atlantic for a couple of decades, along with some illegally dumped nuclear waste. Perhaps then it might finally mutate into something entertaining.

Meg 2 is confident in its schlock, piling on one ridiculous conceit after another at such a pace that the audience can’t help but be swept up in it. That is a harder needle to thread than many filmmakers seem to think -- it’s not enough to just be stupid.
It makes the original look like, well, Jaws by comparison.

Meg 2: The Trench doesn’t overly mess with that formula, but it does muck up the simple strengths of the story with all kinds of unnecessary side plots. In the process, the film goes from Shark Week to shark weak.

There's more, more and more. More Megs. More problems. More ludicrous plot points, more cartoonish villains, and more dialogue cheesier than an overripened Brie wheel left out on a picnic table. But also, in the film's saving grace, more Jason Statham.
Meg 2 often fails on a basic molecular level, sometimes leaving us unclear as to who’s doing what to whom onscreen.
Meg 2: The Trench is better than the first film because, while it repeats everything the first film did wrong, it improves on everything it did right.
The dialogue is truly dire. The heroes say stuff like, “We’re a strong group, we can do this!” A baddie gloats, “We’re making so much money it ceases to have meaning!”
Meg 2, by design, is a completely anonymous bag of lukewarm McDonalds – it’s hard to be mad at it, but only because nothing in it stands out enough to get mad at.
Scene to scene, jump scare to jump scare, Meg 2 gets a D-minus for clarity.
Wheatley's wit seems pointed at the gauche desires of an audience who just want some big, mindless entertainment without being judged for it.
One of the dullest films of the year, a plodding, poorly made giant shark movie that inexplicably lets the giant shark take a backseat to an evil underwater drilling operation.

title: The Marsh King's Daughter | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Ridley delivers her strongest post-Star Wars turn with a deeply empathetic character who is, throughout the drama, on the cusp of a breakdown, or a breakthrough. It’s powerful work.
I was sitting back in my seat, nowhere near the edge of it. I would have liked to have inched towards the edge of it.
The tale is too tame, its savagery held too much in check to truly hold the audience in its thrall.
When we need the churning dread of an intimate tale of generational trauma, The Marsh King’s Daughter goes formulaic, and when we’re primed for exploitation sweats, it gets flabby.
The film’s pacing sags, undercutting the sense of urgency that makes a thriller.
The movie is so afraid of making viewers restless that it shies away from dramatizing anything it can’t resolve in 20 seconds or less.
B-movie material elevated by A-level performances.
Once the film turns into a paranoid home-invasion thriller, there’s no ambiguity left to the tale.

title: The Inventor | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's a role written for Stephen Fry... it's perhaps harder to know exactly who the audience is.
Charming and informative as it is, the film may struggle to engage younger audiences accustomed to more overt comedy in their animated movies and less grave-robbing.
It’s a bit of a bore and a chore, and feels like the kind of “educational” film that will be foisted on kids in class during wet playtime on rainy days.

It asks big questions about life and meaning that might compel adults, but it’s ultimately hard to see this landing anywhere outside of a niche audience. If you appreciate stop-motion as an art, it’s a must. If you want a good story, maybe not.
An animated film suitable for both adults and children that is truly full of marvels.
The movie is marvelous, in a way: It’s enchanting to see Leonardo drifting along in a reverie as his sketches fill the screen and sweet Renaissance-style music decorates the soundtrack.
There's an undeniable boldness to Capobianco's decision to channel a biography through the medium of stop motion, but it's perfect for the untrammeled exuberance and boundless ingenuity of Da Vinci.

“The Inventor” is rife with somewhat didactic lessons — about power, innovation, curiosity — yet a presumably unintended one might be that lessons themselves, however insightful, are not always captivating.
An engaging and amusing history lesson.
Oftentimes da Vinci is pleasantly lost in the cosmos of his mind, what Willy Wonka called “Pure Imagination.” The target audience of “The Inventor” will surely relate.

title: birth/rebirth | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It is the understated, matter-of-fact tone of the story that sucks us in, and the two central performances that help make this effort by Ms. Moss such a singular addition to the monster catalog.
One of the most impactful genre films in recent times, and it's accompanied by a feminist imprint that is never demonstrated to be concessive. [Full review in Spanish]

In teasing out the complex relationship between life and death in relationship to birth and “Frankenstein,” Moss presents a provocative existential quandary, and reminds us that horror stories have been women’s stories all along.
It's amazing how far "birth/rebirth" goes into this amoral territory.
As the women’s behavior grows ever more shocking — and Ariel Marx’s nerve-plucking score intensifies — Moss offers no rebuke to their heedless amorality. There is only the audience to judge.
No insurance premium can cover what this mad doctor is offering.

Habitually shooting her characters through narrow doorways and windows, the better to convey their isolation as well as their squeezed-by-circumstance states, the director fashions a sinister atmosphere, aided by intermittent pregnancy and corpse imagery.
A fiendish and atmospheric riff on classic monster legends and a welcome addition to a certain horror sub-genre propelled by brawny but burdened mamas.
Birth/Rebirth is a uniquely thrilling vision of horror, and Moss is a director to watch. Keep an eye out for both.
Truly haunting stuff.
Maternal horror with a clinical twist.

“Birth/Rebirth” proves just how well the classic tale of scientific hubris and the desire to conquer death maps onto a gory maternity morality play, reanimating the truism that there’s little more (un)deadly than a mother’s love.
Birth/Rebirth serves as a perverse correction, recalibrating decades of dilution to reemphasize the moral weight and emotional anguish at the heart of Shelley’s novel.
The movie is freaky. But it never feigns to become a mere freakshow. It works, in part, because it hurts. It works because it defers that hurt until, at long last, it cannot be avoided.

Moss and co-writer Brendan J. O’Brien give just enough creepy momentum to “birth/rebirth,” knowing that their audience is smart enough to understand that bringing a child back to life comes with a likely set of problems.
A queasily clinical horror debut from Laura Moss that explores the darker sides of child rearing, from birth to death and way beyond.
By the time “birth/rebirth” arrives at its whimper of a finale, few of the film’s ideas have been allowed to develop beyond their most embryonic stage.

title: Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The panoramic intelligence of this film is a wonder.
It's a slow roll, very much about the images, language, thoughts and ideas.

The entire film is marked by the brilliant cinematographic language used by its director and screenwriter Phạm Thiên Ân, who, in his first long-term work, displays an impressive and calm handling of images. [Full review in Spanish]

A demanding meditation on human existence and mortality, it's a film that is as much about what it has to offer, as about what we bring to it on our own as viewers. A film that is as challenging as life itself...
“Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell” blurs the line between surrealism and realism, faith and loss in a subdued search for purpose in the wake of a tragedy.
A three-hour drama whose slender story serves as the skeleton for a formally exquisite examination of loss, faith, family, and connection, it's the year’s first masterpiece.
Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell is an entrancing work of art, but it's also wise enough to leave its deepest mysteries unsolved.
There’s something singularly fulfilling in a film, like this one, that truly demands that most precious commodity: our attention.
First-time feature director Phạm Thiên Ân, and his deeply religious inquiry aims to crack open the trap by forcing Thiện, and the audience, into a confrontation with eternity itself.
An exquisite and thoroughly singular portrait of both an individual in transition and a country in motion, Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell is one hell of a calling card for Phạm Thiên An.
The protagonist may feel cut off from the world, but the film is deeply in harmony with it.
There are too many daring and deft editing choices to believe. Each scene is a filmic victory.

It’s the kind of film that steadily trains you in perceiving and eventually becoming lost in its sense of time, to the extent that you can almost forget the presence of the camera even when it is moving.
Challenging but seductive art cinema that invites comparisons to such titans as Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Tsai Ming-liang and even Theo Angelopoulos, without feeling derivative of any.

title: Vacation Friends 2 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s a creaky, 00s sitcom expanded to a movie, the actors almost waiting for studio laughter to follow their labored jokes.
A perfunctory sequel with an even duller story.

Like John Cena and Meredith Hagner’s characters, this movie's shrill sense of humor barrels into our viewing lives again, begging for our attention and to be seen as cute. Now we have something that’s even worse and more testing than “Vacation Friends.”
As inspired as its title.
If anything, delving into action/comedy territory distracts from what made the original kinda-sorta touching at a few key moments: the heart beneath the hijinks.

title: Coup de Chance (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It is of a piece with Woody’s late-life output, a tale of coincidence, chance, and murder that charms at its best and at its worst evaporates upon contact with your eyeballs.

The film’s closing is abrupt and maybe too tidy, but “Coup de Chance” is still a clever little thriller. It displays an admirable economy of storytelling, and its jazz-heavy soundtrack helps maintain a jaunty mood.

This French bonbon, Woody Allen’s best reviewed film in years, is no career landmark. But its blend of humor and homicide shows Allen, 88, still moving forward, creating the kind of film he made his name on, the kind that makes you laugh till it hurts.
Fifty films into his career – he still makes about one per year -- Allen has his art down to a science.
The result at times carries the whiff of something simultaneously refreshing and nostalgic.
'Coup de Chance' restores the masterful filmmaker to his deserved position as one of the screen’s most profound storytellers.

Would anyone pay particular attention to a French import about love and deception without well-known stars if Woody Allen’s name weren’t attached to it? Perhaps not. But since this is his work—recognizably so—it's worth seeing
Woody Allen’s best work in many years.
“Coup de Chance,” the latest from Woody Allen, looks and plays like many of his recent movies, only better; it sounds like them, too, except that it’s in French.
It's a decently executed version of a movie Allen has made many times before, enlivened by Vittorio Storaro's elegant if overly burnished-looking cinematography.

The movie, aesthetically as lumpy as a latke, nonetheless has a weird and lurid vigor that comes from an altogether different source: Allen’s pleasure in his own imagination—his delight in inventing the plot.
The film is at once among Woody Allen’s most economical works and one of his most free-spirited.
Coup de chance is the 50th film Allen has ­directed and one of his best. It was made in France and is, to all intents and purposes, a French movie.
A tight and effective French-language thriller that is also, among other things, the world’s longest mother-in-law joke.
Coup de Chance is not a major reinvention, but it does have more spirit and joie de vivre than anything Allen has done in a while.
Given his otherwise grim recent form, Allen himself may have simply got lucky with this one, but the charm and sparkle here are real.
As a culture, I wouldn’t be too surprised if we found ourselves debating whether the time has come to give Woody Allen, as a filmmaker, another coup de chance.
Coup de snooze.

Coup de Chance is a pretty slight and minor film, but for an 87-year-old American working in a second language, it can’t help but seem impressive; it’s certainly as good as anything Allen has made since 2013’s Blue Jasmine.
Coup de Chance was never going to dazzle but it doesn’t entirely disappoint. As long as you like very Woody Allen Woody Allen films.

title: El Conde | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The accoutrements of power are telling -- flying in his military cape Pinochet is a fascist superhero -- and Larrain’s gory filmmaking is equally effective as historic prosecution or a macabre fantasy.
The film’s political outlook is a little fuzzy, but it bleeds pure, righteous bitterness. Larraín jumps at the chance to turn political ideology into a literal horror show.
Ed Lachman's cinematography is just luscious. It is just incredibly, richly beautiful in black and white.
What ultimately stays with you, however, is how Larraín has audaciously staked the heart of someone who tore his country apart and still knows that it isn’t enough to slay the beast.
[A] wickedly funny, blood-soaked portrait of a decaying tyrant.
Few jokes, no matter how sick and strong, can be told over and over without beginning to fade.
The satire of Pinochet is gloriously unsubtle.

While the filmmaker has the gall to caricature tyranny, he’s too cynical, or too honest, to wrap up “El Conde” with a satisfying resolution. Larraín has finally faced his monster — but he can’t bring himself to drive a stake through his heart.
El Conde is a visual feast as much as a visceral one, but its artful poise belies its bloodlust. Larraín is making his points here not with fang-like precision, but a gleeful crocodilian chomp.
What saves El Conde is the specificity of its subject and the style of its auteur. They may be monsters, but a modern vampire insists on looking chic.

Few directors take risks this big, and though this film doesn’t yield the most rewards, it’s a fascinatingly project. With Larraín, history never stays firmly in the past; instead, it haunts and lingers like a figure of the undead.

A movie that not only represents a return to (Larraín's) Chilean shores after wading into the waters of Hollywood but it is also his most fanciful, fascinating and darkly, darkly comic twist on history yet.
A visually arresting new entry in the Dracula canon; if only the satire was as biting as its unlikely vampire star.

Are fascist dictators really vampires? That’s the shockingly funny premise behind director Pablo Lorrain’s look at Augusto Pinochet's reign of terror over Larrain’s native Chile. Flaws and all, the film speaks scarily to the undying nature of tyranny.
I longed for a satire that had more bite.
Conde never loses sight of its stark vision and message about tyranny remaining eternal as it repeats itself time and time again through history.
El Conde might stretch its gimmicky premise a little past its welcome, but it is an intoxicating, overwhelming and gruesome cinematic experience nonetheless.
Larraín's satire isn't always subtle and it becomes scattershot as the film wears on; for the skewering of a monstrous figure, it's not quite a stake through the heart.
Bitingly funny, bountifully gory and mercifully filmed in black-and-white, El Conde spins a haunted, hemoglobin-rich origin story for brutal dictator Augusto Pinochet
“El Conde” feels so singular, both as an allegory and as a movie about Pinochet, that its theoretical predictability hardly matters.

title: Happiness for Beginners | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is the movie equivalent of background TV, something to have on while you're paying the bills, or something. There's cinematic comfort food and then there's just comfort, without the food.
Ultimately, the film’s formulaic qualities are too much of a drag.
Like a mapped-out trail, you know where it will end up, but there's enough to enjoy along the way.

If this movie is insufficiently self-possessed to transcend its nature as streaming content and become something more than the sum of its parts, Wight still ensures that each of those parts contribute to a cumulative sense of coziness.

Happiness for Beginners is a shrug of a movie with a side of sweet self-reflection... It’s a bland story executed blandly, with comedy that doesn’t make the cut and a romance that’ll leave you sighing in frustration rather than swooning.
It’s destined to be thrown on in the background of a well-kept Airbnb after a long day of hiking in the Northeast.
In most ways, it’s not worth seeing. Yet everything about this movie goes down easy and never gives you a reason to stop watching.
Throughout it all, Kemper visibly strains to temper her comedic impulses.
The woman at its center remains opaque, her romance is listless and her journey to self-discovery becomes an endurance test.

title: Ehrengard: The Art of Seduction | Rotten Tomatoes
Expend4bles | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's the third best out of the four, but better than [The Expendables 3] -- and still very entertaining.
If Expend4bles turns out to be a swan song, it’s a fitting one, since it so neatly encapsulates the series’ formula.
It's just a huge waste of people with incredible talent.
Dull and tasteless. The insertion of “4” [in the title] is unfortunately just about the most clever thing the fourth installment of this action series has to offer.

This is a dumb-as-rocks exercise in violence and stupidity, which represents a low for a franchise that was already scraping the bottom of the barrel, and it's on the very short list of candidates for the year's worst movie.
The knuckle-headed appeal of this dopey action franchise has finally evaporated with its latest instalment aka Expend-Four-Bles!

“Expend4dbles” wants to be the kind of movie that’s best seen on cable with commercial breaks or on a beat-up VHS tape, but there are far more entertaining classics that can get the job done. There’s no need to enlist this tired team.

Watching the cast of Expend4bles... sweating and straining their way through the “casual banter” section of the screenplay is like watching contestants on The World’s Strongest Man attempting to climb a ladder while carrying a tractor tyre.
“The Disposables” would describe it better.
Plot, you say? What plot? In a word: negligible.
[A] laughably lazy exercise in utility-grade meat-and-potatoes filmmaking.
The bar was already so low, and yet this film manages to sneak under it.

The film’s last reel is so awful — so sneeringly contemptuous of our good-faith efforts to play along with these shenanigans — that we leave the theater still thinking of that shot of a corpse's middle finger. It sure seemed pointed at us.
Expend4bles: wh4t a lo4d of cr4p.
Expendabes 4 is ambushed by its own utter lack of new ideas or better ways to use the talents of the many charismatic actors who did turn up to work for various lengths of time.
It all gets very tiresome. It doesn’t help that the special effects sometimes seem thrown together with about as much care as the script

For all its efforts at wit, Expend4bles offers exactly two kinds of laughs: unintentional (seriously, the explosion effects and green-screen moments are hilarious) and unearned (the joke that lands best is a direct quote from another movie).
Lackluster on practically every level, this ought to be renamed The Disposables as it’s a giant waste of everyone’s time and talent.
... Installment number four of the elite mercenaries series manages to not be entirely extraneous to our entertainment needs, disarming as often with easy charm, as with a high-kick to the hyoid.
The movie is unsurprising and not especially ambitious, but it’s agile enough to vault over most of its flaws.

title: The Out-Laws | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: DeVine manages to make unapologetic dweebishness charming, and the movie is elevated by a mish-mash of wonderful character-actor bit parts.
Everything you need to know about this movie can be gleaned from its title. That's rarely a good sign.
For a Netflix movie that was obviously reverse-engineered from its title, and even more obviously made by the director of The Wrong Missy, Tyler Spindel’s The Out-Laws could be a hell of a lot worse.
Embarrassed laughter isn’t the same as the other kind; a cringe isn’t the same as a smile. And humiliation -- of an actor as well as a character -- isn’t really funny.
Frankly, it’s all a bit too much.
Derivative and desperate and, at the same time, bizarrely pleased with itself.

There seems little chance Netflix will offer us a comedy in the vein of Ernst Lubitsch or Preston Sturges. So make the most of an entertainment that comes in at the altitude of a better Adam Sandler joint.
The wittiest thing about The Out-Laws is its title.
The Out-Laws shines when it spotlights the committed performances of its cast.
[A] watchable if forgettable crime comedy...
...lazy, formulaic, loud and unfunny.
Much of the cast seems to be having fun, but it comes at our expense.
The plot is ludicrous, but this is the sort of film where it’s about hilarious antics not plausibility.
A slight comedy, but it’s also raucous and kickily violent, with several laugh-in-spite-of-your-better-judgment bits.

title: Relax, I'm from the Future | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A sci-fi comedy with a modest sense of humor but tangled message to share with humankind.

title: Lift (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Petersen’s bare-bones, on-the-ground production works well for a story like this, highlighting how vital these small workshops in homeless shelters and community centers can be.
Keep a hanky close. Tears will swell in your eyes, not from grief, but from inspiration.

title: Spy Kids: Armageddon | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's been 22 years since the original movie and whatever might have once seemed fresh and funny about the whole "Spy Kids" universe has long since rotted away.
It’s not going to reinvent the kids’ movie wheel by any means, but if you’re willing to engage with the film on its level, you’ll find a lot of fun to be had.
It’s more of the same, without any discernible improvement in quality, despite the massive technological leaps over the past two decades.
Spy Kids: Armageddon did, at least, remind me of the blind delights of childhood again, and the kids who will likely enjoy this.
The kids’ respective performances feel relatable, authentic, and above all, fun, making “Armageddon” the type of children’s movie where a young audience member could see themselves onscreen...

title: Apocalypse Clown | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s hit and miss. Mostly miss.
Director George Kane keeps the energy up throughout, helped along by a game-for-it cast that know exactly how to pitch the material.
It’s delightfully batty in parts, groan-worthy in others, but overall the ethos is to just keep firing – and some shots land even as others could clearly have been finessed further.

title: The Retirement Plan | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A totally disposable but mostly entertaining action comedy drama with a really stupid plot and a few good laughs.

title: The Pod Generation | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The material they’re [Clarke and Ejiofor] given is often slim and simple, but they lean into it with everything they can offer, and find the relatability in characters who feel more like symbols than like people.
The movie’s core is as inert as an uncharged iPhone, taking most of the sting out of its cautionary satire.
An opaque expression of an overly simple thesis.
In Sophie Barthes' hands, a story of a couple having a pod baby becomes a clever and poignant comedy about the quirks of technology, privilege, and the inhumanity of having it all.
A wickedly funny and fun, if disconcerting, film that arrives right on time for our age of ChatGPT and artificial intelligence doomerism.
After Yang did this theme a tad better. But The Pod Generation scores its own points.
... A cautionary tale of choosing science over nature, albeit one that’s played more for laughs.
The Pod Generation foregrounds Rachel and Alvy’s relationship, exploring how technologies change our most intimate connections and raising questions from a world not so unlike our own.
A warm-bath optimism that swerves into silliness in the final act.
Neither as scary nor as funny as its premise might be, The Pod Generation instead coasts along on a placid, self-satisfied wavelength.
A movie with fascinating ideas but too little POV to drive them home in an interesting way.
For all the movie’s quite credible conjecture about technology rendering nature obsolete and procreation becoming the privilege of the wealthy, The Pod Generation never fully hatches.

Strong performances by both Clarke and Chiwetel Ejiofor, plus compelling production design from Clem Price Thomas recommend the feature, even if some of Barthes’ biggest ideas sometimes feel under-explored by the time the film reaches its conclusion.
A movie needs more than a smart idea and an impressively visualized concept of the future to run smoothly. Two thirds of the way through, “The Pod Generation”‘s battery is already at 1%.
Barthes’ screenplay is clean; for the most part, it’s brainy but not didactic, and thoughtful but not dull.
The cinematography by Andrij Parekh aided by Clement Price-Thomas vibrant set design created an innovative future look that isn't far out of the realm possibility--but that's it.
One of the many things “The Pod Generation” taps into is how the combined forces of technology and corporate power now seem almost designed to divide people off from each other.

title: Fear the Night | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a waste of time and streaming pixels.
It's crafty enough, but it's lacking LaBute's usual acid wit and fearless provocations.
Eventually, it becomes hard to tell if the movie and its canned culture clash/battle of the sexes drama is just self-consciously tedious or also hatefully ungenerous.
A movie that appears not so much written by LaBute as stapled together from a pile of threadbare thriller tropes.

title: Bird Box Barcelona | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is even more drab than the first instalment of the Netflix horror-thriller.
The film has moments of pure and hard terror that should appease those who love the genre.  [Full review in Spanish]
[There's] a new element, which I think is very bright of the film... They pull this thing off again.
The Barcelona edition is essentially a repeat of the first film, flaws and all.
Suspension of disbelief and an appreciation of propulsively destructive action sequences is key. Just don’t expect too many fresh ideas.
Some real creativity could have made all of this cinematically compelling instead of merely sadistic. Unfortunately, Bird Box Barcelona doesn’t have many other ideas beyond its initial ones.
It’s far better than it could have been, a simple retread transformed into something flawed but competently made and narratively unexpected, albeit mildly.
... It soon proves to be less scary than just acutely depressing, with none of the depth or daring of the fatal eye-contact plot device in Jordan Peele’s Nope.
The will to live is missing from Netflix’s not-quite-sequel “Bird Box Barcelona,” and so is our will to watch.
In a world of bombed-out journeys into darkness, it's one apocalypse too many.
... A film whose primary pleasures live in the initial set-up, the early twist and some genuinely thoughtful engagement with the premise.
If seeing is believing, “Bird Box Barcelona” doesn’t have much to show.
While Bird Box: Barcelona has none of the subtle bleakness of Brier's first film, the Pastors still manage to bring an interesting twist to Malerman's excellent original idea.
... A spin-off that’s not as moving as the original, which was boosted by Bullock and had novelty on its side — but it’s still as creepy as hell.
There is no thrill, entertainment or insight to be gleaned in watching the myriad ways people can die by their own hand. It’s just awful.
From a technical standpoint, the Pastors ensure an engaging spinoff. But the emphasis on familiar horror beats and stock archetypes undermine the themes introduced.

Directors Àlex Pastor and David Pastor have come up with a spinoff feature, “Bird Box Barcelona,” minus Bullock but with the addition of a rather nifty — and depressingly credible — faith-based twist.
Thanks to a couple of novel twists, it manages to outpace its predecessor in tension and originality—if not quite reinvigorate the franchise.

Though slick and more expansive in some ways, with bigger action sequences, it proves an overlong, uninvolving entry, in which any attempted fresh wrinkles to this fantasy universe offer scant viewer reward.

A largely uninspiring re-tread of a superior film, this has some decent moments and enough gnarly deaths to keep horror hounds vaguely entertained until the inevitable arrival of ‘Bird Box Santorini’.

title: Animalia | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: If you want sleight-of-hand cinematic atmosphere, a big movie made on a small budget, and a sense of the planet tipping on its axis toward destruction and rebirth, here's your vision of the end times.
Animalia is a quiet, thoughtful film with grand things on its mind that it tackles with impressive confidence, to great success.

With a strong central performance from Oumaïma Barid and remarkable cinematography, the experience of watching the film is arresting enough that its elusiveness becomes an asset rather than a hindrance.
"Animalia" aims for a holistic view of the world, the oneness of all things.
Has an arresting visual sense and handles the blend of social and religious commentary and CGI fantasy with flair.
Meditative, obscure but ultimately rather lovely...
Subverts the genre in compelling ways.

title: My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I was physically uncomfortable the whole way through, because this is just a fever dream of bad choices.
In spite of its third-film shortcomings, My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 has some genuine laughs and a healthy dose of heart.
We’re still left with cute but thinly drawn characters with little personality beyond signature quirks.
It’s a rom-com both com-less and rom-less.
Personally, this series has never done much for me, and that’s the case with this third effort, too. As great as the ensemble might be, Vardalos aims much too low.
My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 should have been a breezy postcard. Instead, no amount of sequences filmed during golden hour can distract from the story’s clunkiness.
Time to bury this franchise.
It’s the best-crafted film in the series, thanks in part to Vardalos taking the reins as director.
A better title may have been My Big Fat Greek Vacation Commercial.
The script functions like a recipe for its own opening shot of baklava; flattened and bland, Toula exists only to constrain the nuts.
An extended commercial for Greek vacations and the idealized immigrant family.

Audience goodwill is the only thing this third take on Greek family bonding has going for it as writer-director star-Nia Vardalos keeps pushing the same brand of ethnic humor. And I mean, really pushing, another reason the movie falls so painfully flat.
Twenty-one years after audiences initially said “I do,” My Big Fat Greek Wedding 3 compels us to start divorce proceedings.
As action-packed as a holiday nap on a hot afternoon, this is a must-see only for Portakalos die-hards.
This latest installation in the “Big Fat Greek” franchise is colorful and celebratory, eager to entertain and wears its heart on its sleeve. There’s something to be said for that.
It’s amiable enough, but devoid of real surprise or jeopardy and full of hokey guff about accepting people for who they really are.
It’s Mamma Mia!, minus ABBA. Don’t say you weren’t warned.
Director Vardalos, the keeper of her half-billion-dollar franchise, mistakes antsiness for energy, cutting constantly, messing up the rhythms.
It's a genial, somewhat bland comedy that plays more like a collection of choppy bits than a movie with a beginning, middle and end.
In keeping with My Big Fat Greek Wedding tradition, if a joke is mildly amusing, it will be repeated until it makes you want to jam your head into the cup holder attached to your stadium seat.

title: Inside Man | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Foster's slick performance as "fixer" Madeleine White adds to the intrigue and suspense, along with the supporting characters...
[A] wily thriller, which revitalizes a familiar premise by turning it inside out.

As unexpected as some of its plot twists is the fact that this unapologetic genre movie was directed by Spike Lee, who has never sold himself as Mr. Entertainment. But here it is, a Spike Lee joint that's downright fun.
Supremely annoying and nonsensical.
A slick, kinetic and relatively straightforward -- which is to say enjoyably twisty-turny -- tranche of cat-and-mouse procedural.

I gloried in the sheer spectacle of Jodie Foster as Madeline White, an exquisitely groomed, fearlessly feline fixer striding on her high heels and her high horse into one supposedly perilous situation after another.
Like everything [Lee] does, it resonates with the buzz and hum of New Yorkers getting on one another's nerves.
It's very satisfying.
Even past the midway point, it's all working -- it's taut, it's funny, it's trenchant, it's stylish. And then it isn't.
Inside Man has an abundance of riches.
Inside Man is a potboiler, but an intriguing one; perhaps Lee should go Hollywood more often.
Inside Man is an exercise in showy, cynical hollowness.
It's a winning contrast of styles as Lee orchestrates one scene after another to contrast Owen's steely resolve, Washington's trained swagger and Foster's venomous insinuation.
Exceptionally well written with clever twists and witty dialogue by first-time screenwriter Russell Gewirtz, Inside Man is adroitly executed by director Spike Lee.
Intercutting post-robbery interrogation scenes with the action at hand, makes Inside Man a substantial and satisfying affair.
Lee seems less interested in scoring easy sociological points than ratcheting up the stakes of Gewirtz's cunning heist scenario, which offers little in the way of wiggle room for latecomers.

Inside Man, a crackling, twisty thriller about a bank heist that shows he [Spike Lee] can make an expensive, mainstream movie that's every bit as well-crafted as the personal, arty films to which he has devoted most of his career.
Lee takes the usual potshots at this stewpot of race, power and politics. Only here it's effective as part of the story, as opposed to when it's wielded like a tire iron in the context of a polemic.
Inside Man may be a genre flick, but its direction is certifiably Lee -- sprinkled with trademark themes and visual cues, including his specialty, the strapped-to-a-factory-belt dolly shot.
Inside Man brings Lee back into the mainstream while still letting him have some fun, and he passes that fun on to the audience.

title: Lil Nas X: Long Live Montero | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “Saying actual words — it’s really hard to do,” Lil Nas X eventually admits. Still, the best parts of this documentary are onstage, where his freedom to be himself tells its own thrilling story.

The job of a good documentary is to speak truths. The job of a music documentary is to do that and mesmerize audiences with alluring vocals, instrumentals, songs and tunes. And in this case, stage performances too... This mus/doc gets the job done.

The result is merely broad, rarely revealing any further details about Lil Nas X’s personal life, his thoughts outside of music, or any component of him that doesn’t exist in the narrowly defined line of the tour.
A fragmented and ultimately pallid portrait of a glittering musician.
He comes on as exactly who he is: the latest star to remake the pop universe, and by the time the film is over it’s hard to imagine the universe without him.

title: Club Zero | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Hausner is clearly talented, and I’m all for a film without easy answers. But I wish this one was less insistently opaque.
Hausner's new film, "Club Zero," is an intense entry in her exploration of ideas run amok, of fantasy overtaking reality to the degree that reality itself is called into question.
No matter where audiences sit on the political spectrum, they’re liable find something discomfiting, if not enraging, in the film.
A horror film told in bright lights and marzipan colors, a dark comedy that rarely gets around to making you laugh — writer/director Jessica Hausner’s “Club Zero” is a tough nut to crack.
[Hausner] walks the satirical line more successfully, eliciting laughs from the audience during scenes that really should be uncomfortable to watch.

There is no doubt whatsoever that Hausner has a clear artistic vision that she has successfully remained unwaveringly true to here, and while that is in itself impressive it sadly does not make Club Zero any the less impenetrable
That's a lot to digest, and some viewers, like the kids at their mealtimes, will simply refuse to swallow it.

Jessica Hausner’s mannered, deadpan film buries body horror inside a satirical facade, using smart ideas about disordered eating... to tell a story about grasping for transcendence in a frightening, confusing world.
It becomes a sharply-told morality tale, critiquing the relationship vulnerable teenagers have with their bodies, as well as how parents can use their wealth both as weapon and inducement
An eerily appropriate conceptual foundation for a film bound to drive away those not on Hausner’s frequency.

But the intentionally halting, anaesthetic performances and odd pan-European casting strategy makes each family unit feel like a dramatic contrivance – much like the school itself, which never convinces as a real institution...
Club Zero fails to offer anything that its predecessors didn’t provide in more succinct and thoughtful ways.
It’s always been hard not to admire Hausner’s audacity, but this time around the boldness of her storytelling finally spills into trollish provocation.
It looks terrific – as always Hausner’s use of colour and costume is striking and eloquent – but this is a thinly-written picture that operates on a largely superficial level.
The problem here is that the satirical arrows don’t really land because the air is too thick with archness and day-glo irony.
[An] exasperating and baffling movie.
Supremely audacious and disturbing...

title: Junior | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The fact remains that patriarchal comedy is the operative mode here, and every gesture made to alter that is strictly salad dressing.
The wait pays off. When the Big Guy starts showing, and begins to get that radiant glow, Junior hits its mellow, endearing comic stride.
A happy, healthy, bouncing baby of a movie.
The plot is a more fertile ground for comedy than the 'sperm milkshake' that made Schwarzenegger and Danny De Vito brothers in Reitman's Twins.

It's goofy and ridiculous and preposterous, and yet it makes you feel good, and there is something oddly heartwarming about the sight of this macho guy melting with feelings of protectiveness and maternal concern.
Junior is passable entertainment, but it could hardly be called fully developed.
A fleecy romantic caper with a dusting of feminism, the picture is basically a one-joke movie successfully nursed by director Ivan Reitman.
As a comedy, Junior has its share of laughs -- but no more than its share.
For the right audience, Junior may deliver. But there's a whole lot of pregnancy to go through first.

title: The Abyss | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Colossally ambitious, this logistically boggling and technically brilliant film from writer-director James Cameron is a visual tour de force, featuring overall, the greatest underwater sequences ever seen on film.
A firstrate underwater suspenser with an otherworldly twist, The Abyss suffers from a payoff unworthy of its buildup.

The attempt to extract the essences of several genres (cold-war submarine thriller, love story, Disney fantasy, pseudomystical SF in the Spielberg mode) and mix them together ultimately leads to giddy incoherence.
This overlong concoction is scuppered by dire dialogue, histrionic performances and maudlin sentimentality.
Pretty great underwater adventure.
Anyone looking for a discouraging word about this stupendously exciting and emotionally engulfing film should read no further. The Abyss confirms James Cameron as a world-class filmmaker.
I'd sooner believe that Moby Dick could swim up the drainpipe.
The human stuff is more than worth the descent.

title: Loop Track | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film finishes as neither arthouse fish or genre-film fowl (more the latter though). Too bad, because it’s performed with conviction on both the satirical and earnest sides of the spectrum, and Ian is a memorable creation.

title: T.I.M. (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a canny film about the uncanny valley, punctuated by fears that don’t yet have specific names and phobias, including deep-fake horror scenarios and “that feeling when one’s phone shills for something you just thought about”.
Stirs up a hornet’s nest of paranoia about AI and deep fake technology, but then rather misses the point with a clunky cyborg stalker plot.
As unnervingly smart and sinister as its insurgent android, this cautionary tale tests our evolving, inverting relationship with our own tools.
I watched wishing for the Black Mirror version; you would think Charlie Brooker would have done something blackly funny, more profound with a bunny-boiling bot.

title: It Lives Inside (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It Lives Inside at least isn’t just another mainstream horror weepy about grief – there’s a lot more that it’s playing around with...
Some fresh ideas spruce up this horror, but it’s an ambitious debut which forgets that less is more. A lack of focus is the real killer.
The early scares from the debut director Bishal Dutta are eerie and evocative, but once the demon itself appears all bets are off.

While the idea of using a supernatural scary movie as a starting point for exploring the second-gen immigrant experience  is rife with possibilities, the end result here doesn’t necessarily make good on the promise of that premise.

All that really saves It Lives Inside from derivative storytelling beats cribbed from a thousand other horror movies is the cultural specificity of its monster as well as the means by which Sam must ultimately face it.
With major deficiencies like plot, themes, and tension holding Dutta’s film back, “It Lives Inside” is merely average on the outside.

Dutta, making his feature film directorial debut, zeroes in on a thread of displacement and assimilation as felt through the immigrant experience, but the metaphor makes for odd bedfellows with the literal monster that is stalking around.
This first feature from the young Indian-American writer-director Bishal Dutta is an intermittently interesting example of the genre, though not an especially skilful one.
It’s a promising debut from Dutta, who offers a fresh premise that proves a natural fit for the genre.
The potency of It Lives Inside — and why it might be worth checking out even if it isn’t wholly satisfying — lies in how it introduces Sam and Tamira’s relationship and links it to Hindu lore.

Something new -- new faces, new themes, a promising filmmaker to watch -- but I wish it would have embraced more of the things that make it unique as opposed to trying to fit in with its genre brethren.

Some of Dutta’s of-the-moment metaphor horror might be blunt but it’s also, in some scenes, bluntly effective as well as effectively dour, his film climaxing with an unsurprising yet unnerving endnote.

A litany of jolt-focused dream sequences do little to escalate the tension or advance the plot, and Dutta hasn’t developed a deep enough skill set for the scares to be as specific to his movie as Sam’s fears are to her immigrant experience.
It Lives Inside is carried by innovative horror imagery, a well-constructed script and great central performances that hold the emotional heart of the story.
One of the better PG-13 horrors of late, it ekes sufficient menace from the familiar story gist of a consuming demonic presence passed from one beleaguered victim to another.
The demon here serves as a perfect metaphor for the film’s frustratingly nebulous qualities.

It Lives Inside plays fairly conventionally with horror’s familiar codes and conventions, the incorporation of Hindu folklore in a story that is fundamentally built around the immigrant experience breathes new life into the otherwise hackneyed storyline.
I kept actively trying to like “It Lives Inside.” It kept pushing me out.

Dutta uses a familiar framework of teen horror as an accessible introduction to underexplored mythology exacerbated by a cultural divide. The gnarly new demon and the complexities of the characters mark this director as one to watch.

title: Solo (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s an uncomfortable watch at times: sharply written and compellingly acted, Simon’s fracturing sense of self and disintegrating confidence is heartbreaking to behold.
“Solo” both honors and transcends its subject matter in its widely evocative, deeply affecting character study — while also happening to have an absolutely banging soundtrack.
“Solo” avoids tired tropes and celebrates drag itself (the scenes of both stars performing are outstanding) and those who step out on the stage while dealing with their own struggles and desires.

As the film’s title reminds us, at the center of Solo is the question not just of what can Glory Gore achieve as a solo performer up on stage but of what Simon can become when he stands on his own (alone, if not lonely) in his life.
Director Sophie Dupuis blends queer euphoria with toxic love in a French-Canadian love letter to drag that skirts past cliche in favour of nuanced celebration.
At its heart is a reverence for the art and culture of drag, and the ambition of “Solo” is an exciting preview to what bother Dupuis and Pellerin have to offer.

Simon’s drag spectacles may be intentionally fierce and operatic, but there’s something refreshing about this drama’s intimate scale and lack of interest in sweeping tragedies, especially in the context of queer cinema.
Despite its intermittent similarities to dated dramas about sad gay guys yearning to be loved, Solo clearly comes from a place of authentic feeling, with characters that never ring false.
A dexterous film that combines bold images with the quiet beat of a heart torn asunder two ways.
Showing equal care for both the dazzling drag performances and the more delicate moments in the film, Dupuis delivers a beautiful reflection of the human spirit.

title: The Re-Education of Molly Singer | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: An ultra-formulaic comedy with maybe a couple mildly funny lines.
Bawdy, insightful, and full of heart, The Re-Education of Molly Singer gets a gold star on its report card.
An unfunny, bloated, and often needlessly cruel spin on what could have been a fluffy little comedy with some genuine life lessons to spare.

title: Deliver Us (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The consistent volatility of “Deliver Us” casts a wonky spell.

title: All Fun and Games | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: All Fun and Games doesn’t use this backstory to complicate or deepen the terrors of its present action... It just stabs itself in the foot and then struggles to run towards its finish line after a strong if straightforward opening act.

title: Pet Sematary: Bloodlines | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A crisp and efficient reminder of King’s line “Sometimes, dead is better,” and that occasionally, sometimes prequels are too.
Not even the jump scares work, in other words, leaving little but sudden jolts of ghoulish carnage to keep the audience awake.
A prequel wanted by few and needed by none.
Bloodlines’ most criminal offense is squandering the talents of David Duchovny.
Cool as the concept of a magic graveyard that brings beloved pets and, later, not so lovely people back from the dead may be, this remains second-rate King movie material.

It’s a prequel that doesn’t care for tidy canon; the aim is to use these familiar characters and the setting to induce scares. It's not helped by editing that feels like much of this choppy story was left on the editing room floor.
“Who asked for this?” is the question such projects invoke, and Lindsey Anderson Beer’s film never comes up with a satisfying answer.

title: Mob Land | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: In the world of Mob Land, nothing good lasts. Disappointingly, despite the cast’s best efforts and a few striking visual flourishes, nothing good lasts in the film itself either.

Mob Land is going all in on the deep southern gothic atmosphere. It’s just a pity that the acting is so conspicuously effortful, the plot is formulaic and the pacing drags like a wounded pig at a hog shoot.
Tired, perhaps, but still brutally effective at times.
Mob Land has sincerity, but it can’t beat a bad case of genre fatigue.
Well, it all hangs together and the final shot rounds it off nicely enough.
I'm watched this movie waiting for it to get bad, but it never does.

Mob Land never quite reaches the heights of the films that inspired it. While Maggio succeeds at painting a tragic backdrop with his drug-addled town, the straightforward revenge story offers audiences little to think about beyond standard tropes.
Echoes of 'No Country for Old Men' reverberate throughout Nicholas Maggio’s rural noir thriller.
John Travolta’s scenes are islands of tranquility in a jittery sea of rote crime-movie pyrotechnics.

title: Megalomaniac | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s a tough but well-made film that raises provocative questions that are certain to make everyone in the audience uncomfortable, as they should.
Writer/Director Karim Ouelhaj crafts extreme confrontational horror that aims to offend as much as it does evoke wrath and societal reflection. It’s at once compelling and uncomfortable to watch.
While it’s undoubtedly an effectively nasty horror picture, linking this inventively unpleasant scenario to an actual case which claimed the lives of five women is perhaps in questionable taste.

title: North of Normal | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Stone handles big and difficult emotions on the gentlest terms.

title: Dead Shot | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's well-paced, very well-acted, and the story itself has a little more depth than just a straight action film because it has a personal edge to it.
The characters are underwritten and the performances underpowered.
[The Guard brothers] bring alarming amounts of precision to a project that could easily have been bogged down in telly drama miserabilism.

Dead Shot could be considered a kind of “Trouble-sploitation” cinema, leveraging street warfare and terror for action gambits and suspense. But the story’s uncompromising ending cuts deep, leaving one off-balance — pulp with a sting in the tail.
If the trajectory feels a bit preordained by dramatic convention, there are still stinging twists in store, especially in the last few minutes.

title: Beaten to Death | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's just 92 minutes of tediously gratuitous suffering that makes you feel like you owe any movie ever dubbed "torture porn" an apology.
No matter the response Beaten to Death elicits in its viewer, there’s no question that filmmaker Sam Curtain delivers a discomforting gauntlet of extreme horror.

title: Haunting of the Queen Mary | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There’s some real dramatic heft at play here – but the bloated running time drags it down, and lots of spooky business in the back half might have been better jettisoned overboard to gain speed.

title: Mother, May I? | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Vannicelli doesn’t quite pull everything together in the last act, but there’s an immense amount of craft on display as well as some terrific acting from the two leads who play off one another so well.
It’s a handsome-looking ghost story, about a man who was haunted by his mother even when she alive.

title: Where the Devil Roams | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Where the Devil Roams may be the family's most complete movie, and its febrile and claustrophobic horrors will sneak into your nightmares.
Their collective filmmaking eye is still so compellingly intentional and full of riches ... the Adams are so gifted at filming bleak Americana, corpses, cloudy days, and rotting hands.

As Where the Devil Roams proves once again, through their collective artistry and shared passion, the Adams Family create uniquely authentic films that contain a sense of creativity and a love for movies that at its heart remains unwaveringly pure.

title: Buck Alamo or (A Phantasmagorical Ballad) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's really Davis' nuanced performance that anchors Buck's story in heartbreak.

title: Maxine's Baby: The Tyler Perry Story | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It has a smidge of depth and takes chances that similarly worshipful documentaries probably wouldn't. But it also cracks a lot of doors without actually opening them up and walking through.
Gelila Bekele and Armani Ortiz's uplifting portrait puts Tyler Perry's career in its proper context, stressing how faith and forgiveness account for the outsider creator's success.

title: TAYLOR SWIFT | THE ERAS TOUR | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "Eras Tour" is a wonderful representation of the music, performance and spectacle of Taylor's fabulous show, which, as a concert, sets the bar as high as "Stop Making Sense" did as a concert film.
It's a really good document of a concert. I feel like I have a sense of what it would have been like to see those shows.

It is wildly entertaining but it is also a curious product that speaks to the larger themes of our IP-based age of content – recycled, reused and repackaged spin-offs that find new, often exciting ways to extract consumers.

With its labyrinthine arc, jumbled chronology and dazzling changes of tone, milieu and costume, it’s Swift’s ode to invention and self-reinvention, the many different lives she’s lived and faces she’s presented over the course of her career.
I couldn’t tell where the crowd noise in the film ended and where the crowd noise around me began.
I did not enter the theater a Swiftie, but I can say with confidence that this immediately goes on the list of great concert documentaries.

As I watched her go through her many eras -- not exactly in order, but expertly paced -- I respect how she’s able to seamlessly weave between fantasy and reality, between the personas she puts on as a front and the ones that allow her to feel seen.
Swift’s command of her audience—and of the moment—is so complete that she instantaneously airbrushes every questionable filmmaking decision into oblivion.
For the devoutly faithful who want to remember what it was like to be in an arena with their idol, or want to feel that communion for the first time, Eras is a formidable kind of merch.
What it reveals about her artistry only heightens my appreciation for the substance and the imagination that goes into the making—indeed, the being—of this pop superstar.
A showcase for the pen and pain that animate Swift’s finest compositions, the fuel that keeps the pistons in her well-oiled business apparatus pumping year after year.
Better than a Swiftie’s wildest dreams.

For Swifties and newbies, here's the musical event  of the movie year, And, yes, you can dance to it as the pop princess shows off her talent for artistic reinvention and a matchless gift for storytelling in song. What's not to like?
Watching the film feels like attending an Eras concert all over again. Or for the first time, if you couldn’t get tickets. Which is kind of the whole point.

One of the delights of “The Eras Tour” is that it makes moviegoing a contact, call-and-response sport, with audiences literally dancing in the aisles and waving at the screen as if their idol can see them.
As fan service, and as a bypass of the conventional Hollywood movie distribution model, “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” has done the job.
It’s an impressive, career-spanning feat from one of our most notable performers that’s worth seeing on the biggest screen you can.

You don’t have to be cray-cray for Tay-Tay to enjoy The Eras Tour. Taylor’s version of a concert flick might not reinvent the music movie wheel but, as a gift to the hardcore or a primer to her immense talent, it works a treat.
The former child star belongs on stage. With Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour, she owns the big screen too.
Simply as a technical spectacle, “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” is a dazzling achievement, capturing the sensation of seeing the pop goddess’ sold-out concerts in all their enormity and intimacy.

title: We Dare to Dream | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: As an uplifting portrait of human endeavour against the odds, this is hard to beat.

It’s a gripping watch, regardless of whether or not you know the outcome. Watching these committed athletes is intensified by the knowledge of what they have been through to survive, let alone become world class Olympians.
We Dare to Dream keeps a determinedly wide lens. Even so, some details inevitably slip out of frame. But this deeply bittersweet film still contains a wealth of powerful stories.
The film is a powerful antidote to the narrative that refugees are nothing but a drain on resources.

title: Society of the Snow | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: J.A. Bayona's film captures the horrors of a plane crash in the Andes as well as the resilience of the human spirit.
This is a hard movie to watch, but that's because it's an honest depiction of a harrowing ordeal.
Bayona ensures this is now the definitive version of this air disaster.
[The characters] didn't pop out to me as individual personalities... but as far as the craft of this movie, it's exceptional.
I thought it was super well done, and it was very, very tense.
As a film that attempts to honor its victims while simultaneously offering graphic details, it both improves upon previous iterations of the material and exposes the limits of the story itself.

This faithful version from Spanish filmmaker J.A. Bayona (The Impossible) is a survival procedural suffused with technical challenges, moral struggle and spiritual reckoning... Bayona has made horror films, but this is not one.
Bayona’s direction accentuates the personal despair, not the horror. He exposes the danger, making it look formidable, but not insurmountable. The ensemble cast shines under his guidance.
The film is very straightforward and earnest... And there is something more moving about seeing this performed by people who actually are Spanish and more authentic to the characters.
No film could fully capture the awfulness of this experience. But despite some of Bayona’s irksome flair, Society of the Snow does a sturdy enough job getting the point across.
Not since Martin Scorsese's Silence has a film so effectively asked us to consider whether faith is benevolence or a blight.
Shouldn’t a true story of life, death, and cannibalism be a little more gripping?
Bayona's approach allows these philosophical and moral questions space to breathe.

As earnest as this new production is, whether that’s enough to make the case for watching it once, much less sitting through a reprise for those who have seen “Alive,” feels, frankly, like a pretty tall mountain to climb.

Society of the Snow is realist cinema on a formidable level of execution, yet it’s troubling to think of such formidable technical expertise being used to minutely recreate real-life horror as Sensurround-type spectacle.
[Bayona's] finest film to date, and a fitting tribute to those who both perished and managed to escape their fateful mountain tomb.
“Society of the Snow” is a perverse movie to watch the way most people will see it — on Netflix, in the comfort of their homes, with a refrigerator nearby.
It may be the best version of this saga told so far. Still, it feels incomplete and doesn’t dig deeper even as it hints at greater pathos beneath the surface.
For all the sensationalism of what was a very real ordeal, any accounting of it requires respect, both for the dead and for the living. Mr. Bayona more than meets that standard.
Though “Society of the Snow” has its moments, it’s difficult to see what was gained by telling the story as a dramatic feature.

title: The Imaginary | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: With no Ghibli film in the offing, The Imaginary is an often delightful way to fill the anime gap.

The movie falters periodically under the weight of its own dream logic, which can be hard to follow or flimsily constructed as the story gains momentum. But it’s mostly easy to move past those flaws in a work of such rich magical realism and heart.
A single frame of “The Imaginary” can outshine the mass-produced, visually uninspired animation in some of the American offerings targeting the same demographic.

At a time when digital animation is breaking radical new ground, it can be tempting to view the hand-drawn sort as its old-fashioned forebear... But Momose’s film elegantly proves otherwise: it has the artistry, but also the visionary spark.
The Imaginary may not be a standout in the rich and wide-ranging oeuvre of its makers, but it is a moving and charming testament to the delights of dreaming.
It should be no surprised that a movie called The Imaginary all but erupts with whimsical ideas, and on that front, this fanciful offering works. But it falls short in other fundamental ways.

Nishimura litters his screenplay with poignant insights about the power of enterprising play that will inspire audiences of all ages to remember a time when they needed only to rely on their minds to conjure new worlds and scenarios.
The Imaginary is an enchanting tale in which reality clashes with imagination in a battle to determine which is more powerful.
This adaptation of A.F. Harrold’s 2014 children’s book is an appealing, emotionally engaging fantasy; the art direction is intricate and exquisite.
This is a poignant, visually pleasant film that animation fans can appreciate, with a healthy dose of age-appropriate terror to ensure kids won’t forget it for a long time.

The Imaginary isn’t as visually or narratively rich as Studio Ponoc's previous film, or as transcendent as Miyazaki's Boy and the Heron. But it does feel like a move in the right direction for Ponoc, an effort at finding its own voice and its own footing.
