A diverting enough entertainment from a group that has repeatedly proven itself to be capable of much more.
The frustrating thing is that Marshall, Herlihy and especially Higgins really are funny, and the film has some huge laughs. That’s enough for a sketch show. It’s not quite enough for a film.
As comedy writers and movie actors, the members of Please Don’t Destroy – Martin Herlihy, John Higgins and Ben Marshall – are out of their depth.
While the group’s short SNL videos are often quite amusing, this feature-length venture doesn’t do them any favors.

title: The Invisible Fight | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: For wuxia fans unconvinced by the shift from Buddhism to the Bible, Sarnet inserts a reading of Matthew 14:26 to remind us that walking on water is a skill shared by both Jet Li and Jesus.
Writer-director Rainer Sarnet’s deliriously weird The Invisible Fight would be irksome if it weren’t crafted so lovingly and with a charming earnestness.

It’s a wacky and frequently nonsensical mish-mosh of elements that don’t quite add up, and yet, the absurdist shock of seeing such incongruous ingredients forced together is typically enough to spark laughter.

title: Trunk - Locked In | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Oh, it’s preposterous, but there are enough unexpected turns in the plot to keep you guessing as you bite those nails down to the quick.

title: Hannah Waddingham: Home for Christmas | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s the least contentious show you could put on during the holiday season, and thankfully succinct.

The extravaganza works through good cheer and the sheer force of Waddinghamness, and at 45 minutes it mercifully doesn’t outstay its welcome... though, should be warned: it really is as cheesy as a baked stilton soufflé.
Home for Christmas sees a consummate pro get the stage she deserves. Up next? World domination, presumably, but I hope she gets a chance to have a little nap first.
The singer, evidently, has always wanted to sing these songs, and isn’t that how singers should make you feel?
This is very gentle, very showbiz, very glittering. The jokes are warm, not hot, but everyone laughs heartily, buoyed by the high spirits around them.

title: Frybread Face and Me | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: We often talk about making films that attempt to find the universal in the local. In the particularity of the Native American experience in Frybread lies the ubiquity of a larger human truth that keeps on echoing in the mind long after the film is over.
Luther’s film may be built on his own coming of age, but there’s both specificity and universality to this story, something for everyone who was ever a kid, Native or not, to connect with.
The movie is overfamiliar and earnest, but you can’t accuse it of not being heartfelt.
[The] film’s gentle approach to storytelling ... and unhurried affect imbues small moments with outsized significance.
Gentle comfort is something the entire world is in need of these days, and “Frybread Face and Me” delivers that in abundance.

Writer/director Billy Luther's warm, tender, and funny debut "Frybread Face and Me," which was executive produced by Taika Waititi, explores the humor and joy in finding your footing with family and the strength that comes from embracing your heritage.

Watching this family interact is a reminder how rare it is to see so many American indigenous actors in a space, weaving the unique and universal into stories that expand our storehouse of their experience.
What Frybread Face and Me lacks in drama, it makes up for in a boundless affection for its characters and an appreciation for the everyday details of their lives.

title: Night of the Hunted (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [You] might enjoy yourself if you’re eager to watch a symbolically vague killer torment yet another sobbing but resilient woman-shaped thought experiment.
Night of the Hunted may fall a bit short of moral substance, but it certainly holds us in its grip.

title: Sister Death | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Is it about a supernatural thing? Yes. What it's really about, though? War, injustice, and cruelty.
Strong enough to be a satisfying watch but not quite able to stand on its own without its superior predecessor, Sister Death is regardless a fun Halloween Netflix essential.

title: Candy Cane Lane | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It does stand out in one area, offering more product placement than any movie in recent memory. It's all very sad.
Reginald Hudlin’s film is self-aware, but it’s very broad and in trying to do too much achieves little.

The best scenes have nothing to do with Christmas, such as Chris and Carol expressing their love and support for each other, and the children telling their father that he’s parenting for himself not them.
“Candy Cane Lane” shows you that the Christmas movie as we’ve known it may be all used up, and that it has now entered its anything-goes surrealist phrase. ‘Tis the season to be batty.
For the most part, though, it’s an exercise in holiday magic that barely musters a spark, executed in such by-the-numbers fashion even a closing outtakes sequence doesn’t yield any laughs.
A frenzied family friendly film as overstuffed as a Christmas stocking, as nutty as a chestnut, and, ultimately, as warm as an open fire.

Murphy gives a lower-key, nearly anti-less performance than we’ve seen from him in the past, letting the concept and the special effects take the lead, with him grounding the fantasy by focusing on Chris as a devoted father.
A madcap medley of deranged ideas that somehow manage to coalesce into a messy but half-decent Crimbo comedy. Just spare a thought for the far more interesting horror film straining to break through.

The bizarro plot might help Candy Cane Lane stand out from the bland, busy crowd of new seasonal movies but it’s just as limp and lacking in spirit as the rest of them. Murphy and Ross deserve better, and so do we, and so does Christmas.
The main thing to say about “Candy Cane Lane” is that Eddie Murphy is funny in it.
It’s all fine. Murphy is so much more than that. Or used to be. You like to think that, given the right material, he will be again. Now that would be a gift.
“Candy Cane Lane” is a stunningly uneven film that careens between cornball family drama, slapstick comedy and special-effects-laden gimmickry.
You want to see Eddie Murphy surrounded by some Christmas-themed silliness. And on that score, it’s fine enough, but destined for regifting.

The result swings between manic and sedative, though not always unpleasantly. The saving graces are a zesty Ellis Ross and the enigma that is Murphy, an actor whose comic timing is still casually brilliant.
The narrative careens through uncompelling territory before ending on a forgettable note.
[It] isn’t a chore or a travesty or anything. But certainly, it’s less than Murphy deserves.

title: Raging Grace | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Peel back the cliches and there’s something interesting here: a gnawing sense of injustice and biting social commentary.
Zarcilla strains so hard to match the politics of the premise with the parameters of horror that he ends up diluting both — imagine Roma meets Poltergeist, or The Maid meets Insidious.
Zarcilla may have more ideas than this film can easily accommodate, or the viewer easily swallow, but he is a distinctly stylish and confident director to keep an eye on.
There is ingenuity here, and good acting, but the film for me feels flawed by its strained melodrama, an absence of scares and by a very odd scene of almost unreal, farcical absurdity.
The final act doesn’t quite hold together, but the overall intent is more than effective.
In his feature debut, writer and director Paris Zarcilla proves he is a master storyteller.
It’s refreshing to see a first feature which isn’t just a calling card, but driven by an authentic need to find a fresh angle on representing an undervalued cultural heritage.
Paris Zarcilla’s debut is carried by the strength of its cultural specificity, perspective, and lead performers.
Raging Grace is too gleefully ridiculous to live up to its didactic ambitions, and too on-the-nose to let its wings of crushed velvet madness truly spread.

Paris Zarcilla, the British-born Filipino writer-director here making his feature debut, does an impressive job of infusing scary movie conventions with the potent urgency of a sharply observed social critique.
Gets its message across despite all the jump-scares and haunted house hysteria.

title: The Marvels | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Unlike the more recent superhero movies that are lengthy and burdened by questions about origin and identity, The Marvels is a breezy entertainer that does not doesn’t take itself too seriously...
Brie Larson leads a super-trio that works hard to blast some fun into this confusing adventure.
While the titular Marvels make for an endearing, women-centric found family, the film’s hyperawareness of its role in a larger universe is its downfall.
It’s silly and makes little sense, but it’s such a fun time at the movies. And isn’t that why we go to see movies in the first place?
DaCosta made room for The Marvels to be bright and playful, filled with characters that are impossible not to love.
You get the sense that everyone involved is going through the motions.

The Marvels is a vibrant and well paced film that's packed with extremely well photographed and choreographed action. It's also brimming with cast chemistry, and rocks a narrative that builds the team *and* the characters as individuals.

Pleasurably lightweight, its story unburdened by the off-screen drama of the studio that made it. The shortest film in the MCU at a runtime of 105 minutes, this sprightly sequel to 2019’s Captain Marvel operates like a breezy road-trip comedy.
This wobbly addition to the overall saga does not pass muster as either a sequel to the 2019 Captain Marvel solo outing or a sum-of-its-parts team-up.

What “The Marvels” has going for it, apart from a 105-minute running time... is the energizing presence of Canada’s Iman Vellani as Kamala Khan, Marvel’s first Muslim superhero. She’s almost enough to save a movie that ultimately is beyond redemption.
The good stuff in The Marvels has been hacked and slashed within an inch of its life.

The Marvels maintains its structure and doesn’t try to function as a springboard to the next Marvel movie or television show. The Marvels gets the space to let the characters just be themselves and for us to better understand what makes them heroes.
It's unfair how much this movie leans on the genuinely joyous Iman Vellani to liven up the incomprehensible mess created by corporate filmmaking and multiverse-wide IP-fracking.

Star Brie Larson seems pretty checked out here — almost as checked out as the jokers who came up with the idea of once again tapping the Beastie Boys for the soundtrack. “Hey, they’re on a spaceship! Let’s use ‘Intergalactic!’”

Poised between goofy and godawful and plagued by rewrites and reshoots, this 33rd entry in the Marvel cinematic universe is in serious disrepair. The MCU, once the spawner of glories, is stuck in a rut. The time for a rethink is now.
In a universe where the movies last well over three hours, the 105 minute runtime of “The Marvels” is as welcome as it is surprising.

DaCosta delivers a family-friendly interplanetary frolic (complete with an impromptu Gilbert and Sullivan-like musical sojourn) filled to the brim with colorful visuals, strong special effects, character-driven humor, and exciting action sequences.
A large portion of The Marvels feels designed to troll the fanboys, and god bless DaCosta for that.
The superhero is as bored as we are, but the Marvel machine grinds on.

The Marvels feels safely bland at a time when Marvel needs to take some chances. Because despite featuring a space-faring hero who can majestically streak into the stars, those heroics come in a movie that only intermittently gets off the ground.

title: Dark Harvest | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Visually clever and directed with giddy, B-movie ferociousness by Hard Candy and 30 Days of Night impresario David Slade, this slick slice of blood-splattered Halloween carnage is worth knocking on doors to see.
Slade's film isn’t too grave about leaving a lasting effect, but it does not take itself seriously enough.
Too silly for words -- a slasher movie with delusions of Shirley Jackson grandeur.
It may not make for requisite annual viewing, but its fearless commitment to slaughtering teens against a cozy Fall backdrop at least makes for a fun enough watch as you carve up jack-o’-lanterns.

title: Role Play (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: French director Thomas Vincent’s feature is lacking in laughs, a genuine marital dynamic, and decent action sequences.

Like a guy at a bar telling you a very long joke. You laugh politely each time the story seems to be winding up, which it isn’t, until the fellow brings things to a close by telling you his house burned down just after he made the last mortgage payment.
Director Thomas Vincent plays it safe which, for an action comedy hinging on the sexy fascination of spying, makes for a flaccid film all around.
The consequence of this confused, jittery writing is a plot-focused sprint that misses every chance to indulge in its content, be it action, comedy, or heart.

Cuoco’s well-honed comic skills are very much on display and Oyelowo, working in a lighter vein than usual, seems to be enjoying himself. Which is more than you’ll be able to say about the viewers of this tired action-comedy retread.
Remains a fun if derivative diversion throughout.
One is quick to forgive faulty plot machinations when an action movie really revs; “Role Play” merely spins its wheels.
What follows is exactly what one would expect – a shootout, a chase, a shadowy organisation – but never enough of what one wouldn’t, a familiar mish-mash in need of a persuaive reason to exist.

title: Hanky Panky | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Hanky Panky is a delightfully unserious horror movie crammed with comedy.
Proudly a B-movie, this gleefully silly slasher plays like the best stoner comedies, offering a world where paranoia is justified and getting high is downright heroic.

title: The Archies | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Writers Kagti, Akhtar and Ayesha Devitre build specificities of the Anglo-Indian community into the narrative.
The movie looks great, it's conceptually interesting, and it has several memorable moments. But it's also interminable.
The Archies humanizes them by giving them humanity...
“The Archies” succeeds by not overthinking its very existence.

It’s an extravagant stunt perked up by moments of absurdity. Reggie invents beat-boxing; the kids applaud a quote from Jean-Luc Godard: “Cinema is truth 24 times a second.” Mostly, however, it’s rote shtick.
A guilt-free pleasure that’s nevertheless super-corny and ridiculous.

title: Fingernails | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This low-key romance is an anti-dote to the dating apps.
This is an affecting romance and a work of compelling social commentary. That's a noteworthy achievement.
It's a really interesting concept that they explore in understated ways.
It’s an exceptional cast, and they fill out the premise with subtle inflections and authentic desire -- the romantic wins out.
Nikou’s sci-fi drama is more failed experiment than a fine, or redefining, romance.
Fingernails won’t satisfy both hearts and minds at the level of its masterful predecessors, but Nikou has written and directed a moving, thought-provoking film.
The restrained performances reflect the emotional numbness of this life.

That provocative element is in those touches where it references other films... when our relationships don't seem to match what we see in those films, when the feelings aren't as strong or as definitive, that's when the doubt creeps in.
For all its whimsy, Fingernails is delicately profound. Its characters aren’t making bold romantic moves; they’re interrogating their assumptions of what is ultimately an unknowable phenomenon.
“Fingernails” won’t be for all tastes, but I found this gracefully acted, lightly dusted sci-fi drama to be one of the most refreshing films about love in a while.

I’d happily watch Buckley and Ahmed read the phone book; they both possess the kind of pensive eyes and ambiguous half-smiles that serve as catnip to funny-sad auteurs. But, like Anna, you can’t help but want a bit more eventually, too.

It’s an interesting premise, the performances are strong and it’s a tight, disciplined story that doesn’t tangent off. But it can feel a little cold even though the always wonderful Jessie Buckley has good chemistry with Riz Ahmed.
Fingernails lacks the leak-proof internal logic that’s necessary to persuade an audience to fully commit to an outlandish central premise.
Nikou’s film is wonderfully astute on love’s unruliness: it wants you to both delight in and despair of it, and have fun doing both.
The Institute of Love plot here, the narrative body of the movie, is mostly pointless and sometimes grating.
Fingernails is funny until it’s not: deeply romantic from the top of your head to the end of your fingernails.

But analogue passion needs a better advert than Anna and Amir. Their will-they-won’t-they might leave you shrugging. And wondering when Hollywood forgot how to make love stories big enough for movies.
Fingernails delivers a beautiful and eccentric articulation of the painstaking feeling of throwing yourself into the romantic unknown.
The film is successful because it manages to create its own logical, nonsensical rules, which love then snaps.
It’s not the familiarity of this setup that irks, but its silliness.

title: Your Lucky Day | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The heart is in the right place for Your Lucky Day, but the execution is a little loose.
It's thrilling and suspenseful, with enough twists to keep you guessing, but the pointed commentary is impossible to ignore.
The film coasts far on the pleasant surprise of some sharp plotting.
Writer-director Daniel Brown’s crime drama is deceptively simple with a beer case’s worth of twists, most of which are unpredictable but make perfect character sense as they unfold.

Brown uses it to craft an intense siege thriller filled with characters making surprising choices and moral concessions. Anchored by Garza’s charismatic, primal turn, Your Lucky Day makes for an impressive debut that’ll leave you on edge.

Your Lucky Day moves along at an engaging pace throughout, although it doesn't reach its brutal potential as a thriller until two-thirds of the way through. Up to that point, it's burdened by clumsy repetition of its central theme.

title: The Sacrifice Game | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A perfect present for horror fans, a bloody homage to ‘70s horror and the tropes that defined it.

Chunky and imperfect, the over-the-top mashup of horror tropes is surprising enough to make streaming it at home feel engrossing, and imaginative enough to feel original in a seasonal subgenre with a limited window to find its audience.
“The Sacrifice Game” wouldn’t feel like such a lumpy blend of genre conventions if its creators remixed the past with greater conviction or technical finesse.
Wexler and Sean Redlitz's script proves strongest when it can be as bonkers as it likes.
Narrative turns, characters that challenge perceptions, and slasher-like bloodletting yield a devilishly fun new entry in holiday horror.

title: Eileen | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A psychological thriller fashioned as a bleak coming-of-age story, this adaptation by author Ottessa Moshfegh and her husband, Luke Goebel, of her breakthrough 2015 novel, works hard to capture the mordant detail and interior unease of the text.
Bound by the events of the novel but absent its enjoyably sociopathic sense of personality, it hits its marks and quietly trails off to nowhere: a trajectory unworthy of its protagonist.
This adaptation of Ottessa Moshfegh’s novel is not a story of repression, but something more prickly, more envious, and more dangerous.
Finding the right ending remains one of the most difficult and persistent challenges in telling a story, so filmmakers deserve some latitude in carving one out, but they rarely miss this badly.
Eileen is triumphant, a rousing directorial success from Oldroyd.
It feels like we’re watching a Todd Haynes film as filtered through the lens of a Hitchcockian tale, with a late-story development that’s bat-bleep crazy but also gripping.
It looks great, it sounds nice, the performances are solid, but none of the choices feel inspired by character or story.
Eileen may ultimately be a little thin, but it’s a bracing watch, powered not just by its two main performances but also by Ireland...
Ultimately, I respected the dramatic destination at which the film arrived, but I kept asking myself if the trip was really necessary. Sometimes you admire a movie more than you like it.
It's stylish, intense, and sexy -- until it Isn't.
A lot of the the pieces are good. They just don't fit together.
It's moody and beguiling, but it doesn't fully deliver on its promise.
Eileen hits you at the two-thirds point with a huge surprise — it’s not a wowza, and it works, as does just about everything else in this demented and twisty thriller.
The thrill of Eileen lies in how McKenzie plays off the film’s inciting spark, a blonde-bobbed enigma played by Anne Hathaway.
A film that is by turns darkly comic and disturbing, both sensations brought into vivid, caustic relief by the film’s mesmerizing star.
The always-good Marin Ireland nearly explodes the film's fabric in her one scene, her trauma so authentic it rips the mask off of all Rebecca's supposedly good intentions.
“Eileen” is a weird little movie. I like weird little movies.
Is this lurid pulp, or something more elevated? The director, and his writers, cannot quite seem to come to an agreement.
McKenzie begins to flex even more of her extremely well-honed actorly chops, Hathaway shows us that her ice-cold-blonde exterior houses an even chillier soul.
Hathaway is magnetic, purring her way around the baked-in misogyny of the potato-faced local men. But then a third-act tonal shift knocks the whole film off balance.

title: Tiger Stripes | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Amanda Nell Eu’s feature debut is a lively coming-of-age story that mixes the mundane and the supernatural with ease.
Eu smartly weaves that universality together with local myths and legends, and the result is a little eerie and unsettling, a film about dark things we’re afraid to speak about.
The message is not always clear, but it’s an entertaining ride.
Eu smartly keeps a distance between the two sides of the story, before drawing them together in mystery and violence.
From the exuberant credits and opening sequence through to the end, “Tiger Stripes” is the work of a confident new talent whose next work will be eagerly awaited.

The drama of girlhood is familiar cinematic territory, and though it might garner a smaller audience than Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret or You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah, Tiger Stripes is a welcome addition to the pack.
[A] well-observed, fiercely female-centred coming-of-age drama.
The performances the director gets from her young cast are tremendous and it is terrifically shot.

title: The Exorcist: Believer | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There are moments in this borderline incoherent mess of a movie in which fans may be convinced that its sole purpose is to try making the original follow-up, 1977’s legendarily godawful Exorcist II: The Heretic, look positively genius by comparison.
They need to stop making Exorcist movies. We don't need any more!

A rock solid first half -- character-driven, strong build of dread, and successful at conveying the sheer terror of watching a loved one, especially a child, slip away & feeling helpless in the fight to get them back. But then it becomes a forced sequel.
It never gets close to recreating the miasmic chill of William Friedkin’s 1973 classic, or generating any fresh frights of its own.
...  To tackle a prestige project that’s steeped in Christian iconography and biblical allusions by simply defanging it with kindness is beyond pointless.

It requires a rare ineptitude to take what is famously one of the most terrifying movies ever made, recycle pretty much everything (including Tubular Bells on the score) but neglect to include the scares.

Much like David Gordon Green’s recent Halloween trilogy, the filmmaker’s attempt to resurrect The Exorcist franchise with The Exorcist: Believer is wildly ambitious. It is also pretty much guaranteed to be equally polarizing.

It’s largely a testament to an almost-50-year-old movie that The Exorcist: Believer delivers so few proper scares, even with an extensive modern-CGI budget and the enthusiastic support of its studio, Universal.
I wouldn’t bet against some future boffin declaring this latest episode an underappreciated classic. It meets all the requirements: it’s terrible; many will certainly fail to appreciate it.
While the elegantly crafted, head-swiveling sequel fails to reach new heights, it delivers on suspense and jump scares, uplifted by returning original cast member Ellen Burstyn, 90!
As a film, it’s at best serviceable, stronger in its world-building than in its climactic exorcism and nowhere near as unnerving as the original.
The build-up to the dual exorcism is so terrible it’s almost funny...
The script is possessed by triteness and the set up is dull.

William Friedkin’s original 1973 take on demonic possession was thrillingly too much. This sorry sequel from David Gordon Green is boringly too little. Believe this: If you let the marketing devils lure you into this one, you’re in for an unholy mess.
Though Green tries all types of terror tactics from sudden jump cuts to graphic gore, there isn’t a single scare in the entire 121-minute runtime.
For most of the running time of "Believer," I was trying to figure out why (other than money) it was made.

Successfully stringing together shocking, disgusting and terrifying moments counts as a solid day’s work for most horror directors, and since The Exorcist: Believer achieves all that it’s competent enough. But I expected better from Mr. Green.
The Exorcist: Believer has its moments, but we’ve had a half-century of this stuff.

Believer is in tortured dialogue with the original Exorcist, attempting to expand that film’s worldview while also paying reverent homage. It seems a bit guilty in its grave robbing -- which is commendable, in a way -- but it’s still doing the robbing.
Between the Burstyn boost, small touches like incorporating the spine-tingling original music “Tubular Bells” and the uneasy first half, The Exorcist: Believer still proves a moderately worthy heir.

title: Silver and the Book of Dreams | Rotten Tomatoes
The Bricklayer (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a lively bullet-riddled adventure that may not stick in the mind, but will leave no one bored for its 110 minutes.

title: The Devil on Trial | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Instead of challenging assumptions, exploring implications or discussing the difficult questions here, Holt merely mines the material for superficial shock value and lurid titillation.
Like everything about this saga, lucid and verifiable specifics are in short supply.

title: Onyx the Fortuitous and the Talisman of Souls | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film knows what it's doing and why it's doing it. It wears its affection on its sleeve.
A handmade horror gem.
Bowser infuses Onyx’s feature film debut with endearing quirkiness, endless ’80s/’90s influences, and horror whimsy.

title: Hopeless | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: While the premise had potential, the execution doesn’t work in tandem with the story,  it draws the audience into 120 minutes of character misery without offering much else.

title: The End We Start From | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film is rarely dull in its sub-two-hour run time, sustaining our curiosity as mother Comer travels across Britain seeking refuge... There are glimmers of a bright future ahead for debut feature director Mahalia Belo.
The film’s quiet strength, in step with Comer’s character, lies in its familiarity.
If the film ends up somewhere a little too neat, Comer makes the journey always worthwhile.
It's a really strong film. Perhaps a little repetitious... But nevertheless the thoughts and the notions going on here are very moving.
A very confident piece of direction from Mahalia Belo.

The concept here is a little more potent than any individual scene, since there’s a tendency to undercut raw emotion with a tidy metaphor. But Comer gracefully draws attention back to the core of Hunter’s story.
The result is the kind of film the UK rarely makes anymore: a clever, propulsive picture with enough mainstream oomph for multiplexes.
The sketchy quality of this material probably worked better on the page than the screen.
More than any other element, it’s Comer that makes “The End We Start From” a success.
Prettily shot and with moments of emotional power thanks to Jodie Comer's performance, The End We Start From is involving and unpredictable, yet strangely cold when it should be searing.
In its relentless focus on Comer's Mother with a capital M, as she is called, I character's almost primal determination, it gets somewhere that feels unforced and, however uneventful, real.
Comer’s vulnerability and idealism are authentic as are her determination and a dash of real ruthlessness... She carries everything with unselfconscious strength and style.
The End We Start From leaves most of its spectacle to the imagination, freeing Belo to train her camera on the whirlwind of emotions that storm across Comer’s face.
“The End We Start From” is an anxiety-inducing experience, not due to loud explosions or effects-driven set pieces, but due to things that feel real and grounded in truthful observations.

The End We Start From isn’t a big, blockbuster disaster movie. It’s quiet and sometimes still and it asks you to think about our existence. But it’s also meaningful, finding unlikely splendor in the midst of destruction.
The End We Start From explores more than motherhood at the end of the world, its subject is every nuance of womanhood at any stage of life.
It’s nourishing, frequently moving, and ends with heroic understatement, where a cruder film would have gone all out for the heartstrings.
The movie’s other strength, besides Comer, is the realism it finds in environmental catastrophe.
Comer’s riveting performance, physically tense with desperation, makes us believe, at least while watching, that we’d do whatever she’s doing.
The film, based on the novel of the same name by Megan Hunter, takes a quiet, emotional approach to the end times, with director Mahalia Belo favoring a meditative visual style.

title: Breakwater (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This twisty tale serves up acting sparks while Rowe injects this Cape Fear-lite effort with welcome doses of dark humor.

title: Share? (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: An ungenerous techno-satire.
The sly “Share?” never overstays its welcome as it wags a finger at social media and does so by giving off the vibe of a shared Zoom-like experience.

title: Lord of Misrule (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: plays out like a reimagining of The Wicker Man, although that film’s uptight male Christian copper has become a laid-back female vicar whose maternal status challenges the original’s patriarchal values.

Director William Brent Bell (best known for the insipid Orphan prequel Orphan: First Kill) can’t work up a proper head of suspense, no matter how many poppets made of human hair and twigs he hangs on trees...
Lord of Misrule can’t fully escape the trappings established by quintessential folk horror films like The Wicker Man, but Bell gives it his all to subvert many of the tropes and make it entertaining.
While the film’s invented version of British folklore gives it some interesting texture and imagery, it lacks a strong point of view.

title: The Mill (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's first-rate genre filmmaking, suspenseful and thoughtful at the same time.
[A] lackluster horror experiment.

The film lacks any well-executed surprises to help it push past one-dimensional satire, and Howery is not strong enough of a dramatic actor to keep a single-setting, single-character film like this consistently engaging.

title: V/H/S/85 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: V/H/S/85 is an absolute blast of gore, laughs, fright, and mayhem.
Truth be told, the only thing stranger than the “V/H/S” franchise waiting six movies to revisit the ’80s is how little it does with the decade when it finally goes there.
Pretty much just a bunch of stuff you’ve seen before, only now with some mildly ironic twists and tweaks to adjust for retrospective tracking.
It relishes its period-specific details while giving the same kind of zippy thrills as great rail runner installments from earlier films.

title: She Is Conann | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: With “She Is Conann,” the writer-director reinforces this fantastical architecture with a clear, propulsive story arc, and the result is his best work to date.
She Is Conann is a politically charged, blood-, sex-, and tears-soaked sword, carving through the helpless arteries to the heart of cinematic mediocrity, and it is Mandico’s strongest vision yet.
It’s more of a fever dream than an actual story, offering a queer counternarrative to the macho vision of the legendary warrior that is as hypnotic as it is gnarly.
Decadent, hermetic, and gleefully hostile to realism, Bertrand Mandico’s film is the cinematic equivalent of a French Symbolist poem.
Those not already on Mandico’s wavelength may find their patience tested, his provocations yielding diminishing returns along the way.

title: Our Son | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: All the characters are rounded, fallible and likable in equal measure, and even if the score is a bit syrupy, it’s a pleasant, engaging watch.
While this New York City-set divorce drama offers enough modern tweaks on a well-worn narrative, its emotional resonance remains elusive, muted even
A simple yet engaging melodrama...
Nothing gels until the 45-minute mark. That’s when the reality of divorce, separating and child custody issue sinks in... Anger, bitterness, sorrow and longing ensue, and the film finds its footing.
There’s too little here to distinguish the film from endless other broken-family dramas that have gone before.

title: Foe (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Paul Mescal and Saoirse Ronan are two of the finest young actors but Foe just doesn't give them their time to shine.
It's suffocating to the point where you're as desperate for an escape from this scorched Earth misery as these characters.
These scenes from a marriage are sometimes evocative, but they don’t tie together.
Overall, the film must be counted as a disappointment, though there are interesting ­elements to this futuristic drama.
A literal and figurative hot mess.
I liked the part where clone Paul Mescal gets shrink-wrapped.

The actors deserve a medal for babbling so much convoluted claptrap with a straight face. Written and directed by Garth Davis from a 2018 novel I never want to read by Iain Reid, Foe is not just a bad dream. It’s a colossal nightmare.
Mescal and Ronan are captivating: her watchful, raw-nerved longing; his stinging sense of betrayal.
It’s an A for effort. But it’s just not enough.
It’s hard not to admire a film that so determinedly zigs when you would expect it to zag.

An emotional, if familiar, take on loyalty and technology in a world where love and survival feel near-impossible. Reid’s writing shines and there’s nobody better than Mescal and Ronan to broadcast heartbreak.
Foe by name, faux by nature.

A sci-fi movie playing in the same sandbox as Blade Runner and Moon, Foe ultimately succeeds as a marriage story about tending to relationships like dying planets, and the people would just as soon abandon their duties to both of those things.
There is an unshakable and electric hum to Foe that ensures director Garth Davis’s work will stay with audiences attuned to its distinct frequency for days, months, perhaps ages.
Davis, though, is shooting for something far grander: a kind of claustrophobic, The Shining-style psychological horror. Sadly he has neither the script nor the imagination to do this.
... The thinness of its plot leaves the film itself feeling somewhat like another’s blank-slate doppelgänger: the mood persuades, but sci-fi cannot live by vibes alone.
A production that unfortunately squanders the talents of Mescal and Ronan and its gorgeous production values.
The whole thing plays like a post-apocalyptic sci-fi flick directed by Terrence Malick: all talk bordering on pretentious poetry and close-ups of body parts.
[Paul Mescal and Saoirse Ronan] give us the lot: tenderness and jealousy, joy and devastation, agonised silences and scorching sex scenes.
We’ve had robo-doppelgänger and bleak futurescapes before but it’s Mescal and Ronan who make this story sing.

title: The Harbinger (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There are flaws, sure, and logical lacunae here and there, but it lingers in the memory long after the final credits roll.
This one slips its claws under the skin and then refuses to retract, latching on in such a way that this vicious chiller leaves a lasting scar.

The Harbinger is the kind of horror movie that becomes personal for each viewer; if one is not afraid of its story's more tangible concepts, Mitton does a credible and careful job of evoking the lasting ethereal ones.

Though their characters aren’t always fully realized in the writing, the actors make it all plausible by emphasizing an understated, everyday quality to figures that might easily have been played in more histrionic keys.

title: Bring Him to Me | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The bag of ensuing twists in “Bring Him to Me” may not entirely redeem the clichés that made them possible, but they do keep one alert.

Bring Him To Me is an impressive drama that prods the psychological side of the criminal underbelly. It takes risks with the characters themselves and with what happens to them. The director does not take the easy way out.

In the same tradition of B-movie abstraction, the main characters are nameless stock types: the Passenger (Jamie Costa) is the fresh-faced kid who’s new to the game, the Driver (Barry Pepper) the cynical old hand.

title: Dangerous Waters (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: An unsubtle and faintly ludicrous outing that at least is never boring.

title: 15 Cameras | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "15 Cameras” lacks the specificity to be either good as satire or an atmospheric mood piece.

title: Everyone Will Burn | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: ... maybe prophecies are sometimes set in place for a reason, and everyone in the little town of León should have burned for being so painfully predictable.
In Hebrero and lead actor Macarena Gómez’s capable hands, Everyone Will Burn offers a devilishly compelling depiction of religious mania run amok.

title: The Loch Ness Horror (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
How the Gringo Stole Christmas | Rotten Tomatoes
Monsters of California | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s a slightly frustrating experience, because the film has got loads going for it but could be just that little bit better.

title: Showdown at the Grand | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Writer/director Orson Oblowitz has lovingly crafted a feature presentation as meta-cinematic as it is nostalgic, conjuring a dying breed of scuzzy old-school cinephilia in an age of digital uniformity.
“Showdown”... provides a good time. That fun will be heightened by whatever knowledge of 1970s and ’80s cult genre films you bring in with you.
[A] misty-eyed, sentimental, sometimes silly love letter to cinema.

title: Suitable Flesh | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This material? Not very strong. These actors? Doing what they can with it and actually getting it to a pretty creepy place.
Lynch never nears the gleefully demented levels of gore and black humor that were Gordon’s hallmarks, but Suitable Flesh is still a fun if relatively mild homage.

There are flashes of HP Lovecraft, but the film is otherwise steeped in tributes to Stuart Gordon, the late king of scuzzy, made-for-VHS horror... Here, that manifests in a splurge of self-parodic fun.

For a movie with such a cluttered, kitchen-sink ramp-up, Suitable Flesh charges to a memorable conclusion that’s perfect for celebratory group viewing, whether at the local multiplex with other die-hard horror fans seeking a seasonal thrill.
Despite its bumpy execution and general thinness, “Suitable Flesh” boasts a playfulness that feels ripe for slicing up and serving anew.
An affectionate homage that captures the psychosexual delirium of its genre inspirations, it’s a throwback chiller steeped in blood, kink, and the terrifying thrill of violation.
It comes off a bit like a revived corpse: It moves, it makes noise, but it isn’t quite the real thing.
Director Joe Lynch haplessly plays much of this supernatural tale as an erotic thriller, the uncertainty of satirical intent leaving his actors looking silly.
While neither particularly profound nor earth-shatteringly scary, “Suitable Flesh” is better than passable grisly horror fun in a very specific tradition.
This is a film about the continuation of an immortal but ever-evolving spirit, and it makes good on that premise inside and out -- entrails and all.
Despite a very game lead performance from Heather Graham, and some amusing 90s-style erotic thriller mannerisms... this left me not knowing quite where to look.
Lynch made a horror-sex-comedy for adults, one in which sexuality isn't something of which to be afraid.
A fun horror flick, one I could imagine finding on VHS in 1989 and losing my mind over.
Lynch captures the humorous, oft-sexy tone of Gordon’s ‘80s/’90s Lovecraftian horror output while putting his own stamp on it through keen instincts and modern storytelling.

title: Locked In (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Aping the format and tease of a novel that you just can’t bear to put down, Locked In is instead a film you wish you would have stopped far earlier.

title: June (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a respectful film, but it does pick a little at the myth of the Johnny’n’June love story.

The bare facts of Carter Cash’s story are such that the filmmakers would have had to really mess up to not produce a movie that entertains and moves a viewer to tears. “June,” rest assured, does the job well.

title: It's a Wonderful Knife | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Sometimes cheap but largely cheerful, this is a fun stocking-filler for horror fans — with plenty of heart to pump all that blood.

But despite a few fun kills, a promising premise, and a few performances that really hit the right tone of the film, it doesn’t live up to those ambitions, a redundant and contrived script holding it back from true slasher glory.
It sort of lurches from moment to moment as far as being dreary and being inspired.
I think it is solidly entertaining.
It’s a Wonderful Knife is just the latest in a string of horror comedies making the same genre jokes Wes Craven did better in the ‘90s.

Long steals the show once again. His have-at-it fun and eerie eyes provide a manic glee that the rest of director Tyler MacIntyre’s oddly tempered slasher riff on Frank Capra’s Christmas classic could stand to match.

Knife speeds through its horror setups without taking time to build actual dread or emotion, leaving behind a trail of cheap, meaningless deaths that hardly seem to impact its heroine, least of all anyone in the audience.
Unfortunately, there are few surprises and only a handful of genuine scares, and the film suffers from subpar lighting and occasionally clunky editing. It’s a “Knife” in need of some sharpening.

The Christmas slasher It’s A Wonderful Knife commits to its pithy premise -- “It’s A Wonderful Life, but with a masked killer” -- with self-aware wit. Solid fundamentals carry the film’s suspense scenes, but the comedy produces more mixed results.
“It’s A Wonderful Knife” has plenty of attributes—charm, blood, and angst—that should fit right in at any family holiday gathering.
This grisly gift was a pleasure to unwrap, a ruby red love letter to both the holiday season and a high-concept horror chestnut that spans multiple generations. I couldn’t have asked Santa for more.
As early Christmas presents go, It's a Wonderful Knife isn't one you'll regift or take back to the store, but it might end up next to that chafing dish you never use.
"Knife” intends to slay, but it suffers from a serious lack of scares and missed opportunities.

MacIntyre’s latest may not quite seamlessly nail its high concept genre mashup, but with some outstanding performances and a sweet gooey emotional center, it effectively tugs at your heartstrings and captures the spirit of Christmas.

title: Geoff McFetridge: Drawing a Life | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: An absorbing profile of an innovative artist.

title: Dune: Part Two | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: As a sequel, it works for the same reasons that make The Empire Strikes Back so many people’s favourite Star Wars film: there’s a darkness, a bleakness, that makes the fist-pumping moments feel all-the-more earned.
As different from the first film as [Ridley Scott's] Alien is to [James Cameron's] Aliens. Same stuff, totally different genre!
There is little character development and it’s not for the literal-minded -- or anyone who has, despite their best efforts, paid some attention.
An epic and spectacular sci-fi allegory with mass appeal.
You know Villeneuve will get the spectacle right. The question is about the human drama… It almost all connected in Part Two.

As in all of these sci-fi epics, there are plenty of scenes in which computer-generated characters drive computer-generated vehicles past computer-generated backdrops but, in "Dune," it feels human, slightly messy and organic.
What is really impressive about Part Two, is that despite how complex and like a miasma the plot becomes... the storytelling is so clear.
Exceeds expectations in every way—except humanity.
The film is all exhilarating buildup leading to an unsatisfactory, and even somewhat perfunctory, payoff.

The second Dune instalment is jaw-on-the-floor spectacular. It elegantly weaves together top-tier special effects and arresting cinematography; it layers muscle, sinew and savagery on to the bones of Part One.

Lawrence of Arrakis meets Dr. Sandworm, or, How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bene Gesserit...The result is a blockbuster space opera that plays like a downbeat drama — we’re a long, long way from that famous galaxy far, far away.

As a feat of project management, Dune: Part Two is undeniable. But given how fundamentally bizarre the world of Dune is—or should be—critical consensus seems like an odd goal. Shouldn't it be weirder?
One of the year’s most anticipated films is nice to look at, but is let down by bland acting and a script that does no great service to its impressive cast.

Even as we marvel at the stunning and immersive and Oscar-level cinematography, editing, score, visual effects, production design and sound in Denis Villeneuve’s Part Two, we’re reminded at every turn that this is an absolutely crazy story...
In an age of ever-increasing runtimes, it’s a rare achievement that the film’s 166-minute length feels earned.
Instead of a theme park, it's more of a cathedral -- solemn, sober, beautiful and forbidding. Greig Fraser's photography and Hans Zimmer's score are full of majesty.

I was a fan of first Dune in this series, although I logged similar complaints about its self-seriousness. This one is a little better; the action is just as thrilling but the characters are given more depth.
Who knew it was possible to be so amazed and so bored at the same time?
Ultimately, we end up with an abundance of craft and a forest of lore wrapped around personal narratives too flimsy to sustain marching feet.

The year’s first surefire blockbuster is a sequel that outdoes Denis Villeneuve’s first epic 2021 sand opera. OK, it’s a tad long and solemn,  but Chalamet and Zendaya are destiny-kissed lovers to die for, and the thundering spectacle is off the charts.

title: The Greatest Night in Pop | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Director Bao Nguyen is also wryly bemused by the now historic celebrity assemblage and thankfully intrigued by the logistical and creative demands of creating an anthem.
Even if the song itself is pretty lame, it doesn’t actually matter. It has a hook and you can donate to it.
It's really fascinating.
I found this endlessly entertaining, and so informative.

The Greatest Night In Pop is a good documentary for Netflix viewing. Fun and fluffy with famous faces, brisk pacing, and plenty of playful tales, it's something you could put on casually while folding laundry. And it is very satisfying on that front.
The Greatest Night in Pop is one of those wonderfully wish fulfilling, “man I wish I could’ve been a fly on the wall during that recording”-type documentaries.
It’s great fun to hear Dionne Warwick’s honey-coated voice meshing with Willie Nelson’s raw but still smooth vocals...
Every cherished moment is here. The emotions, creativity and magnitude of the all-night session are still a wonder.
It's almost like they knew there'd be a film eventually made of this. They have an incredible amount of footage.
One can’t help but enjoy the spectacle of all these stars, who were like gods at the time, standing around getting to know each other like awkward kids at a school social.
At the heart of this mega-celebrity choir, Bob Dylan nervously scowled like a clueless Martian picking up on the ways of Earthlings.
While the making of the song was partially detailed in its long-form video, there’s plenty of new, engaging, and sometimes eyebrow-raising anecdotal material here.
Lionel Richie serves as the de facto tour guide for this trip down memory lane, which fulfills its promise to make a better day (or at least 90-some-odd minutes) for you and me.

While The Greatest Night in Pop may not amount to anything more than a sanitized and somewhat masturbatory look back at one of the wildest get-togethers in the modern history of music, there’s no denying that it’s a lot of fun to watch it all go down.
Music bio-docs may be running out of steam, but “The Greatest Night in Pop” works by being specific and enlightening.
An engaging blitz of nostalgia guaranteed to leave core viewers misty-eyed.
As far as celebratory backward glances go, it’s compelling enough to temporarily brighten one’s day.

title: Cabrini | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: While Monteverde’s film highlights the main character’s incredible work (...), including its encounters with xenophobia, the biopic as a whole falls short of leaving a lasting impression on the spectator.
I actually rather enjoyed this... A pretty faithful biography of Cabrini.

As single-minded as its protagonist, Cabrini drives home in every scene its themes of human dignity—particularly the dignity of women and marginalized groups including immigrants and the poor—and solidarity in the face of prejudice and social injustice.
Cabrini doesn’t reinvent the bio/film genre, but is a solid addition to the faith-based category.
Cabrini’s story is rather absorbing and the film offers a lushly mounted portrait of life in 1880s New York, when immigration was just as much of a contentious issue as it is today.
At a time when movies exist in honor of the strangest oddballs everywhere, I can think of no one more worthy of a life-changing biopic. You can keep your Barbie. I’ll take Mother Cabrini.
Cabrini is the beautiful reminder of the human being behind the name.
Cabrini, while certainly a hagiography, is dramatically and cinematically sound and even, now and then, visually breathtaking.
For all that can be questioned about the makers’ intentions, the movie’s greatest sin is how lifelessly solemn and aesthetically dull it is.
Those attending Cabrini hoping for more hot-potato discourse—or another overheated story of a red-blooded American kicking some ass—will be sorely disappointed.
Its visual splendor is matched by the strong moral convictions and absence of cynicism that characterized many movies of the 1940s, when Catholic heroes were all over the screen.
The production values of "Cabrini" are solid, if obvious and uninspired.
“Cabrini” is in no way a perfect movie, but a damn dignified one that honors the little-known efforts of these fearless women.
Elevated by some beautifully understated performances - Dell’Anna is simply electric here - and a hugely compelling story, this is perhaps Angel's very best film to date.
The gauzy goodness of this film is axiomatic, and its litany of sanctimonious speeches (“the world is too small for what I intend to do”) generally repels inquiry, let alone controversy.
The sumptuous production values are breathtaking...Dell’Anna’s eyes are wonderfully expressive, and she makes the small woman in the severe habit a vital, moving presence.
A stodgy, histrionic, and impossibly dull biopic that drags on for more than 140 minutes despite being thinner than a stained glass window.
For the most part, “Cabrini” raises the bar on quality faith-based entertainment.

The film, which feels overlong at 145 minutes, suffers both from repetition and an over-reliance on melodramatic plot devices. But it nonetheless delivers a compelling portrait of a heroine whose story is too little-known.

title: Madu | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Given the complexity and near-fairy tale improbability of his real-life story, it is not surprising that Anthony is comfortable taking a break from plot to revel in the pure abstraction of movement.

title: Copa 71 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Gooooaaaallll!
[S]tirring, exciting, and lively, a kinetic tale that finally spotlights the revolutionary event that didn’t quite turn the tide but certainly started the wave.

With this poignant tribute, however, the legacy of that glorious summer should finally get the recognition it deserves — even if, according to the film, to this day Fifa still refuses to acknowledge the legitimacy of the tournament.

A timely and galvanising telling of a remarkable story that every football fan should know, and one that will hopefully go some way towards ensuring that Copa 71 finds its way into the sport’s history books.
This is immediately one of the great football documentaries.
Copa 71 is a revolutionary political parable that goes beyond football. A different world is possible; not only that, a different world was not just possible but did in fact exist.
A defining moment in women’s sports history captured in 90 minutes of nostalgia and pure exhilaration.
It’s solid and will do very well for a network like ESPN or Netflix, but it’s a bit too formulaic for the talented athletes it profiles and their finally-reclaimed legacies.
“Copa 71” makes its case succinctly, dropping interesting tidbits while letting the event itself serve as a revelation.
“Copa 71” connects an entire lineage of the sport and reveals that while its popularity has been recognized more recently, it might be even greater if more of it was on the record.
An uplifting and eye-opening love letter.
An easily-digestible, not-too-forensic crowdpleaser which will, like its protagonists, run and run.

title: Ordinary Angels | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The drama is pretty pedestrian; the storytelling is wantonly manipulative, and I have to say that I was manipulated against my better judgment.
The film’s more overtly Christian elements, including calls for divine intervention, dovetail neatly with Sharon’s yearning to be held, supported and, ultimately, forgiven.
The performances are solid and the story is touching — and perhaps that will carry this to its chosen audience. But it's a little flat for true drama.
Taken on its own terms as an old-fashioned character drama and showcase for Ritchson as a dramatic actor (he’s genuinely really good), it does the job it set out to do.
On the other hand, although the approach to things may be too simplistic, the double Oscar winner Hilary Swank holds the entire scaffolding with her excellent performance. [Full review in Spanish]
If you want a better made version of a faith-based film, this could serve as that.
Ordinary Angels takes the faith-based melodrama and injects it with the kind of empathetic energy that could wring tears from even the most godless among us.
The dialogue is as simple as mud, but you can’t ignore the value of a film that finally makes you feel good about the world.
The character’s motivations don’t gel and no amount of Swank moxie can make it work.
I can’t think of a single plot development that will surprise you and sometimes that’s OK. Sometimes it’s enough to sit back and settle in for a Comfort Viewing Movie...

Ordinary Angels is a true story and a remarkable one at that. Living with our two-year old granddaughter has made me especially vulnerable to dramas about young children in peril, and it didn’t take long for this one to open my tear ducts
Just because we know where a movie is going does not mean we don’t enjoy getting there.
This is unambiguously a faith-based film, but it’s one that places its faith in people instead of a higher power. That doesn’t make it good, but it does make it an interesting change of pace.
Luckily Swank is on hand, almost singlehandedly raising the material to a level that keeps you wanting to watch. And sometimes, for a good cry at the movies, that’s really all you need.
Despite its bona fides, the movie's narrative and characterizations practically gorge on clichés.

No magic tricks, no ulterior motives, just the strength of people working together toward a common goal. It doesn't always happen like that, but "Ordinary Angels" is a gentle reminder that it sure is nice when it does.
“Ordinary Angels” has some of the feeling of an after school special, because it’s a heartwarming movie in which everybody is nice. But it’s more well-made than most.

A do-good story about two lost souls who learn to understand and appreciate each other while the community around them comes together to achieve something that goes beyond their individual needs. This one earns its wings.

This film starring Hilary Swank as a Kentucky hairdresser who rallies her community on behalf of a widower and his seriously ill three-year-old daughter proves irresistible with its powerful feel-good story.

What lifts the picture beyond average inspirational fluff is the way director Jon Gunn and company control the slow release of its sweetness so as not to overpower.  Even cynics will be won over by the human kindness on display.

title: Snoopy Presents: Welcome Home, Franklin | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Brown and his buddies may remain in elementary school, but the "Peanuts" franchise is growing up.

“Welcome Home, Franklin” isn’t going to make anyone forget the Christmas or Halloween specials. But it tries to right a wrong and does the right thing. It’s a nice addition to the canon, and it shines a light on what “Peanuts” used to be.

title: Billy & Molly: An Otter Love Story | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Really, this is a film of gentle pleasures, watching the couple’s house gradually becoming otter crazy.

title: Arthur the King | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Film by film, Mr. Wahlberg is using his pull to create a tribute to the world’s tough, decent, humble working guys.
Maybe the movie will direct some eyes toward the existence of the Arthur Foundation, but while the movie goes down easy enough it is, on the whole, a bit unsatisfying.
The movie reminds us that we should pay close attention to the goals we set for ourselves, to decide whether achieving them will really give us what we are hoping for and what it means to win.
It’s fairly standard heartwarming dog fare, often treacly... but edged up with vibrant, handheld cinematography by Jacques Jouffret that gives the film a more adult, action-oriented feel
Watching Arthur the King grab this meatball of a film in his jaws and scurry off with it is a surprisingly pleasing way to spend an hour and a half.
[Simon Cellan Jones] uses the dog to really tug at the audience's heartstrings in increasingly manipulative ways, filling in emotional holes that are otherwise overlooked in the script.

The story is typical paint-by-numbers inspirational — some bids at emotion feel awfully forced. Still, Wahlberg and company manage to hold your attention, and not just because there’s a cute dog in the frame.
“Arthur the King” is so achingly predictable, it gives one paws — err, I mean, pause. It just doesn’t have the chops.
Even when a rousing finale provides a dash of redemption, it’s not enough to rescue a movie that stumbles out of the blocks and never recovers.
Like Arthur himself, the results are sweet and dignified. Watch it on a flight.
Rather than truly being inspiring or moving, Arthur The King manipulates and frustrates.
Is all of this manipulative and cheesy? Yes, and yes. But it ultimately proves irresistible, and will be especially so for younger audience members.

The draw here should be experiencing a story, seeing characters overcoming adversity, and watching them build a bond with an adorable pupper. Yet Arthur The King demonstrates incompetence at doing all three. Only one thing to say to that: Woof.

This true-life tale about perseverance, compassion and second chances cuts right to the quick. While it doesn’t stray from a predictable path, the journey is rarely dull, making our travels and these characters’ travails feel worthy of the big screen.
Since it’s a mashup of sports and animal movies, “Arthur the King” has loads of clichés from which to choose, and it chooses them all.

title: Exhuma | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Jae-hyun Jang combines introspective cultural and historical themes with creepy, gory, and atmospheric horror thrills in an exciting way. It’s fun horror with a lot on its mind.
It makes up for its paucity of scares through the multiple layers of weirdness that it excavates, as one (burial) plot leads to another and as legacy, whether genetic or national, has unseen depths.

title: My Name Is Loh Kiwan | Rotten Tomatoes
Justice League: Crisis on Infinite Earths Part One | Rotten Tomatoes
The Tiger's Apprentice | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I admit we've seen this story a million times in a million forms, but I thought it was nicely done and funny when it meant to be.
A movie that has a couple of amusing moments and nice visual flourishes but not nearly enough to combat the resounding mediocrity of the storytelling.

The animation is less surefooted at the start in a prologue set in Hong Kong, but it quickly improves when the action shifts to San Francisco, gloriously re-created. The vocal cast is mighty impressive and includes the ever-busy Michelle Yeoh.
There’s no word on whether the rest of the trilogy is being considered for adaptation, but if so, it’s off to a solid start, with plenty of room for improvement.
Like a shop-bought char siu bao, it’s over-sweetened but moreish: Chinese-flavoured comfort food in cinematic form.
A game cast and brisk pacing work their spell.

title: The Bloody Hundredth | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Directed by Mark Herzog and Laurent Bouzereau, the nonfiction account of the airborne armada... is intended to augment the dramatic series. But as good as that series may be, it has to take a respectful back seat to the real account and the real men.

It assumes you’ve already seen Masters of the Air. You should indeed watch the drama first, because while the documentary is a perfectly decent summary of the same story, it can’t muster the same romance or spectacle.

title: The Beekeeper (2024) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Clay dispatches his adversaries with characteristic Statham aplomb, which, apologies to Nicole Kidman, is why we come to this place.
Much of it is illogical, preposterous over-the-top ridiculous, which is what makes it such a guilty pleasure and one of Statham’s and Ayer’s best films.

Off we go. Like, way off, leaving even the notion of reality behind like a burned-out barn full of busted honey jars. In its place, a hero who makes James Bond look inconspicuous and John Wick look vincible.
This wacky bit of action fun is wildly entertaining and zips by with the good-natured buzz of a bumblebee. If this is your kind of dumb-movie honey, it’s delectable.
It’s Statham’s movie – a brisk, slick, ultra-violent action onslaught that yet again demonstrates his ability to redeem just about any old tosh.
The shame is that there are flickers of greatness here. Statham, in action, is thunderously convincing. In character, he’s pleasingly ironic.
The Beekeeper, which is both a bee movie and a B movie, falls in the same category as many other Statham-versus-everyone action thrillers: not very good, yet enjoyable enough.
A sad disappointment for bee enthusiasts.
David Ayer has made a special kind of folly this time: an imbecilic and inept pileup of action-movie clichés redeemed only by the occasional hilarity of its caveman excess.
Time and again he’s surrounded by hordes of SWAT guys, Secret Service agents, cops, mercenaries, you name it. And time and again they’re all laid low. It’s nuts. It’s funny.
[Ayer] tackles this assignment without much self-seriousness but doesn’t seem keen to embrace its silliness quotient, either.
The Beekeeper makes honey out of hooey.
There’s a grubby, late-night appeal to [Ayer's] dialled-up trash aesthetic and The Beekeeper mostly works because of it.
What starts out as Statham defending the downtrodden and the defenseless hard-working citizens who get robbed by 21st-century villains turns into something close to toxic tinfoil-hat ranting.

As the movie’s renegade protagonist makes his way closer and closer to the White House, with blood and chaos in his wake, The Beekeeper begins to feel like an uncomfortable B-movie crosspollination of today’s conspiracy theory-marred political landscape.
The Beekeeper is slick, dumb fun... There's plenty of honey here to go around.
Just absolute bee-movie trash.

Glorifying endless violence as these films tend to do (fingers are severed, limbs are torn, cheeks are pierced, heads are blown), The Beekeeper is exactly what it appears to be. Nothing more, nothing less.
It appreciates the virtues of its leading man, who appears to have come by his muscles honestly, and does everything from dialogue to martial arts to gunplay as simply as possible.
It does everything that an action movie needs to do and does it in witty, unexpected ways.

title: Land of Bad | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: We’re in the “try anything once” phase of Russell Crowe’s career, and he’s wearing it well.
The makers of “Land of Bad” mostly reduce their movie’s antagonists to generic obstacles for Kinney, except for a few key scenes that strain to establish why they’re actually the worst.
Moments presumably conceived to create suspense... merely contribute to its longueurs.
Russell Crowe... spends most of the movie sitting in a chair staring at a screen and manages to completely steal it anyway.
Once Land of Bad establishes its stakes – one man versus an army – the film settles all too comfortably into war-machine territory, minus any particularly inventive kills or sense of style.

Headlined by a serviceable Liam Hemsworth and a fantastic Russell Crowe in all his hammy scene-stealing glory, it’s the bro-iest bro-fest that ever bro’d—and I say that with far more affection than condescension.

title: Remembering Gene Wilder | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The actor behind those hit performances comes to the fore in this affectionate biography from director Ron Frank, which uses narration from the now-deceased actor and typically oversized storytelling from former collaborator Mel Brooks to reacquaint us.

“Remembering Gene Wilder,” which Ron Frank directed, is a somewhat unusual documentary, starting with the odd career arc it chronicles. The most unusual thing, and very much in a good way, is that Wilder serves as de facto narrator.
“Remembering Gene Wilder” is a pleasant retro journey for fans and an efficient introduction to a comic genius for cineasts who might not know his work. It could have been so much more.
It's a very lovely film. Warm, affectionate, so many great anecdotes, and I came to appreciate his artistry on a whole different level.
As a documentary, I thought it was pretty okay. It's a lovefest with a lot of usual suspects.

If “Remembering Gene Wilder” isn’t always the most dimensional or penetrating look at an actor’s life and psyche, it still serves as an upbeat tribute to a singular movie star, and a worthy reminder of how much he’s missed.
If the engaging documentary inspires a Wilder streaming marathon, so much the better.
It’s patchy and digressive, and the overreliance on syrupy music becomes off-putting towards the end.

title: Hundreds of Beavers | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Cheslik and Tews execute each gag with great force and speed, stringing the scenes together into a coherent story with callbacks and forward momentum that intensifies as the movie barrels along.
It’s been a long time since I was this clueless about what was going to happen next in a film; the feeling was exhilarating.
It's genuinely quite bananas and it's genuinely quite funny.
Exceeds expectations in every way, including the promise of its title.
A midnight movie for an era of YouTube playthroughs and Twitch livestreams.

What gives Hundreds Of Beavers its special quality is the mixture of no-budget, seemingly haphazard gonzo energy and the well-tooled jokes that can only come from rigorous planning and effervescent ingenuity.
A tale of pelts that pelts along, with more lunacy and creativity than a brace of other films, this film dares to go full beaver.
The sheer sustained silliness of this spoof silent comedy is what finally compels admiration.
Hundreds of Beavers is an immaculately constructed, gloriously bizarre, wholly unique tribute to that basest of comedy pleasures, made by people whose imagination seemingly knows no bounds.
This is the best kind of silly, made with craft, a bottomless well of inventiveness, and maybe a fair share of edibles.
You’d do well to satisfy your craving for knockabout lunacy by checking out “Hundreds of Beavers,” as visionary as any indie in many a moon, and a dam site (ahem) more fun.
The beavers are about as sympathetic as the Caddyshack gopher, and Jean’s a nitwit, so the audience’s only rooting interest is in seeing how crazy things get.
A marvel of slapstick invention that in terms of pure unbridled creativity puts most big-screen comedies to shame.

Hundreds of Beavers works because everyone involved knows to deliver the whimsy with a straight face, treating knitted fish, puppet frogs, and the Wisconsin snowdrifts in which it was filmed all as equally real.
Hundreds of Beavers is fueled by a delirious spirit that reminded me sometimes of “It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World,” and that’s a high compliment indeed.
Part Guy Maddin, part Chuck Jones -- a constant delight.
On paper, it would hardly be expected to remain funny for eight minutes, let alone 108. But this ingeniously home-made lark never runs out of steam.
Hundreds of Beavers starts strange, gets stranger, and yet remains resolutely adorable.

title: Snack Shack | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Armed with a talented cast, writer-director Adam Rehmeier’s 1991-set feature happily squares itself in a tradition of teenage hedonism and broad learning opportunities, settling into a generic but warm glow.
Even with the script’s problems, the film is kinetic, and as in Dinner In America, Rehmeier gets terrific performances from his cast.
With its rambling momentum and quick-witted, almost musical dialogue, it feels less like “Superbad” than a Robert Altman movie, sort of like a pint-size “California Split.”
“Snack Shack” is a sweet stroll down nostalgia lane that’s elevated by Sherry’s and LaBelle’s performances.

title: Upgraded | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I think they set it in this very specific world of art, which, even if it's not entirely accurate, it's specific. So within its own world, it feels developed.

The movie is unevenly directed, and some scenes struggle to clear even the low bar set by more polished streaming originals. But Young succeeds nonetheless in channeling the freshman thrill of plunging into an alluring adult milieu.
This is a story about women supporting women, especially across generations, and that’s what makes Upgraded resonate more than just a frothy rom-com would.

It’s a sweet movie that accidentally expresses ideas that are complicated and perverse. This isn’t enough to make “Upgraded” transcend its formula, but it does make it slightly better than it had to be.

Heartening themes involving holding on tight to one’s dreams and not devaluing one’s self-worth make for an encouraging upgrade from the norm. It’s even better since there are capable filmmakers piloting this transformative journey.

title: Good One: A Show About Jokes  | Rotten Tomatoes
Anaconda | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The monster looks like a maniacal garden hose in a couple of sequences. Still, it delivers the necessary thrills and chills.
Anaconda, directed by Luis Llosa with all of the subtlety of a snake-oil salesman, is in the great tradition of cinematic cheese, as processed as Kraft Singles slices.
A silly and plodding Jaws rip-off about a 40-foot man-eating snake on the prowl in the Brazilian rain forest.
One never questions the realism of the remarkable animatronic and computer-generated effects, but it's hard to credit a snake that screams.
Anaconda is about a snake that eats everybody. That about says it all.
Anaconda is such a classic combination of feckless dramaturgy and rampant excess that giving way to giggles is the only sane response.
A trashily entertaining reptilian version of Jaws set in the steaming heart of the Amazon rain forest.
It's a slick, scary, funny Creature Feature, beautifully photographed and splendidly acted in high adventure style.
It isn't art, but it'll crush your bones.
Charmless, unfrightening, and even devoid of the requisite gratuitous nudity, Anaconda just plain bites.

title: Girls State | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Girls State isn’t quite the explosive takedown and critique of the program that it could be, but it does explore the program's limitations cogently...
The politics lean conservative, but the transformations that occur go beyond ideology.
I wish there had been a little bit more of the get-togethers so we could hear them talk a little more informally, but it's a fascinating movie.
At first it proves every bit as gripping. Then it gets more so.
When thinking about the whole American experiment, nearly 250 years in, it can seem hard to find reasons for optimism. But “Girls State” offers a welcome and necessary helping of it.
In this thought-provoking documentary, girls get the chance to play politics – and their debates about abortion are startlingly nuanced
There’s a formula at work here, a winning and well-proven one, and McBaine and Moss stick to it.
If you’re like me, you’ll come away filled with both dread and more than a little hope.
It is genuinely thrilling to see their integrity, passion, and conviction that they can and must do better. They've got my vote.
Girls State is a powerful documentary that showcases just how invested and determined young women are in their desire to run for the highest office – despite the challenges they face.
If the purpose of Girls State is to give high-school students a taste of how government works in real life, “Girls State” makes a case that it does its job only too well.
The breath of fresh air in the film are the determined young women as they listen to each other, debate and try to fill in the foundation for a better tomorrow.
“Girls State” endears, but it also leaves viewers with the sense that, for a film about young women eager to take on the world’s challenges, the movie could stand to tackle a few more.

Girls State is much more than a gender-flipped version of the previous project. Instead, the film offers a sharp study of how a supposedly empowering environment can simultaneously inspire and limit aspiring female leaders.

Like Boys State, this film presents a fascinating microcosm of American teenagers. Granted, it’s a rather narrow, self-selecting group of kids who choose to spend a week of their summer vacation creating a mock government.
The film’s storytelling structure befits the female experience in American politics.
Girls rule! They really do in this follow-on to the Sundance 2020 documentary prize winner “Boys State,” which was also directed by Amanda McBaine and Jesse Moss.
Undeniably heartwarming and hilarious.
How some of the young leaders in “Girls State” not only handle but also leverage their disappointments provides one of the documentary’s richest lessons.

What unfolds is a riot of interpersonal tensions, betrayals and broken hearts, as key players and potential future politicians are faced with the ethical and personal sacrifices required to claim power.

title: Late Night with the Devil | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Assured in their craft, the Cairnes brothers deliver fulsome ratings satire and sharp scares.
The cast makes Late Night With the Devil more than watchable, but they also raise our hopes for something better.
The Cairnes cite Sidney Lumet’s Network as an influence and I’m not surprised. They have come up with a worthy successor.
Its smart use of mostly practical effects work and its disciplined approach makes for a sometimes tense, often funny and always impressive horror film that even scaredy cats will appreciate.
An inventive and thoroughly entertaining pulp horror movie.

It’s wonderfully creepy and unnervingly familiar, like Alan Partridge by way of The Exorcist. If that doesn’t automatically enter it into the pantheon of classic midnight movies, I don’t know what does.

A story in which there is no shortage of allusions to classics such as “The Exorcist” and “Carrie”, but which has its own identity, keeps us constantly in suspense and leads to an absolutely brilliant final scene.
It becomes 'Alan Partridge goes to hell.'
A smart, original approach makes this much more than just another Exorcist wannabe. You’ll sense that there are horrors coming, but you still won’t quite feel ready.
Smart, cynical and at times devilishly funny, the film delivers a crackle of disruptive static to the demonic possession genre.
[Dastmalchian's] portrait of a Carson wannabe coming undone is the most persuasive thing about the movie, its realest touch.
It takes pieces of things we've seen before and executes them so masterfully into something totally original and cool.
The movie gets in its own way and trips over itself repeatedly.
While "Late Night With the Devil's" ending goes a bit off the rails, it for the most part pulls off its stunt and delivers on its premise.
This is a pressure-cooker film, an exercise in small-budget simplicity that leans on one set and one goal: Keep ’em watching.

Virtually everything about Late Night With The Devil works, from its sets to its costumes to its casting to its impeccable sound design. It’s a gem on every level, and it’s already a contender for the best new horror film of 2024.
A nasty and delicious, unapologetic pastiche with a flair for menace. I had a blast.
A convincingly beige colour grade and analogue glitches complete the look. The blood-splattering effects, mostly practical and in-camera, scream out for a packed cinema.
