Dastmalchian makes a dashing host, with the Cairnes giving him a dark side as well. This has the potential for turning into a cult classic.
This is an irresistible throwback to not only old-school horror, but old-school television.

title: Giannis: The Marvelous Journey | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s a reminder that the sporting world’s celebrated and lavishly compensated larger-than-life figures still have regular-sized emotions, and sometimes, even smaller ones than that.

title: Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The script, there is a plot but it's preposterous tosh and it makes no sense, and it doesn't even try to make sense... Stuff. Stuff. Stuff. ROAR.

While Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire did on occasion test my patience, the overall ride does remain a fun one, and because of that, I’m still willing to remain seated on the Monsterverse’s bandwagon — for now.
This is great fun. A big, dumb movie that tries to explain with scientific language how we get to a place called "Hollow Earth."
Godzilla and King Kong use to have a beef. Now that they’ve kissed and made up, there’s no real meat in this generic big creature smackdown.

These films may be empty, but they can be strangely stimulating. Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire, however, is the MonsterVerse at its weakest: Its spectacle is even duller than its story, which is already nonsensical.
If you want to see massive creatures leveling cities, that’s exactly what you’ll get. If you’re looking for anything more than that, well, you should know by now that you’re in the wrong place.

Dumbed-down and stripped of the symbolic subtext of the earlier movies, the picture is not without seat-shuddering thrills, but it’s like a tag-team wrestling bout for monsters rather than a picture with meaning and even a modicum of thought.
"Godzilla x Kong" is as big and loud as expected, but when the dust is settled, there's nothing to hold onto. The kaiju clash is a crushing bore.

Being in Hollow Earth takes some of the fun out of things... That also leaves Godzilla x Kong residing in a purely CGI arena without even tenuous connections to reality. It's a empty chamber for movie spectacle and nothing else.
The underwhelming effects give you new appreciation for what Godzilla Minus One did at a fraction of the cost.

The live-action and motion capture performances are mostly marvelous, despite the bum dialogue and Wingard’s tendency to rush through sequences and whole relationships that might’ve been extraordinary had they been presented with patience and elegance.
When you multiply Godzilla by Kong, what do you get? When Wingard’s doing the math, it’s an earnest, wacky, hectic ride that often feels like being thrashed about in an Imax seat.

The problem with "Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire" is the same as so many of these franchise-based films: They're all soulless special-effects extravaganzas where CGI takes the place of character development, good writing, and emotional connection.

Wingard’s not a sentimentalist, and “Godzilla x Kong” stumbles whenever he tries to slap phony emotions onto the film to make it more like a generic crowd-pleaser. He’s a showman, a popcorn guy with excellent aesthetics.

Even the title, Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire, sounds like words awkwardly lumped together as if designed only to satisfy best practices in search engine optimization. Like, are we supposed to say the “x?”
Spectacular? I guess, if you're wowed by soulless CGI chaos. Thrilling? Not really. At the end, I was left feeling the way Kong does at the beginning: tired and bored.

Godzilla X Kong: The New Empire is a mouthful of a title. And one that’s surprisingly hard to parse out on its own, especially as it suggests more of a brand collab between those famed cinematic monsters than anything else.
This is a monster movie for monster-movie fans and not more. But hardly 10 minutes goes by without monster action.

Returning director Adam Wingard and his writers really lean into the cartoonish style of the Showa-era Godzilla films from 1954 to ’75. This includes abandoning all pretence of logic or plausibility, never a huge concern in this franchise.
So many effects blockbusters attempt to run before they can walk (mentioning no names), and at least Wingard has the humble intent of a filmmaker who wants to make something simple, coherent and fun.

title: Inshallah a Boy | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a very powerful film.
Its world is so well built out and Palestinian actress Mouna Hawa’s lead performance is so absorbing, the final result is a mesmerizing piece of personal, yet political filmmaking.
Hawa, a Palestinian actress, is commanding as a woman whose future and faith are buffeted by her narrowing options.

Inshallah A Boy is all about resistance and survival against the odds, fighting for the bonafide rights and taking control of one’s destiny, breaking the shackles and finding liberation in something as basic and banal as being able to drive.
“Inshallah a Boy” moves like a sleek thriller, but is full of the unsolved mysteries and dangling question marks of real life...
Patriarchy, misogyny, and the implacable hatred towards women who speak their minds is the toxic mix Amjad Al Rasheed’s debut feature seeks to highlight...

title: The Underdoggs | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There’s still a surprising amount of fun to be had, mostly because The Underdoggs allows the neighborhood and its inhabitants to shine, and everyone is clearly having a blast in this shiny commercial...
If you love Snoop's acting, you'll enjoy “The Underdoggs.” Otherwise, don't bother.
Yes, his thespian range may be pretty limited, but there’s no denying Snoop has a palpable onscreen charisma and a good sense of comic timing that director Charles Stone III skilfully directs around.

While enjoying something like The Underdoggs requires a certain mindset (or maybe a slightly altered one), it's another example that there's still a place for broad comedies, even when they operate from the most familiar of playbooks.
Not good but I love that 30 years after Snoop Dogg was deemed a terrible influence on me. I can share this movie casting him as a role model with my kids.
“The Underdoggs” isn’t memorable, but it is a bit of fun for an afternoon. You could even multitask while watching it and not miss a beat.

Snoop can barely focus on playing a character designed to be as much like his off-camera persona as possible, but he is an able performer and this basic underdog story benefits from being so evidently dear to his heart.
The Underdoggs is thin on plot, character and most other tenets of filmmaking, but it's heavy on laughs, so it meets its goal.
There’s not a single surprise along the way. But there is the comfort of familiarity operating in the movie’s favor. And it’s fun.
What we’re left with instead is the occasional chuckle from Mike Epps as the hapless class clown he usually plays, and the vague outline of other movies that have done this story with more charm.

The results, perhaps suprisingly, are far from disastrous and ultimately quite endearing, though parents should be forewarned of a movie that drops more f- and b-bombs than all the ordnance released during World War II.
Snoop has obviously made a real-life impact in his community. Too bad he couldn’t make one in reel life as well.
There’s only so much that director Charles Stone III can do with the script’s “head held high” cornpone.

title: Kung Fu Panda 4 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Like its villain, “Kung Fu Panda 4” can do an imitation, but we can tell it’s not the genuine article.

If the script was sharper or funnier and if the gags were better maybe you wouldn't notice, but it does feel like a lot of it is a bunch of people in recording booths doing some schtick and them animating around it.
The plot may be cursory — Po has to graduate to spiritual leader of the Valley of Peace and find a successor for his job as dragon warrior — but Black attacks it with knockabout zeal.
Caveats and niggles ultimately don’t dent the magnanimous-natured enjoyment. A lesser Kung Fu Panda movie remains vastly superior to most mainstream animated features.

The script is just as pallid. There’s lots of hackneyed comic repartee but no real vocal chemistry between the players, a trio of cutesy prepubescent hoodlums that may feel awkwardly familiar to anyone who’s seen Disney’s Raya and the Last Dragon...
Whether there’s any kind of larger allegory here might be worth pondering -- though it might also be the real lesson is not to read too much into a series titled Kung Fu Panda.
It failed the wriggle test on my seven-year-old cinema date, who was squirming in her seat around the hour mark.
I would like for it to have built the story a little bit more than it does. It is fun. It is gorgeous to look at.

After letting loose a little, Kung Fu Panda 4 is a fun trip down memory lane, hearkening back on the glory that propelled the treasured panda Po, voiced charmingly as ever by Jack Black, into our hearts.
This dumpling is a little too light on the filling.
This is an enjoyably winning continuation of Po’s story.
I enjoyed the first three adventures of the Dragon Warrior, but the best thing he can do now is to give this series a much needed skadoosh, sending it to rest in the cinematic spirit realm.
Kung Fu Panda 4 leans toward the comforting and familiar, and eventually hits a sentimental note as it genuflects to what came before, something we didn’t see coming.

We do get lessons in teamwork, patience and inner peace, but a flimsy story and a weak villain don't do Po — the big-hearted, Jack Black-voiced, dumpling-loving giant panda at the center of the saga — any favors.
The latest installment of this DreamWorks Animation franchise offers visual and kinetic pleasure, but not a whole lot more.
For its first return in eight years, directors Mike Mitchell and Stephanie Stine, a trio of credited screenwriters and a vast army of technical specialists have recalibrated the Panda format.

Black and Awkwafina and Hoffman do their jobs, but the jokes have a way of arriving like jokes, and sounding like jokes, but not quite being jokes. This is an action movie foremost, which is fine. Or rather, OK-fairly good.

Sure, the kids will giggle, and the animation is well-executed (even if there does seem to be something a little off around the eyes in this version of Po) but it just doesn't land with that same ebullient skadoosh.

Granted, there’s only so much that can be done at this point with this kind of concept beyond recycling it, but director Mike Mitchell keeps the story moving even during the relatively flat exposition.
This is an enjoyable “Kung Fu Panda” movie, even if it’s missing some of the pizazz of the earlier ones.

title: Sleeping Dogs (2024) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The murder mystery Sleeping Dogs is Russell Crowe's best film for a while.
It’s an engrossing plunge into the film noir tradition and it’s a pleasure to watch Crowe embody the very fallible Freeman.

This is certainly not a crime thriller in the dourly realistic “cold case” vein; it is outrageously over-the-top at all times, with crazy and almost dreamlike convolutions of plot, and yet its silliness is enjoyably dramatised.
It’s patchy, it’s badly lit, it’s glum, it’s overloaded with suspects, and it’s almost proud of its contrivances. Yet in its logy, booby-trapped way, it keeps you watching.
Sobering but also rich dramatic material...
Crowe is better than “Sleeping Dogs.” Most actors are.
Russell Crowe continues to prove that he’s better than the B-grade projects he’s now offered, but his convincing performance isn’t enough to elevate this surprise-free mystery.
If you can’t yet guess how it ends, you’re the target audience. Also, you might never have seen any whodunnit movies before in your life.
A sluggishly rendered mystery that audiences will have long stopped caring about before it reaches its conclusion.
Sleeping Dogs isn’t really interested in what haunts its Alzheimer’s-ridden main character so much as it is in how his condition stands in the way of his sleuthing.

title: Stormy (2024) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: After so much media coverage, certain details of the events feel overly familiar. But the director, Sarah Gibson, is often able to put the episodes into fresh contexts.

Stormy might not be confused for any of the other movies that its subject has starred in before, but it shares a few key things in common... It’s poorly shot, severely lacking in character detail, and much longer than most people would ever need it to be.
The team clearly have the utmost respect for the subject and did their best to tell her story.
It’s a successful attempt to strip away the political issues and present its subject as a flesh-and-blood human being, someone with feelings, anxieties, and a great deal of courage.
“Stormy” shows you what the scandal looks like from inside the sensationalist bubble of fame, and by the end of the film you may be a little bit ashamed of us all.
This documentary could have been centered around Stormy Daniels today, and it would have been a better and more truthful movie. It wasn’t and it isn’t.
Fortuitously timed, providing an insider’s view of this most tabloid-y of political tales and the woman at the center of it all.

title: Knox Goes Away | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Keaton has proven himself to be as adept at action seriousness as antic comedy. In Knox, his hand is steady...

This is Keaton’s film to carry every step of the way, and he turns in a typically fine and layered performance as a man who might find relief in the loss of his memories, given all the dark acts he’s committed.
It really all depends on Keaton giving a serviceable performance to salvage whatever is left, but even he falls short.
Knox Goes Away” may take place in the noir capital that is L.A., but it could just as easily be Anywheresville.
With a contrived plot, sluggish rhythm, and unengaging performances, Knox Goes Away ends up being a rather perplexing endeavor.

Knox Goes Away is an exemplary crime drama that looks at old cliches with a fresh slant and gives a reliable but still surprising star a chance to demonstrate the range and depth of character he rarely gets the chance to explore.

Michael Keaton’s second film as star and director stumbles but rises again on the strength of Keaton’s ability to bring his bristling intelligence as an actor to his work behind camera in this darkly comic tale of a hitman losing a battle with dementia.
Its unhurried pacing and mood of quiet deliberation won’t be for everyone; but this low-key thriller resolves its shockingly high stakes with a twisty intelligence.
As Knox Goes Away motors steadily toward redemption and family reconciliation, it leaves all opportunity for real moral reckoning in its rearview mirror.
Keaton perfectly casts himself in his second directorial effort, the neo-noir thriller Knox Goes Away.
[Keaton] is too laid-back here when “Knox” needs some heat, and the always-welcome James Marsden is miscast.
As a director, Keaton’s got style
“Knox Goes Away” is a character study of a disappearing character or maybe a thriller that stays away from actual thrills. However you label the film, it’s low key but satisfying.
The script, by Gregory Poirier, is tautly clever and original, and Keaton directs it with a cunning and skill that are quietly hypnotic.

Ultimately, one just gets the sense that Knox Goes Away is unsure of what it’s supposed to be. On one hand, it leans into the chillingly gruesome; on the other, it wants to laugh at the grimness of its own scenarios.
Clearly, screenwriter Michael Poirier isn’t content to have just one high-concept plotline; he’s gotta have two. The problem is that neither one is remotely convincing.
"Knox Goes Away" isn’t the first (or fifth) genre effort to play with memory, although it might be the flattest.

title: Road House | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Silly, yet plays it straight, and everyone involved knows exactly the type of genre-pleaser they’re making... aspires to be nothing more and nothing less than a goofy experiment in translating the arc of the Western lone gunman to being a bouncer.
...it isn't just so bad it's good. In its own bad way, it really is good!
But in deep "Road House" country... and the undefined made crassly visible, there isn't a whiff of romance anywhere, any more than there's a single jot of common sense.
What results instead is a monstrous hybrid-a grotesquely implausible, oversized character that thoroughly overshadows the poor actor himself.
It's amazing how quickly an explosion, a ripped-out throat, or even four bangs in a row, can make other problems seem insignificant.
The Peruvian marching powder is all but dusting the corners of the frame throughout 'Road House,' which may as well go into a museum for '80s artifacts.
Road House is startling because of the intensity of its violence and because of Swayze's mindless posturing.
All Road House amounts to is a botched southern, and it's not worth a detour.
Eventually it mutates into a paranoid revenge plot that might be called Walking Short.
An immensely enjoyable slice of romanticised fisticuffs, this is a Western in every respect except the stetsons and six guns.
Its vigilante justice, lawlessness and wanton violence feel ludicrous in a modern setting.
Mindless entertainment of the highest order.
Road House is much funnier than most comedies, until it turns vile instead of just stupid.
The grotesque soon drowns out the giggles.
Road House lays out its story with the subtlety of a wrestling match, and probably with less sharpness or savvy.
This is not a good movie. But viewed in the right frame of mind, it is not a boring one, either.

title: Wicked Little Letters | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Colman and Buckley know how to make this material sing, and there are moments when both actors managed to make me squeeze out an authentic tear or two, only to have me enthusiastically giggling a scene or two later.
The range of insults sprinkled in with a healthy dose of f-bombs is truly awe-inspiring. The letters are spicy for the villagers, but for a modern-day audience, they're just delightfully silly.

It’s saved, first by strong performances from Buckley, always effortlessly believable, and Colman, expert at laying bare the clammy soul of easily dismissible women. And second, by the letters themselves...
So much fun, ridiculous, and at the end of the day it's a women's empowerment movie in an odd sort of way.
A very funny little British comedy that I cannot believe was inspired by a true story.
It’s a little story, but it’s wicked fun.
Whether itching for suffrage or to say whatever filthy fucking thing that springs to mind, rebellion is in the air, and it gives this likably goofy whodunit a light tang of the subversive.
The matchup of Jessie Buckley and Olivia Colman produce hilarious, go-for-broke acting fireworks in Thea Sharrock’s irresistible charmer set in a 1920s English village.
It may have been conceived as the kind of classy-but-ribald entertainment that might lure older moviegoers back to theaters. But insulting their intelligence probably isn’t the way to go.
The chief delight in Wicked Little Letters is watching Colman and Buckley in action; it's really not much of a mystery, as the culprit is revealed to us long before the townsfolk catch on.

There are many complaints to be made about "Wicked Little Letters" — its forced humor, its even more forced moral lessons, its tonal unevenness (flat-footed jokiness here, cheap sentimentality there) — but chief among them is wasting Buckley.
“Wicked Little Letters” is for people who like British comedy, but also for people who think British comedies are too refined for their taste. This one isn’t.
"Wicked Little Letters” is benignly enjoyable in its take on a true story of hidden feelings, farcical expression and righteous action.
Hiding somewhere in this seaside caper is a genuinely interesting psychosexual drama, buried beneath suffocating layers of treacly comedy.

Mean tweets 1920 style: The incomparable Olivia Colman and Jessie Buckley turn a flimsy script about poison pen letters that turn friends against each other into irresistible fun. Any resemblance to today’s internet trolling is purely intentional.
The overall tone is one of light-hearted eccentricity, and yet it's flexible enough to allow for real sentiment.

The audience is left to feel sorry for characters we’re meant to find amusingly contemptible and to groan at the way the writing keeps taking potshots at the most obvious targets. When the film thinks it’s being wicked, it’s closer to being trite.
The movie is full of goofy side characters and one-liners, yet elevated occasionally to genuine complexity by Colman and Buckley, who are consistently the best thing about any movie they’re in.

"Wicked" may take great pains to recreate the musty Britain of the 1920s, but don’t be fooled by the cloche hats and frilly frocks. The female rage that powers every frame of this comedy didn’t go away when that decade ended.
It’s not the most sophisticated of satires but it has a gloriously antic spirit and it sends you out on a high -- no small thing these days.

title: Through My Window 3: Looking at You | Rotten Tomatoes
Problemista | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Against all expectations, an odd-couple friendship develops. Or so this needy, Kaufmanesque indie would have us believe. In practice, however, Swinton is massively overblown and Torres too wispy and diffident to balance things out.
Problemista is undeniably inventive, but it’s also rather joyless and ultimately infuriating. Like a Slinky that refuses to walk down stairs.
It’s full of implausible cod-adorable happy-sad touches, the filmic equivalent of a decaf oat latte with a sprinkling of vegan gummy bears.
I want [Julio Torres] to get better as a director... But he's a wonderful actor and a really smart writer.
A whimsical fish-out-of-water tale following a toymaker navigating the U.S. immigration system, Problemista is a deeply considered, fantastical tromp through a mundane wonderland.
An inventive, whimsical and delightfully oddball story of the immigrant experience, "Problemista" marks the promising writing and directing debut of Julio Torres.
The film is very funny, but also so jam-packed – with fairytale imagery, art world tropes, caustic roommates, uncaring institutions – that as you’re watching, it can feel a bit much.
If you’ve ever been lucky enough to find a creative partner who sees the world the way you do, the connection between Elizabeth and Alejandro will hit you joyfully and achingly.
“Problemista” is far from perfect, but it will hit home for anyone in need of reassurance that irrational hope can triumph over even more irrational experience.
Torres gifts Swinton with a frazzled but larger-than-life character and the Oscar-winning actor — one of the best in the business — makes the most of it.
Julio Torres cleverly pairs absurd comedy with real stakes.

To say Problemista is not for everyone isn’t really a negative. My guess is that Julio Torres would readily agree with such an assessment, given how heavily this admirably bold but uneven satire leans into the Surrealist Film Playbook...
Torres’ story isn’t great — “Problemista” feels like a series of sketches — but his ideas are interesting, sometimes even inspired.
Torres keeps a lot of balls in the air. But he tends to downplay the most important one: Alejandro's immigration plight.

It’s a marvelous mixture of surrealism and social satire that depicts the American dream as a nightmare of bureaucracy and phone calls to customer service. There’s nothing more absurd, the film argues, than the mundane.
The film, like its protagonist, feels stuck in a nascent state, leaning into Elizabeth’s shrill voice because it’s not yet certain of its own.
Problemista is smart, sly, and so silly, balancing all its stresses and social commentary with a sense of wonder at the wild world and those who populate it.
It helps to be open to the whimsy, the silly, and the creative essence of “Problemista".
What Torres nails is breathtaking, especially that midnight anxiety at the ATM, the scanning for sketchy cash jobs online and, most sneakily and warmly, a blooming connection.

Given the fact that Torres’ flights of bemused, borderline-quirky fancy work best in small bursts... it may be better that Swinton’s character keeps stealing the focus and jolting the film out of the comedian’s comfort zone.

title: Cottontail | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A delicate gem of a film, with a powerhouse turn from Franky.
Much of its success is down to the gradually heartbreaking performance of the ever-reliable Franky, a regular star for Hirokazu Koreeda.
The curse of Beatrix Potter-associated cinema is lifted, at least temporarily, by the debut feature from Patrick Dickinson, even if his picture’s relationship to Potter’s work is purely tangential.

title: Before I Change My Mind | Rotten Tomatoes
Lover, Stalker, Killer | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Hobkinson deserves credit for creating suspense throughout, with assistance from Nick Foster’s score, which happily flirts with Bernard Herrmann, and cinematography and editing that add to the feeling of disorientation and instability.
Absolutely bizarre and chilling...
Even in a crowded true-crime field, it’s something of a doozy.

True-crime doc watchers who are in committed relationships may see “Lover, Stalker, Killer,” a bracing account of a lurid series of misdeeds directed by Sam Hobkinson, and breathe a sigh of relief over being out of the dating pool.

title: Suncoast | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The cast is very good, but each of them is filling out a role that could have been better illustrated with some extra detail.
Where “Suncoast” stumbles is when it sacrifices specificity for generic sentiment.
It's a compelling drama that relies on strong performances and an understated approach.
This is a terrific little movie and was a surprise for me... The outstanding thing in this movie is Nico Parker. She's just an outstanding actress.

With commendable wit and zero self-pity, Chinn sketches the daily surreality of her teenage analogue, Doris (Nico Parker), and mother, Kristine (Laura Linney), navigating a gantlet of protesters who call the hospice an execution chamber.

Writer-director Laura Chinn tells the semi-autobiographical story about her dying brother and understandably crazed mother, with no-dry-eyes left performances by Nico Parker and Laura Linney, plus an assist from Woody Harrelson for good measure.
Elevated by Laura Linney, the secret weapon behind so many of the Sundance-flavoured indies Suncoast feels inspired by.
When Suncoast focuses on Doris and her emotionally brittle mom — Linney makes you feel the panicky fear of a mother about to lose her child — it’s heartbreaking, and is at its best.
“Suncoast” is a personal and mostly quiet movie, but it has the force of a real expression, of something that somebody just needed to say.

The movie is straightforward enough — unobtrusively shot, sensitively scored, lacking only a sense of urgency in its pacing. As a memory play and a launchpad for both a writer-director and the young actress playing her, it’s a very good start.
Never quite landing with enough of an impact for it to stick around in our heads after the sun has gone in, Suncoast settles for amiable competency.

Amateurishly written and precariously directed by Laura Chinn, Suncoast is neither unbearable nor unforgivable. It’s just another shallow, mediocre coming-of-age movie that makes too many wrong choices and ends up in the file marked familiar and forgotten
Nico Parker delivers an utterly real performance as Doris.

Forswearing anything like a pedantic message and giving the audience plenty of reasons to be sympathetic to the viewpoints of all three characters, Ms. Chinn has created a heartbreakingly real coming-of-age story.
A mostly feel-good film that pulls the characters and audience together to ask questions about ethics, faith, humanity and grief, without offering any real answers. Which is why it works.

This movie’s got everything (you’d expect from a Sundance movie): A period coming-of-age story inspired by the filmmaker’s own life, broader political themes, known stars like Linney and Harrelson playing eccentric characters, and a weepy conclusion.
With an unsubtle and inconsistent 2005 setting, a poorly structured and broadly written script, and an awkwardly apolitical point of view, Suncoast is a disappointment.
Suncoast spends much of its runtime trafficking in tiresome coming-of-age tropes, until the resulting crowd-pleaser has snuffed out much of what’s so singular about its central story.
"Suncoast” joins a more forgettable crop of teen movies, lacking plausible character development and sufficient depth to make its themes resonate.
An amiable ensemble effort, with two sturdy lead performances, “Suncoast” is reminiscent of the minor-key, quirky-charming ’90s dramedies so often discovered by the Sundance Film Festival.

title: Badland Hunters | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: If you like Concrete Utopia, this really extends the madness of that film.

title: Red Right Hand | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Ordinarily, I wouldn’t bother with a waste of time like Red Right Hand, but this is the stuff they’re making now. If you wait for something worthwhile, you might end up writing about only two or three movies a year.
MacDowell also reaches these rarified heights, giving her best performances in years.
Mostly it’s just a dopey mob movie with Southern accents of varying quality — predictable and cliched.
Red Right Hand doesn’t add anything particularly new to the well-worn genre. But it features enough bloody action sequences and shootouts to satisfy fans...

title: Frida | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The screenplay takes a paint-by-numbers approach, but the director, Julie Taymor...  supplies visual exuberance in the spirit of the film’s heroine.

A little better than the run-of-the-mill artist picture, probably because the colorful lives of these figures have an interest that for many people exceeds the interest of their work–or at least enhances it...
Smart, willful, and perverse, this Frida is nobody's servant, and the tiny Hayek plays her with head held high. You may want to laugh now and then, but you won't look away.
Salma Hayek finally ushered her dream project into production, but her impassioned lead performance lacks the necessary gravitas for the role, mistaking empty energy for wild fits of inspiration.
The plodding, glumly literal screenplay holds this otherwise expressive biopic back, but it's still a colourful and entertaining watch.

It wasn't a bad idea to conceive of the film as an epic, complex love story between Frida and Rivera, but the passion between them is more rhetorical than palpable...Taymor and Hayak give us only the rough sketch of a wild soul.
It would be nice to report that the subsequent film, with all of the talent and perseverance that has gone into seeing it to fruition, was worth the heartfelt efforts of all involved.
With splendid supporting turns from the likes of Ashley Judd, Edward Norton, and Geoffrey Rush, and some terrific set pieces, Taymor brings Kahlo's art to life.
While Frida is no masterpiece, it's nevertheless worth the price of admission to see Hayek master her craft.
Taymor's triumph is that her film, despite its distance from us in some ways, is pertinent and enthralling.
Ms. Taymor gets magnificent performances from Ms. Hayek as Frida and Alfred Molina as the oversexed Diego Rivera.
Just as in Kahlo's life, Rivera is the commanding centrifugal force of Taymor's film, and remains the best reason to sit through the otherwise uneven, mildly captivating Frida.
It's a competent and nicely designed biopic that for all of the director's attempts to link surrealist film imagery with Hayek's depiction of Kahlo somehow manages to be generally lackluster.
Passionate, provocative, hilarious, tragic and just dizzyingly beautiful to behold.
[The screenplay's] flatness ultimately defeats a film that's always a treat to look at.
No matter what happens to Hayek from this point on, she leaves us Frida.

Taymor, the creative mind behind Broadway's The Lion King, fills Frida with brilliant, surreal flourishes...a rich, funny and sometimes erotic film about an inspiring and influential figure in 20th-century art.
The greatest movie about an artist since Vincente Minnelli grafted the psychological turmoil of Vincent Van Gogh onto the screen in Lust for Life.
[Hayek] doesn't just act Frida, she inhabits her.
The movie is amazingly flat for a film about Kahlo.

title: Fitting In (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s not up there with the heights of the genre -- Clueless, The Craft and Ginger Snaps (name-checked in the film) can rest easy -- but represents a thematically rich addition to the canon.
Warm, generous and vulnerable.
Fitting In is explicitly a celebration of our different bodies and the disconnect of certain biological markers from gender.
Its revelations about gender, sexuality and identity tend toward the obvious, and sometimes veer into the facile.
Maddie Ziegler gives a fearless performance as a teen girl navigating romance, sex, and a complicated medical diagnosis.

It’s a compelling journey through an unconventional adolescence, but it’s also not a completely foreign depiction of young adulthood, particularly for those who have a complicated relationship with their gender and sexuality.

A sweet, slightly angry clarion call for a world where frank conversations and abundant information about sexual, reproductive, and gynecological health become a more normalized part of the coming-of-age process.
Fitting In is an at-times hilarious and consistently engrossing look at a flawed but earnest teenage girl in the process of redefining her new normal.
While imperfect, “Bloody Hell” does entertainingly offer food for thought via an important overall point made in non-preachy form...
While it beautifully nails some things, others didn’t land so well for me, especially the queerness.

title: Disappear Completely | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Henaine’s film is indeed more frightening in what it’s implying than what it is showing, and that makes it all the more effective.
What this twisted portrait of crumbling personhood lacks in earnest emotions it more than makes up for with a body horror that’s frequently subtle in execution but always brutal in conceit.
While it’s gorgeously shot, Henaine doesn’t allow for a lot of hope. His protagonist thinks he can find a way out of his downward spiral. We know that’s unlikely to happen.

title: The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's devastating. In some ways it felt like a violation... It left me feeling like I had watched a snuff film.

title: The Devil's Bath | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Though not a horror movie in the traditional sense, Fiala and Franz's latest delivers an unblinking portrait of inhumanity and festered faith.
You don’t need to abandon all hope to enter the movie’s painterly frame, but that sort of blind submission often seems to be the only emotional threshold to cross.
An inescapable nightmare that crawls into the psyche and eats it up alive.

This is a relentlessly grim film with an unsettling view of human nature; its audience will be small and self-selecting, but those who like having their guts ripped out by a movie will leave the theater satisfied.
Franz and Fiala are their signature selves, but ... mileage will vary, dictated by your appreciation for methodical avalanches of sorrow driven by puritanical pressures.
The result is one of those films you can’t stop thinking about — but might never want to see again.

Yet the cleverness of this psychodrama, by the Austrian directing duo Veronika Franz and Severin Fiala, is that it employs the tropes and tools of folk horror without any of that genre’s supernatural flourishes.
A fiery sermon of despondency and damnation, as well as a memorable nightmare of marriage, motherhood, and madness.
Veronika Franz and Severin Fiala depict Agnes’s plight with empathy but with a horror maven’s sense of ratcheting unease and encroaching doom.
The Devil’s Bath might be punctuated by the occasional jolt... but the final act of this movie is all the more terrifying because it isn’t softened by genre language or expectations.

As impressive as their past work has been, nothing they have done previously comes even close to the courage, emotional intelligence, stylistic ambition and ferocious intent driving this, their third feature.
The exquisite craftsmanship and powerhouse performances keep you deeply invested in this downward spiral, but buckle up: it’s a downer of the highest order.

While the story is drawn from historical facts and is specific to its period, there are few films, contemporary or otherwise, that capture so unflinchingly the distorting, debilitating symptoms of depression as a disease.
While it’s punishingly grim and has some pacing issues, this is a gripping psychological study by directors operating with formidable command.
If the story is so pitilessly bleak you may want to look away, the filmmaking craft is so compelling that you can’t.

title: Bob Marley: One Love | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The character is not complex here, the character here is really very heroic and very admirable... the issue with that is, that the feature film has a blandness at its heart that I actually don't think was part of the story.
For all the music in it, I don't think you get a real feel for [Bob Marley's] creative process.
This is a real disappointment.

[It's] a worthy addition to the features, docs, series and books that will continue to explore facets of the reggae superstar’s existence. This may not be the ultimate Marley narrative, but this project respectfully keeps his memory and mission alive.
Considering this is unlikely to be the last attempt to dramatise Marley’s life story, next time it wouldn’t hurt if a Jamaican filmmaker had a go.
His music and ideas—and all the people who helped usher them into this fractured world—deserve better.
Sadly, the much overworked script somehow manages to weave in all the cliches and compromises – not to mention the borderline hagiography – that have brought such opprobrium to the genre.
It’s a dutiful addition to a recent wave of such biographies (see “Rocketman” and “Bohemian Rhapsody”), but a largely uninspired one.
A particularly uninspired and deferential plod around the life and legacy of the Jamaican reggae star.
The director's previous film is King Richard...his new film is an interesting if undemanding glimpse into parts of the life of Bob Marley.
Straightforward and conventional, yet consistently involving...
If the film is ambitious, it is also inert.

The film recognizes the value in Marley's relationship to Rita, his impact during Jamaica's political crisis and his search for healing in music. But it never finds the rhythm when weaving those strands together and fails to do them justice.

What could have been daring is ultimately trite, relying on familiar music biopic tropes. It’s a shame, because at the center is a bravura performance from Kingsley Ben-Adir, who is uniquely suited to the title role.

Kingsley Ben-Adir catches the spirit of the Jamaican legend who became the face and voice of reggae and the Rastafarian conscience of his people. But this safe, shallow, family-sanctioned biopic gives us only snippets of songs and scraps of a life.
One Love doesn’t know how to begin exploring this artist and his art in any way that even begins to be interesting.
The next generation won’t learn the artist’s whole life story from this biopic, but they just might be inspired to do some Googling after the credits roll.

Whenever this family-authorized biopic about the Jamaican-born reggae icon who gave us classics such as “Jammin’,” “Everything’s Gonna Be Alright’ and “One Love” loses its storytelling grip, lead Kingsley Ben-Adir saves it and makes everything alright.

Reinaldo Marcus Green applies considerable seriousness to his depiction, which conjures up a plausible feel of the 1970s, in Jamaica and Europe alike. But the result is earnest and a little flat — and occasionally clunky in a showbiz-story way...
“One Love” does a better job of conveying the love reggae superstar Bob Marley’s family has for him than in showing us why we should love him, too.

title: Marmalade (2024) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: half the fun of in writer/director Keir O’Donnell’s genre-twisting romantic noir/escapist road movie is puzzling out where and how exactly the truth lies.
Keir O'Donnell’s delightful feature debut “Marmalade” is the kind of comedy that zigs when you expect it to zag, like a carnival ride that catches you by surprise.
In essence, "Marmalade" pretends to be more dunderheaded than it is, then acts as if it's been smart all along, in a shift that takes it from insulting to incoherent.
Best to just lie back and let wash over you like a soft bubble bath.

title: MoviePass, MovieCrash | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The directorial choice is to use animation in many instances, just to break up the interviews and archival footage... which is amusing enough. But what it all amounts to is a story of arrogance, strategic misrepresentation, and/or a massive scam.
Streaming services are loaded with documentaries about scammy internet-era companies, but “MoviePass, MovieCrash” finds the barely told story in all the juicy facts.
If there's a flaw to "MoviePass, MovieCrash," it's that these elements hardly elevate it beyond the boilerplate documentary structure formulas.

While MoviePass, MovieCrash is certainly an engaging oral history about the creation and destruction of the company, it’s equally absorbing as a searing critique by the filmmaker of systemic racism in an entrepreneurial environment.

Directed with just the right amount of stylistic flair by the talented Muta’Ali, it is a worthy companion to documentaries such as Eat the Rich: The GameStop Saga, and the Fyre Festival documentaries.
An illuminating look at a dream product that ran afoul of reality.
The stakes were and are on the lower side, and the documentary hits softer as a result, but will still resonate with those of us who were “there.”

title: Love Lies Bleeding (2024) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Stewart and O’Brian are terrific together in a credible but decidedly unsentimental romance -- this is a world of sweat, dirt, violence and terrible decisions.
Rose Glass's gory sensibility is put to good use in this steroid-popping, hyper-violent love story.
Once you get the interior ugliness of everyone involved, you may be able to chuckle at some of the violence, ha ha.

And besides: absurdist, gasp-inducing, melodramatic, and often intensely violent right through to the grisly, surrealist end, Love Lies Bleeding is entertaining enough without having to do all of the heavy-lifting.
Not many artists are this brave when it comes to probing at our sexual desires, and what they reveal about us.
If Saint Maude was a slow burn portrait of loneliness and obsession with a killer's sting on its tail, this is a brilliantly visceral sucker punch of a film.
This is a movie that will find its people. And once it does, cult status is more or less assured.
The film is at its most fun and original when it leans into surrealism.

Glass chooses to swerve this hellbound vehicle off the beaten highway, and, as with French body-horror hit Titane... coherence is thrown to the wind. This is essentially a superior B-movie that gets too pumped up on its own aesthetic steroids.

British film-maker Rose Glass lets rip with some pure roid-rage cinema in this uproarious, horribly violent and lethally smart noir thriller sited in the Venn diagram overlap between bodybuilding, murder and sex.
Glass never gets lost in the references, and mostly dispenses with legacy in favour of Jackie and Louise’s increasingly gory (strong stomachs required) and twisted misadventures.

The point really isn’t the crime. Or the bleeding, Or even, despite the palpable chemistry between Stewart and O’Brian, the love. It’s the intimate, passionately intense feel of the thing: the urgent need to escape where you are, and find someplace new.
Visceral and heady, this is a blood-soaked, all-American fable that’s as if Thelma And Louise literally went on steroids. Rose Glass is a force to be reckoned with.
A sharp, pointed movie that makes a movie star out of Katy O'Brian.
Love Lies Bleeding is a sweaty, sensual, dangerous exercise...for that, it’s a must-see.
With Saint Maud and Love Lies Bleeding, Glass has established herself as a daring visual storyteller.

Funny, shocking, and emotionally intoxicating at an almost primordial level, this chaotic love story is an imaginative blast of character-driven nitroglycerin and is guaranteed to be one of the year’s best.

It’s a bare-knuckle ride propelled by strong performances by the ever-watchable Kristen Stewart, the physically imposing Katy O’Brian and a lean and mean Ed Harris, wearing a wig that is a fright scene all on its own.

The best thrillers leave us worn out but satisfied. At the end of Love Lies Bleeding, there’s only exhaustion, and the vague feeling of having been dragged along on a fast ride to nowhere in particular.
Stewart, subtle and fierce, and O’Brian, sinewy and fiercer, prove exceptional at hitting two or three notes at once, and never obviously.

title: Cold Meat | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: If this UK-Canadian thriller has a wind-hardened snowcrust of malice, it’s somewhat less dense under the surface – though still an enjoyable punt from the digital-release ranks.

title: Orion and the Dark | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Turns into the Being John Malkovich of kids movies. Not saying it works. But I was certainly having more fun watching this unfold while my kids turned to me multiple times being like, “what is this??!!”
Whether you have a kid in your life who could use some catharsis or an inner child in need of a lullaby, check out the chaotic yet comforting Orion and the Dark.
This is a smart movie that addresses real and universal childhood fears in an original way.
Endlessly creative, full of alluring colors, and with a pace that grabs hold of viewers and doesn't let go, Orion and the Dark is made up of dynamic characters that you never could have imagined.
This disposable and enervating film marks a rare misstep for Netflix Animation, makers of the superior Leo, My Father’s Dragon and The Sea Beast.
More than a cut above your average rainy-afternoon distraction. It’s really a low-key blast.

Part Inside Out, part A Christmas Carol, with a pinch of Monsters Inc., the DreamWorks production for Netflix turns classic childhood fears into something unexpectedly complex, and occasionally rich and wonderful.
With sharp character design, entertaining dialogue, and positive messaging, “Orion and the Dark” is an early-year Netflix original surprise.

Orion and the Dark takes the clever wisp of a bedtime story provided by its source material and stretches it into a self-aware and sweetly multi-generational meditation on how beautiful the world can be if you learn to live with your fears.

Orion and the Dark is about fear and overcoming it but this movie directed by Sean Charmatz has too much junk clogging up the vision. It’s based on Emma Yarlett’s children’s book but, like its main human character, lacks confidence.

Orion also plays some characteristic Kaufman tricks: this is a stop-start affair that constantly turns itself inside out to muse self-reflexively on the nature of storytelling, like a fusion of Diary of a Wimpy Kid and Tristram Shandy.

Boasts the idiosyncratic anxiety, depression, and angst of its author’s work and the bouncy tone and matching visual style of every other recent cinematic kid’s fable—two flavors that, it turns out, don’t really go well together.
The film’s multiple, wackazoid hero journeys could conceivably leave Joseph Campbell scratching his head. Carl Jung, however, would be amused.

It’s nicely personal as his spin on a Pixar film, but the downside is that [Kaufman] can’t help imitating too many of them at once – which makes it equal parts sweet and hectic, and not a little overambitious.

Kaufman may not be the guy whose bedtime stories you want read to your kids. The moment they’re old enough, though, they should appreciate his deconstruction of predictable tropes they’ve known forever.
Like the best kind of children’s movies, it will make adults tear up and compel children to demand, “Again!” And best of all: not a Minion or Mario in sight.

It is a sweet-natured little tale, indebted to Monsters Inc and the whole Pixar canon but saved from being predictable with other borrowings (Back to the Future, Inception), as well as its various metafictional levels of storytelling.

It might look at first glance like another goofy CG distraction-fest, but this is that rare family-friendly film bursting with ideas and challenging concepts. It’s Charlie Kaufman’s introspective existential dread — for kids!
If the animation is nothing special, the script is better than what drives most animated movies aimed at a young audience. And you can certainly feel Kaufman’s neurotic touch on the material.

title: Ricky Stanicky | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's a good thing that this movie has been promoted as a comedy, because you wouldn't know it from watching.
Good comedies, of course, can make the tragic feel bittersweet, but Ricky Stanicky bungles its tone to the point that the whole affair comes across a little depressing.
Unfortunately, despite the best efforts of a game John Cena in the title role, the laughs are a little thin on the ground.

This is not to disparage the talents of likable stars Zac Efron and John Cena, not to mention a terrific supporting cast. I’m not sure even an out-of-retirement Daniel Day-Lewis and an in-his-prime Eddie Murphy could rescue this material.
Ricky Stanicky is a comedy that delivers nothing but tedium, wasting a clever idea by repeating the same jokes over and over.

It is all quite preposterous, and every time Mr. Cena performs a selection from Rod’s filthy repertoire, one cringes. But he makes the most of the part, abandoning any hint of a post-wrestling persona.
The film is an awkward mix of blithe farce and mawkish life lessons, and when in doubt it doubles down on the middling, madcap tone. The laughs are patchy.
Cena wants it to work so bad you can taste it, but the 16-time World Wrestling Entertainment champion can't salvage material that would be too dopey for a seventh grader's creative writing class.

Nothing seems remotely real, ever, not even the blindingly bright lighting. The one bright spot is Cena, who is quite good. Like his character, who goes above and beyond to adeptly play Ricky Stanicky, Cena really and truly commits.

Playing this filthy-minded, flop-sweating boozehound, Cena barges into the plot with the get-it-while-you-can gusto of a raccoon upending a trash bin.... I found myself rooting for the film to get it together for Cena’s sake — to care as much as he does
So much of “Ricky Stanicky” is juvenile and joyless, playing on drawn out jokes, bottom shelf masturbation punchlines, and varying degrees of cringe comedy.
Efron gets stuck with another slipshod script in Ricky Stanicky, a sad demonstration that what was once considered outrageous, transgressive and anarchic now just seems crass, tired and witless.
Ricky Stanicky might be imaginary and doesn’t measure up to its promise, but in terms of that basket within the wrestler-turned-actor’s filmography, it at least fits Cena like a glove.

Your mileage may vary, but it’s probably safe to assume that most audiences will lose patience with the stale plot machinations of the movie’s second half, when Ricky Stanicky trades its high-key hijinx for a distended mess of sitcom-level shenanigans.
It’s less effective near its overly contrived finale. But Cena’s performance is a revelation — he’s the real deal as both actor and comedian.
The problem with Farrelly as a director now, which may be to his credit as a human being, is that he’s too kind for that sort of broad humor any more.

A raunchy, R-rated return to form for the “Dumb and Dumber” co-director: an unapologetically lowbrow buddy movie, featuring the funniest performance yet from up-for-anything wrestler John Cena in the title role.
There are a few laughs but, at nearly two hours, Ricky Stanicky far outstays its welcome.
Little more than a creaky lark that fails to generate consistent laughs, even if it proves that John Cena is a charming goof-off who’s game for anything.

Where the antics of Tag’s characters effectively captured the stupid joy of acting like your younger self while hanging out with your oldest friends, Ricky Stanicky is stupid in a much less joyful way.

title: The Shamrock Spitfire | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It has an easy swing and self-assurance, thanks in no small part to a well-starched performance by Shane O’Regan as real-life pilot Brendan Finucane, AKA “Spitfire Paddy”.

title: Kiss the Future | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: In its brisk pace, well-deployed song choices and storytelling energy, “Kiss the Future” is skillful at avoiding seeming like an ode to U2 even though the band’s involvement fills over half the movie.

This is history told through emotions as much as through well-documented events, conveying both the resilience of Sarajevans and the power of pop music (without falling into too much celebrity self-regard).
"Kiss the Future” is a portrait of a city and a people who used culture to fight back; it’s also the story of a rock ‘n’ roll band exploring the limits of how its music can impact the real world.
While an interesting ’90s history lesson, Nenad Cicin-Sain's film could have benefited from portraying Sarejevo's resident artists at the close as extensively as it does at the beginning.
A touching reminder of music's ability to change the world.
A polished yet unexpectedly affecting documentary...
This movie is a time-capsule of Europe’s recent tragic past.

title: The Antisocial Network: Memes to Mayhem | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Arthur Jones and Giorgio Angelini’s brisk feature-length documentary is very good on the hive mind of 4chan, where it was all about the lulz, but struggles to encompass how the real-world feedback mutated the site’s peculiar DNA.
It’s more engaging than a lot of this doc subgenre by virtue of the filmmaking acumen of its directors.
Angelini and Jones are desperately pointing out that the virtual house is on fire, and the flames have spread into the real world.

title: Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: After so many mishandled or abandoned series — from “Fantastic Beasts” to “Narnia” to “Percy Jackson” — it’s nice to see one that’s heading in the right direction.

Until Ghostbusters decides if it wants to throw its lot in with one era or the other, it’s always going to be between two worlds. And that purgatory makes for a middling experience that doesn’t quite satisfy.
This newest franchise entry is built on nostalgia and a stacked cast, but not enough to make it worth watching.
It's like the scriptwriters just devoured some plates of Ghostbusters' stuff and went barf... none of it makes any sense.
The plot is pretty much a cut-and-paste duplication of the original film.

There's a lot of self-referential backslapping throughout the film, but overall the problem is that there's too much going on. It's like the filmmakers couldn't figure out what story to tell, so they just threw everything into the mix.

The 1984 original was original and entertaining. This fifth instalment is not the former and barely the latter. The Ghostbusters song asks "Who ya gonna call?" My suggestion is call it quits, but I suspect there's a ghost of a chance of that happening.
If only the filmmakers could’ve shoehorned some actual jokes into this overstuffed confection, or served up action that didn’t look like it was edited in a digital shredder!
Frozen Empire isn’t nearly as glacial or tepid as Afterlife, but it does suffer from a similar desire to drown us in Easter eggs.
Much better than the wobbly reboot, with plenty to delight both long-time fans and newcomers.
The reverence for the past here does nobody any favours. It is as if a 1984 kids’ film tried to get them interested in the collected lore and backstory of Abbott and Costello.
With Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire, busting still makes me feel good.
A blunt Gen X nostalgia play -- a tribute act grinding out the oldies on a cruise ship to nowhere.
Gil Kenan doesn't so much shepherd a story as he does manage the "Ghostbusters" brand for 115 minutes. We get a few winks, a few ghosts, and that's about it.
Aykroyd, who co-wrote the summer of 1984 blockbuster with the late Harold Ramis, is the heart and soul of a film that sets new against old.

My fingers have taken to their death bed simply typing out the basics. Yet, “Frozen Empire” is an eclectic, enjoyable barrage of nonsense — a circus act that kicks off with a Robert Frost poem and climaxes with Ray Parker Jr.’s titular synth banger.
It’s all too much of nothing special and all too little of anything funny or fun.
Aykroyd and Grace are the soul of the thing, to whatever degree a soul exists. At this point, Aykroyd has shed any pretence of ironic distance, emerging as the mournful weirdo he surely always was.
Other than Aykroyd, who admittedly displays a characteristic glee at being in his comfort zone here, nobody seems to want to be there or going through these motions again.
A very busy movie that lacks the emotional hook of its predecessor, while spending too much time on the wrong characters in a way that yields a rather lifeless, chilly affair.

title: Invincible | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A film lacking Herzog's USP -- an ironic and regressive sense of the irreducible power of images -- 'Invincible' feels as though it has been devised by a scholar steeped in Herzog lore, but who at some crucial early stage mistook him for Istvan Szabo.
There's a sugar coating to the way Papale's story unfolds, but not so much that you'll spoil your dinner.
Even Papale's most famous play, recovering a fumble to set up a touchdown, is embellished, as if Disney can't bear to stick with the facts.
When it's good it's very good. When it's bad -- well, it's still pretty good.

Invincible is a working-class jock Cinderella fantasy with the sincerity of a beer commercial, the soul of a Republican incumbent, and the designer-flannel esthetics of an old Bruce Springsteen video.
It may not break new ground, but Invincible is an entertaining film, awash in clichs but leavened by the charismatic performance of Mark Wahlberg as Vince Papale.
What's modestly refreshing about the way this story is told by director Eric Core and writer Brad Gann, is that the person with the largest doubts about going pro is Papele himself.
It's a hard-earned humanity that gives Invincible its vigor.
The movie is shamelessly manipulative.
Wahlberg and his co-stars, including love interest Elizabeth Banks, really seem to believe in the story, with a grave intensity that enhances its underdog appeal.
Credit Invincible with varying the Disney formula just a bit. While still a "feel good" movie, it's a dark and miserable road that must be traveled along the way.
As much as I wanted to root for Invincible, its protagonist comes across as neither ebullient nor vivacious.
Invincible is as much a period piece as it is a sports movie, complete with a non-stop soundtrack of familiar hits that, unfortunately, makes one think of That '70s Show a little too often
They're [Disney] not looking to make a complex, textured analysis of competition and ambition here, they just want a football movie that ends with the audience cheering for the hero.
For a movie about following your dreams, this one is sorely lacking imagination.
The most remarkable accomplishment of Invincible is to make a mid-'70s musical soundtrack sound spectacular.
The genre shows serious signs of wear in this needlessly fictionalized feature about Vince Papale, a 30-year-old bartender who improbably won a spot on the Philadelphia Eagles in 1976.
Wahlberg and the rest of the solid cast sell this ESPN equivalent of a Lifetime movie.
There's a danger in reducing pictures like this to the sum of their lessons, at the expense of recognizing them as satisfying, if flawed, genre exercises.
Put simply, this movie works, and if your heart doesn't beat heartily in appreciation than you better go to a doctor because you just might be dead.

title: Música | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “Música” might seem like it’s hitting beats we’ve grown accustomed to, but Mancuso’s sweet, soulful feature debut doesn’t follow in others’ footsteps. What a gem.
Now that Mancuso has gotten his origin story out onto the screen, it’s exciting to wonder what a sophomore effort could entail for him. For now, “Música” has earned him his filmmaking stripes.
For all that creativity and technical wizardry, the most impressive thing about Música is that, if you’ve been paying attention to Mancuso’s work, nothing present in the movie is entirely new.
Even when its narrative tips into clichéd territory, Música’s aesthetic remains loose and kinetic — an exciting reflection of its creator’s spirit.

Mancuso crams all of his passions into the movie, including the puppets (which, with his cartoonish coif, he resembles). He’s playing a character who is occasionally too passive. Yet, he’s made a film that’s confidently, intentionally overwhelming.
Despite a few unfinished edges and missteps, there’s much to savor in Mancuso’s feature debut.
“Música” heralds the arrival of a filmmaker, an actor, and a musician worth paying attention to, while also delivering a winning and visually inventive musical comedy.

title: The Truth vs. Alex Jones | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The devastating impact of Jones’s conspiracies on families already ripped apart by the Sandy Hook tragedy – which killed 26 – is made clear
The madness of it, and the knowledge that Jones’s rants are giving a certain rabid demographic exactly what they want, the dizzying sense of unreality and the multiplying questions as you watch.
A scathing and well-deserved takedown...

Compared with Reed’s previous work, which includes “Leaving Neverland” and “Four Hours at the Capitol,”  “The Truth vs. Alex Jones” is more sharply targeted and careful not to entirely rely on the audience’s empathy.
“The Truth vs. Alex Jones” offers a lesson in just how vicious and pervasive conspiracy theories can become and a chilling portrait of how little they may trouble their purveyors.
Sharply edited, sensitively constructed, and expertly crafted.
The film is more than a profile of a conspiracy theorist, it's a tribute to the pain of the Sandy Hook families.
Tragically, The Truth vs. Alex Jones doesn’t deliver any closure. What it does provide is a disturbing reminder that the fight against evil will likely be never-ending.

title: Bleeding Love | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Decent performances from both McGregors can’t breathe much spirit (alcoholic or otherwise) into the film’s listless and generic screenplay.
There’s no dramatic tension, our protagonists whine a lot and they seem, at best, like two solipsistic twits driving around the desert and moaning about parenting.
We’ve followed this kind of bicker-and-heal therapeutic arc so many times now, the onus falls on all involved to spike it with truth, or at least novelty.

This unbearably cute joint selfie of a movie is gruesomely indulgent and entitled from the first; it allows Ewan McGregor little or no opportunity to show his natural wit and flair and there is oddly no real chemistry between him and his co-star.
It’s a film that’s been thought out but doesn’t reach any new conclusions; that assembles some good elements, but doesn’t really consider how they all fit together.
Ewan McGregor is polished enough to establish a mood of unflagging realism, undaunted by a script that provides almost no opportunity to keep the momentum going.
It’s hard to see why this movie was made other than to expand Clara McGregor’s résumé.
A meandering road trip that eventually finds its way home.
This uneven indie road-trip drama is at times too by-the-numbers but is always captivating thanks to its two stars, who hold the screen throughout.

title: Bitconned | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Fascinating in ways that range from the brazenly entertaining to the morally queasy, this feature-length documentary is a giddy recap of the absurd heights reached by Ray Trapani.
An enraging account of opportunistic charlatanry, it’s also an entertaining ride in the so-called wild west of crypto.

title: Murder Mubarak | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is the closest any film has come to re-creating Anuja Chauhan’s universe, very few can do the insider-outsider divide with such acuteness, both sharp and warm.

title: Miller's Girl | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: My worst list of 2024 starts right here.
From one scene to the next, a viewer may experience trouble discerning whether this is a merely stupid movie, an amusing specimen of semi-witting camp, or stealth coup of high-wire self-parody.

What cannot be denied is that the film is well shot and that Ortega, like Freeman, fulfills their roles without much fault, which, for many spectators, will be more than sufficient. [Full review in Spanish]
Miller’s Girl just skims the surface, and settles for making that surface look visually sumptuous.
As a showcase for Ortega’s star power, Miller’s Girl does get the job done. But as a piece of pulpy, post-#MeToo storytelling...Bartlett’s dramatic thriller unfortunately comes up short.
The film ultimately commits a truly unforgivable cinematic offense: It turns tedious.
This could have been good trash, as my mom used to say in describing Sidney Sheldon novels, but it never comes close to reaching those heights.
This is pure unintentional camp, striking that wild, so-bad-it’s-entertaining chord vigorously. I can’t recommend “Miller’s Girl” but I also can’t recommend it enough.
Only a generous grader would award this script anything better than a D-plus.
Possesses roughly the intellectual heft of a perfume ad. Dated and creepy in all the wrong ways, it’s a movie that might have escaped derision in the 1980s but deserves to get slapped around today.
A work of glaring artifice, “Miller’s Girl,” written and directed by Jade Halley Bartlett, is being touted as a psychological thriller, but it’s too vapid and silly to do much besides titillate.
For all the ways the film flirts with its thorny topic, proving to be controversial in only a superficial sense, the story is one not even the most inexperienced writer would praise.
A brooding, bookish and bursting-with-pheromones thriller.
Taken together, this movie might be less fun than taking the SATs.
“Miller’s Girl” delivers a tale whose transgressions are stylish but disappointingly predictable, one written with skillful knowledge of form but not the maturity to implement it with originality.

title: While You Were Sleeping | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Bullock gives Lucy just the right amount of edge. Pullman's performance as Peter's down-to-earth younger brother is also a deft mix of moxie and frustration.
[Bullock] knows one of the secrets of doing romantic comedy: treating the romance as a good joke.
Compared to While You Were Sleeping, even the half-baked scenario of the Marisa Tomei-Robert Downey Jr. romance Only You looks witty and inventive.
It's Bullock's first shot at a role in which she plays second fiddle neither to males nor special effects. And she turns out to be every bit as delightful as anyone might have expected.
A cute premise with engaging leads but little else to keep you awake.
It plays like a movie dreamed up by people in a studio marketing department who'd decided to bare their souls.
This year's Sleepless In Seattle. Only better.
Bullock just about knocks herself exhausted being winsome and lovable.
The film's casual warmth may make you tolerate some of the shortcomings -- especially since Bullock seems to be having such a fine time with her first starring role.
Director Jon Turteltaub has a smooth style suited to classic farce and knows just how to pace the material to accentuate the positive.
As cute and cuddly a bedtime story as anyone could wish for.
This is a formula film, but it has the kind of good cheer and fine tuning that occasionally give slickness a good name.
Bullock is a genuinely engaging performer, which at least gives the treacle some minty freshness.
Romantic, sweet without being cloying, and light on its feet.
Recaptures the true spirit of the best kind of modern fairy tale.
A sappy, negligible, thoroughly innocuous romantic comedy vehicle for Sandra Bullock.
A consistently adorable, if utterly predictable, piece of fluff.
Cringe-inducing moments abound.
A lighthearted, charming nougat for romantics.
A feel-good film, warm and good-hearted.

title: Lisa Frankenstein | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It’s not original – in fact it relies too much on its many pop-cultural callbacks – but there’s something universal about Lisa’s emotions that any lovesick, sulky teen girl can revel in.
... a serviceable, fun goth romp.
Just about fun enough to sustain 101 clattering, dusty, dimly lit minutes. Reviews will be mixed. But it has every chance of being resurrected as a cult classic.
Like the creature at the center of it, this starts out creaky... but then, again, like the creature at the center of it, it proceeds to find its feet and indeed its voice.

Like Karyn Kusama’s Jennifer’s Body (2009), also scripted by Diablo Cody, Lisa Frankenstein disinters a murderous monstrousness from female adolescence, empowerment and eros, while gradually reaffirming the (step)sisterhood.
If the central character isn’t consistent or at least credible, what chance does the rest of this sloppily paced, tacked-together mess have?
Cody comes up with some spiky lines... But if ever a film was in need of a 10-gigawatt jolt through the neck, it’s this one.

At best, the film works as a riposte to Hughes’s naff sex comedy Weird Science, with Lisa building an ideal man who is strong, subservient, sexually dynamic and, best of all, silent. So, yes, lovely on paper.
It’s clear Williams knows how to tell a story and with “Lisa Frankenstein” as her first wacky and wonderful calling card, there’s no denying she is a filmmaker to watch.
It succeeds with us having a good time, and is capable of withstanding more than one viewing. [Full review in Spanish]
It's not Heathers.
Though it may struggle to balance tone, Lisa Frankenstein is a crass, unapologetic love letter to the horrors of teenage girlhood, spearheaded by an electric turn from Kathryn Newton.
These filmmakers seem to be making fun of those people [from the '80s], and that kind of bugged me... This just doesn't hold up very well, and it's not directed all that tightly either.
A single-joke skit that’s too self-aware to be distinctively funny, freaky or thrilling.
The result is an interesting misfire, yielding a few amusing moments while adding up to considerably less than the sum of its parts.
The smarter, sharper, funnier version of Lisa Frankenstein hovers tantalizingly over this movie without ever coming to fruition. Back to the morgue with it.
A mood board for 80s goth kids that's more in love with its premise than its characters.

Another Frankenstein throwback (“Poor Things” has nothing to fear) dressed up as a 1980’s teen sex comedy about a goth girl (Kathryn Newton) with the hots for an undead lover (Cole Sprouse). Diablo Cody’s devilish script is sadly tamed by a PG-13 rating.
I laughed throughout, and even with all the goofily dismembered mayhem, there was an innate sweetness that captured my heart and refused to let it go.
An uneven mash-up of 80s teen comedy and horror has some strong ideas but the tone wobbles when it tries to straddle.

title: Scoop | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film is essentially a piece of nostalgia, but it swings along with an insouciance we haven't had from him in a long time.
Nestled as it is amid the clamor of the late-summer blockbusters, it's the kind of small pleasure that can make you feel intensely grateful.
Woody -- enough with the one-liners.
It's full of funny lines and clever inventions.
Scoop is no more than a beguiling trifle. But in the dog days of summer, it's a perk to wallow in inspired silliness.
Scoop has something Match Point didn't, something that none of Allen's films have had to quite this degree in 10 years. It's really, really funny.
A bouncy comedy/mystery about a young would-be journalist (Scarlett Johansson) trying to solve a crime.
If only it were funny instead of just passably amusing, and if only Allen's movies hadn't declined to such a state of rote self-repetition that even passably amusing is tantamount to a compliment.
Scoop is worthwhile viewing for Allen's quips. Just don't expect much of a story.
Scoop, a half-baked amalgam of Manhattan Murder Mystery and Curse of the Jade Scorpion -- sadly demonstrates that Allen has lost much of his comic timing both as a director and an actor.
To see Allen, now 70, trying to reclaim the persona he's been handing off is like watching Willie Mays fall down trying to hit a curve ball during his last season.
Scoop feels like a tentative doodle in the general direction of Match Point, only chronologically reversed and more or less amusing.
Scoop, an amiable romp of lighthearted fun.

It's thin, not really even worth the 90-plus minutes it takes to get from start to finish, but right from the get-go Scoop made me giggle, and I didn't stop until I'd gotten a good five or six steps away from my front door.
The movie is watchable, there's the occasional good one-liner, but it's extremely slight, overly drawn out and never for a moment believable.
Things don't really get ugly in Scoop, they just feel very familiar very quickly, which doesn't mean it's necessarily bad, just awfully lightweight and terribly unoriginal.
A romp of a thing, Scoop won't be mistaken for splendid. Yet for diminutive pleasure, the murder- mystery comedy can rightly be called splendini.
Scoop feels like the leftovers from that [Manhattan Murder Mystery], after they've been strained through The Curse of the Jade Scorpion.
One form of low-rent showbiz Allen depicts in Scoop is Fleet Street journalism, but it's depicted with none of the witty rancor or intelligence of Evelyn Waugh's 1937 Scoop.
It saddens me to report -- Scoop is distinctly minor Allen, with less weight to it than one of his old humor doodles in The New Yorker.

title: No Way Up | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The one selling point of No Way Up is that it makes you scared of being scared, which may be enough for a lazy evening on the couch with a friend, a drink and a meal, though it probably wouldn’t work on sushi night.

title: French Girl | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I just can’t believe this movie came out this year instead of twenty years ago.
For every inventive or simply satisfying rom-com, there are dozens of clumsy, rote ones — “French Girl” falls among the latter.

There are at least a dozen good zingers in here, particularly a three-part punchline from Ed Weeks as a snobbish food critic that kicks off with, “Have you ever seen an emaciated dolphin?” The trouble is none of the performances are on the same wavelength
French Girl’s crude and at times infantile slapstick humour is offset by livelier beats between the cast, whose cross-cultural banter is littered with flashes of genuine wit.

title: Immaculate (2024) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A really charismatic actor can supercharge even the most stolid genre fare, and that’s what Sweeney pulls off as the innocent but fast-learning Cecilia.
The movie’s shockeroo ending made me wince, and it made me laugh. It’s bad-gal blasphemy of the highest order.
Mohan, for his part, films with a great sense of space and frequently presents us with images that remain on the retina. [Full review in Spanish]
It becomes this weirdly, timely kind of inversion of Rosemary's Baby... and then it starts to get really interesting, far more interesting than I expected.
The scare factor is there, but it does go over the line in ways that aren't particularly profitable.
They go places that are very daring and I applaud them for it.
Unfortunately, between Immaculate’s cliches, incoherent direction, and shallow characters, not even the ethereal power of Sydney Sweeney can rescue this nunsploitation flick from damnation.
It would be nothing without a charismatic star at its heart. Sweeney is certainly that – and, as the final shot confirms, she is as game as they come. Nun more fun.

Immaculate, a horror film set in a convent, is a Sweeney showcase in the smartest possible way, devoting much of its running time to her wide-eyed, trembling visage as she encounters all kinds of demonic nastiness.
There’s something about this movie that feels very tactile, and it brings out of Sweeney a hands-on, up-to-her-elbows-in-gore performance.
All that you’re left with, in its final scenes, is the reminder of that other, very famous horror film about pregnancy, Rosemary’s Baby.
If your faith can be shaken by a movie, work on your faith. As a critic, I was underwhelmed and unimpressed.
Sweeney is a likeable presence and truly brings meaning to the term ‘Scream Queen’, but this many decades into religious-based horror, we can do so much better than this.

Sweeney alone is reason enough to dig into Immaculate and its world of secret sins and often surprising gore. Even without its star, it’s a solid enough horror endeavor, but with Sweeney, it’s compulsively, thrillingly watchable.

For all its looking back to cinema past, Immaculate explores a topic that could not be more incendiary in present-day America, , in the wake of the 2022 overturning of Roe vs Wade by a newly conservative-majority Supreme Court.

This is Sweeney’s ballsiest move yet and a must-watch for fans of intelligent horror.  With its blend of campy thrills and social commentary, it proves to be a standout addition to the genre, anchored by Sydney Sweeney's simply divine performance.
In fact, many things in this film have an off-kilter absurdity, for good and bad.
Sweeney delivers a tour de force cry of anguish while holding the camera in an impressively unbroken shot... Scream, queen, scream.
The movie draws out its storytelling in a way that seems all too literal and lacking in the kind of narrative stamina that keeps horror fans on their toes.

Its credentials as a fright fest fall well short of being able to cancel the predictability of its plot or its multiple absurdities. Horror fans may take to it, but I don’t think it’s going to make many converts.

title: Ramy Youssef: More Feelings | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Even when he’s prescriptive Youssef astutely unfolds quandaries and draws laughs from both the incongruous and normally unspoken. The answers here, like the punchlines, are never obvious.
The comic takes a nuanced look at his own role as a Muslim celebrity and at the American response to conflict in the Mideast.
His humor is as sharp an Obsidian blade, and his punchlines often land with a terrific and cheerfully politically incorrect sting.

title: The Greatest Love Story Never Told | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Satisfying as this documentary might be in the greater story of Lopez’s personal growth, it barely hangs together on its own.
