By harnessing not just the drive that made Lopez a superstar but the fragility (especially personal) inherent in its maintenance, Jason Bergh’s film accomplishes something unexpected: offering audiences a truly new way to look at her.

title: Stopmotion | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The first half is mostly just functional... But when Stopmotion gets gross, it gets good.
Stopmotion is a strange, disturbing, exhilaratingly perverse film, which, like stop-motion itself, brings dead objects to life, and vice versa.
It’s a wildly inventive spurt of bug-eyed British gore that pulls the innards out of the creative process. Quite literally, at some points.
A British film that finds a particularly creepy way to generate fear. [Full review in Spanish]
An undeniably grisly but ultimately tedious tiptoe through the genre tropes.
“Stopmotion” isn’t perfect, but each element moves in lock step to forge a deeply troubling intimacy between Ella and her repellent figurines.

Robert Morgan unquestionably has a knack for the extraordinary; it is both a measure of his talent and of its limits that this debut feature stumbles only when it tries to do something on the ordinary side.

Art and storytelling collide in breathtaking yet revolting fashion. Morgan’s knockout debut opens up the veins of a turbulent artist, delivering one creepy melding of mediums to an unsettling, powerful degree.
The film falters when it attempts to mold its best instincts into a discernible narrative shape.
Aside from just being a good old fashioned horror movie, there is an intelligence and ferocity at play here that speaks to much grander things than just simple genre thrills.
It's chilling and tragic in equal measures.

title: The Convert (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The movie takes on a bittersweet note, bringing history to life in all its messy complexity - and the everyday players who shape it.

The Convert manages to combine an entertaining portrayal of an often ignored historical era with universal questions about whether it’s ever possible to build a human society on the foundation of something other than violence.
The Convert is uneven and doesn’t fully live up to its thematic ambitions. But it’s handsomely made and thankfully avoids falling victim to white savior syndrome.
The lush forests and stark, black sand beaches, shot in locations near those used in “The Piano,” help make “The Convert” more than a message movie.
Tamahori's film addresses how New Zealand's indigenous people were mistreated and exploited, but it's also an accomplished character study into the plight of three principles.

All of the time spent on Thomas Munro’s various campaigns for reconciliation and harmony between two Māori tribes hampers the film, which would have been better served had it expounded on the grander conflicts that it only superficially acknowledges.

It starts a little ponderously, as the time and place is set and the characters are fleshed out, but once that haka happens it becomes a gripping historical drama about how faith can be tested in expected and unexpected ways.
Tamahori has given a world rarely seen on the big screen. He’s shown what rich pickings are to be mined from Antipodean history by a filmmaker with the guts and talent to give it a go.
The film does a fine job evoking a vivid sense of place, Tamahori and Loane capturing the might and majesty of a stunning part of the world.
There’s just enough of an interesting theme and strong production value (it’s impossible not to succumb to the breathtakingly imposing landscapes) to earn “The Convert” some grace.

title: Irish Wish | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I really thought this was super charming.
You've got a very charming Lohan, some lovely Irish scenery, and a Hallmark plot. And if that's what you're here for, you'll get it.
A bargain-basement romcom that does its star no favors.
[Lohan] plays Maddie as someone for whom you want the best. And sometimes that’s all you need a romantic-comedy heroine to be.
This disposable, fantasy-light Netflix rom-com timed to St. Patrick’s Day is stridently forgettable, even if the charms of Lindsay Lohan and her BFF Ayesha Curry, and others in the cast, are not.
Irish Wish is an excellent advertisement for a variety of Irish touchstones. But, as a film, it’s as dumb as a box of rocks.
There are no leprechauns in this abysmal romantic comedy. Otherwise, though, pretty much no theme-park Ireland cliche is left unturned...

Cartoonishly colourful cinematography brings emerald-tinted sparkle to Killruddery House, Lough Tay, the Cliffs of Moher and other tourist traps. What else? It’s professionally assembled? Everyone has nice hair?
Lohan is her usually charming self throughout, wasted once again in a cardboard streaming project. This “Wish” is a wash.
... there’s so little feeling in Irish Wish. I’ve cared more about (and cried more during) actual greeting card commercials than anything in this film.
It’s genuinely terrible, but also oddly watchable.
[Lohan] is an undeniable star and has always succeeded as a screwball comedienne
As a fairy-tale romantic rendering of Ireland, Irish Wish is almost offensively bad; as another rung on the ladder for Lindsay Lohan romcom supremacy, it is almost, somehow, beyond reproach.
“Irish Wish” might be more at home on the Hallmark Channel — where it would really stand out — but in the land of Netflix, it just doesn’t shine the way “Falling for Christmas” did.

The movie is as frothy as the foam on a pint of Guinness, as formulaic as the last disposable Netflix rom-com. Yet these two make you believe that they belong together, and not every romantic comedy does that.
If you're in need of a silly rom-com to get through the long, hard days of reality, you've come to the right place.
The curse of auburn-haired American women heading to Ireland for terrible magic-themed romcoms continues, 14 years after Amy Adams took an unfortunate vacation in the detestable Leap Year.
Mostly the movie is a determinedly mild addition to the Lindsay Lohan “what-if” universe.
Irish Wish makes terrific use out of the country’s locations and lulls you into not asking too many questions.

title: If You Were the Last | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “If You Were the Last” is game for fluffy rom-com-like tension, but it fears its own premise. What a missed opportunity.
A romantic comedy that revives the screwball formula where two people talk themselves silly — and we only had to go to the end of the solar system to make it happen.
Sappy and, in terms of its comedy, rather cringe-worthy, never quite finding the sweet spot between romance and laughs.

title: 5lbs of Pressure | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: In a TV series, you would enjoy seeing what dumb thing he has done this episode. But this isn’t a TV series, and as it stands, 5lbs of Pressure falls into the category of a decent rather than particularly great crime movie.
Named after the lethal force behind a handgun’s trigger release, “5lbs” weaves an engaging-enough web of misunderstandings, grudges and doomed trajectories amongst various shady types.

title: The Painter | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “The Painter” never seems like more than a rote shoot-’em-up inadequately juiced by the kind of shocking revelations that are all contrived verbal explication.

title: Lousy Carter | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Lousy Carter might be a reminder that middle age is filled with monotony and unsolvable problems, but that doesn’t mean our movies have to be.
It’s a terrific performance, one that speaks volumes even as it explores the acute limits of Lousy’s emotional intelligence.
Turn the concept of a laugh-out-loud comedy inside-out and you’ll have a feel for Byington’s sense of humor: a sustained cruel hum, the room tone of a crypt.
Even by Byington’s lo-fi standards, Lousy Carter feels ramshackle. It’s got traces of the familiar warm bathos of his sardonic best work. However, like Lousy’s cardigan, it’s all a little threadbare.
Told in just under 80 minutes, "Lousy Carter" made me laugh uncomfortably quite often and then even shocked me at the end.
This low-stakes effort nevertheless proves capable of offering some smart insights into love and death, and a couple of genuinely affecting moments towards the end...
We’ve all seen movies like “Lousy Carter” before, and this one’s adequate, without being particularly insightful or memorable.

title: Einstein and the Bomb | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Packs a wallop in detailing how the man widely considered the father of atomic energy came to influence the innovations of the Manhattan Project, and how he lived to regret it.
A moving and even poetic mixed-media meditation on Albert Einstein...

title: You'll Never Find Me | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A unique and startling film, decidedly its own "thing," albeit steeped in the horror tradition.

You’ll Never Find Me is one more indication that some of the most creative work on screens large and small is being done in genre film, and that there is wisdom in prioritizing soundscape over landscape or visual effects.
Through the use of sound and shadowy cinematography, a great sense of unease cloaks this taut bone-chiller, a chamber piece played to perfection by its two leads.
There’s a feverishly wet and moody ambience to this film; it feels like it’s dripping all over you.
A smart, well-made little thriller.
So much of the joy of You’ll Never Find Me comes from an overwhelming sense that you never really quite know what’s coming next
Indianna Bell and Josiah Allen blend grim, contemporary horror with a classic haunted house aesthetic, resulting in a claustrophobic, oft-unsettling chamber piece.

title: Players | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This is a rom-com where all the emphasis is on comedy and not so much on the romance, for sure.
Nobody should expect too much of a movie in this genre released on Valentine’s Day, and grading on that curve, “Players” happily punches above its weight class and exceeds expectations.
Players is a perfectly fine — occasionally better-than-fine — romantic comedy starring well-known TV actors who know their way around this kind of material.
Mack’s character development is believable because of Rodriguez’s committed performance, which moves with ease between tears and laughter.
The tropes are so front and center that real life barely has any room to breathe.
A middling movie elevated to memorable by the breezy charm of Gina Rodriguez.
“Players” is an old-fashioned romantic comedy, which means you know the end from the start. That’s not a bug; it’s a feature, a well-deployed one in this case.
Director Trish Sie’s middling and at times mawkish film not only makes us hate the game, but also its players.

title: Race for Glory: Audi vs. Lancia | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Mostly, it’s a competent yet uninspired overview of events before and during the globetrotting series of races that comprised the 1983 World Rally Championship.

title: Air Force One Down | Rotten Tomatoes
Argylle | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “Argylle” is fun in spurts with a strong cast of characters that help you get through the overly exaggerated runtime. But the script boxes itself into a corner too often and falls into repetition.

Appreciating all these stars during a single visit to the movie theater is undoubtedly satisfying; but it was reasonable to expect much more from a $200 million mega-production that… is excessively conditioned by the use of CGI. [Full review in Spanish]
Argylle ultimately buckles under the weight of its own ambition, and the end result is a messy, overlong (if entertaining) romp.
Bloated and confusing...
If I was Taylor Swift, and I wrote Argylle, I too would deny the whole thing.
Much like The Flash, this action movie feels less fun and more like a punishment.
This is the most fun a Matthew Vaughn film has been for a very long time.
[Vaughn's movies] are loud, over-the-top films with style and bravado ... So even with all of the twists in Argylle, the spy action movie’s biggest surprise may be how utterly bland it is.
Arg-vile.
For all its generic spy movie glitz – we zip between locations in the US, London, rural France and an aircraft carrier – it has an impoverished, synthetic feel.
Argylle is exhausting.
The spy spoof Argylle is consistently clever, frequently funny and highly entertaining.
The nonstop stunts are CGI heavy, but it’s jolly, ridiculous fun.

Because Vaughn never drops his fantastical, cartoonish style, “reality” ceases to have any true meaning within the context of the film; he keeps trying to up the stakes even as what we’re watching becomes less and less consequential.
When the stakes change every five minutes in a movie, that's the same thing as there being nothing at stake.

Forget the rumor that Taylor Swift wrote the books this sad excuse for fun is based on. Bryce Dallas Howard is wasted as a cat lady who writes thrillers—Henry Cavill and Sam Rockwell play spies—but the whole plodding, cartoonish mess lands with a thud.
A bloated movie that’s more exhausting than interesting.
A movie is like a politician: The more desperately it tries to explain itself, the less appealing it becomes. Mr. Fuchs upends the narrative so many times it becomes a kind of unpleasant mania.
It’s all mindless fun -- although, at two-and-a-half hours plus, it does overestimate its entertainment value.
A spy tale with plenty of twists and turns but no sense of stakes or intrigue, "Argylle" is a convoluted mess of a story in search of a purpose beyond its own self-inflated sense of style.

title: Road Trip | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Vulgar for some parents, but teens will love.
Road Trip is the best dumb party movie of the year; if that's what you've been craving, buckle up.
The movie takes a slice out of the American Pie recipe book by at least making the final screen product funnier than the trailer.
Road Trip is broadly amusing with a few bright spots. But those can't cover up the major gaps in storytelling, characterization and laughs.
It's no masterpiece, you understand, but it doesn't count on the raging hormones of its audience to do all of its work.
As objectionable as its subject matter is, the most objectionable thing is that it's not funny.
Road Trip rides the wave of popularity for base, politically incorrect, outrageous humor.
Multiplexes should be thronged with howling, high-fiving young men deep into summer.
Road Trip may not be an ambitious film, but it doesn't lack for imagination, and the nasty edge of its comedy makes it refreshing.
Slightly more mature and better assembled, Road Trip goes one better on American Pie by teasing out the idiosyncrasies in four guys existing in a personality grab bag.
Road Trip takes a well-traveled highway, but the drivers know exactly what they're doing.
Road Trip is mellow and dirty, which is the wrong combination.
As we all know, bad taste is timeless. And sometimes it can be so funny that you can't help laughing.
Road Trip may not have the all-time-classic status of Animal House, but it's frequently as funny.
Still, although the subject matter is sophomoric it has enough of a plot and key performances to humor more sophisticated moviegoers too.
Road Trip is nothing more than a series of sight gags and put-downs. It's often funny, but it never has anything smart to say.
On the whole it works because its over-the-top humor is supported by the filmmakers' ability to view life with a clear-eyed lack of sentimentality.
Although lively at times, the proceedings are far too perfunctory to generate a 'can-you-top-this' quality. The result is a film that knows some of the words, but not the music.
As the guys continue on their way to Texas, this Road Trip degenerates into a slow-moving game of connect-the-gross-outs.
Road Trip occasionally wills itself to rude, crude life. But most of the time it's pretty limp.

title: Picnic | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: If any integrity of intention was there at the beginning, it has somehow hopelessly miscarried.
Clunky and awkward, with inane dialogue, it's a movie to show how attitudes have changed.

title: Stranger in the Woods | Rotten Tomatoes
Imaginary | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Look beyond the plethora of allusions, and you’ll see a film that’s happily engaging with the genre while still maintaining a solid core of real dread so that it’s not all empty calories.
Not a total catastrophe, but perilously close to being one. Is it too obvious to say Imaginary is simply lacking in imagination?
While a bit unwieldy, Imaginary is a playfully deranged movie that's sure to be a hit at slumber parties. But grown-ups can enjoy its spirited scares, too.

It suffers from the plague of overly convoluted plots that are executed by overly simplistic means: flat expositional dialogue, car commercial visual style, and a seemingly first draft creative concept that never irons out the wrinkles.
If you’re a true horror fan, this film is not your friend.
If you can withstand some of the goofier moments... “Imaginary” might serve as a reasonably effective fright flick during a slow week.
None of this makes much of an impact given how poorly sketched the characters are, and how little there is to distinguish the film from hundreds of other horror movies that come out every year.

Whether it’s the watered-down scares or the terrible performances – no one likes making fun of children, but Braun needs to leave acting to the stage-parented professionals – Imaginary’s myriad faults are all too real.

I’d bet if you tasked any child with a rewrite on this script (credited to director Jeff Wadlow, Greg Erb and Jason Oremland), you’d likely come up with something way more colorful, fun and freaky than the zipless cafeteria food ladled onto our laps.
Imaginary, which starts out as a relatively low-key suspenser with intriguing psychological depth, eventually succumbs to the inanities plaguing so many recent horror efforts.
“Imaginary,” despite a few creepy moments, is starved for scenes that make the fear it’s showing you relatable.
The latest in the Blumhouse catalog of reliably creepy horror movies whose fans typically expect well-executed jump scares, fun plot twists and the occasional rubbery monster.
It’s yet another sub-par day at the Blumhouse factory, production line operating at full, breakneck speed, yet machinery on the perilous verge of total collapse.
A lifeless hodgepodge of the hoariest clichés the genre has to offer.

Despite the dialogue constantly reinforcing the boundless creativity of its heroine, Imaginary is rather low on imagination of its own, instead opting to chart a safe course filled with familiar tropes and horror clichés.
The film never thinks to lean into the blatant silliness that its premise invites.

title: Mean Girls | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Fey does not take the book too seriously, finding plenty of cruel humour in the bitchy battles between Cady and Regina.
One of the movie's achievements is persuading the audience to stay firmly in Cady's camp during her odyssey of self-discovery.
This teen comedy is terrific. Superbly scripted by Saturday Night Live head writer Tina Fey, it explores the viciously divisive cliques that render the American high school a virtual battleground.
Mean Girls offers an enjoyably mean-spirited spin on a subject that most other recent movies... have treated as sacrosanct.
It comes on strong with sharp, biting wit and great energy, then runs out of steam and doesn't know when to call it quits.
One or two good acerbic jokes apart, Mean Girls isn't mean at all.
Fizzes with peculiarly feminine evil, of the kind that comes dripping through a pillowy smirk garnished with baby-pink lipgloss.

While Mean Girls has an uncertain hold on its plot and ends up pulling some of its punches and throwing in teen comedy clichés we have seen before, it's still enjoyable and thought-provoking for teens.

Though better written, better acted and with more wit and subtlety than your average teen flick, the atmosphere in Mean Girls with its promiscuous sex and well, meanness, make it almost as nasty to sit through as these girls are to each other.
Lacks the genuine bile that made Heathers so bracing.
Happily, Fey and Waters gently tweak the studios' usual high-gloss caricature of adolescence and aim for acutely hilarious and surprisingly empathic sociology.
Nails the "survival of the fittest" mentality that permeates high school social life.
A smart little teen picture that, for a change, actually features recognizable teens.
I would be more amused if the topic of rich material girls had not been worn to a thread elsewhere.
There's nothing here you won't have seen a million times before, but -- despite its shortcomings -- it's still one of the better teen movies to come along in a while.
Proof that Hollywood occasionally gets it right
Far from perfect, but it has brains beneath its glossy, vacuum-packed beauty.
A teen movie I enjoyed enormously, much to my surprise.
Steers toward familiar teen-movie hyperbole, but it's the way the girls plot their sabotage while doling out empty compliments that keeps things real.
You might expect this clique comedy to have some bite. It does, in moments -- but not enough to elevate Mean Girls above the pack of teen fare.

title: Handling the Undead | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Hvistendahl treats the audience with respect, her and Lindqvist’s reworking of the latter’s source material respectful, intelligent, and overflowing in empathy.
Composer Peter Raeburn’s beautifully sad soundtrack along with Pål Ulvik Rokseth’s cinematography contribute to creating a tragic mood that’s hard to let go of after the film’s sad conclusion.

The cooking comparison for Handling the Undead would be a sauce that’s broken, its elements having separated. There’s a genuine sense of lived-in sadness here, but this would-be elegy doesn't offer quite enough mesmeric insights to justify its somberness.
“Handling the Undead” also eschews any of the practical questions, but with a more humanist intent: to lean single-mindedly into its characters’ emotions — and also its eerie mythical resonance.
Hvistendahl’s film is absorbing, even captivating at times. But it moves at a pace that can be charitably described as “measured.” (The uncharitable word is “sluggish.”)

It’s an incredibly somber film, one washed in hues of blue and green, and it gets under your skin, making you question how you would react if you could have more time with a lost loved one, even if you knew immediately there would be a cost.
There’s a sense of sadness and dread that haunts every frame; the rolling fog that those left behind know all too well.
For how committed it is to convincing the audience of the profundity of a rudimentary point, the film’s measured pacing comes to feel like a kind of torture.
The film’s strength lies in its narrative, seamlessly connecting three distinct family dynamics linked by the common thread of loss.
The lugubrious pace can be a little too sluggish at times but Hvistendahl handles the last act’s descent into slightly more expected horror well...
A zombie film unlike any other, focused less on mayhem than on grief, loss, and the quiet, tragic terror begat by the dead’s return.
An unexpectedly poignant lament.
A living-dead nightmare with a brain and a heart and, most importantly and inedibly, a soul.

title: Self Reliance | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: ... if you’re a fan of Johnson (and if you’re not, why are you here?), Self Reliance has its charms, particularly those stemming from the actor’s near-perfect comic timing and delivery.
For a movie with such a nose for nuttiness, its human element is genuine and warm.

The movie is too juvenile and too timid to acknowledge the real-world chill of its online cabal of murderous social misfits. The issue is not whether Tommy will survive, but why we should hang around to find out.
There are many laughs in “Self Reliance,” but overall the story is somewhat predictable and peters out to an unsatisfying resolution.
Blissfully, it overcomes the self-indulgence of some of its “isolation is hard” contemporaries through a heaping helping of Johnson’s keen sense of everyman absurdism.
Should have been weirder and wilder.
In the hands of another director, its final act might have been more sharply honed. But it's undeniable that Self Reliance still hits its mark.
There is such potential in Johnson’s script, but the third act is all over the place.
[Jake] Johnson’s film is certainly not a complete failure but it is inelegant and shoddy despite its best attempts at charm and affecting thematics.
Johnson and Kendrick are just terrific together.
An undeniably ambitious project for a first-time filmmaker, but it's a tonal tightrope that should have been attempted with a bit more behind-the-camera experience.
Coming up for connection, Johnson delivers a silly and frequently surprising why-we-need-people parable.

title: The Book of Clarence | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The Book of Clarence stands on its own as a comedy-drama with engaging characters and an emotive narrative, but it’s probably best enjoyed by those vaguely familiar with the Bible, regardless of their beliefs.
Like the fake messiah at its centre, The Book of Clarence has rollicking, lively energy – but it’s hard to believe in.
A raucous stoner comedy dressed as an earnest Bible story, or actually the other way around.
With a cast this talented there will always be decent moments, but they never cohere. Credit for its casting and design, but it’s not the movie messiah, just a very disappointing mess.
Stanfield’s dropout charisma can cushion a role fine, but can’t make this one very interesting.

The film is definitely a comedy, and a lot of the jokes work. But the three chapters or “books” that Samuel divides the film into aren’t evenly weighted. While the first two acts zip by... [the third] drags.
I thought it was well done in a lot of ways, but also kind of confounding in a lot of ways.
Even if [it doesn't] always work... I didn't know where it was going to go from moment to moment, and that in itself is thrilling.
If The Book of Clarence has a purpose, it’s a mystery so hard to unravel that it will puzzle theater or streaming audiences. It’s a treatise on disbelief and belief that never gels.
LaKeith Stanfield shines in a fun biblical comedy that doesn’t always come together.
A big, bold biblical epic that lands roughly half the time, The Book of Clarence is admirable in its scope and vision, even if those ultimately outweigh its execution.
The level of wit on offer is revealed early on, when someone jokes that a supposed messiah is more like a mess. The latter noun is equally applicable to Mr. Samuel’s script.

Samuel has made a movie that imagines a good-hearted sinner slouching toward salvation one desperate measure at a time. But he’s also made a mirror designed to let folks see themselves in this scenario for once.
While it features plenty of directorial promise, the end result is ultimately hollow.
I was ultimately left confused and dissatisfied.
Buoyed by... creative bursts of fresh air and great performances from its ensemble cast, The Book of Clarence has a lot to offer but is weighed down by its tonal irregularities.
What’s good about “The Book of Clarence” is what so many movies lack: taking really, really big swings.
Does it work? I’d say no, and sort of, and in the end, almost.
The results are entertaining, sometimes riotously so, yet also decidedly mixed.
“The Book of Clarence” is ripped, not from the bible, but from fractured memories of past Hollywood biblical epics.

title: Heart of the Hunter | Rotten Tomatoes
I.S.S. | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It doesn't come up with much more than its central theme, but it's an enjoyable B movie in that it's a simple set up, it's convinincly played and directed with enough panache.

While DeBose is impressive, the contrived plot of Gabriela Cowperthwaite’s movie hinges, somewhat preposterously, on rational, highly trained scientific minds devolving overnight into paranoid, murderous maniacs.
With a modest budget of $14m applied to a concept bursting with potential, the film bides its time sensibly enough, but then screws up every remaining phase of its mission.
Moderately tense, with too few ideas to qualify as actively cerebral... what the movie does have is a brilliant performance by West Side Story’s Ariana DeBose as biologist and rookie astronaut Kira.

This high-concept sci-fi thriller set aboard the International Space Station was made... for a relatively paltry $13 million. The results, alas, are ropey visuals, cheap sets and some of the worst zero-G effects in recent space movie history.
Tense and occasionally disturbing, but somehow you’re left with the nagging suspicion that what should have been a meaty psychological drama has been turned into a slightly insipid thriller instead.
I like the tension of the narrative... But what they do with that is make a fairly ordinary and pedestrian thriller.

The plot remains within the confines of a B series due to a lack of character complexity and a succession of illogical decisions, director Gabriela Cowperthwaite manages to grant a certain complexity to the cosmonauts presented. [Full review in Spanish]
I.S.S. asks several troubling and unpleasant questions, and the film refuses to make things easy on the audience by smothering them in obvious answers.
It’s a surprisingly trenchant story for what seems to be a slight genre thriller, but then again, genre thrillers can be the best vessels for these kinds of messages.
In space, no one can hear you yawn.
With “I.S.S.,” [DeBose] takes a giant leap forward as a solid action hero amid a decently gripping mix of human nature and atomic annihilation.
It's mostly pretty tense and pretty well-made for a low budget.

Despite the gravity of the situation (or lack thereof), the promising idea feels too weightless in the spare, underdeveloped execution, operating at the edges of a good movie without reaching that orbit.
It’s odd to think about how these kinds of special effects become so rote and unremarkable so quickly. The movie’s attempts at conflict and intrigue feel just as unremarkable.
The tense, taut space thriller with a spare script and sharp, differentiated performances exposes the overachievers’ battle royal -- who will survive, and to what on earth can they possibly return?

It comes with a level of absurdity that no self-respecting cinephile would tolerate in the other 11 months of the year, but could be exactly what you need to dull the pain of a painful NFL playoff loss.
There are few things more disappointing than a genre movie that forgoes developing its intriguing premise to focus on cheap, failed attempts to thrill.
It is an efficient thrill ride, running about 90 minutes, with every moment used as effectively as possible.

Ariana DeBose and Chris Messina excel in this space thriller that sizzles with Russia vs America tension but all too predictably fizzles into a mild ride that is better than you might expect while falling way short of the wonder it so wants to inspire.

title: The Night They Came Home | Rotten Tomatoes
Out of Darkness (2022) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Horror often has a problem with characters’ annoyingly faulty decision-making; here, their hierarchy of needs, with food and shelter to the fore, makes self-endangering choices more than believable.

The difference here is in the attention to paleolithic detail and the emotional sincerity that the film-makers, including the debut director Andrew Cumming and the debut feature writer Ruth Greenberg, bring to the material.
Atmospheric and chilling, Out Of Darkness doesn’t reinvent the wheel, but adds some thoughtful twists to a well-worn genre.

This first work by British director, Andrew Cumming, counts for a sufficient dose of originality and talent, transforming into a necessary visionary work for lovers of the genre. [Full review in Spanish]
It left me in awe of the survival instinct: how on earth did humans make it through those cold, bloody old times? I’d hurl myself into the nearest loch.
It moves along pretty good... There's a twist that I thought was sort of interesting.
It turns didactic in the end in a way that serves as a disservice... But it is powerful in the sense that it does hold you, it's scary and it's well-shot.
It's a chilling ride.
Out of Darkness is effective enough — and gory — to function as a thriller of the loud-noise-springing variety.

Cumming presents a natural world red in tooth and claw, yet the inevitable lessons learned in this moss-covered and frost-blasted wilderness still have modern resonances – about fear, bigotry, superstition, survival.
It’s an impressively credible and gnarly journey back in time.
Out of the Darkness shines a light on modern troubles, and by dipping into the past, the film asks the audience to consider how tenuous and uncertain humanity’s future survival truly is.
Tense throughout, “Darkness” focuses on the the darkness in human souls rather than imagined creatures of the night, making it all that more disturbing, and — of course — relevant.
Out of Darkness is best when it's ambiguous, and it loses some of its zip as answers begin to come into focus. But in terms of look and feel, it has plenty going for it.
A lean, mean adventure story on the cusp of horror that firsttime feature director Andrew Cumming imbues with tension and handsome visual atmospherics.
The setting may be prehistoric, but there’s nothing primitive about the filmmaking, which molds mostly natural light and an unusually rich soundscape into something both elemental and hostile.
A midnight movie that recognizes that there’s no existence without sacrifice, and no birth without death.
Shot in the Scottish Highlands, Out of Darkness draws on the eerie atmosphere of a place that still feels ancient and steeped in mystery.
Though it struggles to build suspense, the handsomely shot and stunning craft on display makes for an impressive debut by Cummings.

title: Something in the Water | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Still, it’s a mostly fun late-summer film, would likely go down easy with a drinking game.
The female-first vibe is refreshing but Something In The Water is something old, nothing new, a lot that is borrowed and an eyeful of twinkly blue.

Something in the Water is competently filmed, with lots of propulsive underwater shark’s eye shots of the flailing legs of the bridesmaids. But there’s rather too much time spent watching the girls bobbing and bickering in the middle of the ocean.

[There's a] perennial problem with shark films: how to keep people in the water. While Something in the Water can’t claim to be a Jaws-calibre classic, it squares that particular circle very nicely indeed.
Easton Street’s direction is undone by budget limitations. The girls, depending on the shot, seem to be close to shore, out to sea or in a pool in the film studio. And the shark? Oh dear.

Huge sections ... are taken up with the characters gossiping in viscera-thick water as they might while queuing for the bathroom at Wetherspoons. There’s just too much floatin’ and not enough crunchin’. Call it The Daft of the Medusa.
Something in the Water bobs along like many other survivalist shark thrillers, and without finding new ways to jump the shark, it’s just another drop in the subgenre’s ocean.

title: Night Swim | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It opts, in turn, for a Hollywood-esque correct esthetic, lacking in surprises and assuming an air of stubborn solemnity. [Full review in Spanish]

Night Swim might be the first movie to star a haunted pool, but its story beats are interchangeable with any other horror movie in the microgenre of kindly fathers turning mean after a real estate–based possession.
There comes a point where it almost feels as if McGuire was making it up as he went along. So little of this thriller make sense that it’s impossible for it to generate a lasting emotional impact.
McGuire, who executed a trial run of this concept with a 2014 short film, knows exactly what he’s doing, scene after scene, especially when it comes to the deliciously sadistic grammar of suspense.
Night Swim eventually runs out of places to go, but not before it weds some sneaky character development to a few good, solid jump moments. It might not find an audience, but it deserves one.
Night Swim effectively exploits primal fears around water, but its comedy and horror chops aren’t strong enough to keep it from drowning in its more clichéd elements.
While diverting enough for its forgiving 98-minute runtime, Night Swim neither sinks nor floats. It just wades in the waters of “whatever.”
Producers Jason Blum and James Wan, both horror titans, once again show they know how to freak audiences out while maintaining a sly sense of humor.
For the most part... this feature version of “Night Swim” further demonstrates the truism that longer is rarely better when it comes to movies. The original was short, sharp and shocking.
The movie seems destined to sink quickly to the bottom of our cultural memory and, like a few swimmers in this demented pool, vanish altogether.

Condon’s fierce yet heartfelt performance and the underwater sequences keep Night Swim treading water, but the high concept novelty wears out its welcome quickly for seasoned horror fans who’ve seen this scenario play out so many times before.
Last-act let-down aside, this is a confident and creepy ghoul-in-the-pool horror that makes Bryce McGuire a filmmaker to watch. Wusses, bring armbands.
The good news is you can bring the kids. When it comes time for swimming lessons next summer, there’s nothing they’ll remember from this that’ll make them afraid of the water.
The worst movie I’ve seen in years.
As the mysteries behind the strange occurrences are slowly revealed, this underpowered horror film starts to drown in cliches and predictable plot twists.
Nothing in Night Swim will change how you feel about horror, or even swimming, but it fulfils its brief with efficiency and style.

It may be damning with faint praise to describe Night Swim as a solid movie, but horror fans know just how dark and deep the bottoms of their genre can be. We’ll take what McGuire has to offer every day of the week.
As supernatural thrillers go, “Night Swim” is a quick dip — persuasively acted and quite effective in its first half, scattered and woozy in its second.
It just never goes far enough with its ridiculousness to reach pure entertainment, and it certainly can’t be taken seriously enough to justify its melodrama.
I can think of many, many better ways to usher in a new year than the very damp effort that is “Night Swim” — aren’t wet ghosts inherently more sad than scary? — but you play the hand you’re dealt.

title: Brandy Hellville & The Cult of Fast Fashion | Rotten Tomatoes
Drive-Away Dolls | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Drive Away Dolls gets some mileage out of trying to subvert expectations.
It's a mixed-bag of some very familiar stuff... Like a watered-down "Greatest Hits" collection.
Terrible... This is the least fun I've had with a Coen associated-movie since Burn After Reading.

With only one brother in the driver’s seat, this is a sex comedy with the consciously artificial, smart-dumb patter of an old Steve Martin movie. Yet, ushered in alongside is Coen’s partner and longtime collaborator Tricia Cooke...
The film has a boisterous energy, but it’s puerile, phoney and frequently rather cringe.
No good will can wholly brush away the ersatz hokeyness of this venture. It’s as if The Beatles managed to release a record by Herman’s Hermits.
It’s the writing, ultimately, that retains that signature Coen dazzle.

Meanwhile, all the heavy-handed progressive messaging around sex has an embarrassing-parents quality that often had me grinding my teeth: at points I felt as if Coen and Cooke were grinningly handing me a strip of contraceptives...
Uneven, juvenile and a waste of an array of considerable talent, Drive-Away Dolls is a huge disappointment.

Drive-Away Dolls never knows how to be the kind of fun it wants to be. A cue has been taken from transgressive cult classics... In Coen’s hands, though, the results feel studied: an exercise dressed as a joyride.
Drive-Away Dolls just misses the beats all the time, the camera angles mannered to no purpose, slapdash in its editing, perhaps as a homage to pulp movies but nevertheless off-putting.
Viswanathan anchors the movie in a kind of quiet emotional seriousness without which it would quickly feel like flavourless chewing gum. A starring feature film role is what she needs now.
It’s as solid a comedy as the Coens ever made together.

The humor is, as the screenwriters have gleefully acknowledged, "juvenile," but the performances are vivid and, honestly, I'd watch a whole movie starring deadpan Bill Camp as Curlie, who rents the women the car that leads to all of their adventures.

The story doesn’t hold up under scrutiny — don’t overthink it, man — so what you’re left with is the gentle exploration (send-up?) of lesbian culture; the trademark Coen blend of violence, cupidity, and stupidity; and nostalgia for the grindhouse.

Transparently low-budget, it compensates with off-kilter camera angles and aggressively zany scene transitions, as if the filmmakers weren’t highly respected industry veterans, but students trying out the professional equipment for the first time.

Drive Away Dolls is fun and silly, a perfectly diverting way to spend 90 minutes -- and the three lead actresses are a blast to watch. That said, I couldn’t help but feel like this was ersatz Coen Brothers.

There’s little to get excited for watching “Drive-Away Dolls,” even though there is a lot of sex to, presumably, get the audiences’ blood pumping. The problem is it’s all awash in an unfunny, nonexistent plotline that feels about 15 years too late.
What’s remarkable about this freewheeling lark is how it is built on a foundation of intoxicating wholesomeness.
Nearly every note of this alleged romp rings false—except for the presence of one actor, a performer who seems to have been air-dropped from a better, much groovier movie.

title: He Went That Way | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Bizarre subplots and thin performances blunt the impact...
Few things in this laboriously quirky picture mesh at all.
Consistently goes the wrong way.
If nothing else, “He Went That Way” deserves credit for being the most serious effort at reviving the monkey hijinks genre that the festival circuit has seen in years.

title: Cold Copy | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: No one to like. Little reason to watch.
“Cold Copy” is a tense journalism drama that ultimately can’t be saved by a group of strong leads who are running lengths with the material they’ve been given.

Ultimately, the film is less about the ostensible themes of journalism and truth that it starts with than an erratic drama about two out-of-control compromised people, anomalies who deserve each other.
With so many new journalism stories begging to be told, there’s simply no reason to retread old ones this poorly.

title: Scrambled (2023) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A charming comedy-drama. [Full review in Spanish]

McKendrick’s feature speaks with a strong voice, and one that we don’t hear expressed with such realism, faults and all. It’s a funny comedy that unlike so many others stays true to itself, even in the end.
Nellie's world may feel scrambled, but McKendrick knows where she is going and how to take us with her.
It’s a coming-of-age story for the mid-30s set.
This is fertile territory into which McKendrick implants a zingy, quippy, R-rated comedy, inseminated by a TMI sense of humor...
Some of the script is too forced with its emotions, or its humor can be too broad, but "Scrambled" proves to overall be a charismatic directorial debut from a promising writer/director/star.

At times, Scrambled feels like a TV show, which isn’t a bad thing at all. In fact, it’s a compliment: the film has quick quips, good timing, and tight pacing mostly found in nowadays in episodic structures.

title: Dead Man | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Both Blake's journey and composer Neil Young's spare, electric guitar score seem endlessly circular; and people are always asking Blake for tobacco.
The landscape outside and the passengers inside become wilder and woollier with every weary mile.
The film's pleasures are simply too elusive and mild to make up for a lack of narrative propulsion.
[It's a] bizarre, funny, almost mystical take on the Western

[The] metaphysical context benefits enormously from the haunting musical themes that Neil Young wrote, underlining the film's psychedelic/apocalyptic edge, and from the stunning black-and-white camera work of Robby Muller.
When Dead Man is imagining the Wild West as an infernal landscape of death, it is furiously alive. When it tries to reflect on those images, it begins to nod out.
I liked the film at its original length, and I think the shortened version is Jarmusch's best movie.

Blake and Nobody meander through a wilderness as shrubby and nondescript as a '50s B horror movie, all to the accompaniment of an echoey Neil Young guitar score that sounds like something Wayne Campbell made up in his basement.
Dead Man is a strange, slow, unrewarding movie that provides us with more time to think about its meaning than with meaning.
Beautifully shot in high contrast black-and-white, Dead Man fails not because of any one particular flaw, but instead stumbles, caught in a quagmire of metaphysical constructs and Western lore.
I won't pretend that Jarmusch's austere poetry will speak to everyone...No matter. This strange, mystical Western is his most daring work -- his best since Stranger Than Paradise.
Jim Jarmusch's most stunning achievement.

Coy to a fault, the movie collapses under its own weight with 90 minutes to go, despite Robby MÃuller's impressive black-and-white photography, which puts the film on a higher artistic plane than other equally unbearable movies.
A quantum leap by American independent Jim Jarmusch–a hypnotic and beautiful black-and-white western.

title: Megamind vs. the Doom Syndicate | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It is intermittently funny and briefly heartwarming, as though they ran the original through the washing machine a few times, and then faxed it.

title: The Ballad of Davy Crockett | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Colm Meaney steals the show with his villainous turn as the corrupt leader of a fur trading outfit.

title: Departing Seniors | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: These quibbles might be more tolerable if the craft on display were more proficient, or if the pacing were more suspenseful.
Unfortunately, the mystery lacks intrigue, spinning its wheels toward a predictable conclusion.

title: Walk the Line | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Johnny Cash gets the biopic treatment in this superior portrait of the man, his music, the demons he battled and the love that saved him.
The film boasts of extremely competent performances, particularly the extraordinary Phoenix. As for Witherspoon, with her nasal twang and perky persona, she is sweet and sassy...
Walk the Line -- although conspicuously well acted -- is really no different from previous efforts, and that's a good thing. It shares the charm of the (musical biopic) genre.
Not only does the film show just how hungry Cash was to sing his songs, it understands how hungry society was for the cataclysmic changes such music brought.
It's a tidy Hollywood arc imposed on a messy real life, but it gets the job done.
In spite of all it does right, Walk the Line leaves one with the nagging sense of a story unfinished — or rather, with something left out.
I advise you catch up with Walk the Line, if only for Ms. Witherspoon's transcendent joyousness as a still-growing legend within a legend.
[A]n old-fashioned C&W standard.
Coming just a year after Taylor Hackford's Ray, comparisons between this and that Oscar-winning Jamie Foxx biopic are inevitable. On most levels, those comparisons are unfair.
Phoenix as Cash in Walk the Line is the next best thing to having been there, I suppose.

Mangold was wisely generous with the amount of musical performance he included in the film, and the later scenes -- showing Cash and Carter as partners -- are so well shot and edited, they defy you to sit still.
Phoenix's Cash is less an uncanny reproduction of the man and his style than an embodiment that looks and sounds just enough like the real man to pull it off.
If Walk the Line isn't the full story of Johnny Cash, it's at least a crucial corner of it, a way of coaxing a legend down to a human scale, without shrinking that legend away to nothingness.
A Johnny Cash biopic equally packed with music and frustrated love, Walk the Line goes from compelling to enthralling.
[Director] James Mangold's mostly excellent Walk the Line is designed as a Christian epic.
Joaquin Phoenix isn't Johnny Cash. But with the clip-clop of rhythms behind him, aiming his guitar like a gun, he puts on one sensational show.
Walk the Line is less music history than love story, and it comes down to the performances of the two people at its center, both of which are splendid.

The problem is that the movie plays down almost everything that made Cash great: the train rumble of a voice, the direct, poetic truth of his best lyrics, the invention of his outlaw image and his constant creativity.
A passionate, warts-and-all chronicle of an extraordinary American artist, not to mention a love story that can't be beat.
Walk the Line is absolute standard biopic stuff, so familiar that it blatantly echoes last year's Ray, which similarly failed to do justice to the legendary Ray Charles.

title: Boomerang | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Then there's the input from Warrington and Reginald Hudlin, producer and director respectively, who succeed in creating a comedy which, unusually for a Murphy film, also exists around him.
In Boomerang Eddie Murphy straitjackets himself in an ill-fitting comedy vehicle that's desperately in need of a reality check.
The general idea is to exploit a certain amount of role reversal, and Reginald Hudlin, who directed House Party, does a fairly good job of making this fun.
The film is far too slick to be ineffective, but its attempts to play with the sex-war theme are often unbelievably crass.
It's not even funny. Nor does it contain half the wit or charm as the old Doris Day sex comedies it so resembles. In fact, it's downright mean-spirited toward women, as is Murphy's wont.
There's something paradoxical about the ease he radiates in playing a man who is supposed to be a smashing success. As an underdog, Mr. Murphy worked much harder.
For all the sex talk in Boomerang, there's very little nudity. The only thing naked is Murphy's vanity.
Murphy gives his most appealing performance to date, using his smug, self-satisfied, sly smile as a joke on his own well-known screen persona.
Whatever [Murphy] was thinking during the dark days of his career slump, it seems to have paid off handsomely.
Boomerang is the funniest, most sophisticated movie of Eddie Murphy's career.

title: Indigo Girls: It's Only Life After All | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "Life After All" has plenty of music, but the film is more interested in celebrating optimism and bringing viewers one step closer to fine.
If you don't know, if you want to learn more, “It’s Only Life After All" doesn't get the job done, even at 2 hours long.
Existing fans will be mesmerized, but non-fans like me should also get a kick out of “It’s Only Life After All.”

Emily Saliers and Amy Ray of indie folk rockers Indigo Girls convey what they want the audience to experience from their music: self-esteem, a shared experience, and healing, likening it almost to a warm hug... exactly what the film provides.
Emily shares her journey to sobriety, and the duo share many facets of their lives that will delight longtime fans as well as those just discovering their legacy.

Bombach is lucky to have a massive archive of material from their entire career from which to construct a film, but that can be a curse too as “It’s Only Life After All” wears out its welcome at close to two hours, often repeating itself as it unfolds.
Bombach stitches together a portrait of two queer people who were radical for their time and have strived to remain that way to this day.
The rare confessional rockumentary that envelops you like a soft blanket.

Bombach’s movie finds its real flavor in exploring the differences in the duo’s two very distinct personalities, which up till now might have seemed like a fuzzy, singular unit by all but the most hardcore fans.
The most serious flaw of “It’s Only Life After All” is that Bombach has us spend so much time with these women, yet we learn so little about them.
Brimming with previously unseen footage and refreshingly frank interviews with the artists, it’s an adoring opus befitting two long overlooked musicians and activists.

title: Ultraman: Rising | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The idea is to bring father-child stakes into all this mayhem, which works to a degree. But in the movie’s desire to wring tears...The film winds up having it both ways once too often.

Ultraman: Rising will likely touch viewers, especially ages 10 and under, for its story of a young man trying to be a good dad while also reconnecting with his own estranged father, in what ultimate becomes a parable about responsible parenting.
Ultraman: Rising may be a kaleidoscopically color-timed action adventure of throw-down battles, but it’s really about parenting in its many shapes and forms.

“Ultraman: Rising” is a bit longer than it needs to be, but buoyed by a strong voice cast and a unique point of view that blends elements of superhero action with heartfelt family drama, it’s an effective reinvention of a franchise...
“Ultraman: Rising” is a contender for best animated movie of the year, one of the best superhero movies in years, and one of the all-time greatest American adaptations of a Japanese franchise
“Ultraman: Rising” lacks a noteworthy vision of what it means to be a parent, let alone an adult struggling to wear several hats at once.

This is probably the first creature feature where the kaiju functions as a vehicle for a Three Men and a Baby-type narrative about muddling through as a new parent. It’s a decent metaphor as it happens.
If Ultraman wants to conquer the world, he’ll have to try something livelier than a cartoon that looks like a kids movie but lurches about like a saccharine family drama.
Director Shannon Tindle and co-director John Aoshima’s feature needs to pick up its pace and not bang the drums so loudly its message about the importance of family. We get it already.
A fun, sincere, and thoughtfully conceived piece of kids entertainment. And it’s liable to make young viewers more curious about the world around them -- not less.

This English-language charmer boasts vibrant visuals that mostly make up for a fairly pedestrian story about a selfish baseball superstar who begrudgingly accepts his responsibility to be the new Ultraman.

title: Diane von Furstenberg: Woman in Charge | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Taking its tone from its subject -- straight-talking, bemused, dismissive of constraints -- this documentary about the Belgian fashion designer who changed the course of design with the wrap dress is an enjoyable journey.
A celebration of life that captures the designer’s ongoing journey of self-discovery and reinforces her belief that there is always more to accomplish.
It’s breezy and entertaining, certainly, but ultimately feels like little more than a 97-minute ad for the wrap dress.
There is much that is conventional about the construction of “Woman in Charge”... But it is a good story, told by a subject who has a righteous-yet-reasonable sense of her own place in history.
So many fashion documentaries are frigid and vapid; this one, though, from film-makers Trish Dalton and Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy, has a story to tell about someone with something to say.
It’s Diane von Fürstenberg’s life and I’m not even sure the rest of us get to live in it. We’re just allowed to peek through the window and be dazzled.
The film is often informative, but makes for a passively entertaining watch despite the sheer of breadth of life von Furstenberg has lived.
This Diane Von Furstenberg is plenty engaging, but as a tribute to the woman who reinvented the modern dress, it doesn’t reinvent anything itself.
Puffy though it may be, though, this absorbing documentary is easy to like as it presents a life and career worth celebrating.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: A thoroughly enjoyable movie for older kids.
A preposterous, expansive and self-conscious attempt to resurrect the historical spectacular.
A big, vacuous, sometimes exciting glamour-puss of a movie.
The best swashbuckler since The Mask of Zorro.
Dumas's classic tale is such a rattling good yarn, there's nothing you can do to derail it as it hurtles down the track.
Reynolds' remake brings nothing new to the table, but it's still an enjoyable throwback to the swashbucklers of old.
All in all, it's a pretty good execution of a story that's a lot richer than the ones Hollywood action screenwriters usually come up with on their own.
Old-form moviemaking at its best.
There's a thin line between likably old-fashioned and fuddy-duddy, and The Count of Monte Cristo ... never quite settles on either side.
This is middling Dumas all the way.
A rousingly old-fashioned swashbuckler with an abundance of vigorous action and nary a trace of wink-wink irony.
[A] pleasant diversion.
[An] above average piece of junk.
Frequently entertaining and sometimes lovely to look at.
This new movie version of the Alexandre Dumas classic is the stuff of high romance, brought off with considerable wit.
It's a Count for our times.
You can count on snoozing.
It's a fine, old-fashioned-movie movie, which is to say it's unburdened by pretensions to great artistic significance.

Neither among the best nor the worst of the lot, it falls somewhere inconspicuously in between, serving up both lively and ill-fitting performances as well as lush backdrops and the requisite derring-do.
It's quite entertaining.

title: I Am: Celine Dion | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The result is a tribute both to Dion’s resiliency and her talent, making it ideal for fans.
The film lands somewhere between hand-holding fan service and brutal portrait of chronic illness.
Dion’s voice made her a star; this film is keen on making her a person.

Far from a fluffy documentary that fawns over its subject, I Am: Celine Dion is a roller-coaster of emotions that leaves audiences with a mix of elation and uncertainty. But most incredibly, it gives one of music's biggest stars her voice back.
Eschewing talking heads for a portrait in which Dion insisted she do all the talking herself, this is a rare nonfiction chronicle of an artist that also avoids hagiography.
In the film’s final form, that story is told with a broad-strokes approach that keeps the film grounded in Dion’s fraught present.

The simplicity of the documentary’s bilingual title (I Am: Celine Dion / Je Suis: Céline Dion) gets at the simple if elusive question that concerns it: Who is the Grammy-winning singer without her voice, without her stage, without her audience?
A raw, heartbreaking and deeply moving window into the reclusive life of a once-in-a-generation talent cut down in its prime.
We all know we can listen to Celine Dion sing forever. What I learned from this doc is that we can also watch Celine Dion, a hilarious and animated personality, sort through her closet forever.

... What was meant to be a flattering narrative based around her long running Las Vegas residency turned into something far more raw and emotional than anyone might have expected, including the participants.

Like her music, which has cut through the emotional defenses of millions across languages, I Am: Céline Dion is unabashedly sentimental, deeply earnest and, for a true pop diva, mostly devoid of ego, with a few exceptions.
Dion’s life story unfolds here like an inverted fairytale, where a singing-obsessed child from small-town Canada reaches global heights only to be struck down by a curse from within.
This palpable and visceral glimpse into her pain is a jolting reminder of the toll this condition has taken on Dion not just as a star but as a person.
Like all things Celine Dion, “I Am” feels intensely personal and sincere, but also managed to within an inch of its life.
An affecting pageant of intense emotional moments chronicling the Quebec singer’s struggle with stiff person syndrome.

title: Jim Henson Idea Man | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Henson and Howard are a fine match, and the sort of film you’d expect Ron Howard to make – straightforward, skillful, honest and sympathetic – is pretty much the kind of movie you’d want about Jim Henson.

A fairly honest portrait of him thanks to his kids, who are willing to put their fingers into his relationship with his wife, Jane... That lens into Henson's life was completely unfamiliar to me, and I really did appreciate that.
You leave the movie with a better understanding of this monumental figure, while also feeling like he's still something of an enigma. And that's as it should be.

Howard’s genial account of the legendary Muppeteer plays it safe, with a fairly traditional documentary-making approach — but it still manages to be adequately inspirational, celebrational and, yes, even Muppetational.

[Ron Howard] knits a cavalcade of old and new clips and interviews into a film with narrative clarity and emotional force. It would be the very incurious, unreceptive viewer who leaves Idea Man without a heightened appreciation of the human and his work.

Kermit might have sung that it’s not easy being green, but watching “Jim Henson: Idea Man,” it’s very easy appreciating the mind that gave us the Muppets and more, while still acknowledging the human foibles of the hand behind them.
As is the case with Henson’s legacy as a whole, I liked a lot of what I saw in this film—I wish that there had been more to it.
Idea Man is neither overly saccharine nor sanitised.
Watchers will walk away with a deeper understanding of a man who had such an outsized presence in their childhoods.
Sweet, heartwarming and rather unadventurous. If it’s easy to wish “Idea Man” were as bold as its subject, though, it’s just as easy to be won over by this deservedly heartfelt tribute to him.
Anybody with affection for Henson and his work will get the requisite laughs, nostalgia and probably emotions from the footage Howard assembled here.

When it comes to great American lives, Howard is a burnisher not a bloodhound. Still, if his doc is as toothless as Cookie Monster 2.0, it’s still a nostalgic treat to spend time with the man who gave us Kermit, Big Bird and the Goblin King.

In a documentary landscape rife with both star-fronted documentaries and other hagiographic entries, Howard leans into honesty. The film is so much better for it, even as it can’t quite capture the full magic and scope of Henson’s life and work.

title: Big City Greens the Movie: Spacecation | Rotten Tomatoes
Living With Leopards  | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It's fun, light, and one of those escapist things you watch when you just want to relax.
Despite a soundtrack that doesn’t quite fit, Living With Leopards is superior nature content, largely because of the evident devotion of its humans.

title: Dragonkeeper | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: An action-packed kids’ movie with plenty of PG-rated bashing and a real spirit of adventure. The letdown is some fairly average animation, and human characters that move like cheap marionettes with jolty limbs.

title: Federer: Twelve Final Days | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The tone of this film mirrors Roger Federer as a player and human being: elegant, classy, detached and cool.
Like its subject, the film is not particularly revolutionary or groundbreaking in its approach. But again, like its subject, it is a work of unmistakable quality and class.
Federer was unique at being: mild. It’s why so many crying dads love him. On screen this doesn’t play so well.
If you're interested in the sport and in him, he is clearly a remarkable and admirable sportsman, then this is a very loving tribute. It isn't anything other than that.

With the international press and his management team nearly always on the sidelines, there’s little privacy to get personal. One of the more vulnerable moments the film manages to capture comes when Federer wears the wrong dress shirt to a photo call.

Less a career overview than a lengthy valediction, “Twelve Final Days” considers what is meant when a professional athlete has to stare into the post-career abyss. Mr. Federer seems more likely than most not to go blind.
It succeeds as a limited portrait of a decent, deservedly popular champion.

For fans, this handsomely-mounted film’s level of access will be enticement enough, and its emotional peaks are undeniably stirring. But its limited scope and curious demureness prevent it from offering the full-scale portrait that... Federer deserves.

This is no Senna, co-director Asif Kapadia’s most memorable documentary and yet it still very watchable. Federer breaks down as he asks, “what happens next?” when contemplating his future, and it is clear how much he loves tennis.
Twelve Final Days is big on PR but low on actual tennis. Talking heads hymn the beauty of Federer’s silky, seemingly effortless technique but analysis of what made it so is fleeting.
... An entertaining, occasionally illuminating and at times surprisingly moving look at the final bow of a genuine tennis legend.

The paradox is that this film’s original footage, in contrast to the vividly repurposed material of the Senna and Maradona studies, weirdly looks less intimate and more guarded. Everything here looks as if it has been approved at the highest level.
It’s generally entertaining to watch Federer highlights. But it would be difficult to convince anybody without a pre-existing interest that this constitutes compelling storytelling on any level.

title: Periodical | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [Periodical] would make a valuable addition to a sex-ed curriculum and that it’d be a solid (though, you know, not as fun as other options) pick for movie night with kids who are old enough to get their periods.

title: Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: George Miller re-visits his oil-soaked franchise with another brutal, female-dominated action film.
“Furiosa” backs up, fills in the blanks and does a solid job of giving its title character a history that answers questions that its predecessor left in the dust.

While it has you in its grip initially, it gradually loses its way amid marauding tribes, lynch mobs and innumerable chases through the sand dunes on souped-up vehicles. There are moments that take your breath away but don't add up to pack in a wallop.
This script should have been released first. It would've elevated Fury Road... The dynamic here is reversed, though this is still a very good film.
Nothing could ever be Fury Road, but if you want the spectacle and a reason to go back to theaters this summer, this is a great one.
If Furiosa had been a standalone, it would be considered an incredible feat, but as the fifth instalment, it doesn’t evolve on the spectacle we’ve already seen in Fury Road.
A rapturous phoenix.
Furiosa doesn’t offer the same narrative purity, nor does it produce the same propulsive energy, that its predecessor did – but then, few movies have.
What you lose is the tautness of Fury Road... What you gain is Fury Road was pedal to the metal, this is an excercise in comic strip myth building. It's like the Odyssey, a petrol-head Odyssey.
Fury Road was a movie to witness; Furiosa is merely worth seeing.
The newest in the Max Max franchise doesn’t quite fill the shoes of its predecessor, but it’s still a highly compelling odyssey.
Even in moments when the CGI looks a little obvious, the mayhem is staged and shot with the kind of blissful coherence that you rarely see in a Hollywood blockbuster anymore.

It’s a remarkable achievement by Miller – a piece of world-building that is fully realised down to the last diseased pustule on the last burrow-dwelling maggot farmer. And the action sequences are phenomenal.
This is Miller’s world, and I’m ecstatic I’ve been lucky enough to be around to experience every single solitary second of it.

The ending is talky, and it sounds like an authorial statement: Dementus revealing the dark heart of the Mad Max saga. But it also makes way for a nasty, batty, but strangely redemptive segue into Fury Road’s story.

Thanks to a strong ensemble cast, incredible action scenes and production values, and a high-stakes, high-concept chase that lasted for most of the run time, the film gave depth and beauty to its brutal post-apocalyptic wasteland.
Miller stages operatic action set pieces that will be rank as some of best sequences we will see all year. But you also have some drag mainly in terms of backstory we didn’t really need.

Even if one never picks up on any allegorically trans material in Furiosa, there’s still plenty to be enraptured by here. For one, George Miller is still the master and commander of vehicle chase scenes in cinema.
Theron made audiences care for her traumatized Furiosa. In comparison, this gargantuan effort is soulless splatter.
In this thunderous prequel, Anya Taylor-Joy burns with intensity.

title: Baki Hanma vs Kengan Ashura | Rotten Tomatoes
Touch | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The experience of seeing the film is subduing; the movie plays in a muted key.

title: The Idea of You | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Galitzine and Hathaway anchor the film and their chemistry is palpable, making every touch feel electric.
Within ten minutes, the story’s charm, beguiling characters and awkward situations are in full bloom.
This is a substantial movie with the veneer of a frothy romantic comedy.
Anne Hathaway, as Solène, is a vision of relatability, self-sufficiency, and poise, in a film that proves the rom-com isn’t dead.
Hathaway is a talent no matter what she’s in, and Nicholas Galitzine is one to watch. Together, they make what should be an unbearable cringe-fest a convincing and rather enjoyable experience.
The Idea of You is fizzy and diverting, and falls into the “it’s mostly fine” box, but it lacks oomph in its execution. It’s only half a seduction.
I liked Anne Hathaway in it and found it tolerable, but basically it's a harlequin dramedy.

The Idea of You is directed with breezy affection and confidence by the always reliable Michael Showalter . No, it doesn’t have the snappy cleverness of Notting Hill -- what does? -- but it should appeal to folks craving an intelligent and sexy romcom.
In The Idea of You, it’s actually fun to buy into the fantasy.
The Idea of You is off-key. Each touching or funny moment is dulled down by a story that feels unrehearsed. Performances fall flat, and it feels like the last days of any boy band with infighting.
It is absolutely cheese on toast... however, it does have a point.
A sleek, precision-tooled crowd pleaser.
If they gave Oscars for bringing underwritten characters to life, Hathaway and Galitzine would be contenders.
The potential “ick” factor is played for just the right combination of cringe humor and legit insights...
Pleasant, narcotizing romantic-comedy fluff that occasionally steams up your corneas.

There’s a lovely tension between making art that speaks to you and engineering content that appeals to the masses, reflected in so many interactions between these characters (their jobs, relationships) and the gaps between the novel and its adaptation.

A 40-ish single mom hooks up with a 20-ish boy band star. Cue the mush? Not this time. Somehow sensational Anne Hathaway and swoony Nicholas Galitzine make the cliches dance, bringing humor, heat and unexpected heart to a fantasy for daydream fbelievers.
Ultimately, the stars have chemistry -- that suffices.
The third act overdoes it by driving too many wedges too fast between the lovers, but by then you’ll be too hooked to care and just want to see them smooch again — always a good sign for a romance. D
Think of it as one of those movies that really reinforces the adage there are no new ideas, just fresh versions of old ones set to different beats.

title: Turtles All the Way Down | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: “Turtles All the Way Down” makes Aza’s OCD just specific enough to draw us in, then deals with it in a way that’s just manipulative and sugar-coated enough to leave us thinking, “Yep, it’s another YA movie.”
It’s a charming, delightful YA romance that doesn’t bind itself to the sole enjoyment of its target market.
“Turtles,” to its credit, never locates a specious source of Aza’s troubles, nor does it try to unveil a solution to her suffering.
A mostly moving portrait of how one teenager navigates her mind’s unruly terrain.

Being a teenager? It’s not for the faint of heart. Being a Green teen? Well, at least someone is treating you like an adult. The latest Green adaptation, “Turtles All the Way Down,” offers yet another sterling example of that mindset and the power of it.
Manages to bridge the vast and the daily minutiae of high school life with relative aplomb.

title: Alex Edelman: Just For Us | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: With his first HBO special, the writer-comedian disarmingly balances satire, straight comedy, and old-fashioned pathos.

title: Catching Fire: The Story of Anita Pallenberg | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Composed of interviews with those in Pallenberg’s orbit, and home movies that crackle with chaotic energy, Catching Fire is more concerned with the mercurial essence of its subject than it is with the nuts and bolts of her life.
Too bad, then, that her story has been filtered through eyes that still only see her as a mess or a muse, not the complex, imperfect artist, mother, and woman she really was.
It’s a near two-hour exposé, endlessly fascinating yet punishing as we chart the downfall and drugs-based destruction of this pivotal countercultural figure.
Alexis Bloom and Svetlana Zill have adeptly collated a riveting story, and an intensely sobering one.
Maybe Pallenberg could have made it in acting but the lure of mega-celebrity was too enticing … though in this film, nothing about mega-celebrity looks fun.
This profile from Alexis Bloom and Svetlana Zill is a bid to reclaim the valuable heat of Pallenberg’s incandescence, while never shielding viewers from her life’s lasting burn marks.
Pallenberg is finally in focus. But the picture is tough to look at.
The film views her survival as a triumph and in that way, it matches its subject’s approach to life.
“Anita” is a vital portrait, but it’s the current of devastation that makes it essential.

title: Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Kingdom... is more than a big-budget epic: it explores dilemmas that haunt our real world and has so much empathy for its characters you wonder if it wants us to root for the apes, rather than the humans.

Ball’s movie — intended as the start of a new story arc featuring new characters — is the typical bloated and bland franchise fodder that can only come out of a Hollywood that relishes IP as far as its name and no further.

Kingdom is the episode of the series that we didn't know we needed, distinguished by a powerfully set scene, more than decent level acting and a narrative proposal worth appreciating. [Full review in Spanish]

“Kingdom” aims for some sort of anti-fascism and anti-gun statement. But the film tramples on its own undeveloped ideas when it suddenly become a large-scale actioner. It’s as if the studio had a carnage meter that had to hit 11 before fadeout.
An entertaining new entry in the dormant franchise.
An astounding vision, profound writing and originality are missing in this pretender. It’s a shallow knockoff that can’t carry the weight of the legacy it inherited.
If you ranked [the four main characters] on how compelling they are, it arguably would be inverse to how much screen time they get.
It’s visuals, not words, that this film excels at and as it builds to its (rather far-fetched) conclusion it whips you along.
Dull and confusing. The best that can be said about it is the mildly interesting dystopian production design.

It's fine, it really starts slowly. There's a huge amount of waffling at the beginning and then when it gets into the second hour it gets somewhere that suggests that the next chapter is going to be interesting. It's not great. It's not bad. It's mmm.
Wes Ball’s entry to this franchise feels measured, complex, and ripe for sequels.
It’s a thrilling addition to a franchise that swings from strength to strength.

Ball and Friedman keep things emotionally grounded while also ensuring events reside in perennial shades of grey. Nothing is easy. No choice comes without risk, a devastating downside, or the potential for outright disaster.

It all looks great, and there are interesting ideas knocking about in here, but much of the film is also a bit of a slog, because neither Noa nor Mae come across as particularly exciting, complicated characters.

The reason Planet of the Apes endures is because of the element of surprise, which, over the course of six decades has been reduced to formula and routine; a passable but unremarkable exercise in monkey-see, monkey-do lacking the spark of genuine daring.
This is a disappointing instalment in a franchise I’ve been a fan of from the beginning. It monkeys around at the start, is far too long and lacks both the headline ingredient of its predecessors...
Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes, the first movie in seven years and the possible start of a new trilogy, has a chance to actually explore this world rather than be forced to establish it.
All that and a bag of chimps.

There may be few huge ideas here (something about how we misuse distant history, something else about the poisonous power of charisma), but the dedication to spilling out narrative pays dividends as we round on an open-ended, but intriguing, coda.
It’s traditional and robustly crafted, in a way that’s deferential less to the trends of today than to some half-remembered dream of Hollywood’s classical epics.

title: Wonderland | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: From a distance, Val Kilmer still passes as beautiful... But close up, his is the face of corruption: an intense mass of beforehis-time lines. There is certainly a great role out there for him, but reallife former porn star John C Holmes isn't it.
Very sordid and unexpectedly dull; adults only.
Unwarrantedly interested in B-list celebrity-gone-to-seed.
Rarely has so much of so little consequence been so closely examined.
Sometimes Wonderland does make you wonder why you're wasting your time with these losers. But there's also a lot here that stays with you.
The main interest here is the acting, which is, by turns, entertaining or just entertainingly bad, with lots of grungy seriousness and Method-trained twitching, but also some moments of real gusto.
A film whose effects are as hard to wash away as blood.
Overblown, overheated, overdirected, overacted, overlong and over here, in the local bijoux.
Not quite the second coming of Boogie Nights.

If for some reason you are fascinated by the Wonderland murders, look up the Rolling Stone article of 1989 that brought national attention to the gruesome case. Otherwise, your local cineplex has lots of choices with more redeeming social value.
Wonderland may not be the feel-good movie of the year; in fact it feels pretty lousy most of the time. But it offers a dark story well-told with some truly fine performances.
