title: One Battle After Another | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: PTA, the preferred shorthand for the best high-wire director of his generation, wakes up the sleeping giant of American cinema by trip-wiring every scene in this radical blast of action, fun and fervor like an incendiary device that’s primed to explode.

The excellent performances of DiCaprio and Del Toro bring a deep sense of humanism to two characters who, given the dramatic tone employed, always run the risk of coming across as caricatured stereotypes. [Full review in Spanish]
Yes, the revolution has been cinematized. Sometimes it’s a clear vision. Sometimes not.
It is a brilliant mix of chaos and order.

Anderson elicits memorable inflections of dialogue, intent glances, brazen thrashes of energy and outbursts of fury from his charismatic cast, making “One Battle After Another” a feast of inspired and dedicated acting.

Anderson, at his best, represents a cinema of big swings and bold statements. Perhaps not everything lands, but there’s enough that does to make this glorious mess of a movie one of the most thrilling cinema events of the year.
It’s impossible to overstate how much fun this thing is, with twists and welcome detours along the way.
Somehow, a slacker epic decades in the making turns out to be exactly the movie for right now.
A beautifully choreographed fever dream of resistance and reckoning, blending absurdist satire with a poignant meditation on parental legacy.
The film never flags, bounding from moments of high tension to ones that are sublime. The comedy, meanwhile, always feels integral.
Replete with fury-charged performances and sprinkled with obsidian comedy, Anderson strikes a keen balance between tones that ring all too familiar.

Not only does [Paul Thomas Anderson] push himself and really try different things, both visually and narratively, it just feels like everything works together so precisely. Very entertaining. Completely riveted.

The first half hour or so of "One Battle" is as hot as a pistol, buzzing with frenetic energy while clearly establishing the main characters, their conflict and their motivations. It's frenzied but it's grounded, with the story's stakes clearly set.
The whole movie is amazing.

You’re getting the best of both PTAs. One Battle After Another has all the filmmaking mastery of Paul Thomas Anderson's late-career style but is as accessible and entertaining as his earlier work, more so really.
This is ultimately a pointless, overlong movie that occasionally gives some crowdpleasing thrills en route to nowhere.

This is a difficult film to describe or synopsize. It’s easy to recommend, however, so long as you know you’re about to watch an appropriately R-rated movie where nothing is sacred. Kudos to Paul Thomas Anderson for crafting a truly great movie.
For Anderson’s sixth film in a row, Jonny Greenwood’s score is a key modernising ingredient, shaping sequence after sequence with new timbres, tilted beats and bold attacks. It’s a terrific ride.

One Battle After Another, as great an American movie as I’ve seen this year, doesn’t simply meet the moment; with extraordinary tenderness, fury, and imagination, it forges a moment all its own, and insists that better ones could still lie ahead.
While many sequences go whiz-bang, and laughs and dark ironies bubble up, the arch, lengthy film never takes flight, remaining episodic -- just one battle after another.

title: Regretting You | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: At a too-long two hours, Regretting You is at once mild and bumpy, any momentum jolted by basic hits of mourning or uninspired romance, mechanical delivery and off-timed humor.
It's rubbish.
Solid performances can’t keep this from being a tonally erratic disappointment. Here’s hoping the next Hoover adaptation is a little less regrettable.
It's extremely difficult to take any of it seriously when none of the characters seem to know what kind of movie they're in. Maybe it's a frothy beach read, but it's a mess of a movie.

Everyone looks pretty and cries ugly in this glossy, grit-free romance from the bestselling Colleen Hoover that gives soap opera a bad name. Tearjerking hasn’t been this crass since Disney killed Bambi’s mother. You’ve been warned.

It’s hard to tell just how much of the humor in this film is intentional. Perhaps the idea is to show how awkward things can happen in the midst of unspeakable sadness, but here it all feels so choreographed, so telegraphed, that abject lunacy ensues.
The results are often risible, yet also weirdly anthropologically gripping, like watching aliens from the planet Photoshop dance a cryptic gavotte.
It’s formulaic and predictable, with goofy writing and clumsy editing. The saving grace is the actors, who manage to perform even the most ridiculous lines with a straight face.
Thin characterizations, bland acting and a surfeit of bubbly cuteness combine to make a throw-pillow of a movie: It’s soft and decorative without being particularly useful or interesting.

But too much of a good thing can be a bad thing, and in the case of “Regretting You,” the narrative buckles under the number of overblown emotional scenes and the commercial interruptions for product placements.
There is plenty of gloss but very little grit.

Hoover fans will know that, early on, a catastrophe looks to upset the order. Nothing in the film-making suggests, however, this dilemma will not be tidied away by the time of senior prom. Who would want to live in so dull a fantasy?
“Regretting You” ...has its share of grief. But the strange way the tears give way to smiles, quips and then full-on rom-com corniness feels a little awkward — and then just weird and annoying.
“Regretting You” is not a good movie. It is soapy and insipid. But somehow, thanks to its actors, it is still mildly, wait-for-streaming, watchable.
The countless genre clichés helps the film avoid being merely detestable and approach the sublimely ridiculous.
In the end, everything special about “Regretting You” comes down to the performances of Williams, Grace, Thames and Franco.

The decision to have Allison Williams and Dave Franco, both in their late 30s when the film was shot, play their characters as teens may be the most egregious example of Regretting You’s indifference to verisimilitude.

Some of it is moderately funny -- intentionally, I think, although it’s hard to tell -- but the dialogue is so trite and the pace so ponderous that any sense of surprise evaporates in the first half-hour.

Tucked into the melodrama of “Regretting You,” there is a sweet story about a mother and daughter trying to figure things out, but the reliance on their outside romances often detracts from it. That’s a shame.
The line between a good soap opera and a bad soap opera can sometimes be razor-thin. “Regretting You” walks the line for a while but lands on the wrong side of it.

title: Roofman | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Channing Tatum and Kirsten Dunst find the heart but not the bruised soul in a true-life crime drama from director Derek Cianfrance that should have cut deeper and hurt more.

Cianfrance’s touch eventually helps shift the perspective away from the easy comedy of Manchester’s life, and towards a more subtle – and quite moving – portrait of a man desperate for a second shot at normality...
Channing Tatum is a goofy delight in this engaging﻿ if ﻿overlong caper.
It really helps that Kirsten Dunst's character is completely believable.
It’s a film, in the end, about what you compromise for company. And it’s funny too, in places — just not always.
I think more Roofman, less Toys R Us squatter would have made this a more entertaining film.

Cianfrance takes a daring swerve away from his usual melancholic working- class love stories, such as the powerful anti-romance Blue Valentine, to deliver a comedy that delivers big laughs and the occasional thrill.
It’s Derek Cianfrance’s ability to explore the multiplicities in a person, all the good, the bad and the spaces in between, that makes his films such wonderful and complex little gems.
Roofman deftly blends genres to create a low-key crowd-pleaser -- one that avoids merely reveling in what made Manchester notorious in the first place.
As this shaggy story ambles on, you may wait for a message, or a lesson. I wouldn’t. Sometimes, a movie just decides it is enough to say: this happened.

Cianfrance is a gifted director, with an evident love of actors and an equally strong sense of space... But his skills seem to lead him in too many directions at once: Roofman is a sustained exercise in cognitive dissonance.
Roofman has heart, energy and personality fit to burst.
Roofman is partly a lark: it’s fun to watch a clever, likable guy like Tatum’s Manchester beat the system.
Cianfrance is a sensitive, smart filmmaker, and he finds the gentle soul in Tatum's character.
Roofman is simply too odd a bird, a movie that sets out to be a romp but can’t bring itself to smooth over the rougher aspects of its material...

Roofman is predominantly a one-man showcase for the full range of Tatum's talents, but the entire ensemble is crucial for any good caper. Dunst's prowess pushes his own performance, while Peter Dinklage offers levity as the stern store manager Mitch.
Roofman, with its breezy decency, knows how to finesse just the right amount of compassion for larceny.
“Roofman” hooks viewers with its compelling depiction of a person too smart for his own good. It’s funny and moving, however close to or far from the real events it may be.

Here is a protagonist who clearly straddles the line between right and wrong; the trouble is that in “Roofman,” that line wobbles, leaving the movie somewhere between a fun-loving caper and a finger-wagging morality tale.
Lived-in performances and a sensitive screenplay make for a thoroughly engaging comedy-drama.

title: Black Phone 2 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The worst thing the script, written by Derrickson and C. Robert Cargill, does is rely relentlessly on references to the Nightmare on Elm Street saga that end up looking more like imitations than homages. [Full review in Spanish]
Even if it doesn’t all quite work, this is a creepily inventive shocker that grows in mournful power as it moves along.
It’s not as scary or as effective as the first film, but points for the performances, and for trying hard to do something different and fresh.
What’s notable about Black Phone 2 is how unlike The Black Phone it is in some ways. That may provoke disappointment from some quarters, but it also makes for a unique, unexpected experience.
It feels a lot more generically derivative.
For all her ​‘woo-woo’ powers, Gwen remains a refreshingly foul-mouthed teenager, and this time around, her and Finney’s storylines dovetail more neatly and compellingly.
A film whose tension (and inventiveness) waxes and wanes, although courtesy of Hawke’s unforgettable masked fiend, it continues to boast an iconic horror movie visage destined to ruin viewers’ sleep.
Set in the early ’80s, it’s a movie that proudly understands what made the horror genre of its decade a unique beast with steely-sharp fingers.
"“Black Phone 2” commits its own unforgivable crime of being dreadfully boring."
It’s one of the great horror sequels, for about an hour. Then it’s a cautionary tale about how not to make a horror sequel, for about an hour.
It’s a chilling expansion of the franchise, with visually inventive dream sequences.
Black Phone 2 may be a power ballad to the original’s minor chord metal, but it still rocks.
"Black Phone 2" isn't worth answering, but McGraw holds the line all her own.
While the sequel realizes the need to connect the rest of its ghostly parts, it becomes overlong in spots, bogged down by stiff explication. Instead, the movie’s engine is mostly in its new scares.

There are times when Black Phone 2 wears its stylistic influences too heavily on its sleeve. But the extensive borrowings are easily forgiven when the set pieces are delivered with the sort of panache that they are here.
Despite the concept’s inherent nastiness, the film has been well put together.
Black Phone 2, like M3gan 2.0 before it, is a needlessly long and hugely unconvincing argument for the birth of a new franchise. The next time it rings, I recommend not answering.

It’s got fresh ideas, bold visuals, and resonant performances, but once it turns the first movie’s chilling villain, the Grabber (played indelibly by Ethan Hawke), into a rehashed Freddy Krueger, the thrill is very much gone.
But for all of the film's highlights, it lacks the sense of surprise that made "BP1" such a discovery.
There’s still plenty here to make you shiver, but in letting events out of the basement this sequel has also released much of the tension.

title: The Fantastic Four: First Steps | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The first three FFs fell so hard on their fat ones that “First Steps” wins best in show by default.
First Steps is a stand﻿alone picture with no links -- as yet -- to the wider Marvel landscape, and it works relatively well, not least because of the peppy, 60s-style, retro-futurist design choices.
Audiences shouldn’t have to sacrifice eye-catching stunts and imagery for great writing and acting. They should have it all. Should but won’t in this case.
For now, let's enjoy what this efficient commercial product has to offer, which surprisingly lasts less than two hours... [Full review in Spanish]
Even if you don't like the film, it is absolutely worth it for the furniture.

First, the good news: you can take your seat for this semi-standalone Marvel blockbuster and enjoy the zippy action and affectionate banter of its charismatic cast without the nagging concern that you haven’t seen 17 or so other films first.

With lowest common denominator baby jokes, this fair-to-meh superhero movie features a gaggle of great actors working at their lowest gears, while Papa Pascal is on the verge of being 2025’s most over-exposed star.
The Fantastic Four: First Steps is competent at best—a reboot with cosmic ambition that barely attains lift-off.
It’s yet another middling entry in the post-Endgame tradition, a film that doesn’t launch the franchise headlong at the future so much as it glumly drags us toward it.
It’s hard not to walk out of the theater without a happy smile firmly planted on your face.
It's brisk, brightly comic, and most of all, sincere and earnest (this year's superhero mode), a combo that works just as well here as it does for Superman in the DC Universe.

Decades from now, it will still invite us to escape into it, to delight in its larger-than-life characters, its intergalactic battles and its heart-stirring moments of heroism -- and, yes, in its benign, winning, blessed goofiness.
As an effort to breathe new life into a particularly moribund title, First Steps is essentially successful. What it somehow can’t manage to do is have much of a good time in the process.

There’s more energy in the eye-catching production design than in the drama. The director, Matt Shakman, evokes little struggle, terror, or wonder, and the fine cast delivers amiable and mild performances.
It's probably not easy to make a good Fantastic Four movie. The newest version has enough actor-based charm to distract from its jankiest effects, plus a damn cool Silver Surfer,
The dialogue is weak, especially the attempts at humour. Nothing much of interest happens. The superhero movie franchise has its ups and downs. This one is definitely on the downside.
The script never loses a vague, hand-waving quality that leaves its central characters as indistinctly drawn as the moral conflict they ultimately face.
In isolation, First Steps is a pretty good time, even if it feels as though it could push its aesthetic into more daring territory.
It's a nimble, fleet-footed piece of entertainment, which never feels any weightier than a Saturday morning cartoon.
The Fantastic Four: First Steps works on its own terms, it is visually a delight, has three or four jaw dropping moments, some great laughs and compelling performances.

title: Karate Kid: Legends | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: While the film hits all the expected story beats and throws all the right punches, they somehow fail to connect. What’s lacking, as the Han and Dan “Sensei” double act points out in each interminable training montage, is the element of surprise.

Karate Kid: Legends sits at this intersection of something that effectively taps into the nostalgia of the franchise, evokes the warm-and-fuzzies, serves up an enjoyable experience, even if you know that it’s not a great movie.
...Karate Kid: Legends offers little by way of innovation and plenty by way of giving the people what they want. It’s derivative, corny and, in its utterly predictable way, great fun.
Wax on, wax off. Eff on, eff off.

Though it holds back on the emotional punches and occasionally plays it safe with crowd-pleasers, Legends remains a respectful, heartfelt, and surprisingly fresh fusion of everything that’s made the franchise endure.
Karate Kid: Legends is actually an enjoyable little film.
..."Karate Kid: Legends” feels at times like four or five different movies being chopped-and-screwed together, albeit at an enjoyably fast pace, and with a minimum of narrative drag.

I love the Kung Fu Karate training and fight scenes, and the whole thing, and this is true of the series, is played with an air of wholesomeness that's fairly irresistible. I came out with a spring on my step and... I cried.
I can’t imagine anyone remembering Karate Kid: Legends four decades from now. Or next week.
The “Legends” are let downs. All the film’s got going for it is Wang.

There’s no room for this sixth chapter in the series to breathe, characters are one-dimensional archetypes, and everything has to be explicitly spelled out via unnecessary expository avalanches. This latest installment is a true waste of time.
We’re in familiar but not unwelcome territory....No surprises here, but sometimes that’s just fine.

It’s warm, it’s breezy – it’s a burst of summery family fun that is sure to inspire long looks back at the old movies and Cobra Kai episodes while sparking renewed interest in martial arts apprenticeship. Anyone would get a kick out of it.

The problem with “Karate Kid: Legends” is right there in the title: “legends,” as in multiple. Many beloved “Karate Kid” characters and icons of millennial sports movies enter the ring, but in the ensuing melee, no one emerges victorious.
The film struggles tonally, thanks in part to the upbeat music set against a backdrop of violence and trauma.
Instead, it’s more like an outline whose details the filmmakers never got around to filling in.

Hardcore fans may get their kicks from seeing Macchio and Chan together. Everyone else will just feel like tempted to sweep the legs of everyone trying to cash in on a recently revived franchise and wring it dry.
“Karate Kid: Legends” is steeped in nostalgia, which helps paper over a formulaic script and the strange reality that its domestic scenes are more effective than its fight action.

There is at once a roughshod, zippy energy coupled with a sedateness here that results from the simple fact that the film never quite knows how to square the pure awkwardness of two teachers instructing a karate kid at once.
“Karate Kid: Legends” combines the best of all those sequels plus a 2010 remake to contribute a new and worthy chapter to the canon.

title: Final Destination Bloodlines | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This latest instalment is one of the best in a consistently entertaining series: everything from garden rakes and wind chimes to garbage compressors and intimate body piercings are weaponised in eye-watering fashion. It’s an absolute blast.
This is also the series at its best ... [T]he Bloodlines filmmakers have found a way to reinvent the Final Destination wheel — and then promptly crush someone’s head with it.

Maybe the best explanation I can offer for the success of Final Destination is this: It's funny 'cause it's true. When you die, you probably won't go squish, but you'll go, and so will everybody else.

Bloodlines is well plotted and brilliantly grisly, but most important, it knows how to enjoy itself. I’d say that having fun, more than anything, is what people are seeking from the communal cinematic experience.
There are a few breath-snatching moments here and there, but Bloodlines generally strikes a balance between gruesome and funny as it sprints along.
Bloodlines gives us plenty of what we want from a new Final Destination movie, but it also could have given us quite a bit more.
It’s a rare franchise reboot that works as a standalone, even with a few choice callbacks and links to the previous movies.
We’re here for the kills and, again, every single kill in 'Final Destination Bloodlines' is a winner. Every time a head explodes, which is a lot, you’ll want to stand up and cheer.
Lipovsky and Stein elicit not a single solid performance from their cast, and their tale’s twists are illogical even by the material’s established guidelines.
While it might not be the best horror film release this year by any means, Bloodlines is undoubtedly a solid and studied chapter in the Final Destination universe.
It was a mistake to make a Final Destination movie into an almost two-hour-long family drama.
Lipovsky and Stein don't go straight for the jugular, they feel around it and drag out the inevitable, and the fun is in the tension they build and the false finishes they tease.
The acting too is ropey at best (aside from standouts Todd and Richard Harmon, as the sardonic tattoo artist Erik) but even that seems to work within the context of this schlocky delight.

There’s not much more a Final Destination fan could ask for, but Bloodlines — which at times feel more like a dark satire than a straightforward horror movie — reminds us we’re powerless against the world’s morbid whims. Best we can do is laugh about it.
“Bloodlines” reinvigorates “Final Destination” in a way that makes its predecessors proud.
You may watch “Final Destination Bloodlines” through fingers covering your face. But chances are high you’ll be smiling, too.

Are these movies deep? Yeah, in their way. Because they get you thinking about metaphysics, free will, and karma by killing people in chain reaction Destruct-O-Ramas that are framed, lit and edited with all the dark magic at cinema’s disposal.
There’s a decadence in the film-making that isn’t at odds with the campy nature of Final Destination but instead realizing its full potential.

While a canonically satisfying sendoff to the late Tony Todd’s William Bludworth bolsters the series’ morbid gravitas, a cast of playful, mostly likable 20-somethings keep proceedings light in juxtaposition to the filmmakers’ fiendishly inventive kills.

Not only does Bloodlines scratch the itch the original started - the twisted thrill of what happens when you get caught up in death’s design - but it does so by putting a genius spin on the lore, one that well serves its high concept and its characters.

title: Nobody 2 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This sequel reprises ﻿the family man-turned-badass formula but loses the deliriously enjoyable element of surprise and some of the slick efficiency of the mayhem.
My only issue with Nobody 2 is that it is perfectly content to replay what worked best in 2021’s Nobody and not put much thought into doing anything ambitiously different.
There is an interesting kind of Straw Dogs & Home Alone DIY thing about what happens... I always enjoy that sort of stuff.
As the medley of violence continues, Stone’s mugging goes from giddily sinister to hammy and exhausting. Same goes for Nobody 2, and also the post-John Wick wave of action movies it’s part of.
A film this unwilling to make any sort of profound statement needs to at least be dumb and fun, and it actually manages to be neither.
It's bloodier, uglier and angrier than its predecessor, the sequel nobody asked for.
The appeal of the film is basic and, frankly, monotonous.
No one’s heart is in it, even as other body parts are severely damaged.
Hutch is not just a superdad -- he’s essentially a superhero, which makes him less interesting and more predictable. Still, as superhero movies go, this one has more gusto than most.
It’s amusing to watch, in the same cathartic way as the first film, but you can’t help think there could have been more to the story than just a rapidly rising pile of bashed and bloodied bodies.
All the elements were there to make “Nobody 2” a great sequel — it just seems like nobody really thought about what makes the original really work.

Along the lines of a Looney Tunes cartoon, if Hutch was Road Runner AND Wile E. Coyote AND all the blow-up equipment from Acme...it would just be cartoonish without Odenkirk’s ability to make us understand Hutch’s layers of emotion.

The aggro remains front and centre, executed in video game style. But the formula has also been tweaked into something more like what the first movie looked set to be — a berserker romp with an unbroken funny bone.
Bob Odenkirk’s unlikely new career journey as a kickass tough guy continues in this pretty formulaic and forgettable sequel to the amusing original hit.
“What about Bob?” is now a moot question. Odenkirk is an action-movie star now... Nobody 2 exists simply to extend this concept a few steps further, and anything else is merely a bonus.
Making memories it ain't. But making 89 minutes of your life disappear almost painlessly has its place, too.

Nobody didn’t deviate far from the action template, but it has offbeat humor, appealing performers and some tight, wittily choreographed fight sequences that made smart use of Odenkirk’s comedy chops.
Another undemanding installment in the whimsically violent franchise.
[Odenkirk’s] absolute commitment to being as uncharismatic as possible – no mean feat for TV’s favorite sleazy lawyer – makes him perfect as the killer in comfortable sneakers.
Nobody 2 sheds both the novelty value and the style that set the original film apart.

title: Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: ...can't evoke the magnitude of Springsteen’s interiority, straining to literalize the mysteries and anxieties that Nebraska already mined.

Though it barely scratches the surface of a rock icon’s hungry heart, this sliver of a biopic rises above stagnant writing and directing on the power of watching Bruce Springsteen,  studiously acted by Jeremy Allen White, show depression who’s the boss.
The issue isn’t so much that the story being told isn’t authentic but that the presentation confers an uncanny sense of artificiality, like a four-track home recording fed through Pro Tools.
A derivative, if well intentioned, piece of fan fiction.

It is by no means unprecedented that the life of a great performer can be so bifurcated. But to make us begin to understand the anguish on display here, the movie needed more emotional layers and fewer obvious signposts.
White is quietly effective as Bruce, having perfected the singer’s trademark honeycomb rasp.
This is not just a film for fans... I really enjoyed the movie.
It’s a film that feels as if it has many endings, and also many middles, several of them a bit boring.
It’s an imperfect film, obviously, though to Springsteen fantatics (that, I am not) it’ll be a godsend.
At its best, the film gives us a sincere look at the creative process and reveals it to be a sad, scary, at times uncontrollable and destructive thing. Just for that alone, it’s worth seeing.
Unfortunately, what made Nebraska groundbreaking isn’t particularly cinematic. Cooper is forced to rely heavily on that most stagnant of biopic tropes: the creative inspiration montage.
No one expects a bio-pixposé of the Boss, but this movie is so respectful and dignified as to seem like puff.
The film seems interested in the creative process...but largely skips over the unsuccessful full-band recording sessions that convinced Springsteen to release the demos as they were.
...the biopic never finds its groove, lacking the raw, percussive drive and deep connection of Springsteen’s best songs.
The film never catches fire, but White and Strong do their very best to give it a spark.
“Nebraska” was a triumph because it refused to fulfill anyone’s expectations. “Deliver Me From Nowhere” valorizes that decision while missing its chance to do the same.
This will doubtless satisfy the completists. But non-completists – I could have named only two of his songs, tops – may wonder if it’s that interesting.

Cooper spends much of Deliver Me from Nowhere’s runtime convincing us of White’s transformation...Unfortunately, the rest...is reduced in his script to the same pop psychology we’ve come to expect from a music biopic.
[Jeremy Allen White] is wholly convincing in voice, mannerisms and musical performance, even when the film is emotionally inert.

Focusing on Springsteen’s depressive side is a valid approach, but the film doesn’t begin to offer a compelling portrait. It’s an opportunity wasted — a dour, self-important affair, forlorn in the USA.

title: My Oxford Year | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There's no reason to bother with "My Oxford Year" unless you're a YA romance completist.

What should be a tender, feminist-minded story centered on a young woman rediscovering her dormant childhood dreamer turns into a middling melodrama about being with a cute guy in desperate need of her rescue.
They are all very attractive people, as are Dougray Scott and Catherine McCormack as Jamie’s parents. They just aren’t given a lot to do.
Instead of a rote enemies to lovers story, it becomes a limp attempt at being this generation’s About Time.
'My Oxford Year' is shiny and affable, and if that was the assignment it’d get an 'A' for effor- … actually that’s going too far, let’s make it a respectable 'B.' But that’s not the assignment.
Morris is a competent enough director but the script, from Allison Burnett and Melissa Osborne, is devoid of any real electricity, leaving it up to the leads to generate it.
While 'My Oxford Year’ makes for a very good advertisement for studying abroad, it leaves other things to be desired.

title: If I Had Legs I'd Kick You | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Linda is a beast of a role and Rose Byrne plays her with everything’s she’s got and then some.  No list of the year’s great performances would be complete without this tour de force.
Bronstein does a tremendous job of placing viewers inside Linda's head; you understand her mental state because the movie drops the audience inside her headspace without a net.
It’s a bold, claustrophobic movie that wouldn’t work without Byrne.

As difficult as it may be to watch, and as much as it can assault the senses and create an anxiously icky feeling of abhorrent devastation, Byrne’s career-best work makes Bronstein’s first feature-length drama since 2008’s Yeast absolutely essential.
We are not just watching this mother; we begin to feel the pressure she is under.
Despite the intensity of the story, there’s a needed thread of pitch-black humor woven throughout that dares you to laugh at its sheer ridiculousness.
If I Had Legs aims high, and hits harder than most this year – a film guaranteed to knock the breath out of you.
Bryne’s performance is so brilliantly unhinged, such a thing of chaotic beauty, that the film would be worthy of study anyway. Bronstein makes it something more.
Bronstein’s real target is the audience and the limits to its empathy.

It’s a daring choice to force audiences to spend 2 hours with someone they won’t like, but “If I Had Legs, I’d Kick You” is more of an experiment than an empathy machine. It overstays its welcome by at least 30 minutes.
It takes a bold and brave actress to make Linda's unraveling bearable, and Bornstein's film has found that in Rose Byrne, who gives a phenomenal performance.

If I Had Legs I’d Kick You is a movie that feels written and engineered to deliver moments and clips rather than offer any depth on the topics purportedly at hand: the burden of motherhood, feelings of inadequacy, alienation, lopsided gender dynamics.
Downright harrowing in its depiction of a mom beset by a string of personal and professional catastrophes.
Anyone who checks out early will rob themselves of not only the most electric film of the year, but a lead performance that feels singular, towering, even generational.
Byrne manages to keep us empathetic, and Bronstein has the good sense not to judge her. [Full review in Spanish]

Between its marvellous ensemble acting and Bronstein’s propulsive directorial style (abetted by the clever editing of Lucian Johnston), “If I Had Legs I’d Kick You” is never less than watchable and absorbing.

If I Had Legs I’d Kick You is hardly full-on punishment, and in places it’s bitterly funny. But in the end, it’s an enormous relief to walk away from Linda’s problems. Our own don’t seem so bad in comparison.
Only a film this forthright can have such power. Bronstein and Byrne’s dual honesty is as affecting as it gets.
It’s the kind of film that makes you want to call your own mother and apologize.
The script gives Byrne too few moments to modulate the intensity of her performance, or to communicate who Linda is in any register other than blind panic as she careens from one crisis to the next.

title: Freakier Friday | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Including assorted TV spin-offs, this belated sequel to the popular 2003 remake of Freaky Friday is the studio’s seventh variation on the mother-daughter body-swap tale, and there’s not a lot of juice left in the idea.
I laughed a lot, and then I cried.
I went in with no expectations and came out pleasantly surprised.
Far from a perfect movie and definitely a little overlong. But also so earnest and well-intentioned that it papered over a lot of the flaws.

By violating the genre’s numeric rule, director Nisha Ganatra and writer Jordan Weiss prove that double the bodies does not equal double the fun. Everyone is so bland and one-dimensional, it’s easy to forget who’s who.
Freakier Friday is a movie that manages to humiliate everybody.
It’s a good movie for a late-summer legacy sequel, not a candidate for the all-time comedy pantheon.
The films may be separated by more than two decades, but the vibe is very much the same: get the sentiments out, but keep it broad and light, and make things right.
The sequel, Freakier Friday, is freakier in the sense that the mind-body switch goes further, but it isn’t funnier, or even funny full stop.
If you liked the first installment or have any sympathy for its actresses, you won't be able to have a bad time with Freakier Friday. [Full review in Spanish]
It is glossy, family-friendly, wholesome entertainment, presented with a high Disney sheen.
There’s a lot of subterfuge, heart searching and far-fetched life lessons in this glossy fish-out-of-water comedy that may not be fresh, but hasn’t yet lost its juice.

This viewer just wishes that, with such a constellation of talent assembled in one film, ‘Freakier Friday’ had risen to the occasion and pushed them to the outer edges of their abilities instead of putting them through their paces.
Curtis and Lohan remain a rocking comedic duo who know how to bring down the house.
If you feel like catching up with the Colemans and revisiting some early-aughts magic, Freakier Friday is a good choice.
The old crank in me wished that I laughed harder than I did.

“Freakier Friday” feels genuinely restorative, not just for Lohan’s reputation, but for the inner child who once loved movies like this, delighting in silly tropes like food fights, hunks tossing their hair in slow-motion and makeover montages.
Freakier Friday works best if you’re there for the memories. Especially if you’ve learned a lesson or two of your own in the last 22 years.
This old-school confection, smartly reuniting the original cast, delights in every silly scene.
Freakier Friday is an inoffensive product with good intentions and a cardboard heart, but, these days, watching Curtis strut her stuff is an out-of-body experience all on its own.

title: The Conjuring: Last Rites | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Thanks to Wilson and Farmiga, who know the exact register of intensity to play these characters, it’s easy to remain invested in Ed and Lorraine, their work and their love slightly out of time.
It might not conjure something phenomenal, but, for longtime fans, it’s a mostly fitting curtain call for a franchise that always believed in its own ghosts.
Such subtlety has largely vanished by the final reel, sadly, but this is still a suitably shiver-inducing farewell to the Warrens.
“Last Rites” has a sense of humor and that’s worth watching if you’re up for a laugh instead of a scream.

One reason why “The Conjuring: Last Rites” is so uninteresting is it takes one hour, 21 minutes for the Warrens to agree to enter the haunted house that we all know they’re going to enter from minute one.
Last Rites comes from Michael Chaves, the same director as that last film, but returns the series to what it does best, which is dealing with a supernaturally infested home.

I don't mind bunk. But what I mind is 135 minutes in which half of it is sub-Poltergeist Oompa Loompa Ugabooga schlock and the other half is 'oh, the Warrens'... let's be real about this: The Warrens were at best kooks and at worst, conmen.
A fun blend of scares and sentiment, this largely justifies a lengthy run time with effective frights and a valedictory feel.
a sluggishly routine send-off for the Warren family.
As it stands, the film is a disappointing send-off; more an eccentric family drama than a real chiller.
Sticking to a template fans know with a shivery intimacy by now, it brings the series to rest with enough chillingly imaginative touches to make it a winner.
The climax of is as tense and unsettling as you want to be, but it’s also warm and inspiring.
Still more than its predecessors, The Conjuring: Last Rites feels for much of its overlong running time like a syrupy soap opera...

Wilson and Farmiga remain solidity incarnate, capable of enlivening even speculative spiritual dialogue. The film-making pulls no surprises out of the hat, though, and gives no indication that it would if it could.

“The Conjuring: Last Rites” feels crowded from the inside out: it’s as if an earnest domestic drama and a horror flick were thrashing around, trying to occupy the same running time. Neither one is able to cast the other out.

Last Rites is suitably nightmarish where it counts, bringing memorable chills that linger and spilling more blood than usual in a Conjuring film. But it’s more affecting for the way it wears its heart on its sleeves.

As a scary movie, 'The Conjuring: Last Rites' is a generic film, neither good nor bad. It’s practically begging audiences to judge it on a 'pass/fail' basis. As the conclusion of the 'Conjuring' series, it’s a little more successful, but not much.

The Conjuring series was once a trailblazer, elevating mainstream horror by turning simple scares into cinematic experiences. This Last Rites is competent, occasionally tense and features strong performances, but it lacks the sting of the first one.

Last Rights is a decent enough final cinematic prayer for this franchise, combining the personal story of the Warrens and their daughter, Judy, with a new paranormal possession that’s created a freaked-out family.

Cue the creepy attics and doom-filled cellars and horrific visions of ax-wielding maniacs, but these haunted-house trappings no longer carry the fright or the fun that the Conjuring movies once reliably provided.

title: Elio | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The astringent sting and needle-sharp perceptiveness of, say, Inside Out or The Incredibles is missing. Still, it’s a marked improvement on the recent quality lull of Elemental and the barely watchable Lightyear.

The animation is charming, as one would expect from a Pixar production, and the characters are likeable enough to spawn off merch. The swell of music at appropriate times keeps you hooked into the action and emotions.
Visually, it's really fun to watch.

The oddity of Elio is that this subplot is quite a lot more touching than the hero’s journey. A father-son reconciliation between these piglet-sized space slugs is the one thing in danger of moistening the eye.
... The film doesn’t waste anyone’s time, while tackling forever urgent childhood themes: the mysteries of other kids, older kids, adults, yourself.
...[Elio is] inventively animated and neatly plotted in a way that used to be a Pixar hallmark: the surprises are many, both in one-off sight gags and larger twists.
There is a lightness and levity to Pixar’s latest animated spectacle Elio that kept me smiling for every moment of its interstellar comedic adventure.
There’s an unde­ni­able charm to this film that makes it easy to be daz­zled by.
There is enough of a sense of awe here, and enough scale, that it brightens up the big screen as it stares into the ebony black of space.

The sugar highs of this rambunctious thrill ride are fun, in other words, but in the end “Elio” is most memorable when it eases up to celebrate the invisible ties of love and friendship that bind all of us aliens to each other.
By turns appealing and drearily familiar, the movie offers the expected visual pleasures and characters who range from the gently exaggerated to the hyperbolic.

Elio isn't a first-rate Pixar offering, but thanks to sumptuous animation and a warm spirit, it's a cute Wizard of Oz-style journey to the beyond and back. Outer space is cool, but there's no place like home.

Prettily animated in bright pastels and voiced amusingly, the story serves a sweetly conventional set of lessons about friendship, standing up for yourself, and accepting love from allies who share your sensibilities.
Dear Walt, how you wish this trip to the stars wasn’t so beholden to the gravitational pull of being just decent enough.
It's standard, a passable piece of family entertainment, but far from what we once expected from the company that brought us "Up," "WALL-E" and "Inside Out." It's nothing special.
“Elio” is another knockout, a quiet but determined shooting star that earns its place in the galaxy.
“Elio” is a good summer movie of intergalactic fun. It just plays it safe.
Elio is perfectly amiable movie that will delight. Even a second-tier Pixar is better than most things in the known universe.
Pixar’s latest has everything we love about Pixar, a heartwarming story with endless imagination, charm, and wisdom, about an endearing character and the fears and joys of being human.
Schmaltzy yet sincere, “Elio,” the latest from Pixar, is as predictable as they come but as tender as they can get.

title: Caught Stealing | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The film is brutal—filled with bad luck, questionable choices and broken bodies—but it’s also thrilling, propelled by Butler’s performance and Aronofsky’s compassion for the flawed.

A picture with such a high body count﻿ is unlikely to be boring, ﻿but this is a lazily derivative throwback that appropriates ideas and plot points from numerous other movies (think Guy Ritchie’s ﻿After Hours﻿). Caught Stealing indeed.

Aronofsky doesn’t respect his characters. He doesn’t disrespect them as much as he disrespected Brendan Fraser’s title character in “The Whale,” but a friend to the human condition he is not. He also doesn’t respect the audience.
It was darker than I had anticipated from the trailers but still more fun than other Aronofsky films, and there’s a cat in it.
This is a straightforward, entertaining crime thriller.
Caught Stealing is the best movie from Darren Aronofsky... in years, a crazy After Hours-style yarn with a high body count and a buoyant, breathless pace.
It’s Aronofsky near his best.
You enjoy it, you watch it, and you go on about your day.
It's a work with abundant doses of entertainment, vibrantly filmed, and also possesses a tremendous sense of humor, unlike anything its author has done in the past. [Full review in Spanish]
It’s unashamedly derivative but also entertaining.
...the film has so much bloodletting and the casualty rate is so high that its gallows humour tends to be upstaged by the ultra violence. But there’s no looking away.
The pace is fast and propulsive and all characters are expendable, so you're never quite sure where "Caught Stealing" is headed next.

Referencing Scorsese, the forever king of the New York crime movie, is a risk Caught Stealing probably shouldn’t have taken. I spent much of the running time reminiscing on just how thoughtful and composed the best examples of this genre can be.
The entire film is such a refreshing change of pace and tone from Aronofsky’s typically dour material that it feels like the director is intentionally turning a page.
It's not even that Butler is the problem with Caught Stealing. He's more the biggest sign that Aronofsky is pulling his punches, and his fans should be worried.
Aronofsky, whose work I’ve always liked, should retreat back to the dark recesses of the psyche and leave the comically dark underbelly of organized crime to the pros.
A tight, twisty script, meaningful stakes, a top director (Darren Aronofsky), and an A-plus cast have delivered a satisfyingly sharp thriller, ‘Caught Stealing.'
The uneven crime thriller Caught Stealing is an admirable attempt by Darren Aronofsky to be friskier yet more conventional in a genre that often rewards a by-the-numbers approach.
Funny, weird and demented are much more interesting keys to play, and Mr. Aronofsky does so with gusto in a movie that sprawls, rambles and roars.

Caught Stealing finds more pathos in the endangerment of a pet than the death of a female character, and it's forever in a hurry to the next violent confrontation when all of its best parts are the ones in between.

title: Heads of State | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: [Jon Cena and Idris Elba] bicker and blow away bad guys in a formulaic take from Nobody director Ilya Naishuller that has only a hint of the gonzo energy it requires to transcend its limitations.
Like a gym-toned Laurel and Hardy, the mess they get themselves into is — broadly speaking — fine.
There's a decent action scene or two, as far as it goes for low-rent action scenes in streaming slop. That's a pretty low bar.
It works as a fizzy, somewhat kid-friendly throwback to action-packed ‘80s partnerships
It is stupendously idiotic yet eminently watchable.
Torn between action and comedy, irony and sentiment, and rah-rah jingoism and genuine self-reflection, “Heads of State” is a surprisingly entertaining romp
Heads of State succeeds by playing to its stars’ strengths. It’s pacy, funny, and manages to give its slight premise some bite.

Heads of State isn’t going to make us all magically get along, but it at least functions as a welcome reprieve into a fantasy world where our leaders act heroically and selflessly... because they genuinely want the world to be a better place for everyone.
“Heads of State” is infinitely more entertaining than it comes across on paper.

The bickering between Cena and Elba does grow tiresome, but director Ilya Naishuller gives us reasons to forget about that with a series of exhilarating action sequences – including a spectacular car chase in a knock-your-socks-off finale.
A really good, dumb comedy can be a joyous thing, and this is a really good, dumb comedy.
Fun, fiery and totally frivolous, Heads of State is a perfect summer movie with great potential for future sequels.
It’s loud albeit harmless japery, best appreciated with your air-conditioning cranked to movie theater levels.
Not sharp enough to be memorable but just well-crafted enough that you wish everyone involved had tried a little harder...
It’s a painless watch, and, in its cheery, fantastic absurdity, something of a respite from the messier, crazier, more unbelievable world awaiting you once the credits have rolled.

As a blithely likable blunt instrument, “Heads of State” gets the job done, justifying its anesthetized mayhem with a sweet-natured message about the importance of friendship, international alliances and institutional continuity.
All in all, it’s stupid fun, done with enough panache that its thin story and sometimes too-glib attitude doesn’t hurt it too much.
A globetrotting action comedy whose primary selling point is the chemistry of headliners (and The Suicide Squad castmates) Idris Elba and John Cena.
Heads of State is so goddamn fun.

The action tips too far into carnage, and the comedy is not as sharp as it should be. But there are cool locations, the action scenes are exciting, and Jack Quaid shows up midway though to liven things up, so a pleasant streaming time-waster.

title: Novocaine | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: This dark, stylish tale isn't for kids.
This Hitchcockian yarn compensates for its leading man's rather anonymous performance with some well-placed shocks, a morbid sense of humour, and a climax that will literally put your teeth on edge.
The casting is peculiar, the tone is off, the plot is uninteresting and the ending is sorry.
Plays like the sort of silly shared fantasy that a group of dental students might come up with late one night, after too much coffee and cramming for finals.
This movie was not effective.
A coarse, witless and stunningly violent black comedy.
Atkins never finds the right tone for Novocaine. It's not dark enough to be either viciously funny or unsettling.
About as exciting as dry humping a dentist's chair.
With Bonham Carter's been-there, done-that performance and a plot that spins out of control, we end up with a movie that you can't quite sink your teeth into.
Fun but wobbly stuff.
Martin breaks loose from a string of bland studio comedies with Novocaine, a snarkily amusing indie.
An impressive directorial debut, but you wish Atkins had not made his movie's gradual descent seem as inevitable as Frank's.
The laughs aren't warm enough, or the crimes cold enough, to move anyone to shake or shiver.
About two rewrites shy of a real story.
There are many things wrong with Novocaine, but the film's most gnawing pain is its clodhopper farfetchedness.
The action takes on the two-dimensional quality of a clever joke and does a disservice to the actual suspense.
A screwball film noir with a lot of medium laughs and a few great big ones.
[Atkins] brings to his direction of Martin a finesse shared by only a few of the directors who have worked with the comedian-actor.
By the end you may need an aspirin to dispel the hectic racket Novocaine becomes.
It's too bad the movie's intriguing effect wears off ... about two-thirds through.

title: Mickey 17 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: I feel like this movie was made by a Bong Joon-ho admirer who wanted to make a pastiche of Bong Joon-ho movies, but it's just not as good as the other ones.
I assume this works as a narrative for a book -- not so much as a narrative for cinema.
But Mickey 17 doesn’t have Okja’s same level of compassion and humanity, nor is the critique of capitalism and class inequality as acidly rich as it is in Snowpiercer or Parasite.
It’s such a bold, adventurous, scream of a film, but its queerness ends up dampened.

There’s a bit of on-screen torture in the sci-fi black comedy Mickey 17 but the unintended one, I assume, is being forced to watch four-time Oscar nominee Mark Ruffalo and Australia’s Toni Collette mush through two of the cheesiest roles imaginable.
I feel like it has the makings of a cult classic—a dystopian space comedy/adventure with shades of Terry Gilliam.
You wonder if there wasn’t an earlier cut that was much weirder, spiky and bolder.
It would be unfair to expect Bong to make another Parasite. He hasn’t. Neither is his new movie a disaster. It might be something worse. It is passable.

A typically dynamic production, with some great visuals and that more than meets the spectacular requirements of the genre it represents without overusing digital effects or trying to forcefully demonstrate how much it cost... [Full review in Spanish]
Mickey 17 may not end up being the year’s best film, but it will undoubtedly become one of its most essential.
No one else makes films like Bong Joon Ho.
Pattison and Ackie are great and the satire is sharp.
Bong’s peerless storytelling instincts are on display, deftly navigating a tangled nonlinear structure and making light work of the picture’s hefty two-and-a-quarter-hour running time.
It's neither funny, moving, or sharp. The time may feel right for a wry dystopian sci-fi adventure-comedy. But as satires go, this one is more mild than habanero.
Mickey 17 is remarkable for the savagery of its satire of 21st-century capitalism.
As a testament to the human spirit, Mickey 17 is audacious and over the top in all the right ways.
Pattinson’s malleable performances as two warring Mickeys gracefully complement Bong’s playful sensibilities to make “Mickey 17” one of the most galvanizing cinematic experiences this year.

The film’s greatest asset, though, may be Pattinson. The actor’s delightfully offbeat performance anchors the story in an endearing humanity. His choices border on cartoonish, but they’re specific enough to make his character’s plight feel recognizable.

Mickey 17 never seemed likely to be as good as Parasite. It just doesn’t have the same gravitas and edge, but with its maelstrom of nonsense and loveable stars on top form, it’s a rampantly fun cosmic caper.
Of course, Bong Joon Ho is an environmentalist. He recycles his own ideas.

title: Zombies 4: Dawn of the Vampires | Rotten Tomatoes
The Smashing Machine (2025) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: It'll be a hardsell for audiences to accept Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson as a genuine actor ready to emerge from the exhibitionist surface of his wrestler’s body and indestructible movie-star appeal.  But he does that here and passes with flying colors.
This is a machine not worth opposing. [Full review in Spanish]
Surprisingly, Johnson excels most in the dramatic scenes. The emotional tug-of-wars with Blunt and him are scorching.
It's really well made... if it gets award attention is going to be for Dwayne Johnson. The story itself is somewhat unremarkable.
The Smashing Machine mirrors the original doc so closely, it’s more reenactment than reinterpretation.
There’s nothing here that the viewer can’t glean from the documentary, and in fact, the doc is a far more edifying and affecting work than Safdie’s stylish regurgitation.
One gets the impression that Johnson and Blunt are making their characters more interesting than they actually were.

Johnson strips away the glossy veneer and delivers an unexpectedly bruised and naked performance as real-life ﻿mixed martial arts fighter Mark Kerr... It’s new territory for Johnson, and he’s rather good.
You don’t have to be into MMA or sport in general to engage with the characters. Watch it for the human drama and the fine acting.
the kind of film that forces the audience to wrestle with what, exactly, we want to see from these kinds of narratives — tragedy or triumph? Safdie offers both, and neither.
Having established its central foursome, the film doesn't take them anywhere in particular, but it's a sharp showcase for Johnson's remarkable physical transformation, and his acting chops.

I happen to think Johnson is also very good in full movie-star mode... But it’s also captivating to see him so thoroughly settled into a character like he is in “The Smashing Machine” while totally shorn of his charisma.
The picture itself is more workmanlike than transcendent. It marches along but doesn’t soar.
The story of the troubled MMA champion Mark Kerr is a classic redemptive arc - The Rock makes it raw and compelling.
Mostly the story is a drab character sketch of a fairly unremarkable athlete given an enticing personal element by Mr. Johnson’s ring history.
As a newly solo director, Safdie summons a thoughtful and moving mood for this unconventional sports film; as a newly serious dramatic actor, Johnson is about to win some awards.
"The Smashing Machine" works so hard to not be certain things — a by-the-numbers biopic, a typical crowd-pleaser — that it never quite figures out what it's trying to be, or what it is.
These two high-intensity talents, each with something to prove, seem to have egged each other on to be exhaustingly photorealistic.
The Smashing Machine succeeds because Johnson channels contradictions that feel deeply his own—his public armor and private fractures.

Midway through The Smashing Machine, Mark and Dawn argue heatedly, prompting her to yell, “You don’t know a thing about me!” And that line hits hard that far into the movie; I didn’t, in fact, know a single thing about her. Or about him.

title: The Phoenician Scheme | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: "Annoyingly precious," say Wes Anderson detractors who hate his intricate and elitist cinema dioramas that lack the common touch. Maybe.  But this one takes us past the pastel color palettes that windmill in his mind to find the ache that feels human
The Phoenician Scheme is very agreeable and charming.
Is there a future where I revisit Phoenician and find it significantly funnier and more profound (as was the case with Grand Budapest)? Yes, but unlike Korda’s redemption arc, mine isn’t imminent.
If Asteroid City was Wes Anderson’s defense of his own methods... The Phoenician Scheme is his exploration of everything those methods aren’t sufficient to encompass.
What peps up "The Phoenician Scheme" are some of its performances, specifically del Toro's.

But even at their worst, I used to think Anderson’s films were visually interesting. It’s the trait for which he’s most known and celebrated. But as of late, his films have become rife with eye-scorching ugliness.
It's not terrible, but it's an elegantly filmed stumble.

Each set is carefully assembled, with the blocking of each shot perfectly aligned, and Anderson’s rat-a-tat dialogue is delivered exactly as written. Still, there’s a spontaneity to the storytelling and the world it’s moving through.

You know the expression “It’s more than the sum of its parts”? Wes Anderson’s new film, The Phoenician Scheme, is entertaining, humorous and visually striking but its parts...are the reason not to take a toilet break.

Often funny and looks fantastic throughout, but it just never coheres into anything more resonant than a charming object ... by the end, it’s more tiring than exciting to spend time with yet another beloved actor delightedly playing a silly character
The overall theme is redemption, and that gives "The Phoenician Scheme" a warm center amid all its orbiting zaniness.
More charitably, The Phoenician Scheme is a palate cleanser – a lovely lark, a spirits lifter.
At its fleeting best — in its meditation on the transactional and the transcendent — this one feels like it’s reaching for something more than surface charm.
A beautiful mixed bag, let’s say, all told.
I was thoroughly entertained and left a bit cold.
The resulting product is just that: a product, with all of the matte pastel appeal of Anderson’s oeuvre, yet little of its memorable charm.

The result is more digestible, though also less moving, than Anderson’s recent Asteroid City, but it does have a stealth emotional weapon in Threapleton’s Liesl, who exudes the intelligence and self-possession of a young Anna Karina.
Beneath the soporific surfaces lurks an alert satirical intelligence.

Some Wes Anderson movies address loneliness and love and ambition and regret; this is one that communicates the filmmaker’s sadness that he never got to travel First Class on the Orient Express in 1932, or on a TWA intercontinental flight in 1962.
Star-crammed and detailed, The Phoenician Scheme delights.

title: 28 Years Later | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: All these technical marvels can’t stop Danny Boyle's latest trip to zombieland from coming apart at the seams in its tonally erratic final stretch,
You have pretty much everything you ﻿may hope for in the long-awaited third ﻿instalment of the horror series. Everything, that is, except an ending.
Classy, arty, horror. Good enough for genre fans. Mature enough for grownups. More than enough.

If you feared Boyle and Garland might play it safe with their now-seemingly-precious IP, 28 Years Later sufficiently proves otherwise. There’s enough creative gristle to chew on and more than enough to stoke curiosity for what’s next.
I don't know that I was ever scared... but I was never bored. Danny Boyle knows how to do this stuff.
This is a terrific film that will scare you, make you laugh and make you think.
Garland and Boyle have produced an exclusively British horror film, a hokey play on how readily we revert to isolation.
Even near the end, dwarfed by a tower of skulls, it is Comer whose wrenching performance gestures toward the monumental.
Young Fathers’ score for 28 Years Later...is phenomenal...Sadly, nothing else is quite up to [its] level.

Before the movie began, I worried whether Boyle and Garland would be able to top themselves more than two decades after 28 Days Later; by the time it ended, I was laughing at just how fantastical and wild their efforts were.
28 Years Later is more than a return to form. It’s a filmmaker using genre not just to thrill but to reflect.

At its heart, 28 Years Later is a Stephen King-esque coming-of-age story where death becomes a rite of passage for a child who is surrounded by the undead, anchored by young star Alfie Williams’s tender and revelatory performance.
Boyle and Garland refuse to play it safe and, by doing so, make 28 Years Later an essential piece of horror social commentary.

[Danny Boyle’s] use of jump-cuts, of varied focal lengths and exposures, and above all his use of music and sound design (think Trainspotting, times 10) all combine to create and sustain a state of high anxiety in the audience.

With a grim realism and a resilient Britishness that recalls the most desperate days of the Second World War, it has grit, suspense, and heart, albeit with some tonal wobbles and plot twists that are sure to raise eyebrows.
Acting opposite such powerhouses as Fiennes and the ever-excellent Comer, Williams delivers a vivid performance.
The tension between the film’s outsized presentation and its intimate dramaturgy is real and bracing; it’s an epic that grows increasingly overwhelming as it shrinks its field of view.

There’s still enough flesh-rending and severed body parts to sate the average horror fan. More crucially, “28 Years Later” has enough meat on its bones to serve as more than just a warmup for the next installment.
The story is grander and more expansive than what came before. Williams and Comer excel. Their part of the plot has real heft, tied up with time, loss and British childhood.
Mr. Boyle has made more than his share of memorable films, but he has also delivered some stinkers and unfortunately his new one carries the fragrance of a zombie underarm.

title: The Thursday Murder Club | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: There’s plenty of money on screen in the handsome production design, but something meagre and perfunctory about the storytelling.
There is some shock value, but the film goes too far in evading the truth; it nearly forgets to establish an emotional tether between the audience and its suspects.
Sometimes all you need is a nice, safe, and utterly pleasant piece of cinematic diversion that doesn’t insult your intelligence and is made with sturdy, workmanlike competence.
I appreciate seeing a community like this represented…This is all atmosphere and feel and in that way I enjoyed it a lot.
Great actors and a director who gets how to make a movie like this work: What more could you want?
It may be a film rather than a series, but it understands the assignment — and the zeitgeist.
As a mystery, The Thursday Murder Club lacks bite, but as a cosy crime drama it is a pleasant watch—one that works best as a reminder that friendship and cleverness don’t fade with age.
It’s a shame. The book is quite fun, and they’ve assembled a dynamite cast, but there’s too much lost here in the effort to cram it into a two-hour movie. If only they’d turned it into a miniseries.

This is an actor’s vehicle. There may be something bittersweet about the suggestion here that a shrinking pool of great performers is available and appropriate to a story like this. But any poignancy in “The Thursday Murder Club” is purely intentional.
What makes “The Thursday Murder Club,” an adaptation of the first book in the series, click is the casting.
Grab your nan, put the kettle on and enjoy some exceedingly fine thesps hamming it up royally.
Columbus’ touch as a filmmaker is always heavy. Where Osman is tender—particularly in his depiction of Elizabeth’s relationship to Stephen—Columbus is merely sentimental.
It’s pleasant enough to watch the cast parade in their quirky personas for a couple of hours.
If the movie feels slight, especially on character development or even some sharp jokes, it delivers on breeziness, charm and coziness. With this genre, that’s ultimately what matters.
...a grand jamboree of murder and Middle Englishness.

There’s a very welcome absence of condescension and sentimentality that is often used in the portrayal of elderly people on film, particularly when they engage in activities not typically associated with their age.
The script could certainly be sharper, the comedy more clever. But for two hours on Netflix, Coopers Chase is rather a comfy place to be, with some moments to cherish.
Chris Columbus’ movie wants to evoke cozy British whodunits but has only polish in place of a personality.
It says a lot about the global success of Richard Osman's Thursday Murder Club series that this first adaptation arrives with the self-conscious swagger of a ready-made franchise.
Cosy and comforting? Absolutely. Cutting edge? Not a bit. Just as the data ordered.

title: Spinal Tap II: The End Continues | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The weakness of the material and the familiarity of the structure﻿ are problems. But there’s also the fact that ﻿Spinal Tap II returns to a cultural landscape that is beyond parody﻿.
This sequel feels as long as an extended guitar solo you did not ask for, in a concert that started two hours late.

The worst part is that at only 82 minutes, you’ll still find yourself restless and wondering when is it going to wrap up. There wasn’t even enough funny material to sustain that length with the final act basically just a concert film.
It's nice to be back in the company of these people, particularly when they've aged... but it is a footnote. It is not in the same ball park as Spinal Tap at all.

This reunion could’ve all been cringe-worthy, but Spinal Tap was never exactly about dignity, was it? Still, there are sufficient laughs and a wistful, honest reckoning with aging... It’s stupidly sincere. Or sincerely stupid. Take your pick.
One of the many joys of the first film was its typically flawed array of backstage operators facilitating – and hindering – the band’s progress. There are fewer this time, but they make their mark.
It’s not as fall-down funny nor as fresh as the original, but there are enough chuckles and musical performances to make this sequel worth seeing.

... it seemingly hopes that the sight of our beloved trio gathered together, mostly on chairs and improvising badly, will be enough in itself. The results, alas, are less The Majesty of Rock and more Shit Sandwich.
Thankfully, nothing in “Spinal Tap II” will kill off the original’s legacy. It’s just a nostalgia lap you wish had more 11.
The core issue, however, is that it just isn’t very funny.
Spinal Tap II is more touching than it is laugh-out-loud funny.
The End Continues feints at rich, elegiac emotions but never quite accesses them.

Though it never reaches the heights of the original—if that film went to 11, this one tops out at around 7.5—Spinal Tap II also never feels like a soulless cash grab or a betrayal of the first movie’s impish comic spirit.

It’s funny and a wee bit poignant, and the main trio has the good taste not to ask us to feel too deeply about three guys whose chief appeal is that they’re miserable and petty and witheringly sarcastic and don’t try to hide it.

At best, this is a late-period diversion that most fans will either ignore or try to forget, while at worst, it does reach the point where you feel as if it might be actively working against the band’s legacy.
This collection of tired jokes is enough to prompt the question, “What day did the Lord create Spinal Tap II: The End Continues, and couldn’t he have rested on that day too?”

Is Spinal Tap II funny? I’ll give you a qualified yes. The sensation of a new comic universe popping into being is absent, because you can do that only once, but the original elements are still vital.
Playing a little too much like the hagiographic brand of music doc that Spinal Tap once ruthlessly skewered Spinal Tap Mark II offers what David St Hubbins once called a little too much perspective.
The joys of this film are similar to the joys of a beloved (real) band’s reunion concert: watching decades of personal and musical history play out onstage...

“The End Continues” is the same thing again, only different. And not that different, as it plays on a lot of the same tropes, while also being self-referential. Why not? They’ve earned it. But it doesn’t do a lot for the movie.

title: Den of Thieves: Pantera | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Feel free to nap through the first hour of Pantera, however – the last 90 minutes is all that redeems this fun but vapid sequel.

As a franchise, we saw The Fast and the Furious center on a cop... cross the line and join the criminals as friend and then family. This appears to be the path that this Den of Thieves sequel is now treading.

...even more convoluted than the original Den of Thieves... Yet, it’s hard to care when [it] does such a great job establishing his two central characters and taking the time to show all the meticulous work they must carry out to pull off the impossible.

While completely different to the original film there is still something to like about Pantera. It's sleek at seems to want to follow in the footsteps of The Fast & The Furious although the fact that Big Nick feels like a cliche this time is annoying.
Gerard Butler and O’Shea Jackson Jr. duel across lovely locales in serviceable thriller
Nothing really stands out in this ho-hum follow up, it's not awful but very average

It won’t win points for originality or sophistication, but this is another muscular, well-pitched heist thriller with strong character work from Butler and Jackson Jr. We wait with bated breath for The Further Adventures Of Big Nick.

…Den of Thieves: Pantera is a deliberately languorous but highly enjoyable copshow, with Gerry Butler and 50 Cent enjoying their repartee, with enough action for writer and director Christian Gudegast to stretch his legs….

The resulting film is as unmoored as Butler’s frequently sozzled character, with far too many tedious and indulgent bonding scenes between Butler and Jackson drawing the running time out...instead of getting down to business with actual action.
Pummels suspension of disbelief into something murky and tiresome until the lingering effect is only exhaustion.
A distinct improvement over its junky predecessor, this heist movie still eventually drops the ball with too many dumb twists jammed into a numbingly excessive running time.
Den of Thieves Pantera needed some tighter editing, but the performances are solid, and the European setting adds a stunning visual element.
Gerard Butler and O'Shea Jackson Jr. reunite in Den of Thieves: Pantera, a gripping sequel packed with heists, diamond thieves, and the infamous Panther mafia.

Ends in clunky, neverending sequel bait, what comes before is a true masterwork in the examination of its troubled protagonist before delivering a palm-sweating, edge-of-your-seat heist that’s as good as what Soderbergh stages.

It won’t change your life and might be forgotten in a few days, but it can turn a bad day around like few others—reminding us how satisfying a solid, no-frills thriller can be when everyone else is chasing perfection.

Den of Thieves 2: Pantera doesn't regurgitate the formula of its predecessor. Taking its story to Europe, the film changes style and tone as well. If the first Den of Thieves is a mashup of Heat and Ocean's Eleven, this is more akin to Ocean's Twelve.
...Den of Thieves begins to move away from the world of Michael Mann ...to become a buddy movie and a B-grade police film with more European overtones.... [Full review in Spanish]
Where the first film’s more action-heavy influences gave us a more ruthless, tactical violence... this sequel offers viewers something of a Melville-esque job of work.
Den of Thieves 2 is an enjoyable lark populated with characters who are more tangible than the usual genre dudes and dames, thus making their implausible adventures feel a little more plausible.
I honestly expected more action in this sequel, but the most memorable (and funny!) scene in the film is when Gerard Butler, O'Shea Jackson Jr. and crew party hard in France!

title: Happy Gilmore 2 | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: The sense of if-it-ain’t-broke-don’t-fix-it suits a movie with no great aim but to call back to the original. A modern critic might point out the irony of yesterday’s outsider becoming today’s guardian of old-school wisdom.
We get some light chuckles and one-off jokes, but the story, with bones to be genuinely gripping, flatlines thanks to an onslaught of half-assed gags and cameos.
There are laughs to be had, here and there; the good news is, the sequel isn’t terrible. It’s just not anything special, nothing with the spark of the original.
Like the original movie, this isn’t super funny, unless burping, farting and people being hit in the groin with golf balls is your thing.
Takes a page from some of the worst sequels in recent memory.
If it has any worth at all, Happy Gilmore 2 will at least be irrefutable proof that, more often than not, the humor we loved decades ago will age.

This movie is an astonishing feat of booking, a real master class of getting famous people to answer a producer’s calls. It’s just not a satisfying follow-up to one of the most enjoyable movies of Sandler’s career.
Sandler’s sequel to his hole-in-one comedy is an unfortunate slice into the sand.
Rather than aim for the flagstick, “Happy Gilmore 2” seems all too content to lay up in search of one gimme putt after another.
Happy Gilmore 2’s issues are, mostly, your standard Netflix-movie ones, which is to say that it feels haphazardly made, like it’s just aiming to be good enough.
Director Kyle Newacheck, taking over for the original’s Dennis Dugan, keeps things moving as quickly as he can, given the sprawling cast and truckload of cameos.
Yeah, it’s a bit messy and self-indulgent, but it’s often great, stupid, harmless fun.
It's a harmless return to the links, if a disappointment to anyone looking for anything more from this round of 18.
The rule for sequels is: give them the same, only different. Happy Gilmore 2 adheres to this concept beautifully, along with doling out enough blatant fan service to choke a one-eyed alligator.

These are all big questions, if occasionally funny ones, and “Happy Gilmore 2” attempts to answer them with humor and a touch of sadness. More often than not, it makes the shot. Thirty years on, that’s not too bad of a comeback.

Sandler’s desire to go low had always been an aesthetic choice, a conscious embrace of the elemental in himself. He was American screen comedy’s first and greatest cathartically disreputable Jewish punk-rock comedian. In “Happy Gilmore 2,” he still is.

The result is less a continuation than an exercise in fan service. If you’re watching Happy Gilmore 2 at home, don’t be surprised if some of the castmembers show up at your door offering autographed pictures for a fee.
For the generations who still quote summer comedies from eons ago (ahem), Sandler’s second round offers a refreshing trip down memory lane.
Arguably the least inspired film in the actor’s canon, if not all of movie history.

Between Happy’s family life and a whole new series of challenges for him to tackle, there’s enough freshness to the plot to keep it from feeling like a total rehash of what came before, while still delivering wild golf stunts and a huge range of cameos.

title: The Luckiest Man in America | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Is it real? The acting is, from Shaunette Renée Wilson and Damian Young as vaguely defined CBS functionaries to Messrs. Strathairn, Anderson and Hauser, whose Michael Larson is the stuff a particular American dream is made of.

So much more than just an exploration of this anomalous oddball story and character who managed to outsmart the media. The focus on the control-room panic illustrates how these corporate narratives shape the myth of the American Dream.
It's difficult getting to know Larson or his drive, and he's portrayed as bashful and shrinking by Hauser.

It’s an example of how to make a low-budget movie that immerses you in a long-gone world and the minds of people who lived in it, all while maintaining a tight geographical focus on a small number of characters.
It is still fun to watch Michael and CBS compete for the upper hand.
With such a wealth of talent at its disposal, “The Luckiest Man in America” is strangely never as satisfying as it should be.
With Paul Walter Hauser capturing the specific quirks and buried anxieties of the titular “luckiest man,” it’s a film that provides a strange snapshot — even if it may fade away just as quickly.
A delightfully sleazy ensemble thriller that goes down easy in 90 minutes -- and yet another reminder that Hauser is one of his generation’s most interesting movie stars.

The Luckiest Man in America is plenty evocative, full of retro flair tinged with dread or dreaminess. But as a character study or a narrative, it’s too rooted in its particular place to extend its impact beyond it.
Oliveros is lucky that he got people as talented as Hauser, Goggins, Strathairn, and Anderson to play his game because otherwise, this would have been a complete disaster.
Strives in vain to use its tale to say something about destiny, ambition, cunning, and the American Dream. It’s a pleasant and well-acted curio, and little more.

title: The Wrong Paris | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Even with classic rivalries and storybook romance attempts, ‘The Wrong Paris’ just doesn’t scratch a genuine itch.

The Wrong Paris, written by Nicole Henrich and directed by Janeen Damian, somehow serves the synthetic sugar of both The Bachelor and the Hallmark movie without any sweetness. The formula is there, but not the flavor.
While the movie’s production design has considerable mojo, the anodyne writing reins in whatever satire one might have expected.

title: The Perfect Neighbor (2025) | Rotten Tomatoes
reviews: Captured entirely from police cam footage, this Oscar-buzzed documentary about a white Florida woman who murders her Black neighbor indicts an entire society. It's also the scariest movie you’ll see this Halloween season.
“The Perfect Neighbor” deserves to be broadly seen, discussed and heeded.
It’s a tough but important watch that sounds the alarm on a number of issues – racism, gun ownership and mental health, to name a few.
I haven’t felt such visceral and intensely gendered loathing for a documentary termagant since “Dear Zachary.”
As a way of capturing the horrors of that night, the spareness of the film-making is powerful. But in terms of giving us the full picture, it falls short.
The climax, in which police slowly drag the truth out of the central figure, is harrowing.
